lifetime: Mikloth is recorded as one of the sons of Jeiel, the ancestor of Gibeon (1 Chronicles 9:35-37). He is mentioned together with the other sons of Jeiel: Abdon, Zur, Kish, Baal, Nadab, Gedor, Ahio, and Zecher (1 Chronicles 8:29-32).
event: He lived in Jerusalem with his brothers (1 Chronicles 8:32).

call: Levite who distributed the sacred offerings in the time of Hezekiah
introduce: A Levite who was active in the time of Hezekiah king of Judah and who carried out the duty of distributing the goods of the temple.
lifetime: During the reign of King Hezekiah, together with Eden, Jeshua, Shemaiah, Amariah, and Shecaniah, he lived in the cities of the priests and was in charge of distributing the sacred offerings fairly to their brothers, according to their divisions and duties (2 Chronicles 31:15).
event: When King Hezekiah reorganized the temple worship and the portions of the priests and Levites, he was responsible for the administrative work of distributing the sacred offerings to those who lived in the towns of the priests and carried out their duties, together with their children and wives (2 Chronicles 31:15).

introduce: He was a Persian official who managed the vessels of the temple in the time of Cyrus king of Persia. He is recorded in Ezra 1:8 as the treasurer of King Cyrus.
lifetime: At the command of Cyrus king of Persia, he brought out the vessels of the house of the LORD that Nebuchadnezzar had carried off from Jerusalem and placed in the temple of his gods, counted them, and delivered them to Sheshbazzar the prince of Judah (Ezra 1:7-8).
event: The counting of the temple vessels that Cyrus brought out and delivering them to Sheshbazzar is the only record about him (Ezra 1:7-8). The number of those vessels is recorded as 30 gold dishes, 1,000 silver dishes, 29 knives, 30 gold bowls, 410 silver bowls of lesser quality, and 1,000 other vessels, with the total of the gold and silver vessels being 5,400 (Ezra 1:9-11). Sheshbazzar brought all those vessels with him when he brought the captives up from Babylon to Jerusalem (Ezra 1:11).

introduce: Midian is the fourth son whom Abraham had by his later wife Keturah (Genesis 25:2). His name later became the origin of the people he formed and of the land of Midian, the place where they lived.
lifetime: He was born as a descendant of Abraham (Genesis 25:2), and while Abraham was still alive he gave him gifts and sent him to the east, to live far away from Isaac (Genesis 25:6).
event: His descendants appear frequently in biblical history under the name of the Midianites. Abraham gave gifts to the sons of his concubines and, during his lifetime, sent them away from his son Isaac to the east, that is, the eastern country (Genesis 25:6). When Moses fled from Pharaoh and stayed in the land of Midian, the priest of that land gave his daughter Zipporah to Moses, and he is recorded as Moses' father-in-law, the Midianite priest Jethro (Exodus 2:15-21, 3:1).

introduce: Mirmah is a figure recorded in the genealogy of the descendants of Benjamin in 1 Chronicles 8, one of the sons of Shaharaim, and these sons are recorded as heads of families (1 Chronicles 8:10).
lifetime: Mirmah was born as a son of Shaharaim (1 Chronicles 8:10). He is recorded as one of seven sons, together with Jobab, Zibia, Mesha, Malcam, Jeuz, and Sachia, whom Shaharaim fathered by his wife Hodesh in the land of Moab after he had sent away his two wives Hushim and Baara (1 Chronicles 8:8-10).

call: Sister of Moses and Aaron (prophetess of the Exodus)
introduce: Miriam is a woman in the Book of Exodus in the Old Testament, the sister of Moses and Aaron, a person of the tribe of Levi. She played a leading role in the course of Israel's Exodus, and Scripture records her as a prophetess.
lifetime: She watched from nearby to protect the baby Moses who had been abandoned by the Nile, and introduced Moses' mother to the princess as a nurse for Moses (Exodus 2:4-8). After the Israelites crossed the Red Sea she led the song of victory (Exodus 15:20-21), and when she criticized Moses over the Cushite woman, she was struck with leprosy, but was healed through Aaron's intercession and Moses' prayer (Numbers 12:1-15). Afterward, during the wilderness life, she died at Kadesh in the wilderness of Zin and was buried there (Numbers 20:1).
event: After crossing the Red Sea she took a tambourine and, dancing with the women, led the song of victory (Exodus 15:20). She challenged the authority of Moses and criticized him together with Aaron, but because of this she incurred the wrath of God and received the discipline of being confined outside the camp for seven days (Numbers 12:1-15). In the Book of Micah she is mentioned as one of the leaders whom God sent to guide Israel (Micah 6:4).
character: In her childhood she showed the resolve to act wisely to protect Moses (Exodus 2:4). As a leader of the women of Israel she had the artistic gift of leading praise and worship (Exodus 15:20), and she was a person with spiritual influence such that she was called a prophetess (Exodus 15:20). Yet at the same time she is also seen to have had a willful side, interfering in the personal life of Moses and challenging his authority (Numbers 12:1-2).

introduce: Mizzah was a descendant of Reuel the son of Esau, recorded as one of the chiefs of the descendants of Reuel in the land of Edom (Genesis 36:13, 17).
lifetime: Esau's wife Basemath bore Reuel (Genesis 36:4), and the sons of Reuel were Nahath, Zerah, Shammah, and Mizzah (Genesis 36:13). Mizzah, as a son of Reuel and a grandson of Esau, is recorded as one of the chiefs of the descendants of Reuel in the land of Edom (Genesis 36:17).

introduce: Mishael was one of the three sons of Uzziel, the son of Kohath of the tribe of Levi, and a figure who appears in Exodus 6:22 and Leviticus 10:4.
lifetime: He was born to Uzziel the son of Kohath, and together with Elzaphan and Sithri formed a brotherhood (Exodus 6:22). His family line made up one branch of the descendants of Kohath.
event: As a son of Uzziel, the uncle of Aaron, after Aaron's sons Nadab and Abihu died before the LORD, Moses called Mishael and Elzaphan and told them to carry their brothers away from the front of the sanctuary to outside the camp, and as Moses had commanded they carried the bodies, still in their tunics, outside the camp (Leviticus 10:4-5).

introduce: Misham was a descendant of the tribe of Benjamin, recorded as a son of Elpaal (1 Chronicles 8:12). He is placed within the genealogy of the descendants of Benjamin (1 Chronicles 8:1).
lifetime: Misham was a son of Elpaal and is mentioned as one of the three brothers Eber, Misham, and Shemed (1 Chronicles 8:12). In the family genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin he is classified as a descendant of Elpaal (1 Chronicles 8:12).
event: No specific achievement of Misham's nor any particular event during his life is recorded; it is confirmed through the genealogy only that he was a brother of Shemed, who built Ono and Lod with its villages (1 Chronicles 8:12).

introduce: Mizraim was the second son of Ham the son of Noah, a man recorded in the biblical genealogical system as the ancestor of the ancient Egyptian people.
lifetime: As a son of Ham, he was a brother of Cush, Put, and Canaan (Genesis 10:6). Mizraim fathered the Ludites, Anamites, Lehabites, and Naphtuhites (Genesis 10:13), and the Pathrusites, Casluhites, and Caphtorites (Genesis 10:14).
event: His descendants make up the peoples that run through the Ludites, Anamites, Lehabites, Naphtuhites, Pathrusites, Casluhites, and Caphtorites (Genesis 10:13-14). The Philistine people are recorded as having come from the Casluhites (Genesis 10:14, 1 Chronicles 1:12).

introduce: Mishma is the fifth of the twelve sons of Ishmael, who was born to Abraham and Hagar (Genesis 25:12-14).
lifetime: As a son of Ishmael, his name is mentioned for the first time in Genesis 25:14 (Genesis 25:14). His genealogy is also reconfirmed through the genealogy in 1 Chronicles 1:30 (1 Chronicles 1:30).
event: No personal achievement or specific event of his is recorded in Scripture. There is only the record that the names of Ishmael's sons were names by their villages and encampments, and that according to their tribes they were twelve princes (Genesis 25:16).

introduce: Mishmannah was one of the mighty men of the Gadites who came to David at a rugged stronghold, a man recorded in 1 Chronicles 12 (1 Chronicles 12:8, 10).
lifetime: The mighty men from among the Gadites who came to David at a rugged stronghold were experienced in battle and able to handle shield and spear (1 Chronicles 12:8), and Mishmannah is recorded as one of them (1 Chronicles 12:10).
event: He is listed fourth among the eleven mighty men of the tribe of Gad who came to help David (1 Chronicles 12:10).

introduce: Mispar is a man recorded in Ezra 2:2 in the Old Testament as having come with Zerubbabel, Jeshua, and others.
lifetime: Among those who were carried away captive from Babylon and returned to Jerusalem and Judah, he is recorded as one who came with Zerubbabel, Jeshua, Nehemiah, Seraiah, Reelaiah, Mordecai, Bilshan, Mispar, Bigvai, Rehum, Baanah, and others (Ezra 2:1-2). In the parallel list in Nehemiah 7:7, some other names, such as Mispereth, appear in this place.
event: His name is on the list recording the count of the people of Israel who came with Zerubbabel and others (Ezra 2:2).

introduce: Mispereth is one of the people of Israel who, having ended their life in the Babylonian exile, returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel.
lifetime: His name is recorded in the list of returnees who came back from Babylon to Jerusalem (Nehemiah 7:6-7).
event: He is mentioned as one who came with Zerubbabel, Jeshua, Nehemiah, Azariah, Raamiah, Nahamani, Mordecai, Bilshan, Mispereth, Bigvai, Nehum, Baanah, and others (Nehemiah 7:7).

meaning: Born of the right hand, blessed one
introduce: Mijamin was one of the priestly families recorded in 1 Chronicles in the Old Testament, a man who was in charge of the sixth course when David divided the priests into twenty-four courses.
lifetime: David divided the descendants of Aaron's sons Eleazar and Ithamar, together with Zadok of the descendants of Eleazar and Ahimelech of the descendants of Ithamar, and assigned each their duties of service, dividing them by casting lots (1 Chronicles 24:1-3, 5). The family recorded sixth at that time is the course of Mijamin (1 Chronicles 24:9). Mijamin's name also appears again in the list of the priests who returned with Zerubbabel and Jeshua (Nehemiah 12:1, 5).
event: In the casting of lots to decide the order of the priestly duties in David's time, it was recorded sixth and became the family of the sixth course (1 Chronicles 24:5, 9). Later, after the kingdom of Judah fell and the Babylonian exile had passed, Mijamin is included in the list of the priests who returned with Zerubbabel and Jeshua (Nehemiah 12:1, 5).

introduce: Mikneiah was a Levite of David's time, a man appointed as a player of instruments when the ark of God was moved.
lifetime: Mikneiah was one of the Levites appointed when David commanded the heads of the Levites to appoint singers and to sound instruments (1 Chronicles 15:16, 15:18). Together with Mattithiah, Eliphelehu, Obed-edom, Jeiel, and Azaziah, he is recorded as one who led by playing the lyre to the eighth tone (1 Chronicles 15:21).

introduce: Milcah was the wife of Nahor and the daughter of Haran, and the sister of Lot, the nephew of Abraham.
lifetime: Milcah was born as the daughter of Haran (Genesis 11:29) and married Nahor, the brother of Abraham (Genesis 11:29). By Nahor she bore eight sons: Uz, Buz, Kemuel, Chesed, Hazo, Pildash, Jidlaph, and Bethuel (Genesis 22:20-23).
event: One of her sons, Bethuel, became the father of Rebekah (Genesis 22:23), and through this Milcah became the grandmother of Rebekah, the wife of Isaac (Genesis 24:15).

introduce: Milalai is a man listed as a brother of Zechariah, a descendant of the priests who held trumpets at the dedication of the wall of Jerusalem (Nehemiah 12:35-36).
lifetime: When Nehemiah divided the company of those giving thanks and praise into two groups and had them go in procession along the top of the wall (Nehemiah 12:31), Milalai, together with Shemaiah, Azarel, Gilalai, Maai, Nethanel, Judah, and Hanani, held the instruments of David the man of God (Nehemiah 12:36). The procession advanced to the place where one goes up to the city by the Fountain Gate, with Ezra the scribe going before them (Nehemiah 12:36-37).
event: At the dedication held after the wall of Jerusalem was completed, he took part in the procession holding David's instruments (Nehemiah 12:27, 36).

introduce: Mibsam is the fourth of the twelve sons born to Abraham's son Ishmael. He is classified as one of the chiefs of the tribes that sprang from Ishmael's family line.
lifetime: As a son of Ishmael, his name is mentioned in Genesis (Genesis 25:13). He is included in the list as one of the twelve sons born to Ishmael (1 Chronicles 1:29).

introduce: Mibhar is a man recorded among the mighty men of David, David's military organization (1 Chronicles 11:38).
lifetime: After David became king over all Israel, his name was entered, as the son of Hagri, in the list of the mighty men who helped strengthen David's power and gain the kingdom (1 Chronicles 11:10, 11:38).
event: As one of the prominent mighty men who supported David, he was included in the list that shows the military solidarity of David (1 Chronicles 11:38).

introduce: Mizzah was a son of Reuel the son of Esau, a man recorded in the genealogy of the descendants in 1 Chronicles 1 (1 Chronicles 1:35, 37).
lifetime: Mizzah is recorded as one of the sons of Reuel, the son of Esau (1 Chronicles 1:37). His line belongs to the family line that begins with Esau and continues through Reuel (1 Chronicles 1:35-37).

introduce: Pagiel was a man of the tribe of Asher, the son of Ocran, who acted as a representative of his tribe in the census of Israel and the dedication of the tabernacle in the early wilderness period.
lifetime: At the census carried out by Moses and Aaron, Pagiel is recorded as the son of Ocran who represented the tribe of Asher among those, one chief from each tribe, who were made to stand with them (Numbers 1:4-5, 13). When they encamped in the wilderness, he was recorded as the leader of the descendants of Asher (Numbers 2:27). He is also recorded as the one who presented his offering on the eleventh day of the dedication of the tabernacle (Numbers 7:72). He is once again specified as the one who commanded the army of the tribe of the descendants of Asher during the march of the Israelites (Numbers 10:26).
event: For the dedication of the tabernacle he presented as his offering one silver platter weighing 130 shekels, one silver bowl weighing 70 shekels, one gold dish weighing 10 shekels, together with a burnt offering, a sin offering, and peace offerings, and this was an offering presented according to the sanctuary shekel (Numbers 7:72-77).

introduce: Barnabas is an early Christian leader and evangelist who appears in the Book of Acts in the New Testament. His given name was Joseph, and he was a Levite born in Cyprus. He is recorded as one who helped Paul's early ministry and laid the foundation of the church in Antioch.
lifetime: Barnabas sold his field and brought the proceeds and laid them at the apostles' feet, devoting himself to the community (Acts 4:36-37). When Saul went to Jerusalem and tried to join the disciples, but they were all afraid and did not believe, he took him and went to the apostles and told them how Saul had seen the Lord on the road and how he had spoken boldly in Damascus (Acts 9:26-27). The church in Jerusalem sent him as far as Antioch, and when he saw the grace of God he rejoiced and exhorted them; he went to Tarsus to look for Saul, found him, and brought him to Antioch (Acts 11:22-26). Later, in the church at Antioch, when the Holy Spirit said to set apart Barnabas and Saul, they fasted and prayed, received the laying on of hands, and were sent off (Acts 13:2-3). He was among those sent with Paul to the apostles and elders in Jerusalem (Acts 15:2). After a sharp dispute with Paul over the matter of taking Mark along, they parted company, and he took Mark and sailed to Cyprus (Acts 15:37-39).
event: In Antioch, together with Saul, for a year he met with the church and taught a great number of people, and it was then that the disciples were first called Christians at Antioch (Acts 11:26). When a famine came, together with Saul he delivered to the elders the relief that the disciples had decided to send to the brothers living in Judea (Acts 11:29-30). In Lystra, when the crowds saw what Paul had done, they called Barnabas Zeus and Paul Hermes (Acts 14:11-12).
character: The apostles gave him the nickname Barnabas, meaning Son of Encouragement (Acts 4:36). He is described as a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and of faith (Acts 11:24). Although Mark had withdrawn partway through the first missionary journey, he appears as a person of inclusive and encouraging temperament toward others, so much that he came into conflict with Paul over wanting to take Mark along again (Acts 15:37-39).

직업/직위: leader of the church at Antioch (Joseph, Son of Encouragement)

introduce: Phanuel was a man of the tribe of Asher who appears only once, in the Gospel of Luke in the New Testament, and is recorded as the father of the prophetess Anna.
lifetime: He was the father of Anna, a daughter of the tribe of Asher, and no specific information about the rest of his life is recorded in Scripture (Luke 2:36).

introduce: Bani is a Gadite whose name is recorded in the list of David's mighty men (2 Samuel 23:36).
lifetime: Bani is recorded as a Gadite in the list of David's mighty men, together with Igal son of Nathan of Zobah (2 Samuel 23:36), and this list totaled thirty-seven men (2 Samuel 23:39). No other part of his life is recorded in Scripture.
event: His name is recorded in the list of David's mighty men (2 Samuel 23:36). His individual exploits are not recorded in the text.

introduce: Padon is the name of a family recorded as "the descendants of Padon" in the list of the Nethinim who returned from Babylon to Judah (Ezra 2:44, Nehemiah 7:47).
lifetime: The descendants of Padon are recorded under the Nethinim in the list of those who returned from Babylon (Ezra 2:43-44). In the genealogy of the returnees recorded in Nehemiah 7 as well, the descendants of Padon appear among the Nethinim (Nehemiah 7:46-47). No other part of his life is recorded in Scripture.
event: He is registered as the descendants of Padon among the Nethinim in the list of those who returned from Babylon (Ezra 2:44, Nehemiah 7:47).

introduce: Patrobas was a member of the church in Rome, one of the group to whom the apostle Paul sends greetings in Romans 16 (Romans 16:14).
lifetime: That Patrobas lived in Rome is confirmed through the apostle Paul's instruction to greet Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermes, Patrobas, Hermas, and the brothers who are with them (Romans 16:14). Other concrete information about his life, such as his birth, upbringing, and death, is not recorded in Scripture (Romans 16:14).
event: The biblical text contains no description of any special achievement or specific event of Patrobas (Romans 16:14).
character: The biblical text provides no information from which Patrobas's character or personal traits could be inferred (Romans 16:14).

introduce: The Pathrusites are a group of descendants who branched off from Mizraim, the son of Noah's son Ham, a name in the genealogy recording the peoples of the ancient Near East (Genesis 10:14, 1 Chronicles 1:12).
lifetime: The Pathrusites are mentioned as one of the descendants fathered by Mizraim the son of Ham, and in the genealogy they stand together with the Casluhites, from whom the Philistines came (Genesis 10:14, 1 Chronicles 1:12).

introduce: Bartimaeus is a figure who appears in the Gospel of Mark in the New Testament, a blind beggar near the city of Jericho. His name means "son of Timaeus" in Aramaic.
lifetime: Bartimaeus was one who sat begging by the roadside of Jericho (Mark 10:46). When Jesus, his disciples, and a great crowd were leaving Jericho, he heard them passing by and called out to Jesus (Mark 10:46-47). After being called by Jesus, he threw off his cloak, jumped up, and came to Jesus (Mark 10:50). After Jesus healed him, he followed Jesus along the road (Mark 10:52).
event: Confessing that Jesus was the Son of David, he cried out loudly for him to have mercy on him (Mark 10:47-48). Though those around him rebuked him and told him to be quiet, he cried out all the more loudly, showing his determination (Mark 10:48). Jesus called him, stopped him, and said that his faith had saved him, and he gave him sight (Mark 10:51-52).
character: Despite the restraint and discouragement of those around him, he did not give up and showed an assertive disposition in persistently conveying his request (Mark 10:48). He called Jesus the Son of David, having known about him beforehand (Mark 10:47). When Jesus called him, he showed decisiveness by immediately throwing off the cloak he was wearing (Mark 10:50).

introduce: Berechiah is a man recorded as the father of Zechariah, mentioned when Jesus Christ rebuked the scribes and Pharisees in Matthew 23 in the New Testament (Matthew 23:35).
lifetime: In the biblical record nothing is known of the specific life of Berechiah, and he is mentioned only as the father of Zechariah (Matthew 23:35).
event: Jesus Christ said that all the righteous blood, up to the blood of Zechariah son of Berechiah, whom you murdered between the temple and the altar, would come upon this generation (Matthew 23:35). Whether to regard this Zechariah as the same person as Zechariah son of Jehoiada recorded in 2 Chronicles 24:20-22 is not stated in the text. In Luke 11:51 only the blood of Zechariah is mentioned, and the name of his father does not appear.

introduce: Barachel is a figure in the Old Testament, mentioned as the father of Elihu the Buzite (Job 32:2).
lifetime: Barachel is known as a Buzite of the family of Ram (Job 32:2). No account of his taking any direct action appears in the biblical record; his name is mentioned only in the course of explaining the genealogy of his son Elihu (Job 32:6).
event: Within the biblical record there is no account of any independent achievement or specific event of Barachel as an individual (Job 32:2).

introduce: He is the prisoner who was released by Pontius Pilate, the Roman governor, at the time of the trial of Jesus Christ. He is recorded as one who was imprisoned for an insurrection that had occurred in the city and for murder (Luke 23:19).
lifetime: Barabbas had been bound and put in prison for the crime of killing a man in an insurrection (Mark 15:7, Luke 23:19). There was a custom that at the festival the governor would release one prisoner to the crowd, whomever they wished; when Pilate asked whether they wanted Barabbas or Jesus who is called Christ, the crowd asked for Barabbas, and he was released (Matthew 27:15-17, 21, 26).
event: He was in prison because of an insurrection that had occurred in the city and because of murder (Luke 23:19). The chief priests stirred up the crowd to have Barabbas released instead (Mark 15:11), and when the crowd shouted for Barabbas and not for Jesus (John 18:39-40), Pilate released Barabbas, and had Jesus flogged and handed over to be crucified (Matthew 27:26).
character: He was a participant in a rebellion against the Roman system of rule and is recorded as a murderer (Mark 15:7). In the New Testament he is referred to simply as a sinner or a robber (John 18:40).

직업/직위: prisoner jailed for insurrection and murder

introduce: Barak was the son of Abinoam, a military leader of Israel from Kedesh in Naphtali, who in the time of the judges, together with Deborah, defeated Sisera, the commander of the army of Jabin king of Canaan.
lifetime: Called by the prophetess Deborah, who lived in the hill country of Ephraim, Barak led an army of ten thousand men of Israel and advanced to Mount Tabor (Judges 4:6). Together with Deborah he gathered men at Kedesh and went up leading ten thousand of the descendants of Zebulun and Naphtali (Judges 4:10). After the victory in the war against the army of Canaan he pursued Sisera, and found that he was already dead in the tent of Jael (Judges 4:22).
event: At Deborah's command he mobilized ten thousand soldiers and fought on Mount Tabor against the nine hundred iron chariots of Canaan led by Sisera, winning a great victory (Judges 4:13-15). When Sisera abandoned his camp and fled during the battle, Barak pursued him and came to the tent of Jael, the wife of Heber, where he saw that Sisera was dead (Judges 4:22). Afterward Barak sang, together with Deborah, a song commemorating the victory in this war (Judges 5:1).
character: In carrying out God's command, he showed a cautious attitude, saying that he would not go unless Deborah went with him (Judges 4:8). Because of this conditional acceptance, he was told in a prophecy that the honor of killing Sisera would be given to a woman, Jael (Judges 4:9). The writer of Hebrews mentions him as one of those who by faith conquered kingdoms (Hebrews 11:32-33).

introduce: Pharaoh Hophra was the king of Egypt in the time of Zedekiah king of Judah, a man whose fate the prophet Jeremiah foretold (Jeremiah 44:30).
lifetime: He is recorded as Pharaoh Hophra king of Egypt (Jeremiah 44:30), and when the army of Pharaoh came out of Egypt, the Chaldeans who were besieging Jerusalem heard the report and withdrew from Jerusalem (Jeremiah 37:5). Nothing else about his life is recorded in Scripture.
event: The LORD said that the army of Pharaoh, which had come out to help Judah, would return to its own land of Egypt, and that the Chaldeans would come back and attack this city (Jeremiah 37:7-8). The LORD also said to Jeremiah that just as He had given Zedekiah king of Judah into the hand of his enemy Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, who sought his life, so He would give Pharaoh Hophra king of Egypt into the hand of his enemies, who sought his life (Jeremiah 44:30).

introduce: Pharaoh Neco refers to Necho II, a pharaoh of the Twenty-sixth Dynasty who ruled Egypt in the late seventh century BC, and he appears in Scripture as a figure connected with the kingdom of Judah.
lifetime: While going up to the river Euphrates to attack the king of Assyria, when King Josiah went out to defend against him, he met Josiah at Megiddo and killed him (2 Kings 23:29). Afterward he imprisoned Jehoahaz at Riblah in the land of Hamath so that he could not reign in Jerusalem, set up Josiah's son Eliakim as king in place of his father and changed his name to Jehoiakim, and took Jehoahaz to Egypt (2 Kings 23:33-34). His army was defeated by Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon at Carchemish on the bank of the Euphrates (Jeremiah 46:2), and the king of Babylon took all that had belonged to the king of Egypt, from the river of Egypt to the river Euphrates (2 Kings 24:7).
event: He made the land of Judah pay a fine of a hundred talents of silver and a talent of gold (2 Kings 23:33), and Jehoiakim, as Pharaoh Neco commanded, taxed the land, assessing it at a fixed amount, and collected the silver and gold and gave it to Pharaoh (2 Kings 23:35). Also, as he was coming up to attack Carchemish on the Euphrates, he confronted King Josiah at Megiddo, and Josiah was killed (2 Kings 23:29, 2 Chronicles 35:20-22).
character: For his own military purposes, he demanded passage of his army from Josiah, a foreign king, and showed an aggressive disposition in the confrontation (2 Chronicles 35:21). By installing and deposing the sons of Josiah as kings, he revealed himself as a political ruler who tried to manage Judah like a vassal state in the Near East of that day (2 Kings 23:34).

meaning: Son of Qos, the god of Edom
introduce: Barkos is the name of a family of the Nethinim, or of the ancestor of that family, appearing in Ezra and Nehemiah in the Old Testament (Ezra 2:53, Nehemiah 7:55).
lifetime: Barkos means the head of a family among the Nethinim who returned from the Babylonian exile, or that family itself. As members of the Nethinim who assisted with the various tasks of the temple, the descendants of Barkos were included in the list of the returnees from the Babylonian exile (Ezra 2:53, Nehemiah 7:55). They are recorded in the list of those who returned from Babylon to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:1-2, Nehemiah 7:6-7).
event: It is recorded as one family in the list of the Nethinim of the community of returnees. The number of the Nethinim and the descendants of the servants of Solomon together was 392 (Ezra 2:53, 58).

introduce: Joseph, who was also called Barsabbas and had the nickname Justus, was a member of the early church in Jerusalem, nominated as a candidate to carry out the apostleship after Judas Iscariot.
lifetime: He was one of those who had accompanied the apostles all the time from the baptism of Jesus until the day He was taken up (Acts 1:21-22). The apostle Peter sought a suitable man from among those who had followed Jesus to be a witness to the resurrection, and Joseph Barsabbas was proposed together with Matthias as a final candidate (Acts 1:23).
event: He was nominated as a candidate for apostle to take the place of Judas Iscariot, one of the twelve apostles, but as the lot fell upon Matthias, he did not succeed to the apostleship (Acts 1:26).
character: Having accompanied Jesus throughout the time he was with Him, he was regarded as a man of such orthodoxy of faith and qualifications that he earned the recommendation of the apostles for his faithfulness (Acts 1:21-23).

call: Ancestor of a priestly family that returned with Zerubbabel
introduce: Pashhur is a figure who appears in Ezra and Nehemiah in the Old Testament, referring to the ancestor of a priestly family that returned from the Babylonian exile to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel, or to the name of that family. He belongs to the priestly line of the descendants of Aaron and is mentioned in the process of the rebuilding of the Jewish community in the Persian period.
lifetime: The family of Pashhur was one of the priestly families that returned from Babylon to Jerusalem and Judah, and the descendants of Pashhur are recorded as 1,247 (Ezra 2:38). In the list in Nehemiah 7 as well, the descendants of Pashhur are recorded as 1,247 (Nehemiah 7:41).
event: In Ezra 10, in the list of the priests who had taken foreign women as wives, Elioenai, Maaseiah, Ishmael, Nethanel, Jozabad, and Elasah are recorded from among the descendants of Pashhur (Ezra 10:18-22).

introduce: Baasha was the third king of the northern kingdom of Israel, the son of Ahijah, of the tribe of Issachar. He killed Nadab, seized the throne, and ruled Israel for twenty-four years.
lifetime: When Nadab and all Israel were besieging Gibbethon, which belonged to the Philistines, Baasha conspired against him, killed him, and became king (1 Kings 15:27). Immediately after taking the throne he exterminated the whole house of Jeroboam (1 Kings 15:29), and throughout his reign he continued to be at war with Asa king of Judah in the south (1 Kings 15:32). After his death he was buried in Tirzah, and his son Elah succeeded him as king (1 Kings 16:6).
event: He came up against Judah and built Ramah in order to keep anyone from going out or coming in to Asa king of Judah (1 Kings 15:17). Then King Asa sent a gift of silver and gold to Ben-hadad king of Aram to have him break his treaty with Baasha (1 Kings 15:18-19), and Baasha stopped building Ramah and stayed in Tirzah (1 Kings 15:21). He also received a rebuke through Jehu son of Hanani, to whom the word of the LORD came, that his house would become like the house of Jeroboam (1 Kings 16:1-3).
character: Baasha is recorded as one who walked in the way of Jeroboam, caused Israel to sin, and did evil in the sight of the LORD (1 Kings 15:34). He took power by violent means, and to maintain his own power he showed a cruelty that thoroughly destroyed the house of Jeroboam (1 Kings 15:29).

introduce: Baalis was the king of the Ammonites, a figure who appears in the Book of Jeremiah in the time of Gedaliah, whom the king of Babylon appointed governor of the land of Judah (Jeremiah 40:14).
lifetime: He is mentioned as king of the Ammonites in the time of Gedaliah son of Ahikam, whom the king of Babylon appointed governor over the cities of Judah (Jeremiah 40:5, 14). Johanan son of Kareah and the commanders of the forces told Gedaliah that Baalis had sent Ishmael son of Nethaniah to take Gedaliah's life, but Gedaliah did not believe them (Jeremiah 40:13-14).
event: Baalis was named as the one who had sent Ishmael son of Nethaniah to take Gedaliah's life (Jeremiah 40:14). Ishmael afterward struck Gedaliah down with the sword and killed him (Jeremiah 41:2). That Baalis had sent Ishmael is the report of Johanan and others, and there is no record in the text of his motive.
character: He was a man who took a cunning and aggressive foreign policy, employing the political means of assassination in order to wipe out the remnant forces of Judah (Jeremiah 40:14). He showed a pragmatic side, seeking his own country's interests by exploiting the situation of Judah under Babylonian influence (Jeremiah 40:14).

introduce: Baal-hanan was the seventh king to rule the land of Edom, the son of Achbor, a ruler who became king after Saul in the genealogy of the kings of Edom.
lifetime: Baal-hanan, as the son of Achbor, succeeded to the throne of Edom (Genesis 36:38, 1 Chronicles 1:49). He became king in his place after the death of Saul of Rehoboth by the River.
event: After his death Hadad became king in his place (Genesis 36:39). The records of the name of the capital city, Pau, and of the wife, Mehetabel (the daughter of Matred and the granddaughter of Me-zahab), concern not Baal-hanan but his successor Hadad (Genesis 36:39, 1 Chronicles 1:50).

introduce: Bar-Jesus is a figure in the Book of Acts in the New Testament, a Jewish sorcerer and false prophet who was active on the island of Cyprus. He is also known by the name Elymas.
lifetime: Bar-Jesus was one who stayed by the side of Sergius Paulus, the proconsul of the island of Cyprus, and exercised influence (Acts 13:6). When Paul and Barnabas met the proconsul to proclaim the gospel, he was present, but he acted to hinder the proconsul from hearing the word (Acts 13:8). Immediately after receiving Paul's stern rebuke, the hand of the Lord came upon him and he became unable to see for a time (Acts 13:11).
event: Also called Elymas, he strove to oppose the apostles so that the proconsul would not believe (Acts 13:8). He tried to turn away the interest of the proconsul Sergius Paulus, but was rebuked by the apostle Paul as a child of the devil and an enemy of all righteousness (Acts 13:10). After the hand of the Lord was upon him and he became blind, he found himself seeking people to lead him by the hand (Acts 13:11).
character: As a Jewish sorcerer, he showed a disposition to enjoy displaying his power before people and exerting influence on them (Acts 13:6). He had an aggressive attitude of actively opposing and obstructing the ministry of the apostles (Acts 13:8). He used his knowledge and his standing as a sorcerer to maintain a close relationship with those in power (Acts 13:7).

introduce: Paul was originally called Saul, a Jew from Tarsus in Cilicia, and a key figure who led the mission to the Gentiles in the history of early Christianity. He held Roman citizenship and had received a Pharisaic education; after converting to Christianity he founded many churches centered on the Mediterranean coast and wrote a number of letters.
lifetime: He grew up receiving a strict education in the law at the feet of Gamaliel (Acts 22:3). In the early period he took the lead in persecuting Christians and was present at the scene when Stephen was martyred (Acts 7:58). He converted to Christianity after an experience of Jesus on the road to Damascus (Acts 9:3-9). Afterward, with the church in Antioch as his base, he carried out three large-scale missionary journeys (Acts 13:1-21:17). In his later years he was arrested in Jerusalem and held in custody in Caesarea, and was sent under guard to Rome, where he worked while under house arrest (Acts 28:16-31).
event: He planted several churches and spread the gospel throughout Asia Minor and Europe (Acts 16:9-15). Through his first to third missionary journeys he carried out organized missionary work in major cities such as Ephesus, Corinth, and Philippi (Acts 18:1-11). He wrote several of the letters of the New Testament, including Romans, and through them contributed to forming the theological framework of the early Christian community of his time (Romans 1:1). He was arrested by the Jews in Jerusalem, and went through a trial process in which he appealed to the Roman emperor, invoking his Roman citizenship (Acts 25:10-12).
character: He was well versed in the law of Judaism and lived the life of a strict Pharisee (Philippians 3:5). He had the cool judgment to suit the situation, to the point of declaring his status as a Roman citizen (Acts 16:37), and his occupation was making tents (Acts 18:3). He himself mentioned that in the course of carrying out his ministry he suffered a pain that he described as a thorn in the flesh (2 Corinthians 12:7), and he showed an uncompromising, passionate temperament (Galatians 2:11).

introduce: Paltiel is a figure in the Book of Numbers in the Old Testament, a chief belonging to the tribe of Issachar and the son of Azzan.
lifetime: When the LORD commanded Moses to have the land of Canaan divided as an inheritance for the Israelites, Paltiel is recorded as the chief of the tribe of the descendants of Issachar among the chiefs, one from each tribe, who were chosen to divide the land of inheritance (Numbers 34:18, 26).
event: The LORD told Moses to choose one chief from each tribe to divide the land of inheritance (Numbers 34:18), and among their names Paltiel son of Azzan was recorded as the chief of the tribe of the descendants of Issachar (Numbers 34:26). Those who divided the land as an inheritance were the priest Eleazar and Joshua son of Nun (Numbers 34:17).

introduce: Baladan is a man recorded as the father of Merodach-baladan king of Babylon (Berodach-baladan in 2 Kings 20:12), whose son appears as the one who sent a letter and a gift to Hezekiah king of Judah in the time of King Hezekiah.
lifetime: He is recorded only as the father of Merodach-baladan king of Babylon, and no other specific personal life, nor any record of his birth or death, appears in Scripture (2 Kings 20:12, Isaiah 39:1).
event: There is no record of any direct achievement or activity of his; he is mentioned as the father only in the account in which his son, Merodach-baladan king of Babylon, heard that Hezekiah had been sick and had recovered and sent Hezekiah a letter and a gift (2 Kings 20:12, Isaiah 39:1).

introduce: Balaam was the son of Beor, from Pethor, a man described in Scripture as a prophet or diviner. He was hired by Balak king of Moab to curse Israel, but in the process he underwent a unique religious experience and left prophecies concerning Israel.
lifetime: Balak king of Moab sent envoys with fees for divination, asking him to curse the people of Israel (Numbers 22:5-7). After inquiring of God for his instructions, Balaam set out for Moab (Numbers 22:12-21). Afterward, looking out over the camp of Israel, he proclaimed prophecies of blessing instead of curses (Numbers 23:18-24). At the end of his life he was killed with the sword by Israel during the war against Midian (Numbers 31:8).
event: While on the road he did not see the angel of the LORD, but when his donkey stopped, he struck the donkey, and in the course of this the donkey spoke (Numbers 22:22-30). Three times he tried to curse Israel, but in the end, moved by the LORD, he left four oracles blessing Israel (Numbers 23:7-24:24). After his death it is mentioned that he had enticed the people of Israel to sin in the incident at Peor (Numbers 31:16).
character: Balaam had a disposition of covetousness and loved the wages of wickedness (2 Peter 2:15), and he is regarded as one who linked his prophetic ability with money (Numbers 22:7). Even while hearing God's direct command, he showed a double-minded attitude, trying to compromise for his own gain (Numbers 22:18-19). Scripture defines him as a diviner and records him as the one who led Israel astray into apostasy (Revelation 2:14).

call: Second son of Benjamin (mighty warrior and chief)
introduce: Becher was a son of Benjamin, a man of the tribe of Benjamin recorded in 1 Chronicles 7:6 and 7:8. His sons are recorded as heads of their families and mighty men of valor (1 Chronicles 7:8-9).
lifetime: The sons of Benjamin are recorded as three: Bela, Becher, and Jediael (1 Chronicles 7:6). The sons of Becher were Zemirah, Joash, Eliezer, Elioenai, Omri, Jeremoth, Abijah, Anathoth, and Alemeth (1 Chronicles 7:8).
event: His descendants each became chiefs and formed families, and it is recorded that the mighty men of their families numbered 20,200 (1 Chronicles 7:8-9).
character: He is described as the head of a family and a capable warrior, and he and his descendants are regarded as a family that held considerable military influence within the tribe of Benjamin (1 Chronicles 7:8).

introduce: Barak is a figure mentioned in 1 Samuel 12:11, whose name appears as one the LORD sent while Samuel was recalling how the LORD had delivered Israel from the hand of its enemies. His identity and detailed activities are not recorded in Scripture.
lifetime: His name appears when Samuel, speaking to the people of Israel, recalls how the LORD had delivered them from the hand of their enemies (1 Samuel 12:11). Nothing about his birth or the course of his life is recorded in Scripture.
event: It is recorded that the LORD sent Jerubbaal, Barak, Jephthah, and Samuel, and delivered Israel from the hand of its enemies on every side so that they dwelt securely (1 Samuel 12:11). What specifically Barak did is not recorded in Scripture.

introduce: He is recorded in the genealogy of the descendants of Judah (1 Chronicles 4) as one fathered by Eshton, and is described as a man of Recah (1 Chronicles 4:12).
lifetime: He is recorded as one of those fathered by Eshton: Beth-rapha, Paseah, and Tehinnah the father of Ir-nahash (1 Chronicles 4:12).
event: In the biblical text no record of any personal achievement or specific event is found in connection with Beth-rapha (1 Chronicles 4:12).

introduce: Peresh, who appears in 1 Chronicles 7:16, is a son born to Maacah, the wife of Machir of the tribe of Manasseh. He is mentioned in the genealogy of the descendants of Manasseh together with his brother Sheresh (1 Chronicles 7:16).
lifetime: Peresh was born as a son of Machir the son of Manasseh (1 Chronicles 7:14, 7:16). He was born to Machir's wife Maacah (1 Chronicles 7:16).
event: Peresh had a brother named Sheresh, and they are recorded as descendants who made up the family of Machir (1 Chronicles 7:16). The biblical text contains no account of any specific achievement or particular event of his (1 Chronicles 7:16).

introduce: Porcius Festus was the governor of the Roman province of Judea in the first century, a man who took office as successor to Felix. Within the Roman system of rule he was in charge of the administrative and judicial affairs of the region of Judea.
lifetime: Festus took office as governor of Judea in place of Felix (Acts 24:27). Three days after arriving he went up from Caesarea to Jerusalem (Acts 25:1), where the chief priests and the leading men among the Jews brought charges against Paul (Acts 25:2). After spending eight or ten days there, he went down to Caesarea, took his seat on the tribunal, and ordered Paul to be brought (Acts 25:6). When Paul appealed to Caesar, he conferred with those who sat with him and said that he would go to Caesar (Acts 25:12), and when King Agrippa visited, he laid Paul's case before the king (Acts 25:13-14).
event: The Jewish religious leaders asked that Paul be transferred to Jerusalem, but Festus answered that Paul was being held in Caesarea, and he took his seat on the tribunal in Caesarea (Acts 25:3-6). Wishing to win the favor of the Jews, he asked Paul whether he would go up to Jerusalem to be examined, but Paul said that he would be examined before Caesar's tribunal and appealed to Caesar (Acts 25:9-11). Festus accepted Paul's appeal and decided to send him to Caesar (Acts 25:12), and he explained the circumstances of Paul's case to King Agrippa (Acts 25:14-21). He also said that he had found nothing in Paul deserving death (Acts 25:25).
character: He showed a practical side, giving priority to the Roman legal system and administrative procedure over Jewish customs (Acts 25:16). Hearing Paul's eloquence, he even judged that Paul was out of his mind (Acts 25:24), and he had an attitude of seeking to observe the due legal process for one who held Roman citizenship (Acts 25:25-27).

introduce: He was a district governor who administered one of the twelve administrative districts of Israel in the time of Solomon's reign. He is recorded as one who governed the region including Ramoth-gilead and was responsible for supplying provisions for the royal household.
lifetime: He appears as one of the twelve governors whom Solomon set over all Israel (1 Kings 4:7, 4:13). Being at Ramoth-gilead, he had charge of all the villages of Jair son of Manasseh in Gilead, and of the region of Argob in Bashan, sixty great cities with walls and bronze bars (1 Kings 4:13).
event: His main duty was to provide food for King Solomon and the royal household for one month of the year (1 Kings 4:7). The region he administered consisted of the principal strongholds east of the Jordan, and the cities had high walls and bronze bars installed (1 Kings 4:13).

introduce: Ben-deker was a regional official who administered one of the twelve administrative districts of Israel in the time of King Solomon's reign.
lifetime: He was one of the twelve regional governors appointed by King Solomon and governed the district comprising Makaz, Shaalbim, Beth-shemesh, and Elon-beth-hanan (1 Kings 4:9).
event: In the administrative district entrusted to him, he carried out the duty of providing food for King Solomon and his royal household for one month of the year (1 Kings 4:7).

introduce: Ben-zoheth is a man recorded as a descendant of the tribe of Judah. He is mentioned in the genealogy in which the sons of Ishi are listed (1 Chronicles 4:20).
lifetime: In the family tree of the tribe of Judah he appears as one of the sons of Ishi (1 Chronicles 4:20).
event: The biblical text mentions him only as a son of Ishi and does not record any specific achievement of his or any historical event connected with him (1 Chronicles 4:20).

introduce: Ben-abinadab is a man mentioned in 1 Kings 4:11, one of the twelve district governors in charge of the administrative districts of King Solomon. He was given responsibility for the whole region of the heights of Dor.
lifetime: He took Taphath, the daughter of Solomon, as his wife and so became the king's son-in-law, and he held the office over the whole region of the heights of Dor (1 Kings 4:11).
event: As one of Solomon's twelve governors, he was responsible for providing food for the king and the royal household for one month of the year (1 Kings 4:7, 4:11).

call: Ben-hadad I, king of Aram (ally of Asa)
introduce: Ben-hadad I was a king who ruled from Damascus, the capital of ancient Aram, and who contended for supremacy in the northern region through political and military interests with the kingdom of Israel. According to the biblical record, he is mentioned as the son of Tabrimmon and the grandson of Hezion.
lifetime: When Baasha king of northern Israel built Ramah and pressed upon Judah, Asa king of Judah sent the silver and gold from the treasuries of the house of the LORD and of the king's palace and asked an alliance of Ben-hadad king of Aram, who lived in Damascus (1 Kings 15:17-18). Ben-hadad accepted Asa's proposal and attacked the cities of Israel, and Baasha stopped building Ramah and stayed in Tirzah (1 Kings 15:20-21). No detailed record of his personal birth or later years appears in Scripture.
event: Ben-hadad sent the commanders of his armies against the cities of Israel, and the targets were Ijon, Dan, Abel-beth-maacah, all Chinnereth, and all the land of Naphtali (1 Kings 15:20). As a result Baasha stopped building Ramah and stayed in Tirzah (1 Kings 15:21), and this followed Asa's request, with the gift of silver and gold, that he break his treaty with Baasha (1 Kings 15:19).
character: He showed a pragmatic and calculating course of rule, breaking an existing treaty for the sake of his own political interests and accepting Asa's bribe to attack Israel (1 Kings 15:19). He is also described as a leader with an active will to expand, using the military strength of Aram to enlarge the territory and extend the influence of Aram over neighboring countries (1 Kings 15:20).

introduce: Belial is a term derived from the Hebrew word beliyya'al. In Scripture it is used chiefly not as the proper name of a particular individual but as an abstract noun meaning worthlessness, wickedness, and depravity. In the New Testament it is also used as another name referring to Satan.
event: The original word (H1100) used in the Old Testament in "sons of Belial" is rendered in the Korean Revised Version (Gaeyeok Hangul) as "ruffians," "worthless men," and the like. The expression appears in the incident in which the ruffians of that city surrounded the house where a Levite was staying and demanded that the man who had come into the house be brought out (Judges 19:22), in the ruffians who despised Saul and brought him no gifts (1 Samuel 10:27), and in Abigail's words calling Nabal a "worthless man" (1 Samuel 25:25).
character: In the biblical text Belial is used as a byword for wickedness and uselessness. By the New Testament period Paul, emphasizing that Christ and Belial cannot be in harmony, identified it with an evil spiritual being or Satan (2 Corinthians 6:15). The word appears as a personal attribute symbolizing a worthless person, a depraved person, or a force opposed to God (Deuteronomy 13:13).

introduce: Belshazzar is known as the last king of Babylon, and according to the Book of Daniel, on the very night he was holding a great banquet he was slain as king of the Chaldeans, and Darius the Mede received the kingdom (Daniel 5:30-31). Daniel 7 and 8 record the dream and the vision that Daniel received in his first year and third year (Daniel 7:1, 8:1).
lifetime: The Book of Daniel records Nebuchadnezzar as Belshazzar's father and Belshazzar as his son (Daniel 5:2, 5:22). He gave a great banquet for a thousand of his nobles and drank wine in front of them (Daniel 5:1). Belshazzar commanded that Daniel be clothed in purple and a gold chain be put around his neck, and issued a decree making him the third ruler of the kingdom (Daniel 5:29). That very night Belshazzar king of the Chaldeans was slain (Daniel 5:30).
event: During the banquet Belshazzar had the gold and silver vessels that his father Nebuchadnezzar had taken from the temple in Jerusalem brought in so that the king and his nobles could drink from them (Daniel 5:2-3). Then the fingers of a human hand appeared and wrote on the plaster of the wall of the king's palace opposite the lampstand (Daniel 5:5). The king called the enchanters, the Chaldean astrologers, the diviners, and the wise men of Babylon, but none of them could read the writing (Daniel 5:7-8); and on the word of the queen mother, Daniel was summoned (Daniel 5:10-16) and interpreted the writing. Daniel made known that the writing was MENE, MENE, TEKEL, PARSIN, and interpreted that the king's kingdom was at an end and would be given to the Medes and Persians (Daniel 5:25-28).
character: He showed a sacrilegious attitude, such as bringing the vessels of the temple in Jerusalem and using them as drinking cups (Daniel 5:2-3). When the prophetic warning appeared, his face turned pale, his thoughts troubled him, and his hip joints gave way, revealing extreme fear and bewilderment (Daniel 5:6). He showed a realistic side in trying to solve the problem by promising great rewards to his wise men (Daniel 5:7). Although he knew the example of Nebuchadnezzar, he was judged to have exalted himself and hardened his heart (Daniel 5:22).

introduce: A man belonging to the genealogy of the tribe of Judah, a male classified as one of the descendants of Caleb.
lifetime: He is mentioned as the son of Maon. 1 Chronicles 2:45 records Beth-zur as the son of Maon, saying, "The son of Shammai was Maon, and Maon was the father of Beth-zur.", and this verse is within the genealogy of the descendants of Caleb, the brother of Jerahmeel (1 Chronicles 2:42-45).

introduce: Pochereth-hazzebaim is a family among the descendants of the servants of Solomon, a name recorded in the list when the people of Israel returned to Jerusalem and Judah after finishing the Babylonian exile.
lifetime: It is a family recorded in the list of returnees from the Babylonian exile as descendants of the servants of Solomon, and it is included in the count of the people of Israel who came with Zerubbabel and others (Ezra 2:2, 2:55-57). Where Nehemiah found the register of the genealogy of those who had come up at first and recorded it, it is again mentioned as the descendants of Pochereth-hazzebaim among the descendants of the servants of Solomon (Nehemiah 7:5, 7:57-59).
event: As a member of the community of Israel, its name was entered in the list of those who returned from Babylon to Judah (Ezra 2:1, 2:57). The same family is also recorded in the list of Nehemiah 7:59 as one of the families among the descendants of the servants of Solomon.

meaning: Pilate, the one bearing a spear
introduce: Pontius Pilate was the fifth governor to rule the province of Judea under Tiberius Caesar of the Roman Empire, and served from AD 26 to 36. Historically he is recorded as the one who tried Jesus and pronounced the sentence of crucifixion.
lifetime: As a Roman administrator, he was governor of Judea in the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar (Luke 3:1). He presided over the trial of Jesus, who had been accused by the Jewish leaders (Matthew 27:2); no clear record of him after this appears in Scripture.
event: As governor of Judea he was in charge of the trial of Jesus, and at the demand of the Jewish crowd he had Jesus flogged and handed over to be crucified (Matthew 27:26). Seeing that a riot was about to break out before the execution, he washed his hands in front of the crowd and said that he was innocent of this man's blood (Matthew 27:24). On the cross of Jesus he had a notice written and fastened, "Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews" (John 19:19). It was reported to Jesus that Pilate had mixed the blood of certain Galileans with their sacrifices (Luke 13:1).
character: Fearing the pressure of the Jewish crowd and the possibility of an uprising, he showed a political compromising nature, putting the mood of the masses ahead of his own legal judgment (Mark 15:15). Finding no particular charge against Jesus, he tried several times to release him, revealing a side of him that agonized as an enforcer of Roman law (John 19:12). After the death sentence he showed an attitude of trying to evade his own responsibility (Matthew 27:24).

introduce: Merodach-baladan was the son of Baladan, king of Babylon, a man who appears in 2 Kings and Isaiah. Hearing that Hezekiah had been sick and had recovered, he sent a letter and a gift to Judah (2 Kings 20:12; Isaiah 39:1).
lifetime: He was the son of Baladan, king of Babylon, and hearing that Hezekiah had been sick, he sent a letter and a gift to Hezekiah (2 Kings 20:12). Isaiah 39:1 records that, hearing that Hezekiah had been sick and had recovered, he sent a letter and a gift, and there his name is written "Merodach-baladan."
event: Hearing the words of the envoys he sent, Hezekiah showed the envoys everything in his treasure house: the silver and gold, the spices and precious oil, and the armory and all that was in his treasuries (2 Kings 20:13). Afterward the prophet Isaiah delivered to Hezekiah the word of the LORD that everything in the royal palace and all that his fathers had stored up would be carried off to Babylon (2 Kings 20:17; Isaiah 39:6).

call: Third son of Ham (ancestor of Put in North Africa)
introduce: A son of Ham, classified as a figure associated with the region of North Africa in the ancient Near East and in biblical geography. He is mentioned in the list of the sons of Ham, son of Noah, after Cush and Mizraim and before Canaan (Genesis 10:6).
lifetime: He was born as a son of Ham after Noah's flood, and his name is registered in the genealogy of Noah (Genesis 10:6). His name is also stated again in Chronicles as a descendant of Ham (1 Chronicles 1:8).
event: Scripture records no specific deeds of Put himself; his name appears only as one of the sons of Ham (Genesis 10:6; 1 Chronicles 1:8).

meaning: The LORD has opened his eyes
introduce: He was the seventeenth king of the northern kingdom of Israel, the son of Menahem, a man who reigned for a short time in the middle of the eighth century BC.
lifetime: He became king of Israel in Samaria and ruled for two years (2 Kings 15:22-23). His reign began as the successor of his father Menahem, but it ended when he was killed by his officer Pekah in the second year of his reign (2 Kings 15:25).
event: The key event during his reign was the rebellion and murder carried out by his officer Pekah. Together with fifty men of Gilead, Pekah killed the king, Argob, and Arieh in the citadel of the king's palace in Samaria and became king in his place (2 Kings 15:25).
character: According to the biblical record, he is judged to have done as Jeroboam son of Nebat did, not turning away from the sins of his ancestors, and causing Israel to sin (2 Kings 15:24). Beyond this, nothing specific is described about his personal character or his philosophy of rule.

introduce: Bunah is a figure in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah, a son of Jerahmeel, the firstborn of Hezron (1 Chronicles 2:25).
lifetime: He is recorded as a son of Jerahmeel, the firstborn of Hezron (1 Chronicles 2:25). As sons of Jerahmeel are listed the firstborn Ram, then Bunah, Oren, Ozem, and Ahijah (1 Chronicles 2:25).

introduce: Benaiah was a military leader active in the time of King David and King Solomon, the son of Jehoiada and the commander of David's bodyguard, composed of Cherethites and Pelethites. Afterward, in the time of Solomon, he was appointed commander-in-chief of the army and took control of the military in succession to Joab.
lifetime: Benaiah is recorded as the grandson of a mighty man of Kabzeel and the son of Jehoiada (2 Samuel 23:20). He won a name among the three mighty men, but was more honored than the Thirty and did not attain to the first three, and David set him over his bodyguard (2 Samuel 23:22-23). During David's reign he was over the Cherethites and the Pelethites (2 Samuel 8:18). Before David's death he assisted in the process of Solomon's succession to the throne (1 Kings 1:32-38), and after Solomon's accession he executed the opposing forces and became commander of the army in place of Joab (1 Kings 2:35).
event: He killed two sons of Ariel of Moab, and on a day when snow had fallen he went down into a pit and killed a lion (2 Samuel 23:20). He also killed a mighty Egyptian; the man had a spear in his hand, but Benaiah went down to him with a staff, snatched the spear from his hand, and killed him with his own spear (2 Samuel 23:21). When Adonijah tried to seize the throne, he stood on Solomon's side and took part in setting Solomon on King David's mule and escorting him to Gihon (1 Kings 1:38). At Solomon's command he struck down and killed Adonijah, Joab, and Shimei (1 Kings 2:25, 2:34, 2:46).
character: Benaiah was a man utterly loyal to David, and he had the decisiveness to carry out the king's commands without hesitation (1 Kings 1:36). He was a warrior with outstanding physical ability and martial skill, and held a position of special respect even among David's mighty men (2 Samuel 23:22). In the process of removing unrighteous forces he showed the figure of a strict enforcer of the law (1 Kings 2:25-46).

직업/직위: commander in chief of Solomon's army

introduce: Beno was a man belonging to the descendants of Merari of the tribe of Levi, recorded as the son of Jaaziah (1 Chronicles 24:26).
lifetime: Beno was a son of Jaaziah, a descendant of Merari (1 Chronicles 24:26). As those born of Jaaziah, Beno, Shoham, Zaccur, and Ibri are recorded (1 Chronicles 24:27).

introduce: A man who appears in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah, recorded as born to Hur, the firstborn of Ephrathah (1 Chronicles 4:4).
lifetime: He is recorded as born to Hur, the firstborn of Ephrathah, the father of Bethlehem (1 Chronicles 4:4).
event: In the Korean Revised Version (Gaeyeok Hangul) it reads "Penuel, the father of Gedor" (1 Chronicles 4:4). No other deeds are recorded.

introduce: One of the Levites included in the list of those who sealed the covenant after the rebuilding of the wall of Jerusalem in the time of Nehemiah (Nehemiah 10:9).
lifetime: He is on the list of the Levites among those who set their seal to the covenant led by Nehemiah (Nehemiah 10:1, 10:9-13).
event: He put his name on the list of those who sealed, in which the people of Israel pledged before God, taking on themselves a curse and an oath, to walk in the law and to keep the ordinances and commandments (Nehemiah 10:29).

introduce: She was one of the two wives of Elkanah the Ephraimite, a woman who together with Hannah made up Elkanah's household.
lifetime: As the wife of Elkanah, she had children (1 Samuel 1:2). Elkanah went up every year to Shiloh to offer sacrifice, and on the day of sacrifice he gave portions of the offering to Peninnah and all her sons and daughters (1 Samuel 1:3-4).
event: Because the LORD had closed Hannah's womb, her rival Peninnah provoked her severely to irritate her (1 Samuel 1:6). Elkanah gave Hannah a double portion (1 Samuel 1:5), but every year when Hannah went up to the house of the LORD, Peninnah provoked her, and Hannah wept and would not eat (1 Samuel 1:7).
character: She showed an attitude of mocking and tormenting Hannah, who could not bear children (1 Samuel 1:6). She formed a competitive arrangement within Elkanah's family and was at the center of the conflict (1 Samuel 1:7).

기타관계: Hannah#3022(kinsman of the tribe of Ephraim)

introduce: Pedahzur is a man recorded in the Book of Numbers as the father of Gamaliel, the chief of the descendants of Manasseh (Numbers 1:10).
lifetime: Scripture records no deeds of Pedahzur himself. His son Gamaliel is introduced as "the son of Pedahzur" as chief of the descendants of Manasseh in the census list (Numbers 1:10), in the arrangement of the camp (Numbers 2:20), and in the march (Numbers 10:23).
event: No event of Pedahzur himself is recorded. His son Gamaliel, as chief of the descendants of Manasseh, presented an offering for the dedication of the tabernacle on the eighth day, and the peace offering consisted of two bulls, five rams, five male goats, and five male lambs a year old (Numbers 7:54, 7:59).

introduce: Pedaiah, from Rumah, was the father of Zebidah, the wife of King Josiah and the mother of King Jehoiakim. That is, he was the maternal grandfather of Jehoiakim.
lifetime: He is known to have been from Rumah, and his daughter Zebidah was the mother of Jehoiakim, the son of Josiah (2 Kings 23:34, 23:36).
event: In the biblical record no specific deeds of Pedaiah himself nor any national events concerning him appear (2 Kings 23:36).

introduce: Pedahel was a chief of the tribe of the descendants of Naphtali, the son of Ammihud (Numbers 34:28).
lifetime: He is one of the chiefs named in accordance with the command to choose one chief from each tribe when the people of Israel divided the land of Canaan as an inheritance, and he is recorded as the chief of the tribe of the descendants of Naphtali (Numbers 34:18, 34:28).
event: When the LORD told Moses the names of those who were to divide the inheritance, he was named as the chief of the tribe of the descendants of Naphtali, and these were said to be the men whom the LORD commanded to divide the inheritance among the people of Israel in the land of Canaan (Numbers 34:28-29).

introduce: Pethahiah was a Levite, a man belonging to the nineteenth of the twenty-four divisions determined by lot for the duties of the priesthood in the time of David.
lifetime: In the course of systematizing the genealogies and duties of the Levites during the reign of King David, he was recorded in the list of the divisions of the priests (1 Chronicles 24:16).
event: He is recorded as the one on whom the nineteenth lot fell when David divided the descendants of Eleazar and the descendants of Ithamar by lot (1 Chronicles 24:3-5, 24:16), and according to this order of service they entered the house of the LORD and ministered according to the ordinance given them by Aaron (1 Chronicles 24:19).

meaning: Son of judgment, or son of Dan
introduce: Bedan is a figure who appears in the genealogy of the tribe of Manasseh, recorded as the son of Ulam (1 Chronicles 7:17).
lifetime: Bedan was the son of Ulam, and these were all said to be descendants of Gilead. Gilead was the son of Machir and the grandson of Manasseh (1 Chronicles 7:17).

introduce: Bedad is a man recorded as the father of Hadad, king of Edom (Genesis 36:35, 1 Chronicles 1:46).
lifetime: Bedad is mentioned only as the father of Hadad, in the record that after Husham died his son Hadad reigned in his place (Genesis 36:35, 1 Chronicles 1:46), and Scripture has no record of Bedad's own life.
event: It is recorded that Bedad's son Hadad struck Midian in the field of Moab (Genesis 36:35, 1 Chronicles 1:46). This is a deed of his son Hadad, and no event of Bedad himself is recorded in Scripture.

introduce: Bethuel is recorded as the eighth of the eight sons of Nahor, Abraham's brother, and Milcah, and was a member of a family of Arameans who lived in the region of Paddan-aram. As the father of Rebekah, who became Isaac's wife, and of Laban, the father-in-law of Jacob, he serves as a genealogical link between the patriarchal families.
lifetime: He was one of the eight sons born between Nahor and Milcah, and he fathered Rebekah (Genesis 22:22-23). He is recorded as an Aramean of Paddan-aram, with Rebekah as his daughter and Laban as his son (Genesis 25:20, 28:5). When Abraham's servant came to the city of Nahor (Genesis 24:10), Rebekah was introduced as the daughter of Bethuel, the son whom Milcah bore to Nahor (Genesis 24:15, 24:24).
event: When Abraham's servant asked for Rebekah to be the wife of Isaac, he, together with Rebekah's brother Laban, answered, "The matter comes from the LORD; we cannot speak to you either bad or good," and said that Rebekah should become the wife of his master's son (Genesis 24:50-51).

introduce: Fortunatus is a figure who appears in 1 Corinthians in the New Testament, recorded as one who came to the apostle Paul together with Stephanas and Achaicus (1 Corinthians 16:17).
lifetime: At the time when Paul intended to stay in Ephesus until Pentecost (1 Corinthians 16:8), he is recorded as having come to Paul together with Stephanas and Achaicus (1 Corinthians 16:17).
event: He is recorded as one of those who supplied what was lacking on the part of the church in Corinth and refreshed Paul's spirit (1 Corinthians 16:17-18).

introduce: Beracah is one of the mighty men of the tribe of Benjamin who joined David when David stayed at Ziklag to escape from Saul (1 Chronicles 12:3).
lifetime: Beracah came from the tribe of Benjamin, Saul's kinsmen, and is included in the list of the mighty men who came to Ziklag to help David while he was living there (1 Chronicles 12:1-3).
event: He is recorded as one of the mighty men who came to David and helped him in battle while David was in hiding at Ziklag because of Saul son of Kish; they were men armed with the bow, who used both the right hand and the left in slinging stones and shooting arrows (1 Chronicles 12:1-3).

introduce: Beraiah is a figure who appears in the genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin, recorded as one of the sons of Shimei (1 Chronicles 8:21).
lifetime: Beraiah is recorded as a son of Shimei together with Adaiah and Shimrath (1 Chronicles 8:21), and it is said that all the men in this list were heads of families, chiefs throughout their generations, and lived in Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 8:28).
event: He is recorded as one of those who lived in Jerusalem and served as heads of their families (1 Chronicles 8:21, 1 Chronicles 8:28).

introduce: Prochorus is a man chosen as one of the seven whom the apostles told the church to select over the matter of relief in the early church in Jerusalem (Acts 6:3, 6:5).
lifetime: When, in the early church in Jerusalem, the Hellenistic Jews complained against the Hebrews over the matter of relief (Acts 6:1), he became one of the seven chosen according to the word of the apostles to select seven men of good repute, full of the Holy Spirit and of wisdom (Acts 6:3, 6:5). He was set before the apostles and received their prayer and the laying on of hands (Acts 6:6).
event: He is one of the seven chosen to be entrusted with "this task" so that the apostles might devote themselves to prayer and to the ministry of the word (Acts 6:2-5).
character: He was acknowledged by the church in Jerusalem as a man full of the Holy Spirit and of wisdom, and was a man held in good regard within the community (Acts 6:3, 6:5).

introduce: Peruda is one of those who returned to Jerusalem and Judah, at the decree of Cyrus king of Persia, after the end of the Babylonian exile (Ezra 2:55). He is recorded as a man belonging to the genealogy of the descendants of Solomon's servants (Ezra 2:55).
lifetime: His name is entered in the list of the returnees who came back from Babylon to Jerusalem as one of the descendants of Solomon's servants (Ezra 2:55). Scripture has no further record of his deeds after the return from the Babylonian captivity or of the specific period of his life (Ezra 2:55).
event: He joined the community that was released from the Babylonian captivity and returned to Jerusalem (Ezra 2:55). Apart from the fact that he entered his name on the list of returnees while retaining the genealogical identity of a descendant of Solomon's servants, no special accomplishment of his is recorded in Scripture (Ezra 2:55).

introduce: Perida is one of the members of the community of Judah who returned from the Babylonian captivity, a man whose name is entered in the list of the descendants of the servants of Solomon (Nehemiah 7:57).
lifetime: Perida is one of the descendants of the servants of Solomon who, among the descendants carried away captive to Babylon, returned to Jerusalem and to the cities of Judah (Nehemiah 7:57). The same list is also in Ezra 2:55, but there it is written as "the descendants of Peruda" (Ezra 2:55).
event: After the return from the Babylonian captivity, in the census conducted for the rebuilding of the wall of Jerusalem and the reorganization of the community, he was officially recorded as included in the list of the descendants of the servants of Solomon (Nehemiah 7:57).

introduce: Prisca is a woman who appears in the New Testament, the wife of Aquila and a helper who took part in Christian mission work in the time of the early church. Together with her husband she was active, going back and forth between Rome, Corinth, and Ephesus.
lifetime: She was the wife of Aquila, a Jew born in Pontus, and had recently come from Italy with her husband because Claudius had ordered all the Jews to leave Rome, and Paul went to them (Acts 18:2). Because they were of the same trade, Paul stayed with them and worked at making tents (Acts 18:3); afterward she accompanied him when Paul set sail for Syria (Acts 18:18), and Paul left them at Ephesus (Acts 18:19). In Romans 16, Paul told the believers in Rome to greet them (Romans 16:3).
event: In Corinth Paul went to them, and because they were of the same trade, he stayed with them and worked (Acts 18:2-3). In Ephesus, when she and Aquila heard Apollos, a native of Alexandria who knew only the baptism of John, begin to speak boldly in the synagogue, they took him aside and explained the way of God to him more accurately (Acts 18:24-26). Paul called them his fellow workers in Christ Jesus, and wrote that they had risked their own necks for his life (Romans 16:3-4). Paul also told them to greet her church (Romans 16:5).
character: In the biblical record her name is always mentioned together with her husband Aquila, and sometimes her name is written before her husband's, which suggests that she had considerable influence in the early church (Acts 18:18, Romans 16:3). She showed an open and devoted attitude, offering her own house as a meeting place for the church (Romans 16:5). She was intelligent and of high theological understanding, with the ability to instruct even a leader-level figure such as Apollos in doctrine (Acts 18:26).

introduce: Priscilla is a woman who appears in the Acts of the Apostles and the Epistles of the New Testament, a person who was active in the community of the early church together with her husband Aquila. Paul called them his fellow workers in Christ Jesus (Romans 16:3).
lifetime: Together with her husband Aquila, Priscilla had recently come from Italy because Claudius had ordered all the Jews to leave Rome, and Paul went to them (Acts 18:2). Because they were of the same trade, Paul stayed with them and worked at making tents (Acts 18:3). Afterward she accompanied him when Paul set sail for Syria (Acts 18:18), and in Ephesus, hearing Apollos begin to speak boldly in the synagogue, they took him aside and explained the way of God to him more accurately (Acts 18:26). In Romans 16, Paul told the believers to greet them and also to greet her church (Romans 16:3-5).
event: In Corinth Paul went to them, and because they were of the same trade, he stayed with them and worked at making tents (Acts 18:2-3). In Ephesus, hearing Apollos, a Jew from Alexandria, begin to speak boldly in the synagogue, they took him aside and explained the way of God to him more accurately (Acts 18:24-26). Paul called them his fellow workers, and wrote that they had risked their very necks for Paul's life (Romans 16:3-4). Paul also told them to greet her church (Romans 16:5).
character: In Scripture Priscilla is always mentioned together with her husband Aquila, and the couple exerted influence in the early church as independent agents (Acts 18:18, 1 Corinthians 16:19). On the basis of a deep understanding of Christian doctrine she had the intellectual capacity to teach others (Acts 18:26), and she showed an attitude of active devotion to ministry, such as offering her own house as a place for the church (Romans 16:5). She is portrayed as a person of strong conviction and a spirit of sacrifice, to the extent of being recognized by the apostle Paul as his fellow worker (Romans 16:3-4).

기타관계: Claudius#237(Roman emperor who ordered the expulsion)

call: Son of Asher (ancestor of the Beriite clan)
introduce: Beriah was a son of Asher, the eighth son of Jacob, and became the ancestor of the Beriite family belonging to the tribe of Asher.
lifetime: Beriah was born as a son of Asher; his brothers were Imnah, Ishvah, and Ishvi, and his sister was Serah (Genesis 46:17). He is recorded as a son of Asher in the list of the family of Israel who went down to Egypt (Genesis 46:8, 46:17).
event: He became the ancestor of the Beriite family (Numbers 26:44). He also had two sons, Heber and Malchiel (Genesis 46:17), and from them came the Heberite family and the Malchielite family (Numbers 26:45).

introduce: Bezalel, the grandson of Hur of the tribe of Judah and the son of Uri, was the craftsman for making the tabernacle whom the LORD named and called in Exodus, and his name carries the meaning "in the shadow of God" (Exodus 31:2).
lifetime: Bezalel was a man of the tribe of Judah, the grandson of Hur and the son of Uri (Exodus 31:2), and he was endowed by God with wisdom, understanding, knowledge, and all kinds of craftsmanship (Exodus 31:3). The LORD stirred up him and Oholiab son of Ahisamach of the tribe of Dan to teach (Exodus 35:30-34).
event: Bezalel made all that the LORD had commanded Moses (Exodus 38:22). He made the ark of acacia wood and overlaid it with pure gold, and made the mercy seat (Exodus 37:1-6); he made the table of the bread of the Presence, the lampstand, the altar of incense, the anointing oil and the incense (Exodus 37:10-29). He also made the altar of burnt offering and the basin, and made the court, equipping it with hangings of fine linen, pillars, and so on (Exodus 38:1-20).
character: Bezalel possessed fine skill across the whole range of the crafts: the working of gold, silver, and bronze, the cutting and setting of stones, and the carving of wood (Exodus 31:4-5). He had the educational quality to teach craftsmen of outstanding talent (Exodus 35:34), and he showed accuracy and faithfulness in designing and making the tabernacle as Moses had commanded (Exodus 38:22).

직업/직위: master craftsman in charge of building the tabernacle

meaning: One who knows the secret of the LORD
introduce: Besodeiah is a man recorded in Nehemiah 3 as the father of Meshullam (Nehemiah 3:6).
lifetime: There is no direct record about Besodeiah; among those who repaired the wall when the wall of Jerusalem was rebuilt, one who repaired the Old Gate is introduced as "Meshullam son of Besodeiah" (Nehemiah 3:6).
event: His son Meshullam, together with Joiada son of Paseah, repaired the Old Gate, laid its beams, installed its doors, and fitted its bolts and bars (Nehemiah 3:6). This is the work of his son Meshullam, and Scripture has no record of Besodeiah's own deeds.

introduce: Bealiah is one of the mighty men of the tribe of Benjamin who joined David when David stayed at Ziklag to escape from Saul (1 Chronicles 12:5).
lifetime: Bealiah belonged to the tribe of Benjamin, the same tribe as Saul, but he is recorded as one of those who came to Ziklag to help David, who was being pursued by Saul (1 Chronicles 12:2, 12:5).
event: When David was hiding at Ziklag to escape from Saul, the mighty men of the tribe of Benjamin, including Bealiah, came to David and sought to cooperate with him militarily (1 Chronicles 12:1, 12:5).

introduce: Two men with the same name, Beerah, appear in 1 Chronicles. One is a chief of the Reubenites, the son of Baal (1 Chronicles 5:5-6), and the other is one of the sons of Zophah of the tribe of Asher (1 Chronicles 7:36-37).
lifetime: Beerah of the Reubenites is recorded as the son of Baal, and he is the one carried away captive by Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria (1 Chronicles 5:5-6). Beerah of the tribe of Asher is named last among the sons of Zophah (1 Chronicles 7:36-37).

introduce: Beeri is a figure who appears in Genesis in the Old Testament, a man of the Hittite people, recorded as the father of Judith, one of Esau's wives.
lifetime: Beeri is recorded as a man of the Hittite people (Genesis 26:34). His daughter Judith was taken as a wife by Esau when he was forty years old (Genesis 26:34).
