event: Because Esau took his daughter Judith as a wife, he entered into a marriage relationship with Esau (Genesis 26:34). No other deeds of Beeri himself are recorded in Scripture.

introduce: Peullethai is a man recorded as the eighth son among the sons of Obed-edom, who belonged to the division of the gatekeepers (1 Chronicles 26:1, 26:4-5).
lifetime: In the time of David, when the duties of the Levites were apportioned, he was counted as one of the sons of Obed-edom (1 Chronicles 26:4-5).
event: He is recorded as the eighth of the sons of Obed-edom, and it is said that this was because God had blessed Obed-edom (1 Chronicles 26:5). The descendants of Obed-edom were able men, who performed their duties well (1 Chronicles 26:8).

introduce: Pelatiah is a descendant of David, one of the figures who carried on the genealogy of the royal house of Judah after the Babylonian exile. He is mentioned as a son of Hananiah in the list of the descendants of the house of David recorded in 1 Chronicles 3.
lifetime: Pelatiah was a son of Hananiah and belongs to the same Davidic royal line as the descendants of Zerubbabel (1 Chronicles 3:21). No historical record remains of his specific life or the period of his activity.
event: Scripture mentions no specific accomplishment of Pelatiah or any special event connected with him (1 Chronicles 3:21).
character: The biblical text gives no information about Pelatiah's character or personal traits (1 Chronicles 3:21).

introduce: Blastus was a man who held a high position in the royal household of Herod Agrippa I, an official close to the king whom the people of Tyre and Sidon approached in order to make peace with Herod (Acts 12:20).
lifetime: At the time when Herod was angry with the people of Tyre and Sidon, he is recorded as the king's chamberlain (Acts 12:20).
event: Herod was highly displeased with the people of Tyre and Sidon, and because their region was fed from the king's country, they came to Herod with one accord, and having won over Blastus, the king's chamberlain, asked for peace (Acts 12:20).

introduce: A figure who appears in 1 Chronicles 3:24, a descendant of Solomon and a son of Elioenai, recorded through the genealogy of the house of David.
lifetime: As a son of Elioenai, he belongs to a late generation recorded in the royal genealogy of David (1 Chronicles 3:24).

introduce: One of those to whom the apostle Paul sent greetings near the end of Romans in the New Testament, presumed to have been a Christian belonging to the church in Rome.
lifetime: His name is included in the list of final greetings in the letter sent to the believers in Rome (Romans 16:14).
event: He was mentioned when Paul sent greetings to the believers of the church in Rome, and was named as a recipient of greetings together with the brothers who were with him (Romans 16:14).

introduce: Phicol is a figure who appears in the Old Testament, who held the office of commander of the army of Abimelech, king of Gerar. In the diplomatic process of making treaties with Abraham and Isaac, he accompanied the king as an aide and the one militarily responsible.
lifetime: He is recorded as the commander of the army who assisted Abimelech, king of Gerar (Genesis 21:22). He spoke to Abraham together with Abimelech (Genesis 21:22), and after Abraham and Abimelech made a covenant at Beersheba, he returned with Abimelech to the land of the Philistines (Genesis 21:32). Later, in the time of Isaac, when Abimelech came to Isaac from Gerar with his friend Ahuzzath and Phicol the commander of his army and proposed that they make an oath and a covenant, he was present (Genesis 26:26-28).
event: He took part in the process in which a covenant was made with Abraham at Beersheba to keep friendship and good faith with each other (Genesis 21:22-32). Also, after Isaac prospered in Gerar and Abimelech asked him to leave, he attended in his capacity as commander of the army when a peace treaty was finally concluded with Isaac (Genesis 26:26-31).
character: As a military commander trusted by Abimelech, he showed the figure of a faithful official who carried out and assisted the king's diplomatic decisions on the spot (Genesis 21:22, Genesis 26:26). In relations with foreigners, he performed the role of a mediator who brought about peaceful agreement and alliance rather than armed confrontation (Genesis 21:31, Genesis 26:31).

introduce: Bichri is a man recorded in 2 Samuel only as the father of Sheba. His son Sheba is introduced as a Benjamite (2 Samuel 20:1).
lifetime: Scripture has no record of Bichri's own deeds; he appears only as an identification when Sheba rebelled against David, in which Sheba is called "the son of Bichri" (2 Samuel 20:1).
event: When his son Sheba blew the trumpet and said there was no share with David, all the men of Israel stopped following David and followed Sheba (2 Samuel 20:1-2). David had Abishai pursue Sheba (2 Samuel 20:6-7), and Sheba son of Bichri, from the hill country of Ephraim, had his head cut off by the townspeople through the wisdom of a woman and thrown to Joab (2 Samuel 20:21-22). All of this is the doing of his son Sheba and is not recorded as a deed of Bichri.

call: Leader of the return with Zerubbabel
introduce: Bigvai is a man whose name is recorded in the list of the people of Israel who came out of Babylon with Zerubbabel, Jeshua, and others (Ezra 2:2).
lifetime: Bigvai's name is recorded among those who came out together with Zerubbabel, Jeshua, Nehemiah, Seraiah, Reelaiah, Mordecai, Bilshan, Mispar, Rehum, and Baanah (Ezra 2:2). He appears under the same name in the list of Nehemiah 7:7 (Nehemiah 7:7).
event: His name was entered in the list that recorded the number of the people of Israel who came out with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:2, Nehemiah 7:7). Apart from this, no deeds of Bigvai personally are recorded in Scripture.

introduce: Binea is a figure recorded in 1 Chronicles of the Hebrew Bible, a descendant of the house of Saul who belonged to the tribe of Benjamin.
lifetime: Binea was the son of Moza (1 Chronicles 8:37). He belongs to the genealogy that runs from Merib-baal, the son of Saul's son Jonathan, through Micah, Ahaz, Jehoaddah, Zimri, and Moza (1 Chronicles 8:33-37). His son was Rapha (1 Chronicles 8:37), and in 1 Chronicles 9:43 he appears as Rephaiah.
character: The biblical record gives no specific description of Binea's character or personal traits (1 Chronicles 8:37).

introduce: Phinehas, the grandson of Aaron and the son of Eleazar, was the third high priest of Israel. He was a man of the tribe of Levi who was active during the Exodus and the early period of the conquest of Canaan.
lifetime: He was the grandson of Aaron and the son of Eleazar (Exodus 6:25, Numbers 25:7). After the incident at Shittim, God gave him and his descendants the covenant of a perpetual priesthood (Numbers 25:13). When Moses sent an army from each tribe to fight against Midian, he sent Phinehas with them, with the vessels of the sanctuary and the trumpets for signaling in his hand (Numbers 31:6), and the people of Israel sent him to the land of Gilead to see the descendants of Reuben, the descendants of Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh (Joshua 22:13). When his father Eleazar died, the people buried him on the hill that Phinehas had received in the hill country of Ephraim (Joshua 24:33). At the time of the incident at Gibeah, he stood in attendance before the ark of the covenant (Judges 20:27-28).
event: At Shittim, when the people of Israel were committing sexual immorality with the women of Moab and an Israelite man brought a Midianite woman, he took a spear, followed the man into the tent, and killed both of them, and the plague stopped (Numbers 25:1, 6-8). In the war with Midian he went out with the army, carrying the vessels of the sanctuary and the trumpets for signaling (Numbers 31:6). When it was said that the descendants of Reuben, the descendants of Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh had built an altar, the people of Israel sent him to the land of Gilead; he listened to their words and thought them good, said, "we know that the LORD is among us," and returned and reported, so that the people of Israel did not again speak of fighting against them (Joshua 22:13, 30-33). At the time of the fighting against the tribe of Benjamin, he stood in attendance before the ark of the covenant, and the people of Israel inquired of the LORD (Judges 20:27-28).
character: He took God's jealousy as his own jealousy and showed an attitude of immediate and resolute response to the sin of the community (Numbers 25:11). He maintained strictness regarding God's law and ordinances, and is portrayed as a man who valued the unity and purity of the community (Joshua 22:16-20).

introduce: Pithon is a figure who appears in the genealogy of the house of Saul, classified within the genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin as a descendant of Saul.
lifetime: Pithon is recorded as one of the sons of Micah (1 Chronicles 8:35, 1 Chronicles 9:41). Because Merib-baal, the son of Jonathan, fathered Micah (1 Chronicles 8:34, 1 Chronicles 9:40), Pithon was a great-grandson of Jonathan.

introduce: Bithiah is a woman recorded in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah as the daughter of Pharaoh, the wife whom Mered took (1 Chronicles 4:18).
lifetime: Bithiah, the daughter of Pharaoh, was the wife whom Mered took (1 Chronicles 4:18). Miriam, Shammai, and Ishbah, the father of Eshtemoa, whom Mered fathered, are recorded as the offspring of Bithiah, the daughter of Pharaoh whom Mered took (1 Chronicles 4:17-18). Jether, Mered, Epher, and Jalon are the sons of Ezrah (1 Chronicles 4:17).
event: Jered, the father of Gedor, Heber, the father of Soco, and Jekuthiel, the father of Zanoah, are recorded as those born to "his wife Jehudijah," and are not recorded as the offspring of Bithiah (1 Chronicles 4:18).

introduce: Piram is a man mentioned as king of Jarmuth at the time of the war to conquer Canaan (Joshua 10:3).
lifetime: Piram was king of Jarmuth (Joshua 10:3). When Adoni-zedek king of Jerusalem heard that Gibeon had made peace with Israel, he sent word to him proposing to strike Gibeon (Joshua 10:1-4), and Piram, as one of the five kings of the Amorites, gathered with them and fought against Gibeon (Joshua 10:5). After they were defeated before Israel, the five kings hid in the cave at Makkedah and were brought out (Joshua 10:10, 16-23), and Joshua struck those kings dead and hanged them on trees (Joshua 10:26).
event: Adoni-zedek king of Jerusalem sent word to Hoham king of Hebron, Piram king of Jarmuth, Japhia king of Lachish, and Debir king of Eglon, asking them to come up and help him strike Gibeon (Joshua 10:3-4). Then the five kings of the Amorites all went up with their armies, camped against Gibeon, and fought against it (Joshua 10:5). Piram hid with the five kings in the cave at Makkedah and was brought out of the cave (Joshua 10:16-23), and Joshua struck the kings dead and hanged them on five trees until evening, and at sunset took the bodies down and threw them into the cave where they had hidden (Joshua 10:26-27).

introduce: Birsha is a man recorded in Genesis 14 as king of Gomorrah, one of the five kings together with Bera king of Sodom and others (Genesis 14:2).
lifetime: Birsha, as king of Gomorrah, was one of the five kings who fought against the four kings, including Chedorlaomer king of Elam (Genesis 14:1-2, 9). They all gathered in the Valley of Siddim (Genesis 14:3). Scripture has no further record of Birsha's deeds after this war.
event: The king of Sodom, the king of Gomorrah, the king of Admah, the king of Zeboiim, and the king of Bela, that is, Zoar, went out and joined battle with the four kings in the Valley of Siddim (Genesis 14:8-9). The Valley of Siddim was full of tar pits, and when the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah fled, some of their men fell into them, and the rest fled to the hills (Genesis 14:10); the four kings took all the goods and food of Sodom and Gomorrah (Genesis 14:11).

introduce: Birzaith is a figure in the genealogy of the tribe of Asher recorded in 1 Chronicles 7:31 of the Old Testament, whose father is recorded as Malchiel, the son of Beriah (1 Chronicles 7:31).
lifetime: The sons of Beriah, the son of Asher, were Heber and Malchiel, and Malchiel was the father of Birzaith (1 Chronicles 7:30-31). Therefore Birzaith was a grandson of Beriah, the son of Asher. Apart from this, no deeds of his are recorded in Scripture.

introduce: Biztha was one of the seven eunuchs who served King Xerxes of the Persian Empire (Esther 1:10).
lifetime: He served at the court of King Xerxes as a eunuch, an attendant who carried out the king's orders (Esther 1:10).
event: He is one of the seven eunuchs who received the command when, on the seventh day, the heart of King Xerxes was merry with wine and he ordered the seven eunuchs who served in his presence to bring Queen Vashti before him wearing her royal crown (Esther 1:10-11).

introduce: Pispa is a descendant of the tribe of Asher, a figure who appears in 1 Chronicles 7:38. In the genealogy of the tribe of Asher he is recorded as one of the sons of Jether.
lifetime: Pispa is recorded as one of the sons of Jether: Jephunneh, Pispa, and Ara (1 Chronicles 7:38). Concerning his life, apart from his name being listed in the genealogical register of 1 Chronicles 7:38, there is no detailed record of his birth, upbringing, death, and the like.

introduce: Bishlam is a man recorded as one of those who, in the time of Artaxerxes, wrote a letter to Artaxerxes king of Persia together with Mithredath, Tabeel, and their associates (Ezra 4:7).
lifetime: His name is recorded among those who, in the time of Artaxerxes, wrote a letter to Artaxerxes king of Persia together with Mithredath, Tabeel, and their associates (Ezra 4:7). That letter was written in Aramaic script and in the Aramaic language (Ezra 4:7). His other deeds are not recorded in Scripture.
event: Together with Mithredath, Tabeel, and their associates, he wrote a letter to Artaxerxes king of Persia (Ezra 4:7). The ones who sent the letter accusing the people of Jerusalem were the commander Rehum and the scribe Shimshai (Ezra 4:8), and the king's decree to stop the work was also sent to Rehum, the scribe Shimshai, and their associates (Ezra 4:17, 21-23). There is no record that Bishlam was directly involved in this matter.

introduce: Bigtha was one of the seven eunuchs who served King Xerxes of the Persian Empire (Esther 1:10).
lifetime: He is recorded as one of the eunuchs who served in the presence of the king during the time when King Xerxes reigned (Esther 1:10).
event: He is one of the seven eunuchs who received the command when, on the seventh day, the heart of King Xerxes was merry with wine and he ordered the seven eunuchs who served in his presence to bring Queen Vashti before him wearing her royal crown (Esther 1:10-11).

introduce: Bigthana was a eunuch who served King Xerxes of the Persian Empire, one of the two eunuchs of the king who guarded the door (Esther 6:2).
lifetime: Bigthana is recorded as a eunuch of the king who guarded the door (Esther 6:2). There is no record of since when he had served; the plot he and Teresh made to assassinate the king was discovered, and the two were hanged on a tree (Esther 2:21-23).
event: Bigthana, together with Teresh, sought to assassinate King Xerxes (Esther 6:2). Mordecai learned of it and told Queen Esther, and Esther told the king in Mordecai's name (Esther 2:22). When the matter was investigated and found to be so, the two were hanged on a tree, and the matter was recorded in the court records in the presence of the king (Esther 2:23).

introduce: Bigthan was one of the two eunuchs who guarded the palace door during the reign of Xerxes, king of Persia. He is recorded as a man who took part in a plot to assassinate the king.
lifetime: Bigthan was a eunuch of the king who guarded the door of the king's palace (Esther 2:21). Together with Teresh, the eunuch who guarded the door with him, he resented the king and sought to assassinate him (Esther 2:21). Mordecai learned of this and told Queen Esther, and Esther told the king in Mordecai's name (Esther 2:22). When the matter was investigated and found to be so, the two were hanged on a tree (Esther 2:23).
event: He tried to carry out a plot to assassinate the king (Esther 2:21). Their conspiracy was discovered by Mordecai and recorded in the court records (Esther 2:23). In the end this incident became the decisive occasion on which Mordecai later came to receive the king's favor (Esther 6:2).
character: He was a man who plotted treason against the king whom he was supposed to guard (Esther 2:21). Though he had power as one close to the king, he showed a course lacking in political loyalty, to the point of attempting an assassination by abusing it (Esther 2:21).

call: Son of Henadad (weigher of the temple vessels)
introduce: Binnui is a man recorded in Nehemiah 10:9 as one of the descendants of Henadad, and in Nehemiah 12:8 as a Levite who returned with Zerubbabel and Jeshua. In Ezra 8:33 his son Noadiah appears.
lifetime: His name is recorded among the Levites who returned with Zerubbabel and Jeshua (Nehemiah 12:1, 8). Among the Levites who sealed the covenant in the time of Nehemiah, Jeshua son of Azaniah, Binnui of the descendants of Henadad, and Kadmiel are recorded (Nehemiah 10:9).
event: He is recorded as Binnui of the descendants of Henadad among the Levites who sealed the covenant in the time of Nehemiah (Nehemiah 10:9). The one who was present when the silver, the gold, and the vessels were weighed in the house of our God on the fourth day and put into the hand of the priest Meremoth is Binnui's son Noadiah (Ezra 8:33). His name also appears in the list of Levites in Nehemiah 12:8, and the one said to be in charge of the songs of thanksgiving is Mattaniah (Nehemiah 12:8).

call: Chief of the fifteenth division of priests
introduce: Bilgah is the head of the priests who took charge of the fifteenth of the twenty-four divisions determined by lot for the duties of the priesthood in the time of David.
lifetime: David, together with Zadok of the descendants of Eleazar and Ahimelech of the descendants of Ithamar, divided the divisions of the descendants of Aaron and assigned them each their duties of service (1 Chronicles 24:3), and there were sixteen chiefs of the descendants of Eleazar and eight of the descendants of Ithamar, and they were divided by lot (1 Chronicles 24:4-5). At that time Bilgah was recorded as the fifteenth division (1 Chronicles 24:14).
event: When David systematized the duties of the priests for the service of the temple, he was chosen by lot as the head of the fifteenth division and came to perform his duties (1 Chronicles 24:14).

introduce: Bilgai is a man recorded as a priest among those who sealed the covenant in the time of Nehemiah (Nehemiah 10:8).
lifetime: Bilgai is recorded as a priest among those who sealed, together with Maaziah and Shemaiah (Nehemiah 10:8). That list begins with Nehemiah the governor and Zedekiah, among others (Nehemiah 10:1).
event: He is recorded as one of the priests who sealed the covenant (Nehemiah 10:29) in which they swore to keep the law of God given through Moses, the servant of God (Nehemiah 10:8).

introduce: Pildash is one of the eight sons born between Nahor, the brother of Abraham, and his wife Milcah (Genesis 22:22).
lifetime: He is recorded as a son born between Nahor and Milcah, and he is a nephew of Abraham (Genesis 22:22).

introduce: A figure who appears in the Book of Job in the Old Testament, the Shuhite mentioned second among Job's three friends. He was a man who upheld the traditional principle of wisdom and retribution and tried to interpret Job's suffering.
lifetime: When Bildad the Shuhite heard of the calamity that had come upon Job, he, together with Eliphaz and Zophar, made an appointment and went to visit Job to comfort him (Job 2:11). He argued concerning Job's suffering three times (Job 8:1, 18:1, 25:1), and afterward he found himself in the situation of having incurred God's wrath, so that he had to offer a burnt offering and ask Job to pray (Job 42:7-9).
event: In the debate with Job, he said that Job's children had sinned against God and had been delivered into the hand of their transgression, and that if Job diligently sought God and was pure and upright, God would watch over him (Job 8:4-6). He put forward ancient wisdom, telling Job to inquire of the ancestors (Job 8:8-10), and he emphasized the destruction of the wicked, saying that the light of the wicked is put out and their steps grow weary (Job 18:5-21). In his last speech he spoke of the worthlessness of man before the majesty of God (Job 25:2-6). Afterward the LORD said to Eliphaz, "My wrath is kindled against you and your two friends, for you have not spoken about Me accurately, as My servant Job has" (Job 42:7).
character: He is regarded as a man with a traditionalist and conservative way of thinking. Rather than sympathizing with Job's pain, he had a strong tendency to interpret the phenomenon according to the doctrines and norms he knew (Job 8:8-10). Rather than examining the other's situation, he showed an obstinate aspect, trying to press through his own logic, and in response to Job's rebuttal he even took an aggressive attitude, raising the level of his reproach (Job 18:2-4).

introduce: Piltai is a man of the clan of Miniamin, that is, Moadiah, recorded as a head of the priests in the time of Joiakim.
lifetime: In the list of those who were heads of the priests in the time of Joiakim (Nehemiah 12:12-21), Zichri is recorded for the clan of Abijah and Piltai for the clan of Miniamin, that is, Moadiah (Nehemiah 12:17).
event: In the time of Joiakim he was entered in the list as the man representing the clan of Miniamin, that is, Moadiah, as a head of the priests (Nehemiah 12:12, 17).

introduce: Philetus is a man mentioned in 2 Timothy in the New Testament, one of those whom the apostle Paul named by name while warning against false teaching.
lifetime: Scripture has no record of Philetus's birthplace or the specific course of his life. He is mentioned by name together with Hymenaeus only in 2 Timothy 2:17 (2 Timothy 2:17).
event: Philetus was mentioned together with Hymenaeus, and it is said that they had deviated from the truth, saying that the resurrection had already taken place, and so they were undermining the faith of some (2 Timothy 2:17-18). Paul told Timothy to avoid profane and empty chatter, saying that such men would progress further in ungodliness (2 Timothy 2:16), and that their talk would spread like gangrene (2 Timothy 2:17).

meaning: One who holds love, an affectionate one
introduce: He is the recipient of the New Testament letter to Philemon and an early Christian believer in the region of Colossae. The apostle Paul sent him a personal letter while Paul was imprisoned, and Paul called him a beloved one and a fellow worker.
lifetime: Philemon is a man whom Paul called a beloved fellow worker (Philemon 1:1). Paul said that he owed Paul even his own self (Philemon 1:19). There was a church in his house (Philemon 1:2), and he appears as the central figure of the letter in the matter of sending back to him Onesimus, whom Paul had begotten while in prison (Philemon 1:10-12).
event: Paul sent a letter to the church in his house (Philemon 1:2). He also received Paul's request to welcome Onesimus, who had been a slave, no longer as a slave but as a beloved brother (Philemon 1:15-17).
character: He was commended by Paul as a man who had love and faith toward all the saints (Philemon 1:5). He gave joy and comfort to fellow believers (Philemon 1:7), and Paul called him a fellow worker in the ministry (Philemon 1:1).

introduce: Philologus is a man who appears in Romans 16 in the New Testament, a believer included in the list of those to whom Paul sent greetings among the Christians in Rome.
lifetime: Philologus is a person mentioned together with Julia, and his name was recorded when Paul sent greetings to the members of the church community in Rome (Romans 16:15). Scripture shows no other information about his birth or the specific course of his life (Romans 16:15).
event: In the course of Paul's sending greetings to the saints in Rome, Philologus was recorded as one mentioned, together with Julia, along with all the saints (Romans 16:15). No separate independent ministry or event is described in Scripture (Romans 16:15).

introduce: Bilshan is a man whose name is recorded as one who came out with Zerubbabel, Jeshua, and others among those who returned from the Babylonian exile.
lifetime: His name is recorded in Ezra 2:2 as one who came out of the Babylonian captivity with Zerubbabel, Jeshua, and others (Ezra 2:2). When Nehemiah first obtained the genealogy of those who had returned, his name is again confirmed in the same list in that record (Nehemiah 7:5, 7:7).
event: When the people of Israel returned from Babylon, he was included in the list of those who came out with Zerubbabel, Jeshua, and others (Ezra 2:2). His name is also entered in the same list in Nehemiah 7:7 (Nehemiah 7:7). No other personal event is recorded in Scripture.

call: Rachel's maidservant (mother of Dan and Naphtali)
introduce: Bilhah was the maidservant whom Laban gave to his daughter Rachel, and whom Rachel gave to her husband Jacob as a concubine. She bore Dan and Naphtali, the fifth and sixth sons of Jacob.
lifetime: She was given as Rachel's maidservant when Laban gave his daughter Rachel in marriage to Jacob (Genesis 29:29). When Rachel could not bear children, she sent Bilhah in to Jacob in order to obtain children, and Bilhah bore Dan and Naphtali by Jacob (Genesis 30:3-8). Afterward Reuben, Jacob's son, lay with Bilhah, his father's concubine, and Israel heard of it (Genesis 35:22).
event: She gave birth to Jacob's sons Dan and Naphtali, bearing those who became ancestors of the twelve tribes of Israel (Genesis 30:4-8). Reuben, Jacob's firstborn, lay with Bilhah, his father's concubine, and Israel heard of it (Genesis 35:22). Jacob later said to Reuben that he had gone up to his father's bed and defiled it (Genesis 49:4), and Reuben's birthright went to the descendants of Joseph (1 Chronicles 5:1).

call: Son of Ezer (chief of the Horites)
introduce: Bilhan is a son of Ezer, a descendant of Seir of the Horite clan in the land of Edom. His name is recorded in the genealogy of the Horite clan in Genesis 36 (Genesis 36:27).
lifetime: Bilhan is recorded as a son of Ezer, a descendant of Seir of the Horite clan (Genesis 36:27, 1 Chronicles 1:42). His brothers were Zaavan and Akan (the same name appears in 1 Chronicles 1:42) (Genesis 36:27).
event: Scripture shows no specific accomplishment or individual event performed by Bilhan. As a member of the genealogy of Edom, he is mentioned only in the list that attests his genealogical position (Genesis 36:27).

introduce: Bimhal is a man mentioned in the genealogy of the tribe of Asher in 1 Chronicles 7 of the Old Testament, a son of Japhlet. Because Heber, the son of Beriah son of Asher, fathered Japhlet, he belongs to the descendants of Asher.
lifetime: Heber was born to Beriah, the son of Asher, and Heber fathered Japhlet (1 Chronicles 7:30-32), and the sons of Japhlet are Pasach, Bimhal, and Ashvath (1 Chronicles 7:33).
event: Scripture shows no information about personal accomplishments or specific events performed by Bimhal (1 Chronicles 7:33).

introduce: Bidkar is the man whom Jehu called "his officer," the one to whom Jehu commanded that the body of Joram be thrown into the field of Naboth the Jezreelite (2 Kings 9:25).
lifetime: He is recorded as Jehu's officer, and Jehu said to him that he would remember how, when you and I rode together following his father Ahab, the LORD prophesied concerning Ahab's affair (2 Kings 9:25). His birth and the rest of his life are not recorded in Scripture.
event: After Jehu shot Joram with his bow and killed him, he commanded his officer Bidkar to throw the body into the field of Naboth (2 Kings 9:24-25). Jehu reminded him that when he and Bidkar rode together following Ahab, the LORD had prophesied concerning Ahab, and that prophecy was the word that the LORD had seen the blood of Naboth and the blood of his sons and would repay it on this plot of ground (2 Kings 9:25-26).

introduce: A figure mentioned by Jesus Christ, included in the line of righteous martyrs reaching from Abel to Zechariah in Old Testament times. He is recorded as having been killed between the temple and the altar.
lifetime: He is called the son of Berechiah (Matthew 23:35), and apart from the fact that he was killed between the temple and the altar, no specific dates or deeds of his life are recorded in Scripture (Matthew 23:35, Luke 11:51).
event: He underwent the event of being murdered between the temple and the altar, and was mentioned by Jesus as a pattern of the martyrs who shed righteous blood in history (Matthew 23:35, Luke 11:51).

call: A Hararite (father of one of David's mighty men)
introduce: Sachar is a figure who appears in 1 Chronicles 11 of the Old Testament, recorded as a Hararite and the father of Ahiam, one of David's mighty men.
lifetime: Sachar is known as a Hararite, and from the fact that his son Ahiam served as one of David's thirty mighty men, it can be seen that he was a man who lived in the time of David (1 Chronicles 11:35).
event: The biblical text gives no record of any independent accomplishment or specific event of Sachar himself; he is mentioned only as the father of Ahiam, David's mighty man, in the record of Ahiam's lineage (1 Chronicles 11:35).

introduce: Sachia is a man recorded in the genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin in 1 Chronicles 8, one of the sons born to Shaharaim, and recorded as a chief.
lifetime: Sachia is one of the children born to Shaharaim after he sent away his two wives, Hushim and Baara, in the land of Moab (1 Chronicles 8:8). Jobab, Zibia, Mesha, Malcam, Jeuz, Sachia, and Mirmah were born to Shaharaim's wife Hodesh (1 Chronicles 8:9-10), and these sons were chiefs (1 Chronicles 8:10).

introduce: Zanoah is a name that appears in the phrase "Jekuthiel the father of Zanoah" in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah in 1 Chronicles 4 (1 Chronicles 4:18). The same name appears as the name of a city in Joshua 15:34, 15:56 and in Nehemiah 3:13, 11:30.
lifetime: In 1 Chronicles 4:18, Jekuthiel is recorded as "the father of Zanoah," and Scripture has no record of Zanoah's own birth or parents (1 Chronicles 4:18).
event: Scripture shows no information about personal accomplishments or events of Zanoah (1 Chronicles 4:18).

introduce: A name derived from the Hebrew satan and the Greek satanas, referring within Scripture to a supernatural being who opposes the will of God and accuses and tempts human beings. In Scripture he appears as the one to whom the LORD and Jesus speak, calling him "Satan" (Zechariah 3:2, Matthew 4:10).
lifetime: In the Book of Zechariah he appears standing at the right hand of Joshua the high priest, who stood before the angel of the LORD, in order to oppose him (Zechariah 3:1). In Mark, the life of Jesus is recorded as being tempted by Satan for forty days in the wilderness (Mark 1:13). In Matthew, there is a scene in which Jesus himself calls him by the name Satan and commands him to go away (Matthew 4:10).
event: In a vision that Zechariah saw, he stood at the right hand of Joshua the high priest and opposed him (Zechariah 3:1). Then the LORD rebuked Satan, saying that the LORD who has chosen Jerusalem rebukes you (Zechariah 3:2). In Matthew and Mark, Jesus said that if Satan casts out Satan, he is divided against himself, and his kingdom cannot stand (Matthew 12:26, Mark 3:23, Mark 3:26). Also, in the parable of the sower, he is depicted as the one who comes at once and takes away the word sown along the path (Mark 4:15). When Peter tried to dissuade Jesus from his suffering, Jesus called Peter Satan and rebuked him, saying that he did not have in mind the things of God but the things of men (Matthew 16:23, Mark 8:33).
character: Before the judgment of God, he shows a disposition as an adversary who accuses human beings (Zechariah 3:1). He also has the oppositional characteristic of tempting Jesus (Mark 1:13, Matthew 4:10) and trying to block God's plan (Matthew 16:23, Mark 8:33). He is defined as a being who intervenes in human ways of thinking and hinders the will of God (Matthew 16:23, Mark 8:33).

introduce: Zadok was a high priest of the line of Eleazar, a descendant of Aaron, who was active during the reigns of David and Solomon. He served as a key religious figure who safeguarded the legitimacy of the Davidic dynasty.
lifetime: Zadok is recorded as the son of Ahitub, and he became a priest in the time of David (2 Samuel 8:17, 1 Chronicles 6:8). When David was about to bring up the ark of God, he called the priests Zadok and Abiathar and had them, together with the chiefs of the Levites, consecrate themselves and bring up the ark (1 Chronicles 15:11-14). When David's son Absalom rebelled, Zadok came out carrying the ark of the covenant of God together with all the Levites, but David told them to carry the ark back to the city and to return to the city in peace with his son Ahimaaz and Abiathar's son Jonathan, so he remained in the city (2 Samuel 15:24-29). When Solomon was enthroned, the priest Zadok took the horn of oil from the tabernacle and anointed Solomon (1 Kings 1:39).
event: David told the two priests Zadok and Abiathar to report to them what they heard in the palace, and Zadok's son Ahimaaz and Abiathar's son Jonathan were designated as the ones to carry the message (2 Samuel 15:35-36). When Adonijah tried to make himself king, the priest Zadok did not side with Adonijah (1 Kings 1:8), and at David's command he anointed Solomon at Gihon together with the prophet Nathan and made him king over Israel (1 Kings 1:32-34, 1:45). Solomon put the priest Zadok in the place of Abiathar (1 Kings 2:35).
character: Even in a time of political upheaval, Zadok maintained unwavering loyalty to the house of David (2 Samuel 15:29). He showed an obedient aspect, carrying out David's commands immediately, and through his religious authority he played the role of strengthening the legitimacy of the Davidic dynasty (1 Kings 1:38-39). After Abiathar was expelled for taking part in the rebellion, he occupied the position of sole high priest and strengthened his ties with the royal house (1 Kings 2:35).

introduce: Shadrach was a young Jewish man taken captive when Babylon invaded Judah; his Hebrew name was Hananiah. In the Babylonian royal palace he was educated in Chaldean learning and language and was appointed to a high office.
lifetime: In the third year of Jehoiakim king of Judah, he was carried off captive to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon (Daniel 1:1-3). He refused the king's delicacies and wine, chose vegetables and water, and underwent a test (Daniel 1:8-15); after three years of education, in the presence of the king his wisdom and understanding were recognized as surpassing that of the other wise men (Daniel 1:17-20). Afterward he was appointed as an official to manage the affairs of the province of Babylon (Daniel 2:49).
event: Because he refused to bow down to the golden image that Nebuchadnezzar had set up, he was thrown into the fiery furnace, but God sent an angel and delivered him, so that he came out alive without even a hair of his head singed (Daniel 3:12-28). Because of this, King Nebuchadnezzar praised the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, issued a decree to punish anyone who spoke against that God, and promoted the three men still further in the province of Babylon (Daniel 3:28-30).
character: He showed resolve in defying the king's command in order to keep his own faith and values (Daniel 3:16-18). He also had thorough self-control, to the point of resolving together with his companions to refuse the king's food (Daniel 1:8). He had an upright character that did not yield even in front of the king (Daniel 3:16).

직업/직위: one of the three friends who survived the furnace in Babylon (Hananiah)

introduce: Sarah was the wife of Abraham and the mother of Isaac, the half-sister of Abram, and a woman central to the patriarchal history of the Hebrew people. Her original name was Sarai, but afterward it was changed to Sarah.
lifetime: She became the wife of Abram (Genesis 11:29), and in the course of moving to Canaan she went down to Egypt, concealed that she was Abram's wife, and passed herself off as his sister (Genesis 12:13). After returning to Canaan, because she had no children, she gave her maidservant Hagar to Abram to bear Ishmael (Genesis 16:2-3). At the age of ninety she gave birth to Isaac according to God's promise (Genesis 17:17, 21:2), and at the age of 127 she died at Hebron, that is, Kiriath-arba (Genesis 23:1-2).
event: When her maidservant Hagar became pregnant and despised her, Sarai mistreated Hagar and Hagar fled; but the angel of the LORD told her to go back and submit, and Hagar returned (Genesis 16:4-9). When the LORD appeared to Abraham and said that Sarah would have a son, she heard that word at the tent door and laughed to herself (Genesis 18:10-12), but afterward she bore her son Isaac as promised (Genesis 21:2). When she saw Hagar's son mocking Isaac, she strongly demanded of Abraham that the maidservant and her son be driven out (Genesis 21:9-10). After her death she was buried by Abraham in the cave of Machpelah (Genesis 23:19).
character: She showed the resolve to press her husband strongly in order to carry through her own position (Genesis 21:10), and in the pain of barrenness she also made a realistic judgment, such as proposing a surrogate mother (Genesis 16:2). When she heard the news that she would conceive at an advanced age, she is recorded as having laughed out of human doubt (Genesis 18:12).

introduce: Sharar is a man recorded as a Hararite in the list of David's mighty men in 2 Samuel 23, mentioned as the father of the mighty man Ahiam (2 Samuel 23:33).
lifetime: Sharar is recorded as a Hararite, and his son Ahiam is entered in the list of David's mighty men (2 Samuel 23:33). Scripture has no record of Sharar's own birth or life.
event: Scripture has no record of personal accomplishments or events of Sharar, and he is mentioned only in the phrase that identifies the mighty man Ahiam ("Ahiam son of Sharar the Hararite") (2 Samuel 23:33).

introduce: Sharezer was a son of Sennacherib king of Assyria, who together with his brother Adrammelech struck down his father the king with the sword. According to the biblical record, after killing his father the king he fled to the land of Ararat, and Sennacherib's son Esar-haddon became king in his place.
lifetime: He was a son of Sennacherib king of Assyria (Isaiah 37:38). When Sennacherib was worshiping in the temple of his god Nisroch, he struck him down with the sword together with Adrammelech (2 Kings 19:37) and fled to the land of Ararat (2 Kings 19:37).
event: Together with his brother Adrammelech, he struck down his father the king Sennacherib with the sword and fled to the land of Ararat (2 Kings 19:37, Isaiah 37:38). Sennacherib's son Esar-haddon became king in his place, and Scripture has no record that Sharezer succeeded to the throne (2 Kings 19:37).

introduce: Sargon is a king of Assyria whose name appears in the Book of Isaiah, the one who sent the commander of the army to Ashdod to attack and capture Ashdod (Isaiah 20:1).
lifetime: Sargon is mentioned as king of Assyria in Isaiah 20:1. Nothing about his life, such as his birth, accession, or lineage, is recorded in Scripture (Isaiah 20:1).
event: Sargon king of Assyria sent the commander of the army to Ashdod, and he came and attacked and captured Ashdod (Isaiah 20:1). In that year the LORD spoke to Isaiah son of Amoz (Isaiah 20:1-2).

call: Son of Hotham (one of David's mighty men)
introduce: Shama is a man entered in the list of David's mighty men, the son of Hotham the Aroerite, a figure recorded in 1 Chronicles 11:44.
lifetime: He is included in the list of David's mighty men in 1 Chronicles 11 (1 Chronicles 11:26-47), and is recorded as "the son of Hotham the Aroerite" (1 Chronicles 11:44).
event: In the list of David's mighty men, his name is recorded as the son of Hotham the Aroerite (1 Chronicles 11:44). Other personal deeds of his are not recorded in Scripture.

meaning: Asked of God, God has heard
introduce: Samuel was a man who served as both judge and prophet at the end of the period of the judges. He was the son of Elkanah, who lived in the hill country of Ephraim, and in the genealogy of 1 Chronicles 6 he is recorded as a descendant of Kohath, the son of Levi; in the transitional period connecting the era of the judges and the era of the monarchy, he served as a political and religious leader of Israel.
lifetime: He was born as the son of Elkanah and Hannah and was raised under the priest Eli in the sanctuary at Shiloh (1 Samuel 1:20, 2:11). He experienced the call of the LORD in his childhood (1 Samuel 3:10), and all Israel came to know that he had been established as a prophet of the LORD (1 Samuel 3:20). After he grew up, he governed Israel by going on a circuit every year to Bethel, Gilgal, and Mizpah (1 Samuel 7:16); in his old age he made his sons judges, but when they took bribes and perverted justice, the people came to demand a king (1 Samuel 8:1-5). Afterward he anointed Saul and set him up (1 Samuel 10:1), and he anointed David (1 Samuel 16:13). He died at Ramah and was buried there at his house (1 Samuel 25:1).
event: When Israel gathered at Mizpah, fasted, and repented, Samuel prayed for them; and as Samuel offered a burnt offering and cried out, the LORD thundered with a mighty voice against the Philistines and threw them into confusion, and the men of Israel struck down the Philistines (1 Samuel 7:5-11). When Israel demanded a king, he anointed Saul and set him up as leader over his inheritance (1 Samuel 8:4-5, 10:1). After the battle with Amalek, he declared that because Saul had rejected the word of the LORD, the LORD had also rejected him from being king (1 Samuel 15:23). He also went to Bethlehem and anointed David (1 Samuel 16:4, 16:13).
character: From his childhood he dwelt in the temple of the LORD and kept a pure life (1 Samuel 3:1). When he went on circuit in Israel as judge, he judged honestly and fairly and took no bribes (1 Samuel 12:3-4). He is portrayed as a man who did not cease to pray for the people without ceasing (1 Samuel 12:23). When the word of God came to him, he showed firmness in delivering its content to King Saul as it was, without compromise (1 Samuel 15:16-19).

직업/직위: last judge and great prophet of Israel

기타관계: David#468(second king of united Israel, principal author of Psalms, shepherd)
Tohu#537(fellow worker of the tribe of Levi)
Abiasaph#2058(fellow worker of the tribe of Levi)

introduce: Samlah was one of the kings who ruled the land of Edom, a man from Masrekah (1 Chronicles 1:47). He is recorded as having exercised rule after Hadad in the line of rulers of the ancient Edomite region (1 Chronicles 1:48).
lifetime: After Hadad died, Samlah took the throne as king of Edom and ruled that land (1 Chronicles 1:48). His place of origin was Masrekah, and after his death Saul succeeded to the throne (1 Chronicles 1:48).
event: Apart from the fact that he exercised kingship as ruler of the Edomite region after Hadad, no specific accomplishment or individual historical event is recorded in Scripture (1 Chronicles 1:48).

introduce: Shalmai is one of the families of the Nethinim who returned to Jerusalem after finishing the Babylonian exile (Ezra 2:46). The Nethinim denotes a class of servants who took charge of the miscellaneous duties of the temple.
lifetime: He is included in the list of the community of Israel that returned from the Babylonian captivity, and his name is recorded in the list of the Nethinim who returned to Jerusalem and to the cities of Judah (Ezra 2:46).
event: He belongs to the list of returnees who came back from Babylon to Jerusalem and Judah following Zerubbabel and Jeshua (Ezra 2:1, 2:46).

introduce: Shamir was a descendant of Kohath of the tribe of Levi, a man mentioned in the process of determining by lot the duties of the Levites in the time of David. He is recorded as one of the sons of Micah, the son of Uzziel (1 Chronicles 24:24).
lifetime: Shamir is recorded as one of the sons of Micah, the son of Uzziel (1 Chronicles 23:12), the son of Kohath (1 Chronicles 24:24).
event: When the descendants of Levi were chosen by lot, like their brothers the descendants of Aaron, before King David, Zadok, Ahimelech, and the priests and the chiefs of the Levites (1 Chronicles 24:31), Shamir was entered in that list as one of the sons of Micah, the son of Uzziel (1 Chronicles 24:24).

call: Son of Azaliah (scribe of King Josiah)
introduce: Shaphan was a scribe who was active in the time of Josiah, king of Judah, the son of Azaliah and the grandson of Meshullam. He was an official who worked between the king and the high priest Hilkiah in the repair of the temple and the discovery of the book of the law.
lifetime: In the eighteenth year of King Josiah, at the king's command, he was sent to the high priest Hilkiah in connection with the repair of the temple (2 Kings 22:3). He received from Hilkiah the book of the law that had been found in the temple, read it, and also read it aloud before the king (2 Kings 22:8, 22:10). When King Josiah heard the contents of the law and commanded them to inquire of the LORD, he went with Hilkiah, Ahikam, Achbor, and Asaiah to the prophetess Huldah (2 Kings 22:12-14).
event: He was involved in counting the silver that the people had brought for the repair of the temple and putting it into the hands of the overseers (2 Kings 22:4-9). He received the book of the law that the high priest Hilkiah had found in the temple, read it, told the king about it, and read it before the king (2 Kings 22:8-10). His son Ahikam protected Jeremiah and did not give him into the hands of the people (Jeremiah 26:24), Baruch read the words of Jeremiah in the chamber of his son Gemariah, and his grandson Micaiah heard those words and reported them to the officials (Jeremiah 36:10-13). These are the deeds not of Shaphan himself but of his son and grandson.
character: As a high official who enjoyed the deep trust of King Josiah, he showed public competence in carrying out the king's commands immediately (2 Kings 22:3). In the course of conveying the word of God to the king and informing the king of the prophet's warning, he maintained a professional attitude as a scribe who gathered and recorded information (2 Kings 22:10, Jeremiah 36:11). His sons Ahikam, Elasah, Gemariah, and Jaazaniah later held important political and religious positions in the kingdom of Judah and kept their influence (2 Kings 22:12, Jeremiah 36:10-12, Ezekiel 8:11).

기타관계: Josiah#2723(kinsman of the tribe of Judah)

introduce: Shapham is a man who appears in 1 Chronicles 5 of the Old Testament, a member of the clan belonging to the descendants of Gad, the son of Jacob. In the genealogical system of the tribe of Gad he is classified as the one mentioned after Joel (1 Chronicles 5:12).
lifetime: Shapham is the one mentioned after Joel, the chief, among the descendants of Gad, and after him follow Janai and Shaphat, who lived in Bashan (1 Chronicles 5:12). The descendants of Gad lived in the land of Bashan as far as Salecah (1 Chronicles 5:11).
event: Scripture does not describe any specific accomplishment or particular event of Shapham himself; only his name and identity are stated in the course of the genealogical record of the tribe of Gad (1 Chronicles 5:12).

introduce: Shaphat is a man who appears in Numbers in the Old Testament, one of the twelve spies sent to spy out the land of Canaan. He was a man in a leading position chosen to represent the tribe of Simeon (Numbers 13:5).
lifetime: Shaphat was born as a son of Hori of the tribe of Simeon (Numbers 13:5). At the command of Moses he served as one of the twelve tribal representatives chosen to spy out the land of Canaan (Numbers 13:2, 13:5).
event: He had his name entered in the list of the representatives of each tribe whom Moses sent to spy out the land of Canaan, and as one of them he carried out the mission of spying out the land of Canaan (Numbers 13:5, 13:16). Afterward the spies, including Shaphat, having finished spying, returned and reported the result of their search to Moses and Aaron and the whole congregation of the people of Israel (Numbers 13:26).

introduce: Zabud is a man recorded as the son of Nathan, a principal officer among the officials of King Solomon, and the king's friend (1 Kings 4:5).
lifetime: Zabud is recorded as the son of Nathan (1 Kings 4:5). In the list enumerating the officials of King Solomon, he appears as a principal officer, the king's friend (1 Kings 4:2-6).
event: Zabud is recorded in the list of King Solomon's officials as "a principal officer, the king's friend" (1 Kings 4:5). In the same verse, Azariah son of Nathan is recorded together with him as chief of the governors (1 Kings 4:5).
character: Zabud is recorded in the list of Solomon's officials as the king's friend (1 Kings 4:5). The text does not specifically describe his personal character.

introduce: Shabbethai is recorded as one of those who, when Ezra read the book of the law, together with Jeshua, Bani, and others, made the people who stood in their places understand the law (Nehemiah 8:7).
lifetime: He was a member of the returned community that came back to Jerusalem after finishing the Babylonian exile, and after the rebuilding of the wall of Jerusalem he took part in the gathering for the reading of the law held in the square before the Water Gate (Nehemiah 8:1, 8:7).
event: When Ezra the scribe read the book of the law of God to the people of Israel in the square before the Water Gate, together with Jeshua, Bani, Sherebiah, Jamin, Akkub, Hodiah, Maaseiah, Kelita, Azariah, Jozabad, Hanan, and Pelaiah, he did the work of making the people who stood in their places understand the law (Nehemiah 8:3, 8:7).

introduce: Zaza, who appears in 1 Chronicles 2:33, is a man belonging to the family genealogy of the tribe of Judah, a son of Jonathan of the descendants of Jerahmeel (1 Chronicles 2:33).
lifetime: Zaza is recorded as the son of Jonathan and appears together with Peleth (1 Chronicles 2:33). Jonathan is the son of Jada (1 Chronicles 2:32), Jada is the son of Onam (1 Chronicles 2:28), and Onam is the son of Jerahmeel (1 Chronicles 2:26); thus Zaza is listed among the descendants of Jerahmeel (1 Chronicles 2:33). In the same genealogy it is said that Jether, another son of Jada, died without sons (1 Chronicles 2:32), but this is not a matter concerning Zaza.
event: The biblical text does not describe any specific accomplishment or particular event of Zaza, but only states that he was a member of the house of Jerahmeel in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah (1 Chronicles 2:33).

introduce: Shashak is a man who appears in the genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin recorded in 1 Chronicles 8 of the Old Testament, recorded as one of the sons of Beriah (1 Chronicles 8:14, 8:16).
lifetime: Shashak is listed among the sons of Beriah together with Ahio, Jeremoth, and others (1 Chronicles 8:14-16). It is also recorded that Ishpan, Eber, Eliel, Abdon, Zichri, Hanan, Hananiah, Elam, Anthothijah, Iphdeiah, and Penuel were all sons of Shashak (1 Chronicles 8:22-25).
event: No specific accomplishment of Shashak himself, nor any historical event that he led, is described in Scripture (1 Chronicles 8:25).
character: The biblical text provides no information whatsoever about Shashak's character or personal traits (-)

introduce: Shashai is a man recorded as one of the descendants of Bani in the list of those who took foreign women as wives in the time of Ezra (Ezra 10:34, 10:40, 10:44).
lifetime: He belonged to the company of the people of Israel who returned after finishing the Babylonian exile, and when Ezra pointed out the problem of marriage with foreign women (Ezra 10:10-11), his name was recorded in the list of those who had taken foreign women (Ezra 10:40, 10:44).
event: In the course of the movement to restore religious purity led by Ezra, he was singled out as one who had a foreign wife and was included in that list (Ezra 10:40).

call: Eunuch in charge of the concubines of King Xerxes
introduce: He was a eunuch of King Xerxes of the Persian Empire, an official in charge of the concubines (Esther 2:14).
lifetime:
The Bible gives no specific record of his birth, personal life, family, or death (Esther 2:14).
He served as a eunuch in the royal palace during the reign of King Xerxes and held the duty of being in charge of the concubines (Esther 2:14).
event:
When the young woman who had gone in to the king in the evening returned in the morning to the second harem, she came under the care of Shaashgaz, the eunuch in charge of the concubines (Esther 2:14).
She could not go in to the king again unless the king delighted in her and called her by name (Esther 2:14).

introduce: Zaavan was one of the sons of Ezer, of the Horite clan that lived in the land of Edom, and he appears in Genesis and 1 Chronicles, which record the genealogy of Edom.
lifetime: Zaavan was born as a son of Ezer, a descendant of Seir of the Horite clan. His brothers were Bilhan and Akan (Genesis 36:27). He is also mentioned, in the genealogical records of Chronicles, as one of the sons of Ezer, a descendant of Seir (1 Chronicles 1:42).

introduce: Shaaph is a person whose name is recorded in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah in the Old Testament (1 Chronicles 2:47).
lifetime: He is recorded in the genealogy as a brother together with Regem, Jotham, Geshan, Pelet, and Ephah, the sons of Jahdai of the tribe of Judah (1 Chronicles 2:47).

call: Sixth king of Edom (Shaul of Rehoboth)
introduce: Shaul was the sixth of the kings who ruled the land of Edom, and he is recorded as being from Rehoboth by the Euphrates River. He is a different person from Saul, the first king of Israel, and is mentioned as a ruler in the genealogy of the ancient Edomite monarchy.
lifetime: He was from Rehoboth and became king of Edom after Samlah (Genesis 36:37). After his reign, Baal-hanan succeeded him on the throne (Genesis 36:38).
event: No specific conquests or building projects are described in the Bible in connection with his reign; only the fact that he is included in the list of the kings of Edom and succeeded to the throne appears (Genesis 36:37).

introduce: Shaharaim is a person recorded in the genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin; after sending away his two wives Hushim and Baara, he had children in the land of Moab (1 Chronicles 8:8).
lifetime: After sending away his two wives Hushim and Baara, he had children in the land of Moab (1 Chronicles 8:8). By his wife Hodesh he fathered Jobab, Zibia, Mesha, Malcam, Jeuz, Sachia, and Mirmah, and these sons were heads of families (1 Chronicles 8:9-10). By his wife Hushim he also fathered Abitub and Elpaal (1 Chronicles 8:11).
event: It is recorded that he had children in the land of Moab after sending away his two wives Hushim and Baara (1 Chronicles 8:8). The sons born to Hodesh were heads of families (1 Chronicles 8:9-10).

introduce: Zaham was a son of Rehoboam king of Judah, one of the three sons whom Rehoboam had by Mahalath (2 Chronicles 11:19).
lifetime: He was born to Rehoboam king of Judah and Mahalath, the daughter of Jerimoth, a son of David (2 Chronicles 11:18). Mahalath bore Jeush, Shemariah, and Zaham (2 Chronicles 11:19).

introduce: Zaccai is a person who appears as a family name ("descendants of Zaccai") in the list of those who returned from the Babylonian exile. In the lists of Ezra 2 and Nehemiah 7, the descendants of Zaccai are recorded as seven hundred sixty.
lifetime: The descendants of Zaccai belong to those who were carried away captive to Babylon by Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, were released, and returned to Jerusalem and Judah; they are recorded in the list of the people who came out with Zerubbabel and others (Ezra 2:1, 2:2, 2:9). In the genealogical register of those who first returned, which Nehemiah found, the descendants of Zaccai are likewise recorded as seven hundred sixty (Nehemiah 7:5, 7:14).

introduce: Zacchaeus is a figure who appears in the Gospel of Luke in the New Testament; he was a chief tax collector and a rich man in the region of Jericho. In Jewish society, which was under the colonial rule of the Roman Empire, he was in charge of collecting taxes.
lifetime: He was a chief tax collector of Jericho and was rich (Luke 19:2). When Jesus was passing through Jericho (Luke 19:1), he wanted to see who Jesus was, but because he was short and there was a crowd, he ran on ahead and climbed up a sycamore tree (Luke 19:3-4). When Jesus called him by name and said that He must stay at his house, he came down quickly and welcomed Him joyfully (Luke 19:5-6).
event: He declared that he would give half of his possessions to the poor, and announced that if he had defrauded anyone of anything, he would pay back four times as much (Luke 19:8). Concerning this, Jesus remarked that salvation had come to this house (Luke 19:9).
character: He had the physical characteristic of being short, so that he could not see Jesus among the crowd (Luke 19:3). To the Jews of the time, tax collecting was an occupation whose members were treated as sinners (Luke 19:7), yet he showed the zeal to set aside his dignity and climb up a tree in order to meet Jesus (Luke 19:4).

직업/직위: wealthy man, later a disciple of Jesus

call: Father of Shammua (father of a spy)
introduce: Zaccur was a man of the tribe of Reuben and the father of Shammua, one of the twelve spies sent to spy out the land of Canaan.
lifetime: Zaccur is mentioned as the father of Shammua, a descendant of Reuben (Numbers 13:4).
event: His son Shammua was chosen at the command of Moses as one of the twelve spies to spy out the land of Canaan, and he carried out that task (Numbers 13:4). No other specific accomplishments or events of Zaccur himself are recorded.

introduce: Sanballat was a Horonite who mocked Nehemiah and sought to harm him when Nehemiah was building the wall of Jerusalem, and he is recorded as Nehemiah's adversary (Nehemiah 2:10, 4:1, 6:1-2).
lifetime: He was a Horonite (Nehemiah 2:10), and when he heard that a man had come to seek the welfare of the people of Israel, he was greatly distressed (Nehemiah 2:10). Together with Tobiah the Ammonite and Geshem the Arab, he despised and mocked Nehemiah and his companions and asked whether they were rebelling against the king (Nehemiah 2:19). Afterward, he and Geshem sent word to Nehemiah to meet together in one of the villages on the plain of Ono, but Nehemiah knew that they intended to harm him and did not go (Nehemiah 6:2-3). One of the sons of Jehoiada, the grandson of Eliashib the high priest, had become a son-in-law of Sanballat the Horonite, so Nehemiah drove him away (Nehemiah 13:28).
event: When Sanballat heard that we were building the wall, he became very angry and mocked the Jews (Nehemiah 4:1). Together with Tobiah, the Arabs, the Ammonites, and the Ashdodites, he was greatly angered when he heard that the repairs of the walls of Jerusalem were going forward (Nehemiah 4:7), and they all plotted together to come and fight against Jerusalem and cause confusion in it (Nehemiah 4:8). When Nehemiah had rebuilt the wall so that no breach was left in it, but had not yet set the doors in the gates, Sanballat, together with Tobiah, Geshem, and others, sent to Nehemiah asking to meet; they sent four times in this way, but Nehemiah gave the same answer each time (Nehemiah 6:1-4). The fifth time he sent an open letter in the hand of his servant, and its writing said that there was a rumor that Nehemiah and the Jews were plotting rebellion, that he was building the wall, and that he wished to become king (Nehemiah 6:5-7).
character: He showed an opportunistic side, using religious and kinship ties for the sake of political interests (Nehemiah 13:28). He was cunning and meticulous in character, not hesitating to use scheming and false rumors to achieve his purpose (Nehemiah 6:5-7). Furthermore, toward the forces opposed to him he displayed strong hostility and maintained an aggressive attitude, even plotting direct use of force (Nehemiah 4:7-8).

introduce: Sennacherib was the king of Assyria who invaded Judah in the time of King Hezekiah (2 Kings 18:13). He sought to attack Jerusalem and, through his servants and by letters, reviled the LORD God (2 Chronicles 32:9-17).
lifetime: In the fourteenth year of King Hezekiah he came up and attacked and captured all the fortified cities of Judah (2 Kings 18:13), and he sent the Tartan, the Rabsaris, and the Rabshakeh with a great army from Lachish to Jerusalem to attack King Hezekiah (2 Kings 18:17). When the angel of the LORD struck down 185,000 men in the camp of the Assyrians, Sennacherib departed, returned, and dwelt at Nineveh (2 Kings 19:35-36); and while he was worshiping in the shrine of his god Nisroch, his sons Adrammelech and Sharezer struck him down with the sword, and another son, Esar-haddon, became king in his place (2 Kings 19:37; Isaiah 37:38).
event: In the fourteenth year of Hezekiah, Sennacherib attacked and captured all the fortified cities of Judah (2 Kings 18:13). While he was attacking Lachish with all his army, he sent his servants to Jerusalem to speak to Hezekiah king of Judah and to the people of Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 32:9), and the Rabshakeh, speaking as the word of the king of Assyria, demanded of Hezekiah in what he trusted (2 Kings 18:19-25). He also wrote letters to insult and revile the LORD, the God of Israel (2 Chronicles 32:17; 2 Kings 19:16).
character: Through wars of conquest he displayed his own might, and employed the strategy of psychologically intimidating the opposing nation (2 Kings 18:28-35). He absolutely trusted his own gods and power and showed an arrogant attitude that belittled the gods of other peoples (2 Kings 19:10-12); and it appears that struggles over the kingship and internal politics were so unstable that he was murdered by his own sons (2 Kings 19:37).

introduce: Zalaph is a person recorded as the father of Hanun, who repaired one section of the wall at the rebuilding of the wall of Jerusalem (Nehemiah 3:30).
lifetime: Zalaph is recorded as having Hanun as his sixth son (Nehemiah 3:30). His son Hanun, together with Hananiah son of Shelemiah, repaired a section of the wall (Nehemiah 3:30).
event: The Bible does not record Zalaph's own deeds; it reports that his sixth son Hanun, together with Hananiah son of Shelemiah, repaired a section of the wall of Jerusalem (Nehemiah 3:30).

call: Descendant of Benjamin who lived in Jerusalem
introduce: Sallai was one of the descendants of Benjamin who lived in Jerusalem after the return from exile, a person recorded in the census and residence list of the time of Nehemiah (Nehemiah 11:8).
lifetime: He was a member of a clan of the tribe of Benjamin who returned from the Babylonian exile and settled in Jerusalem after the rebuilding of the wall of Jerusalem (Nehemiah 11:4, 11:8).
event: His name was entered in the list as one of the descendants of Benjamin who volunteered or were chosen to dwell in Jerusalem (Nehemiah 11:8).

call: Woman disciple of the early church (wife of Zebedee)
introduce: Salome was one of the women who visited the site of Jesus' crucifixion and the tomb, a person who can be identified through the records of the Gospels. She is mentioned as one of the women who followed and served Him during the period of Jesus' public ministry.
lifetime: Salome was one of the women who followed and served Jesus from the time He ministered in Galilee (Mark 15:41). She was watching from a distance at the time of Jesus' crucifixion (Mark 15:40), and is recorded as one of those who bought spices and went to the tomb when Jesus rose on the first day after the Sabbath (Mark 16:1).
event: She was one of the several women who were present at the scene of Jesus' suffering on the cross (Mark 15:40). Also, after the Sabbath was over, together with Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of James, she prepared spices to anoint the body of Jesus and headed for the tomb (Mark 16:1).

call: Father of Zimri (father of the Simeonite chief)
introduce: Salu is a person who appears in Numbers in the Old Testament, the father of Zimri, the leader of a Simeonite family (Numbers 25:14).
lifetime: He came from a family of the tribe of Simeon, and his son Zimri was the Israelite man who, at the incident of Baal-peor, brought the Midianite woman Cozbi before the congregation and was killed together with her by Phinehas (Numbers 25:6-8, 25:14-15).
event: There is no record of any personal accomplishments of his, and in the Bible he is mentioned only as family information to explain the sin of his son Zimri in the incident of Baal-peor (Numbers 25:14).

introduce: Shallun was one of those who took part in rebuilding the wall of Jerusalem after the return from the Babylonian exile, an official who ruled the district of Mizpah (Nehemiah 3:15).
lifetime: After returning from the Babylonian exile, he took part in the historic process of rebuilding the wall of Jerusalem, and as the ruler of the district of Mizpah at that time, he took responsibility for repairing a particular section of the wall (Nehemiah 3:15).
event: At the time of the project of rebuilding the wall of Jerusalem, he repaired the Fountain Gate, rebuilt it, roofed it, and installed its doors, bolts, and bars (Nehemiah 3:15). He also repaired the wall of the Pool of Shelah near the king's garden as far as the stairs that descend from the City of David (Nehemiah 3:15).

call: Son of Jabesh (king of northern Israel)
introduce: Shallum was the fifteenth king of the northern kingdom of Israel and a son of Jabesh, who killed King Zechariah and usurped the throne. His reign was very short; he ruled for one month in Samaria (2 Kings 15:13).
lifetime: Shallum was a son of Jabesh (2 Kings 15:10, 15:13). He conspired against King Zechariah, struck him down before the people, and became king in his place (2 Kings 15:10). He ruled the northern kingdom of Israel for one month in Samaria (2 Kings 15:13); afterward Menahem son of Gadi went up from Tirzah to Samaria, killed Shallum there, and succeeded to the throne (2 Kings 15:14).
event: Shallum conspired against King Zechariah, struck him down before the people, and became king (2 Kings 15:10). The text records that the word the LORD had spoken to Jehu, "Four generations of your sons will sit on the throne of Israel," was fulfilled exactly (2 Kings 15:12). In the thirty-ninth year of Uzziah king of Judah he became king in Samaria, and after ruling for one month he was put to death by Menahem (2 Kings 15:13-14). It is said that the rest of his deeds and the conspiracy he led were written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel (2 Kings 15:15).

introduce: He was the king of Assyria who invaded Israel in the time of Hoshea, the last king of the northern kingdom, besieged Samaria, and finally brought about the destruction of the northern kingdom (2 Kings 17:3).
lifetime:
After ascending the throne as king of Assyria, he came up against the northern kingdom of Israel, subdued King Hoshea, made him a vassal, and made him pay tribute (2 Kings 17:3).
When King Hoshea conspired with So king of Egypt and stopped paying the tribute he had paid year by year, he perceived Hoshea's betrayal, seized him, and imprisoned him (2 Kings 17:4).
Afterward he attacked all the land of Israel, went up to Samaria, and besieged the city for three years (2 Kings 17:5).
In the ninth year of Hoshea he finally captured Samaria and carried the people of Israel away captive to Assyria (2 Kings 17:6).
event:
In the seventh year of King Hoshea of the northern kingdom, that is, the fourth year of King Hezekiah of the southern kingdom of Judah, he carried out a military expedition, going up to Samaria and besieging the city (2 Kings 18:9).
In the ninth year of Hoshea, three years after laying siege to the city, he completely occupied Samaria (2 Kings 18:10).
After the occupation he carried out a policy of forcibly relocating the people of Israel to Halah, to Gozan by the Habor River, and to the cities of the Medes (2 Kings 18:11).
He is regarded as the same person as the Shalman mentioned in the record of the prophet Hosea as having devastated Beth-arbel in the day of battle, when he destroyed the city and mothers were dashed to pieces along with their children (Hosea 10:14).

introduce: Shalmai is a name recorded as "descendants of Shalmai" in the list of the Nethinim among the people who came back from the Babylonian exile (Nehemiah 7:48).
lifetime: He belongs to the list of the people of Israel who, after being carried away captive by Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, were released and returned to Jerusalem and Judah (Nehemiah 7:6), and who came with Zerubbabel, Jeshua, and others (Nehemiah 7:7). He is recorded as "descendants of Shalmai" in the list of the Nethinim (Nehemiah 7:48), and the Bible contains no record of the life of Shalmai himself.
event: His name appears as "descendants of Shalmai" in the list of the Nethinim in Nehemiah 7:48. In the list of the Nethinim in Ezra 2:46 the descendants of Shalmai are recorded, but the text does not state whether the two names belong to the same family (Ezra 2:46).

introduce: Salmon is a person of the tribe of Judah, a son of Nahshon, who fathered Boaz by Rahab (Ruth 4:20-21, Matthew 1:4-5). In 1 Chronicles 2:11 he is written as Salma.
lifetime: Salmon is recorded as a son of Nahshon (Ruth 4:20), and he fathered Boaz by Rahab (Matthew 1:5). He belongs to the genealogy that reaches David through Boaz, Obed, and Jesse, and is David's great-great-grandfather (Ruth 4:21-22).
event: He fathered Boaz by Rahab (Matthew 1:5). Thus Salmon belongs to the genealogy that continues to David through Boaz, Obed, and Jesse (Ruth 4:21-22).

introduce: Salma was a descendant of Judah in the line of Caleb and Hur, a person recorded as the founder or representative ancestor of a clan formed around Bethlehem.
lifetime: The descendants of Salma are recorded as Bethlehem, the Netophathites, Atroth-beth-joab, half of the Manahathites, and the Zorites (1 Chronicles 2:54).

introduce: Zalmunna was one of the kings of Midian, a person who engaged in battle with the army of Gideon. In the biblical record he is portrayed, together with Zebah, as a military leader of Midian.
lifetime: As a king of Midian who oppressed Israel, he stood in opposition to Gideon, a judge of Israel (Judges 8:5). Though he fled when pursued by Gideon (Judges 8:12), he was captured and was afterward put to death by Gideon (Judges 8:21).
event: He invaded Israel and oppressed them by seizing their produce (Judges 6:3-5). He was at Karkor (Judges 8:10) and fled, but was captured when Gideon pursued him (Judges 8:12). Gideon said that the men whom Zebah and Zalmunna had killed at Tabor were his brothers (Judges 8:18-19), and told his firstborn, Jether, to kill them, but the boy was afraid and did not draw his sword (Judges 8:20). Then Zebah and Zalmunna told Gideon to rise and strike them himself, and Gideon rose and killed them (Judges 8:21).
character: He was a man who tried to keep his dignity, to the point of boldly demanding that Gideon kill them himself, in order to save his own life (Judges 8:21). Even during the war he showed a keen eye for observing his opponent, to the extent of remembering and describing the appearance of Gideon's brothers (Judges 8:18).

introduce: Nebo-sarsekim was one of the officials of the king of Babylon who sat in the Middle Gate when Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon captured Jerusalem, a person recorded with the title of chief of the eunuchs (Jeremiah 39:3).
lifetime: When the city of Jerusalem was captured on the ninth day of the fourth month of the eleventh year of Zedekiah king of Judah (Jeremiah 39:2), the officials of the king of Babylon came and sat in the Middle Gate, and among them was Nebo-sarsekim, the chief of the eunuchs (Jeremiah 39:3).
event: As an official of the king of Babylon, he is recorded as chief of the eunuchs in the list of the officials who sat in the Middle Gate after Jerusalem was captured (Jeremiah 39:3). No other deeds of his are recorded in the Bible.

introduce: Shamgar is the third judge of Israel mentioned in the book of Judges in the Old Testament, the one who saved Israel after Ehud. He is recorded as a son of Anath, and the specific chronology of the period of his activity as a judge is not stated.
lifetime: Shamgar is recorded as a son of Anath (Judges 3:31, 5:6) and was judge after Ehud (Judges 3:31). No further details about the place of his birth or about his lineage are recorded in the Bible.
event: Shamgar struck down six hundred Philistines with an ox goad and saved Israel (Judges 3:31). This is recorded as an event that shows the distinctiveness of the instrument.
character: The Bible gives no separate description of what kind of character he ordinarily had. However, from the fact that he made an ox goad his weapon, it can be inferred that he was a member of an agricultural society or was in a situation in which he could make use of humble tools (Judges 3:31).

introduce: Samgar was one of the officials of the king of Babylon who sat in the Middle Gate when Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon captured Jerusalem (Jeremiah 39:1-3).
lifetime: When Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon besieged and attacked Jerusalem and the city was captured, all the officials of the king of Babylon came and sat in the Middle Gate, and Samgar is recorded among their names (Jeremiah 39:1-3).
event: After Jerusalem was captured on the ninth day of the fourth month of the eleventh year of Zedekiah king of Judah (Jeremiah 39:2), Samgar sat in the Middle Gate as one of the officials of the king of Babylon (Jeremiah 39:3).

introduce: Samlah is a person who appears in the genealogy of the kings who ruled the land of Edom, in which Samlah of Masrekah and Shaul of Rehoboth are recorded separately. The Bible mentions him as a ruler in the list of the kings of Edom in Genesis 36.
lifetime: Samlah was from Masrekah and was the king who ruled Edom after Hadad (Genesis 36:36). After his death Shaul of Rehoboth succeeded to the throne (Genesis 36:37).
event: It is not recorded what specific acts of government Samlah performed as king of Edom or what historical events he brought about (Genesis 36:36). He is, however, confirmed as a person who is included in the genealogy of the kings of Edom, who succeeded to the throne and passed it on (Genesis 36:36, Genesis 36:37).

introduce: Shammah was a son of Reuel, the son of Esau, and one of the chiefs of the descendants of Reuel in the land of Edom (Genesis 36:13, 36:17).
lifetime: He is recorded as one of the four sons (Nahath, Zerah, Shammah, and Mizzah) of Reuel (Genesis 36:10), the son borne by Esau's wife Basemath, and he is a descendant of Esau's wife Basemath (Genesis 36:13, 1 Chronicles 1:37).
event: He is recorded as Chief Shammah among the chiefs who came from Reuel in the land of Edom (Genesis 36:17). No other deeds are recorded in the Bible.

introduce: Shammai is a person mentioned in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah; he was the son of Onam, the son of Jerahmeel, the firstborn of Hezron, and the elder brother of Jada (1 Chronicles 2:25-28, 2:32).
lifetime: Shammai was a son of Onam, who is recorded as the son born to Atarah, the wife of Jerahmeel (1 Chronicles 2:26, 2:28). Shammai had a younger brother, Jada (1 Chronicles 2:28, 2:32).
event: Shammai had two sons, Nadab and Abishur (1 Chronicles 2:28). The sons of Nadab are recorded as Seled and Appaim, and Seled died without children (1 Chronicles 2:30).

introduce: Shammua is a person who appears in Numbers in the Old Testament, one of the twelve spies chosen to spy out the land of Canaan as representative of the tribe of Reuben.
lifetime: Shammua was born as a son of Zaccur of the tribe of Reuben (Numbers 13:4). After the Exodus, during the journey in the wilderness, he was included in the list of spies, one chosen from each tribe, whom God commanded Moses to select (Numbers 13:2-3).
event: At the command of Moses he carried out the mission of spying out the land of Canaan for 40 days (Numbers 13:25). After finishing the spying, he returned with the other spies and reported on the condition of the land of Canaan; they acknowledged that the land of Canaan was a land flowing with milk and honey, but presented the negative opinion that its inhabitants were strong and its cities were fortified (Numbers 13:27-28).

introduce: He was a man of the tribe of Dan who appears in the latter part of the book of Judges, set apart as a Nazirite, and a judge who began to deliver Israel from the Philistines.
lifetime: He was born as a son of Manoah of the tribe of Dan in the land of Zorah and was dedicated as a Nazirite from the womb (Judges 13:2-5). He took a Philistine woman as his wife in Timnah, but because of the riddle he became very angry and went up to his father's house, and his wife was given to his companion (Judges 14:1-20). Afterward he stood against the Philistines at Ashkelon (Judges 14:19), Gaza (Judges 16:1-3), and other places. While he loved Delilah of the Valley of Sorek, his hair was cut and he lost his strength, was seized by the Philistines, and with his eyes gouged out was made to turn the mill (Judges 16:4-21). At the end of his life he bowed with all his might in the temple of Dagon, and the house fell, and he died together with the Philistines who were in it; those whom he killed at his death were more than those whom he had killed in his life (Judges 16:28-31).
event: While going down to Timnah, he tore a lion apart with his bare hands, and he ate honey he took from the carcass of the dead lion (Judges 14:5-9). Because of the riddle he posed to the Philistines, he killed thirty men of Ashkelon and took their clothing (Judges 14:12-19). He tied torches to the tails of 300 foxes and burned the Philistines' grain fields, inflicting great damage on their crops (Judges 15:4-5). With one jawbone of a donkey he killed 1,000 Philistine soldiers (Judges 15:15-16). He pulled out the doors of the gate of Gaza, with the gateposts and the bar, and carried them to the top of the hill facing Hebron (Judges 16:3).
character: When the Spirit of the LORD came upon him he displayed supernatural physical ability, but in temperament he showed an impulsive and emotional disposition (Judges 14:6, 14:19). He showed a flexible or indifferent attitude toward religious norms, as when he violated the rule that a Nazirite must stay away from wine and took honey from the body of a dead lion (Judges 14:8-9). In his relations with women he lost self-control and divulged his secret, showing himself vulnerable to emotional bonds rather than to strategic judgment (Judges 16:17). As a judge who throughout his life confronted the Philistines alone and took the lead in physical clashes, he repeatedly waged struggles of the nature of personal revenge rather than communal military action (Judges 15:11-13).

introduce: Shamsherai is one of the persons recorded in the genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin, appearing as one of the sons of Jeroham (1 Chronicles 8:26-27).
