Nehemiah served as governor in the land of Judah from the twentieth year to the thirty-second year of this king (Nehemiah 5:14), and in the thirty-second year he went to the king, and after some days asked leave of him (Nehemiah 13:6).
character: He showed a relatively tolerant attitude toward Jewish religious customs and administrative autonomy. Seeing Nehemiah's sorrowful countenance, he listened to his request, and he valued communication with his subjects to the point of conversing with him even while the queen was sitting beside him (Nehemiah 2:6). While aiming at centralized rule, he pursued a pragmatic diplomatic policy, trusting the leaders of subject peoples and providing them with administrative assistance.

introduce: Athaliah is recorded as a daughter of Ahab, king of northern Israel (2 Kings 8:18), and also as a granddaughter of Omri (2 Kings 8:26); she was the wife of Jehoram king of Judah and the only female ruler of the kingdom of Judah. After her husband and son died, she destroyed all the royal offspring and ruled Judah for six years.
lifetime: Athaliah, as the daughter of Ahab, became the wife of Jehoram king of Judah (2 Kings 8:18). After her son Ahaziah became king and was killed in the revolt of Jehu, Athaliah destroyed all the royal offspring, but Joash, the son of Ahaziah, was hidden and escaped being put to death (2 Kings 11:1-2). Afterward she reigned over the land for six years (2 Kings 11:3), but when Joash was set up as king under the leadership of the priest Jehoiada, she was driven out from the ranks and was put to death on the way by which the horses enter the king's house (2 Kings 11:15-16).
event: When she saw that her son Ahaziah was dead, she rose up and destroyed all the royal offspring of the house of Judah (2 Chronicles 22:10), and she reigned over the land during the six years that Joash was in hiding (2 Kings 11:3). The sons of Athaliah broke into the house of God and gave all the holy things of the house of the LORD to the Baals (2 Chronicles 24:7). In the seventh year the priest Jehoiada made a covenant with the captains of hundreds and showed them the king's son (2 Kings 11:4); Athaliah went into the house of the LORD, tore her clothes, and cried, "Treason!" (2 Kings 11:13-14), but at Jehoiada's command she was driven out from the ranks and was put to death on the way by which the horses enter the king's house (2 Kings 11:15-16).
character: Athaliah influenced her husband Jehoram to walk in evil ways (2 Chronicles 21:6), and showed a cruelty that ruthlessly killed even her own blood relatives to maintain her power (2 Kings 11:1). She is regarded as a person who actively promoted the worship of Baal and tried to strongly transplant the religious coloring of her father's house, the royal house of northern Israel, into Judean society (2 Chronicles 24:7).

call: Father of Jeshaiah (of the descendants of Elam)
meaning: The LORD is great, the LORD afflicted
introduce: He is the father of Jeshaiah of the descendants of Elam, who came up from Babylon with Ezra in the era of the return from the Babylonian exile. He is a different man from Athaliah, the queen of Judah.
lifetime: His name is mentioned as the father of Jeshaiah, of the descendants of Elam, in the list of the heads of families who came up from Babylon with Ezra (Ezra 8:1, 8:7). Nothing is recorded in Scripture about his own life.
event: Although his own direct deeds are not recorded in Scripture, his name was recorded in the list of returnees when his son Jeshaiah, in the time of King Artaxerxes, led seventy men of the descendants of Elam in returning from Babylon to Jerusalem with Ezra (Ezra 8:7).

introduce: According to the biblical record, he is portrayed as the ancestor of humanity and the first man. He is recorded as having been formed from the dust and as having become a living being by receiving the breath of life from God.
lifetime: God formed man from the dust of the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and so created Adam (Genesis 2:7). Afterward he was given the role of working and keeping the garden of Eden, and carried out the task of naming the animals (Genesis 2:15, 2:19). He married Eve and had several children, including Cain, Abel, and Seth, and lived 930 years and died (Genesis 4:1, 4:2, 5:3, 5:5).
event: He gave names to all the livestock and the birds of the heavens in the garden of Eden (Genesis 2:20). He disobeyed the command not to eat the fruit of the forbidden tree of the knowledge of good and evil, and ate the fruit together with Eve (Genesis 3:6). After this event he was driven out of the garden of Eden and came to be in the situation of tilling the ground and laboring (Genesis 3:23).
character: Until he obtained a helper, he lived alone, and on seeing Eve he called her bone of his bones and flesh of his flesh, expressing a deep sense of oneness (Genesis 2:23). After eating the forbidden fruit, he felt fear and hid, or showed an attitude of shifting responsibility onto Eve (Genesis 3:10, 3:12).

introduce: A figure who appears in the New Testament, one of Paul's coworkers, mentioned in the letter Paul sent to Titus.
lifetime: He is mentioned in the letter Paul sent to Titus, who was staying in Crete, and appears in the passage where Paul states his plan to send Artemas or Tychicus to Titus (Titus 3:12).
event: He was named as a candidate to be sent to help Paul's ministry, and was mentioned to fill the place of Titus, who was instructed to come to Paul at Nicopolis (Titus 3:12).

introduce: Artemis is a goddess who appears in ancient Greco-Roman mythology, a goddess of fertility and fruitfulness who was worshiped in the region of Ephesus. In the Bible she is mentioned as the chief idol of the city of Ephesus, the setting of the book of Acts, and is described as a being who exercised an enormous social and economic influence at that time.
event: Demetrius, a silversmith of Ephesus, made silver shrines of Artemis and brought no small profit to the craftsmen (Acts 19:24). The silversmiths, fearing that because of Paul's evangelistic work the standing of Artemis would fall and her influence would diminish, stirred up an uproar (Acts 19:25-27). The citizens of Ephesus cried out with a loud voice for about two hours, "Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!" (Acts 19:34). The city clerk of Ephesus quieted the crowd, saying, "Who does not know that the city of the Ephesians is the guardian of the temple of the great Artemis and of the image that fell down from Zeus?" (Acts 19:35).
character: She is described as the great goddess whom all Asia and the world worship (Acts 19:27). To the people of Ephesus, Artemis was regarded as the god whom the temple served, and the temple was both the center and the symbol of their faith (Acts 19:35).

introduce: Ater is a figure mentioned as the ancestor of the descendants of Ater among the people of Israel who returned from the Babylonian exile. According to the records of Ezra and Nehemiah, Ater appears as a name designating the head of a family included in the list of returnees, or the founder of that family.
lifetime: Among those who returned from the Babylonian exile, the descendants of Ater, that is, of Hezekiah, are recorded as ninety-eight (Ezra 2:16). Also, Ater is among the descendants of the temple gatekeepers, and the total of the descendants of Shallum, Ater, Talmon, Akkub, Hatita, and Shobai is 139 (Ezra 2:42). In the list of returnees in the book of Nehemiah, the ninety-eight descendants of Ater, that is, of Hezekiah, are mentioned again (Nehemiah 7:21). The descendants of Ater are also included in the list of gatekeepers, and the total of the six gatekeeper families is recorded as 138 (Nehemiah 7:45). Afterward his name appears in the list of the chiefs of the people who sealed the covenant (Nehemiah 10:17).
event: The family of Ater is recorded as a member of the returning community that came back from Babylon to Jerusalem (Ezra 2:16, Nehemiah 7:21). The descendants of Ater are included among the descendants of the gatekeepers (Ezra 2:42, Nehemiah 7:45). In the time of Nehemiah, the name of Ater appears in the list of the chiefs of the people who sealed the covenant (Nehemiah 10:17).

meaning: Lord of Bezek, lord of lightning
introduce: Adoni-bezek was a Canaanite king who ruled the region of Bezek, and was a man who was defeated in the war with the tribes of Israel and had parts of his body cut off.
lifetime: When the tribe of Judah, united with the tribe of Simeon, fought against the Canaanites, they met Adoni-bezek at Bezek (Judges 1:4-5). Defeated in the battle, Adoni-bezek fled and was caught, and in the process he received the punishment of having his thumbs and big toes cut off (Judges 1:6). Afterward he was brought to Jerusalem and died there (Judges 1:7).
event: He was defeated in the battle of Bezek, the war with the tribes of Israel (Judges 1:5). He himself stated that in the past he had captured seventy kings, cut off their thumbs and big toes, and made them gather scraps of food under his table (Judges 1:7). After his defeat, he received a retaliatory punishment in which his thumbs and big toes were cut off by the army of Israel in the very same way he had done (Judges 1:6).
character: He had a cruel and authoritarian way of ruling, to the point of forcing on the kings he had subdued sadistic bodily mutilation and humiliating labor (Judges 1:7). He showed a cynical side, acknowledging his own defeat while himself referring to the justice of his own deeds (Judges 1:7).

introduce: Adonikam refers to the leader of a family, or the name of that family, among the people of Israel who returned to Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile; in Hebrew it has the meaning "my lord has arisen."
lifetime: Six hundred sixty-six descendants of Adonikam returned from Babylon to Jerusalem and Judah with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:13). Later, when Ezra went up, sixty men went up with the last of the descendants of Adonikam, Eliphelet, Jeuel, and Shemaiah (Ezra 8:13).
event: In the list of those who returned from the Babylonian exile, the number of the descendants of Adonikam is recorded as 666 (Ezra 2:13), while in the list in the book of Nehemiah it is recorded as 667 (Nehemiah 7:18). Also, in the list of the heads of families who came up from Babylon with Ezra, the last of the descendants of Adonikam are recorded as having come up with the men who were with them (Ezra 8:13).

introduce: Adoniram was an official who oversaw forced labor during the reigns of King David, King Solomon, and King Rehoboam of ancient Israel. In the history of Israel he is recorded as the administrative head concerned with the nation's large-scale building projects.
lifetime: Adoniram is recorded as the one in charge of forced labor in the time of King David (2 Samuel 20:24). In the time of King Solomon too, Adoniram the son of Abda is recorded as being in charge of forced labor (1 Kings 4:6). In the time of King Rehoboam he is recorded as the overseer of the forced laborers, and when King Rehoboam sent him, all Israel stoned him to death (1 Kings 12:18).
event: Adoniram was the overseer when Solomon raised a labor force of thirty thousand men out of all Israel and sent them to Lebanon in shifts of ten thousand a month (1 Kings 5:13-14). When Rehoboam came to Shechem to be made king, the assembly of Israel asked him to lighten the hard service and the heavy yoke, but Rehoboam answered that he would make the yoke even heavier (1 Kings 12:3-4, 12:13-14); afterward King Rehoboam sent Adoniram, who was over the forced labor, and all Israel stoned him to death (1 Kings 12:18).
character: In the biblical record there is no direct description of Adoniram's personal character, but he has the characteristic of a practical official who carried out forced labor on the people on behalf of the authority of the royal power (1 Kings 4:6). Within the administrative system of the dynasty spanning the three generations of David, Solomon, and Rehoboam, he faithfully performed his role as an official, but in the end he came to stand in the position of a political scapegoat who had to bear the full brunt of the people's anger (1 Kings 12:18).

introduce: He was the king of the Amorites who ruled Jerusalem at the time of the conquest of Canaan. Upon hearing of Israel's entry into Canaan and that Gibeon had made peace with Israel, he was the figure who led the alliance of the southern Canaanite city-states.
lifetime: Hearing that the inhabitants of Gibeon had made peace with Israel, he sent word to Hoham king of Hebron, Piram king of Jarmuth, Japhia king of Lachish, and Debir king of Eglon, and formed an allied force (Joshua 10:3). He led this allied force to attack Gibeon, but was defeated by a surprise attack from Joshua (Joshua 10:5-10). Afterward he fled and hid in the cave at Makkedah, but was discovered, and by Joshua's command he was executed and hung on a tree (Joshua 10:16-26).
event: Hearing that Gibeon had made peace with Israel, he was greatly afraid (Joshua 10:1-2) and sent to the other kings proposing that they strike Gibeon (Joshua 10:3-4). The five kings of the Amorites drew up against Gibeon and fought, but because the LORD caused them to be defeated before Israel, Joshua slaughtered them with a great slaughter at Gibeon and pursued them on the descent from Beth-horon, as far as Azekah and Makkedah (Joshua 10:5-10). This king hid in the cave at Makkedah and was brought out; Joshua had the commanders put their feet on his neck, then struck him down and hung him on trees, and at sunset took down the bodies and threw them into the cave where they had hidden (Joshua 10:22-27).
character: As a leader who exercised political influence over the southern region of Canaan, he reacted sensitively to developments near his own territory and showed the organizing ability to rally many city-states into an alliance (Joshua 10:3-4). He had a belligerent side that preferred an immediate military response to forces that resisted or were hostile to his rule (Joshua 10:4).

call: Fourth son of David (aspirant to the throne)
introduce: Adonijah was the fourth son born to King David and Haggith, and was regarded as the candidate to succeed to David's right of the firstborn after the death of Absalom. In David's old age he tried to make himself king but failed, and was later executed in the course of Solomon's strengthening of his royal authority.
lifetime: Adonijah was born at Hebron (2 Samuel 3:2-4). When David became old and feeble, he proclaimed himself that he would be king, and won over Joab the commander of the army and Abiathar the priest (1 Kings 1:5-7). But when David designated Solomon as king, his plan of accession came to nothing, and he caught hold of the horns of the altar and begged for his life (1 Kings 1:33-51). After Solomon became king, Adonijah asked that Abishag the Shunammite, who had attended David, be given to him as a wife, and by the command of Solomon, who interpreted this as an intention to usurp the throne, he was put to death by Benaiah (1 Kings 2:13-25).
event: In David's old age he prepared for himself chariots and horsemen and fifty men to run before him, displaying the majesty of a king (1 Kings 1:5). Beside the Stone of Zoheleth, which is by En-rogel, he sacrificed sheep, oxen, and fattened calves, and invited his brothers and the king's servants to hold an enthronement feast (1 Kings 1:9). After Solomon's accession he was briefly pardoned, but he showed an attitude of seeming to challenge Solomon's royal authority again by requesting Abishag, and in the end was put to death (1 Kings 2:23-25).
character: The Bible records that Adonijah was a very handsome man, and that he was a person in David's favor, to the extent that David had never displeased him at any time since he was born (1 Kings 1:6). He was ambitious enough to come forward to make himself king, but after Solomon's power became firm, he also showed a weakness, feeling fear and fleeing to the altar (1 Kings 1:50-51).

call: Commander of thousands of Manasseh (mighty man at Ziklag)
introduce: Adnah was one of the commanders of thousands of the tribe of Manasseh who defected to David when he went to Ziklag. The company that came with him helped David against the raiding bands, and they were all mighty warriors and commanders in the army.
lifetime: Adnah was one of those of the tribe of Manasseh who defected to David when he went to Ziklag, after having earlier gone with the Philistines to fight against Saul (1 Chronicles 12:19-20). He was a commander of thousands in Manasseh, and this company helped David against the raiding bands (1 Chronicles 12:20-21).
event: Adnah was one of the commanders of thousands of Manasseh who defected to David from the tribe of Manasseh when he went to Ziklag (1 Chronicles 12:20). This company helped David against the raiding bands, and all of them were mighty warriors and commanders in the army (1 Chronicles 12:21).
character: The Bible calls Adnah a commander of thousands of the tribe of Manasseh, and classifies him as one of the capable mighty men who were with David (1 Chronicles 12:20). No specific personal character or individual episodes concerning him are recorded.

introduce: Adrammelech is a figure who appears in the biblical books of 2 Kings and Isaiah, a son of Sennacherib, king of the Assyrian empire. He is a historical figure who murdered his father and fled with his brother Sharezer to the land of Ararat.
lifetime: He was a son of Sennacherib, king of Assyria (Isaiah 37:38). While his father Sennacherib was worshiping in the house of his god Nisroch, he and his brother Sharezer struck their father down with the sword (2 Kings 19:37). After murdering his father, he fled to the land of Ararat (Isaiah 37:38).
event: With Sharezer he struck down his father the king, Sennacherib, with the sword in the house of Nisroch (2 Kings 19:37). Afterward he fled with Sharezer to the land of Ararat, and Esar-haddon, a son of Sennacherib, became king in his place (Isaiah 37:38).
character: He had a power-seeking and violent disposition, to the extent of murdering his own father, the king, in a temple (2 Kings 19:37). Judging from his action of fleeing after failing to seize power once he had assassinated his father, he is regarded as a person who was deeply involved in the political friction within Assyria and in the question of succession to the throne (Isaiah 37:38).

introduce: Adriel is a figure who appears in the Old Testament, the son of Barzillai the Meholathite and the husband of Merab, the daughter of King Saul.
lifetime: Originally Saul said he would give his elder daughter Merab to David (1 Samuel 18:17), but at the time Merab should have been given to David, she was given as a wife to Adriel the Meholathite (1 Samuel 18:19). Afterward, the five sons of Adriel born of Merab, Saul's daughter, are recorded (2 Samuel 21:8).
event: When the Gibeonites demanded men of the house of Saul, the five sons born to Adriel and Merab were handed over to the Gibeonites and put to death (2 Samuel 21:8-9).

introduce: Admatha was one of the seven nobles who had access to the king in the time of King Xerxes of the Persian empire and sat first in the kingdom. He is recorded as a noble of Persia and Media (Esther 1:14).
lifetime: In the time of King Xerxes, Admatha was one of the seven nobles of Persia and Media who had access to the king, saw the king's face, and sat first in the kingdom (Esther 1:14).
event: When Queen Vashti did not obey the king's command, the king asked those who knew the law and judgment, and Admatha is introduced, together with Carshena, Shethar, Tarshish, Meres, Marsena, and Memucan, as one of the seven nobles who had access to the king (Esther 1:13-14). The one recorded as answering before the king and the nobles was Memucan (Esther 1:16).

call: Father of Shaphat (father of the manager of the royal herds)
introduce: Adlai is a figure recorded as the father of Shaphat, who was the manager of the royal herds in the time of King David. Apart from the fact that he was Shaphat's father, no other information about his specific deeds or personal details is given in the Bible.
lifetime: He is mentioned as the father who begot Shaphat, who held the office of managing the royal herds during the reign of King David (1 Chronicles 27:29).

introduce: Adina is a figure who appears in the Old Testament book of 1 Chronicles, one of the mighty men of the tribe of Reuben who belonged to David's army.
lifetime: Adina was the son of Shiza, a chief of the Reubenites, and he is recorded in the list of David's mighty men together with the thirty who were with him (1 Chronicles 11:42).
event: Adina was the son of Shiza and a chief of the Reubenites, and is recorded together with the thirty who were with him (1 Chronicles 11:42). No other specific deeds are recorded in the text.
character: The Bible classifies him as a head of the Reubenites and one of the thirty mighty men, so it can be seen that he was a person with leadership within the military organization of the time (1 Chronicles 11:42).

call: Chief of the tribe of Simeon (conqueror of Gedor)
introduce: Adiel is a figure who appears in the Old Testament book of 1 Chronicles, one of the chiefs of the tribe of Simeon. His name is in the list of chiefs concerning the settlement of the chiefs of the tribe of Simeon, who obtained pasture in the region of Gedor in the time of King Hezekiah (1 Chronicles 4:36-41).
lifetime: Adiel's name is in the list of the chiefs of the tribe of Simeon (1 Chronicles 4:36, 4:38), and those recorded in this list sought pasture for their flocks and came to the entrance of Gedor, on the east side of the valley, and in the time of Hezekiah king of Judah came to dwell there (1 Chronicles 4:39, 4:41).
event: The chiefs recorded in this list sought pasture for their flocks and came to the entrance of Gedor, on the east side of the valley, and found rich and good pasture (1 Chronicles 4:39-40); in the days of Hezekiah they went and struck down the tents of the people there and destroyed the Meunites utterly, and dwelt in their place (1 Chronicles 4:41). Adiel's name is in this list, but his individual deeds are not recorded separately.

call: Ancestor of a family that returned with Zerubbabel
introduce: Adin was the ancestor of a family of Israel that returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel from the Babylonian exile, a figure recorded in the lists of returnees in Ezra and Nehemiah.
lifetime: The descendants of Adin are recorded in the list of the people of Israel who returned from the Babylonian exile (Ezra 2:15). The descendants of Adin are also recorded in the list of returnees in the book of Nehemiah (Nehemiah 7:20).
event: In the lists of those who came up from Babylon with Zerubbabel, the number of the descendants of Adin is recorded as 454 in the book of Ezra (Ezra 2:15) and as 655 in the book of Nehemiah (Nehemiah 7:20).

introduce: Ara is a figure who appears in the genealogy of the tribe of Asher, recorded as a son of Jether.
lifetime: Ara is recorded in the genealogy of the tribe of Asher as one of the sons of Jether: Jephunneh, Pispa, and Ara (1 Chronicles 7:38).
event: In the biblical record, nothing is mentioned about any specific achievement or special event of Ara himself (1 Chronicles 7:38).

introduce: Araunah was a Jebusite who owned the threshing floor of Jerusalem in the time of King David. In the Bible he is also called by the name Ornan.
lifetime: After David took the census and the calamity was falling, the angel of the LORD stood by the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite (1 Chronicles 21:15). David went up as Gad had spoken in the name of the LORD (1 Chronicles 21:18-19). Ornan, while threshing wheat, turned and saw the angel, and hid with his four sons (1 Chronicles 21:20). When David came, Ornan saw David, went out from the threshing floor, and bowed down to him with his face to the ground (1 Chronicles 21:21). After David took the census and the calamity fell, according to Gad's word he went up to build an altar to the LORD on the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite (2 Samuel 24:18-19). Araunah, seeing the king and his servants coming toward him, went out and bowed down before the king with his face to the ground (2 Samuel 24:20). When David said he would buy the threshing floor and build an altar, Araunah said he would give it to the king without charge (2 Samuel 24:21-23). Afterward David bought the place for a price (2 Samuel 24:24).
event: Araunah offered David not only the threshing floor but also the oxen for the burnt offering, and the threshing sledges and the yokes of the oxen for the wood (2 Samuel 24:22-23). But David refused, saying he would not offer a burnt offering without cost, and in 1 Chronicles he paid Ornan six hundred shekels of gold by weight for the site (1 Chronicles 21:24-25). Second Samuel records the same transaction as a purchase of the threshing floor and the oxen for fifty shekels of silver (2 Samuel 24:24). This place later became the site where Solomon built the temple of Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 3:1).
character: As soon as he saw King David, Araunah bowed down with his face to the ground and showed a courteous attitude of respect (2 Samuel 24:20). He had a generous side, being willing to give up his own possessions to the king (1 Chronicles 21:23).

call: Son of Shem (ancestor of the Aramean people)
introduce: The fifth son of Shem, son of Noah, recorded as the ancestor of the Aramean people, who took shape mainly in northern Mesopotamia and the region of Syria.
lifetime: He was born as a son of Shem and is mentioned as one of the persons who make up the genealogy of Shem (Genesis 10:22). In 1 Chronicles 1:17 also, his name is recorded in the same way in the genealogy that lists the descendants of Shem (1 Chronicles 1:17).

introduce: Aretas is a king mentioned in 2 Corinthians in the New Testament, whose governor tried to seize Paul in Damascus (2 Corinthians 11:32). Historically, it is generally held that he refers to Aretas IV, king of the Nabateans.
lifetime: The governor under King Aretas guarded the city of Damascus in order to seize the apostle Paul (2 Corinthians 11:32).
event: When the apostle Paul escaped from Damascus, the governor under King Aretas was guarding the city and trying to seize Paul (2 Corinthians 11:32). At that time Paul was let down through a window in the wall in a basket and escaped from his hands (2 Corinthians 11:33).

introduce: Areli is a figure mentioned in Genesis and Numbers, one of the seven sons of Gad, a son of Jacob and one of the ancestors of the twelve tribes of Israel.
lifetime: He was included in the list of the sons of Gad when Jacob went down to Egypt with his sons (Genesis 46:16). Afterward, when a census was taken in the period before the conquest of Canaan, he was recorded as the ancestor who formed the Arelite clan of the tribe of Gad (Numbers 26:17).
event: He fulfilled the role of continuing the family-level genealogy by forming the Arelite clan within the tribe of Gad (Numbers 26:17).

introduce: The sixth of the seven sons born to Gad, a son of Jacob, and one of the persons who make up the genealogy of the tribe of Gad.
lifetime: He was a son of Gad, son of Jacob, and was included in the list of the descendants whom Zilpah bore to Jacob, and went down to Egypt (Genesis 46:16, 46:18).
event: Apart from his name being recorded as a son of Gad in the list of Jacob's family who went down to Egypt in Genesis 46:16, no individual event of his is recorded in Scripture.

introduce: Aaron was a son of Amram of the tribe of Levi and the elder brother of Moses, and was appointed the first high priest in the history of Israel. He served as Moses' spokesman in the course of the exodus, and his descendants became the family that inherited the priestly office through the generations.
lifetime: In Egypt, Aaron received the command given when the LORD spoke to Moses and Aaron to bring the people of Israel out of the land of Egypt (Exodus 6:13). He went with Moses to Pharaoh and demanded the liberation of Israel (Exodus 5:1), and as the LORD had commanded Moses, when Aaron and his sons came forward before the congregation assembled at the entrance of the tent of meeting to be ordained, he was anointed with the anointing oil and set apart as holy (Leviticus 8:1-3, 8:12). Together with Moses, at the incident of the waters of Meribah at Kadesh, he heard the word that the LORD would not bring this assembly into the land He had given them (Numbers 20:12-13), and in the fortieth year after the people of Israel came out of the land of Egypt, in the fifth month, on the first day of the month, Aaron the priest went up Mount Hor on the border of Edom at the command of the LORD and died there at the age of 123 (Numbers 33:37-39).
event: The LORD commanded Moses to have Aaron take his staff and stretch out his arm over the waters of Egypt, and Moses and Aaron did so, and when he struck the river, all its water turned to blood (Exodus 7:19-20). While Israel was encamped at Mount Sinai, Aaron received the gold rings the people brought, cast them, and made the form of a calf (Exodus 32:2-4). Afterward, on the eighth day, Moses called Aaron and his sons and had Aaron offer a calf for the sin offering and a ram for the burnt offering before the LORD (Leviticus 9:1-2). Also, there is a record that at the rebellion of Korah's company, at Moses' command he took the censer, ran to the congregation, and made atonement for the people, so that the plague was stopped (Numbers 16:47-48).
character: Aaron is described as an eloquent person and was chosen as Moses' spokesman (Exodus 4:14). Together with his sister Miriam he spoke against Moses and was struck with leprosy, showing human failings (Numbers 12:1-10). As a leader he showed a weak side that easily yielded to the pressure of the people (Exodus 32:22-24), but in the priestly office he showed himself observing the strict ordinances (Leviticus 10:3).

introduce: Arod is a figure who appears in the Old Testament book of Numbers, one of the sons of Gad of the tribe of Gad of Israel, and the founder of the Arodite clan, descendants of Gad (Numbers 26:17).
lifetime: Arod is recorded by the name of the Arodite family among the clans of the descendants of Gad (Numbers 26:15, 26:17). This record belongs to the passage of the census that Moses and the priest Eleazar spoke to the people of Israel on the plains of Moab by the Jordan at Jericho (Numbers 26:3).
event: In the census record of Numbers 26, his name is recorded as the Arodite family among the clans of the descendants of Gad (Numbers 26:17). Those numbered of all the clans of the descendants of Gad were forty thousand five hundred (Numbers 26:18).

introduce: Argob is a figure who appears in the Old Testament book of 2 Kings, recorded as a man whom Pekah, an officer, killed together with the king and Arieh in the citadel of the royal palace at Samaria when he rebelled in the time of Pekahiah king of Israel (2 Kings 15:25).
lifetime: When Pekah the son of Remaliah, an officer, rebelled in the time of Pekahiah king of Israel, he was killed together with the king and Arieh in the citadel of the royal palace at Samaria (2 Kings 15:23-25).
event: Pekah the son of Remaliah, an officer, rebelled with fifty men of the Gileadites, killed the king, Argob, and Arieh in the citadel of the royal palace at Samaria, and became king in his place (2 Kings 15:25). Argob is the one who was killed at that time, and his individual deeds are not recorded in Scripture.

introduce: Arnan is a figure belonging to the genealogy of the royal house of David, one of the descendants of David who appear in the genealogy after the Babylonian exile.
lifetime: Arnan is recorded in 1 Chronicles 3:21 as "Arnan the son of Rephaiah"; this verse lists, following Pelatiah the son of Hananiah and Jeshaiah, the sons of Arnan the son of Rephaiah, the sons of Obadiah, and the sons of Shecaniah (1 Chronicles 3:21). He is listed in the passage that records the descendants of Zerubbabel (1 Chronicles 3:19-21) within the genealogy of David's descendants in 1 Chronicles 3.

introduce: Ardon is a figure who appears in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah, a descendant of Judah and a son of Caleb, son of Hezron (1 Chronicles 2:18).
lifetime: He is recorded as one of the sons Jesher, Shobab, and Ardon whom Caleb, son of Hezron, had by his wives Azubah and Jerioth (1 Chronicles 2:18).

introduce: Arba is a figure whose name remains in Kiriath-arba, the old name of Hebron; the Bible records him as the father of Anak and says he was the greatest man among the Anakim (Joshua 14:15, 15:13).
lifetime: Arba was the greatest man among the Anakim (Joshua 14:15). The old name of Hebron was Kiriath-arba (Joshua 14:15), and Hebron was also called "the city of Arba" (Joshua 21:11). The Bible does not record his individual deeds.
event: The city of Kiriath-arba, that is, Hebron, was given by Joshua, as the LORD had commanded, to Caleb the son of Jephunneh as a portion among the descendants of Judah (Joshua 15:13), and Kiriath-arba, the city of Arba the father of Anak, that is, Hebron, with its surrounding pasturelands, was given to the descendants of Aaron, of the Kohathite family among the descendants of Levi (Joshua 14:13, 21:10-11).
character: The Bible describes him as the greatest man among the Anakim, indicating that he was a person of physical dignity and strength (Joshua 14:15).

introduce: A son of Shem, born two years after the flood of Noah, recorded through the genealogies of the Bible as continuing the line of Shem (Genesis 10:22, 11:10). He is one of the principal figures who make up the early bloodline of the Semites leading to the ancestor of the Hebrew people (Luke 3:36).
lifetime: Shem begot him at the age of one hundred, that is, two years after the flood (Genesis 11:10); he begot Shelah at the age of thirty-five (Genesis 11:12), and after begetting Shelah he lived four hundred three years and had other children (Genesis 11:13). In the genealogy of Jesus in Luke 3:36 he is recorded under the spelling "Arphaxad" in the generation immediately after Shem.

introduce: Arza was the steward of the palace of Elah, king of northern Israel, a figure whose house is recorded as the place where Elah drank himself drunk at Tirzah (1 Kings 16:9).
lifetime: Arza was the steward of the palace in the time of Elah, king of northern Israel (1 Kings 16:9). While Elah was at Tirzah, drinking himself drunk in the house of Arza, the steward of the palace, Zimri conspired against the king (1 Kings 16:9).
event: While King Elah was drinking himself drunk in Arza's house, Zimri, Elah's servant and the commander of half of his chariots, conspired, went in, struck Elah down, and became king in his place (1 Kings 16:9-10). In this incident the actions of Arza himself are not recorded.

introduce: Ard was a son of Benjamin, one of the descendants of Jacob, and a person belonging to the family line of the descendants of Benjamin (Genesis 46:21).
lifetime: When Jacob went down to Egypt leading his sons and families, he was included in the list of the sons of Benjamin (Genesis 46:21). As a son of Benjamin, he is recorded in the genealogy of the descendants of Jacob (Genesis 46:21).
event: Apart from the event of his name being entered in the list as a member of the family of Jacob who went down to Egypt, no specific achievement or individual event is recorded in Scripture (Genesis 46:21).

introduce: Aridatha was a figure active in the time of Xerxes, king of Persia, recorded as one of the ten sons of Haman (Esther 9:8, 9:10).
lifetime: Aridatha is recorded as one of the ten sons of Haman, the son of Hammedatha the Agagite (Esther 3:1, 9:8, 9:10). After the plot of his father Haman to destroy the Jews failed, he met his death when the Jews killed five hundred men and the ten sons of Haman in the citadel of Susa (Esther 9:6-10).
event: His name is recorded as one of the ten sons of Haman, the enemy of the Jews, and he was killed by the Jews in the citadel of Susa (Esther 9:8, 9:10). Afterward the bodies of Haman's ten sons were hanged on the gallows (Esther 9:13-14).

introduce: Aridai was a figure active in the time of Xerxes, king of Persia, recorded as one of the ten sons of Haman (Esther 9:9).
lifetime: Aridai is one of the ten sons of Haman whose name is recorded in Esther 9:9. After Haman's attempt to destroy Mordecai and the Jews, he is included among the ten sons of Haman who were killed by the Jews in the citadel of Susa (Esther 9:6-10).
event: On the day the Jews struck down and slaughtered their enemies, the ten sons of Haman were killed in the citadel of Susa, and Aridai was one of them (Esther 9:5-10). At Esther's request the king granted permission, and the bodies of Haman's ten sons were hanged on the gallows (Esther 9:13-14).

introduce: Arisai is a figure mentioned as one of the ten sons of Haman in the time of Xerxes, king of Persia (Esther 9:9).
lifetime: Arisai is recorded as the eighth of the ten sons of Haman, the son of Hammedatha the Agagite (Esther 3:1, 9:7-9). After the plan of his father Haman to destroy the Jews in the Persian kingdom failed, he was killed by the Jews in the citadel of Susa (Esther 9:6-10).
event: When the Jews struck down and slaughtered their enemies, Arisai was killed in the citadel of Susa as one of the ten sons of Haman (Esther 9:5-10). Afterward, when the bodies of Haman's ten sons were hanged on the gallows, he was included among those ten sons (Esther 9:13-14).

introduce: Aristarchus was a man from Thessalonica in Macedonia who accompanied and assisted the apostle Paul from Paul's third missionary journey through the period of his imprisonment in Rome.
lifetime: In the confusion that came from Ephesus, the crowd seized Gaius and Aristarchus, Macedonians who were traveling with Paul, and rushed together into the theater (Acts 19:29). Aristarchus of Thessalonica is recorded as one of those who accompanied Paul as far as Asia (Acts 20:4), and when Paul, who had been entrusted to the centurion Julius to go to Italy, boarded a ship of Adramyttium, Aristarchus, a Thessalonian of Macedonia, was with him (Acts 27:1-2). In Colossians, Paul called him "Aristarchus my fellow prisoner" (Colossians 4:10), and in Philemon he is recorded among "my fellow workers" who send greetings (Philemon 1:24).
event: In the confusion that came from Ephesus, the crowd seized Gaius and Aristarchus, who were traveling with Paul, and rushed together into the theater (Acts 19:29). When Paul boarded a ship of Adramyttium to go to Italy, Aristarchus was with him (Acts 27:1-2). Paul called him "Aristarchus my fellow prisoner" (Colossians 4:10).
character: Since he never left Paul but accompanied him through the period of his imprisonment in Rome, he is regarded as a very loyal person (Colossians 4:10). He showed strong loyalty and a devoted attitude toward Paul, being seized together with him even in a dangerous situation (Acts 19:29) and accepting the long voyage to Rome with him as a prisoner (Acts 27:2). Having received from Paul the direct mention "my fellow worker," he was a trusted person within the early Christian community (Philemon 1:24).

introduce: Aristobulus is a figure mentioned near the end of the New Testament book of Romans, one whose household Paul told the believers to greet in Romans 16:10.
lifetime: In the greetings he sent in Romans 16, Paul told the believers to greet the household of Aristobulus (Romans 16:10).
event: Apart from the fact that his household received Paul's greetings, no specifically recorded activity or particular event has been handed down (Romans 16:10).
character: The biblical text gives no information describing his personal character or outward traits (-)

introduce: Arieh is a figure who appears in the Old Testament book of 2 Kings, recorded as a man whom Pekah, an officer, killed together with the king and Argob in the citadel of the royal palace at Samaria when he rebelled in the time of Pekahiah king of Israel (2 Kings 15:25).
lifetime: When Pekah the son of Remaliah, an officer, rebelled in the time of Pekahiah king of Israel, he was killed together with the king and Argob in the citadel of the royal palace at Samaria (2 Kings 15:23-25).
event: Pekah the son of Remaliah, an officer, rebelled with fifty men of the Gileadites, killed the king, Argob, and Arieh in the citadel of the royal palace at Samaria, and became king in his place (2 Kings 15:25). Arieh is the one who was killed at that time, and his office and individual deeds are not recorded in Scripture.

introduce: Ariel is one of the leaders whom Ezra summoned when he gathered the people at the canal that flows toward Ahava (Ezra 8:15-16). Ezra 8:16-17 records that Ezra sent these leaders to the region of Casiphia, to Iddo, the leader there, to bring ministers for the house of God.
lifetime: When Ezra gathered the people at the canal that flows toward Ahava and looked them over and found none of the sons of Levi (Ezra 8:15), Ariel was one of the leaders whom Ezra summoned (Ezra 8:16). Ezra sent them to Iddo, the leader in the region of Casiphia, and his brothers, to bring ministers (Ezra 8:17). Afterward nothing further is recorded in Scripture about his personal life or deeds.
event: Ezra summoned the leaders Eliezer, Ariel, Shemaiah, Elnathan, Jarib, Elnathan, Nathan, Zechariah, and Meshullam, and the men of understanding Joiarib and Elnathan (Ezra 8:16), and sent them to the region of Casiphia, telling them what to say to Iddo and his brothers, the temple servants, that they should bring ministers for the house of God (Ezra 8:17). By the good hand of God upon them, they brought a man of understanding from the sons of Levi, along with Sherebiah and his sons and brothers, Hashabiah and Jeshaiah with his brothers and sons, and 220 of the temple servants (Ezra 8:18-20).

introduce: In the Bible, Ariel is a symbolic name for Jerusalem that appears in the book of Isaiah, and in Hebrew it carries the meaning "lion of God" or "altar."
lifetime: In the context of the book of Isaiah, Ariel is used as another name for the city of Jerusalem, where David encamped (Isaiah 29:1).
event: As another name for Jerusalem, Ariel is the one the LORD said He would distress, and is mentioned as a city that will mourn and lament (Isaiah 29:2). Also, it was said that the multitude of all the nations that fight against Ariel will be like a dream, like a vision of the night (Isaiah 29:7).
character: In the biblical record there is no concrete description of the character of Ariel as a person, but from the fact that Ezra designated him as a member of the delegation sent to Iddo, one can infer that he was a trusted person in the community with the ability to communicate (Ezra 8:16). As a name, Ariel is used as a literary device that simultaneously symbolizes the sacred altar function of Jerusalem and the crisis of its destruction (Isaiah 29:2).

introduce: Arioch was the king of Ellasar, one of the four kings in Genesis 14 who, together with Amraphel king of Shinar, Chedorlaomer king of Elam, and Tidal king of Goiim, fought against the five kings including the king of Sodom (Genesis 14:1, 14:9).
lifetime: Arioch is the king of Ellasar recorded in Genesis 14:1 together with Amraphel king of Shinar, Chedorlaomer king of Elam, and Tidal king of Goiim. The five kings, including the king of Sodom, served Chedorlaomer for twelve years and rebelled in the thirteenth year (Genesis 14:2-4), and Arioch, as one of the four kings, fought with these five kings in the valley of Siddim (Genesis 14:8-9).
event: Arioch, as one of the four kings including Chedorlaomer, fought with the five kings including the king of Sodom (Genesis 14:9-10), and the four kings took all the goods and food of Sodom and Gomorrah, and also captured Lot, Abram's nephew, who lived in Sodom, and plundered his goods (Genesis 14:11-12). But Abram, leading 318 trained men born in his house, pursued them and attacked them by night and defeated them, and brought back all the goods that had been taken, and his nephew Lot with his goods, and also the women and the people (Genesis 14:14-16).

introduce: Amariah is a descendant of Aaron recorded in 1 Chronicles 6 and a figure belonging to the genealogy of the high priestly family. He is the son of Meraioth, and is recorded as the grandfather of Zadok and the father of Ahitub.
lifetime: Amariah was a figure who continued the genealogy of Eleazar, Aaron's son, and was born as a son of Meraioth (1 Chronicles 6:3-7). As the father of Ahitub and the grandfather of Zadok, he fulfilled the role of continuing the bloodline legitimacy of the high priestly family (1 Chronicles 6:7-8).
event: In the biblical record, no specific public activity or historical event carried out by Amariah is mentioned; he appears mainly as a figure within the genealogy that establishes the genealogy of Aaron's high priestly family (1 Chronicles 6:7-8).

introduce: Amasa was a nephew of King David and a military commander of Israel, born to Abigail, David's sister, and Jether the Ishmaelite (1 Chronicles 2:16-17). 2 Samuel 17:25 records him as the son of Ithra the Israelite, and says that his mother Abigail was a younger sister of Zeruiah, Joab's mother. At the time of Absalom's rebellion he was the commander whom Absalom set up in place of Joab, and afterward he was the one whom David said he would make commander in place of Joab (2 Samuel 17:25, 19:13).
lifetime: Amasa, as David's nephew, is connected with David's family line (1 Chronicles 2:16-17). When Absalom rebelled, Absalom made Amasa commander of the army in place of Joab (2 Samuel 17:25). After Absalom's rebellion was put down, David had word sent to Amasa that he would make him commander before him continually in place of Joab (2 Samuel 19:13). At the time of Sheba's revolt David told Amasa to summon the men of Judah within three days, but Amasa went to summon them and was delayed beyond the time the king had set (2 Samuel 20:4-5). Afterward, at the great stone that is in Gibeon, Joab stabbed him in the belly with a sword and he died (2 Samuel 20:8-10).
event: Absalom made Amasa commander in place of Joab (2 Samuel 17:25). David had word sent to Amasa of his intention to make him commander in place of Joab (2 Samuel 19:13), and all the men of Judah, with one heart, asked the king to return (2 Samuel 19:14). At the time of Sheba's revolt, David commanded Amasa to summon the men of Judah within three days, and Amasa went to summon the men of Judah (2 Samuel 20:4-5).
character: A cousin of Joab, he showed the trait of failing to discern the intentions of Joab, who was a rival, so that he let down his guard against Joab and was killed, stabbed by the sword (2 Samuel 20:9-10).

meaning: One who bears a heavy burden
introduce: Amasai was a Levite of the descendants of Kohath, one of the ancestors of Heman, who was in charge of praise in the temple in the time of David. In the genealogy of Scripture he is recorded as a descendant of Izhar, the son of Kohath.
lifetime: Amasai is recorded as the son of Elkanah and the father of Mahath (1 Chronicles 6:35-36). In the genealogy of Heman the singer, of the Kohathites (1 Chronicles 6:33-35), above him follow Elkanah, Joel, Azariah, Zephaniah, Tahath, Assir, Ebiasaph, and Korah, and Korah was the son of Izhar, and Izhar was the son of Kohath (1 Chronicles 6:36-38).
event: No concrete activity or historical event directly shown in the biblical text is recorded, but his name is listed in the genealogy as an ancestor of Heman, one of those to whom David assigned the work of singing in the house of the LORD (1 Chronicles 6:31-36).

introduce: The ninth king of the southern kingdom of Judah, the son of Joash and the father of Uzziah. His reign lasted about 29 years, and he ruled in Jerusalem.
lifetime: Amaziah came to the throne at the age of 25 and reigned 29 years (2 Kings 14:1-2). He put to death the servants who had killed his father Joash, but did not put their children to death, acting according to the law (2 Chronicles 25:3-4). After his victory in the war with Edom he brought back the gods of Edom and worshiped them (2 Chronicles 25:14), and was defeated in the war with Joash king of Israel, so that the wall of Jerusalem was broken down and the treasures of the temple were plundered (2 Chronicles 25:21-24). Afterward a conspiracy arose against him in Jerusalem, and he fled to Lachish, but was killed there (2 Chronicles 25:27).
event: In the Valley of Salt he killed ten thousand Edomites (descendants of Seir), and struck Sela and took it, and named it Joktheel (2 Kings 14:7; 2 Chronicles 25:11). He sent messengers to Joash king of Israel proposing that they meet face to face, but at Beth-shemesh Judah was defeated and Amaziah was taken captive (2 Kings 14:8, 11-13). The wall of Jerusalem was broken down for four hundred cubits, from the Gate of Ephraim to the Corner Gate (2 Kings 14:13).
character: He did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, yet not like his father David (2 Kings 14:3). He brought the gods of Edom, set them up as his own gods, and burned incense before them (2 Chronicles 25:14). He showed a stubborn side, to the point of rebuking the man of God who warned him and sending him away (2 Chronicles 25:16).

introduce: A military commander active in the time of Jehoshaphat, king of the southern kingdom of Judah, a man who devoted himself to the LORD.
lifetime: He is recorded as one of the commanders who led the army of Judah during the reign of King Jehoshaphat (2 Chronicles 17:16).
event: He is recorded as the son of Zichri, one who willingly offered himself to the LORD, and he commanded two hundred thousand mighty men of valor (2 Chronicles 17:16).
character: He is regarded as a person who showed a willingness to devote himself voluntarily to the LORD and had a zealous attitude in his military duties (2 Chronicles 17:16).

introduce: Amal is a figure recorded as a son of Helem in the genealogy of the tribe of Asher (1 Chronicles 7:30-35).
lifetime: In the genealogy of the tribe of Asher he is recorded as a son of Helem, together with Zophah, Imna, and Shelesh, and Helem was the younger brother of Shomer (1 Chronicles 7:34-35).

meaning: One who dwells in the valley
introduce: Amalek was a son born to Esau's firstborn Eliphaz by his concubine Timna, a grandson of Esau, and a figure recorded as one of the chiefs in the land of Edom.
lifetime: Esau, that is Edom, lived in the hill country of Seir (Genesis 36:8), and Timna, the concubine of his son Eliphaz, bore Amalek to Eliphaz (Genesis 36:12). Amalek is recorded as one of the chiefs in the land of Edom who came from Eliphaz (Genesis 36:16).
event: In the biblical record, no specific achievement of Amalek himself or individual event in his life is mentioned; the only thing stated is that he formed a family as a chief of Edom (Genesis 36:16).
character: The biblical text gives no direct description of Amalek's personal character or physical traits. It shows only that he became the ancestor of the Amalekite people, who inherited the bloodline of the Edomite clans and came to form a historically hostile relationship with Israel (Genesis 36:12).

introduce: Amashai was a figure of a priestly family who lived in Jerusalem after the return from the Babylonian exile, the son of Azarel, the grandson of Ahzai, the great-grandson of Meshillemoth, and the great-great-grandson of Immer (Nehemiah 11:13).
lifetime: Amashai is recorded as the son of Azarel and one of a priestly family who lived in Jerusalem (Nehemiah 11:10-13). His family background is confirmed through the genealogy that he was the son of Azarel, the grandson of Ahzai, the great-grandson of Meshillemoth, and the great-great-grandson of Immer (Nehemiah 11:13).
event: In Nehemiah 11:13, following the record "his brothers, heads of fathers' houses, 242 in all," Amashai the son of Azarel is recorded, and no other individual events are recorded.

introduce: Amok, who appears in the biblical record, is a figure mentioned as the ancestor of Amok, one of the priestly families that served in the temple at Jerusalem after the return from the Babylonian exile.
lifetime: Amok was among the priests who returned with Zerubbabel and Jeshua (Nehemiah 12:1), and was one of the heads of the priests and of their brothers in the days of Jeshua (Nehemiah 12:7).
event: In the days of Joiakim, among the heads of the priests' houses, Eber was over the family of Amok (Nehemiah 12:12, 20).

introduce: A king of Shinar who appears in Genesis 14, one of the four kings who allied with Chedorlaomer king of Elam and fought against the five kings, including those of Sodom and Gomorrah.
lifetime: As king of Shinar, together with Chedorlaomer king of Elam, Arioch king of Ellasar, and Tidal king of Goiim, he fought against five kings, including Bera king of Sodom (Genesis 14:1-2, 14:9). The five kings, including those of Sodom and Gomorrah, served Chedorlaomer for twelve years and rebelled in the thirteenth year, and in the fourteenth year the kings allied with Chedorlaomer came out (Genesis 14:4-5). In the valley of Siddim the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah fled, and the four kings took all the goods and food of Sodom and Gomorrah, and also captured Lot, Abram's nephew, who lived in Sodom (Genesis 14:8-12).
event: He is recorded as one of the four kings who fought in the valley of Siddim against the five kings, including those of Sodom and Gomorrah (Genesis 14:8-9). The four kings took the goods of Sodom and Gomorrah and captured Lot, Abram's nephew (Genesis 14:11-12), but Abram, leading 318 trained men born in his house, pursued them and struck them by night, pursuing them as far as Hobah to the left of Damascus, and brought back Lot and the goods that had been taken (Genesis 14:14-16).

introduce: The son of Kohath and grandson of Levi, and the father of Moses, Aaron, and Miriam. He is recorded as a key figure in the family among the descendants of Jacob that produced the leaders of the exodus.
lifetime: Born as a son of Kohath, he took Jochebed, his father's sister, as his wife (Exodus 6:20). By her he fathered Aaron and Moses (Exodus 6:20), and Amram lived to the age of 137 and died (Exodus 6:20).
event: Amram, the son of Kohath, took Jochebed, his father's sister, as his wife and fathered Aaron and Moses (Exodus 6:20). Jochebed bore to Amram Aaron and Moses and their sister Miriam (Numbers 26:59). The sons of Aaron, a child of Amram, continue in the genealogy (1 Chronicles 6:3).

introduce: Ami was a member of the community of Israel that returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel after the Babylonian exile, a figure classified among the descendants of the servants of Solomon (Ezra 2:57).
lifetime: His name is entered in the list of the returnees, among those who had been taken captive to Babylon and came back to Jerusalem and Judah (Ezra 2:1, 2:57). He was included in the genealogy of the returnees together with the descendants of the servants of Solomon (Ezra 2:55, 2:57).
event: Apart from the event of being recorded in the list as a member of the returning community that came back from Babylon to Jerusalem, no personal achievement or particular event is described in Scripture (Ezra 2:57).

introduce: Amasai was a priest active in the time of David, one of those who blew the trumpets before the ark in the course of moving the ark of God (1 Chronicles 15:24).
lifetime: When David moved the ark of God, he is recorded as one of those who blew the trumpets before the ark of God, together with the priests Shebaniah, Joshaphat, Nethanel, Zechariah, Benaiah, and Eliezer (1 Chronicles 15:24).
event: He is recorded as one of the priests assigned the duty of blowing the trumpets before the ark of God (1 Chronicles 15:24).

introduce: Amittai is a figure mentioned in the Old Testament book of Jonah, the father of the prophet Jonah. The Hebrew name Amittai carries the meaning "a truthful person" or "my truth."
lifetime: Other than the fact that he was the father of the prophet Jonah, who was from Gath-hepher, there is no concrete information recorded about his life (2 Kings 14:25).
event: There is no record of any direct activity or particular event; his name appears only in the context explaining Jonah's family line (Jonah 1:1).

introduce: Abaddon is the name used in the Hebrew form; in the book of Revelation he is recorded as the king of the locusts and the angel of the Abyss. In the Greek form he is called Apollyon.
lifetime: According to the biblical record, Abaddon is not a person with a human life, but appears in the vision of Revelation 9 as the king of the locusts that came out of the Abyss (Revelation 9:3, 9:11).
event: When the fifth angel blew his trumpet, a star that had fallen from heaven to earth was given the key to the Abyss and opened the Abyss, and out of the smoke locusts came upon the earth (Revelation 9:1-3). The locusts were told to harm only those people who do not have the seal of God on their foreheads (Revelation 9:4), and Abaddon is recorded as the king of these locusts (Revelation 9:11).
character: As the angel of the Abyss he presides over destruction, and his very name carries the meaning of destroyer (Revelation 9:11).

introduce: He is one of the seven eunuchs of King Xerxes of Persia who appear in the book of Esther.
lifetime: He is mentioned as one of the seven eunuchs who attended the king in the palace of King Xerxes (Esther 1:10).
event: When King Xerxes, merry with wine, commanded the seven eunuchs who served in his presence to bring Queen Vashti before the king wearing her royal crown, Vashti refused to come at the king's command conveyed by the eunuchs; Abagtha is recorded as one of the seven eunuchs who received this command (Esther 1:10-12).

introduce: Ahban is a figure who appears in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah, a son born, together with Molid, to Abishur the son of Shammai and his wife Abihail (1 Chronicles 2:28-29).
lifetime: He is recorded as a son of Abishur and Abihail (1 Chronicles 2:29). Abishur was the son of Shammai, Shammai was the son of Onam, and Onam was the son of Jerahmeel, the firstborn of Hezron (1 Chronicles 2:25-26, 2:28).

introduce: The second son of Adam and Eve, a biblical figure recorded as the first person murdered in human history.
lifetime: He was born between Adam and Eve and was the younger brother of Cain (Genesis 4:1-2). He lived as a keeper of sheep, and after some time his elder brother Cain brought an offering to the LORD from the fruit of the ground, and Abel from the firstborn of his flock and their fat portions (Genesis 4:2-4). Afterward he was killed by his elder brother Cain in the field (Genesis 4:8).
event: He offered to the LORD the firstborn of his flock and their fat portions, and the LORD had regard for Abel and his offering but did not have regard for Cain and his offering (Genesis 4:4-5). Because of this, Cain became angry and killed him in the field, and he became the victim of the first murder (Genesis 4:5-8).
character: The biblical text does not describe Abel's character or words directly, but through the attitude God showed toward the offering he brought, a differentiated evaluation of his sacrificial rite and conduct appears (Genesis 4:4). There is no direct portrayal of the person; his existence is mentioned only through the figurative expression that his blood, shed after his death, cries out from the ground (Genesis 4:10).

introduce: Apelles is a figure who appears in Romans 16, one approved in Christ, mentioned when the apostle Paul sent greetings to the believers in Rome (Romans 16:10).
lifetime: The Bible records nothing about Apelles' birth, upbringing, specific occupation, or field of ministry; his name appears only among those whom the apostle Paul told the believers at the end of Romans to greet, as one "approved in Christ" (Romans 16:10).
event: Apelles is regarded as a person approved in Christ, and as a member of the church mentioned by the apostle Paul he became an object of greeting (Romans 16:10).

introduce: A figure from Judah who was taken captive to Babylon, whose original name was Azariah. The chief of the eunuchs changed his name and called him Abednego (Daniel 1:7).
lifetime: A descendant of Judah, he was among the boys of royal and noble families of the people of Israel who were taken to Babylon after Jerusalem was besieged (Daniel 1:1-6). In the royal palace of Babylon he was made to learn the literature and language of the Chaldeans, and was given vegetables to eat in place of the king's delicacies (Daniel 1:4-16). Afterward, at Daniel's request, he was appointed, together with Shadrach and Meshach, to administer the affairs of the province of Babylon (Daniel 2:49).
event: Because he did not bow down to the golden image King Nebuchadnezzar had set up, he was thrown into the burning fiery furnace, but the fire had no power to harm their bodies (Daniel 3:12-27). After this event the king praised their God, and promoted Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego further in the province of Babylon (Daniel 3:28-30).
character: To keep his religious identity, he showed the resolve to refuse the king's delicacies and wine (Daniel 1:8). Even under the threat of death he held to his convictions and maintained an attitude of not yielding (Daniel 3:16-18).

introduce: A Jew from Alexandria, an intellectual and preacher who stood out in the early history of Christianity. He is a figure who contributed to the spread of early Christianity, centered on the regions of Ephesus and Corinth.
lifetime: Born in Alexandria, a learned man mighty in the Scriptures, he arrived at Ephesus (Acts 18:24). He had been instructed in the way of the Lord and, fervent in spirit, spoke and taught accurately the things concerning Jesus, though he knew only the baptism of John (Acts 18:25). Priscilla and Aquila, a husband and wife who observed this, took him aside and explained the way of God to him more accurately (Acts 18:26). Afterward he crossed over to Achaia and greatly helped those who through grace had believed there (Acts 18:27). In Corinth he vigorously refuted the Jews in public, showing by the Scriptures that Jesus is the Christ (Acts 18:28).
event: In the church at Corinth there was division, saying "I follow Paul" and "I follow Apollos," and Apollos was mentioned together with Paul (1 Corinthians 1:12, 3:4). Paul said that he and Apollos were servants through whom they believed, as the Lord assigned to each, and that Paul planted and Apollos watered (1 Corinthians 3:5-6). Paul strongly urged Apollos to go to Corinth with the brothers, but he was not at all willing to go at that time, saying he would go when he had the opportunity (1 Corinthians 16:12). Also Paul urged Titus to send Zenas the lawyer and Apollos on their way quickly, so that they would lack nothing (Titus 3:13).
character: He was regarded as a person of great eloquence (Acts 18:24). He was well versed in the knowledge of the Scriptures and had the ability to argue logically on the basis of the Scriptures in public settings (Acts 18:28). He showed a receptive attitude, humbly accepting from Priscilla and Aquila what was lacking in his own knowledge and knowing how to correct his teaching (Acts 18:26).

introduce: Apollyon is a being who appears in the book of Revelation; in the Hebrew form he is called Abaddon, and he is the king of the locusts and the angel of the Abyss.
lifetime: In the biblical text no narrative record concerning the birth or ordinary life of this being appears (Revelation 9:11).
event: When the fifth angel blew his trumpet, a star that had fallen from heaven to earth was given the key to the Abyss and opened it, and out of the smoke locusts came upon the earth (Revelation 9:1-3); Apollyon is recorded as the king of these locusts (Revelation 9:11).
character: He has the name Abaddon in Hebrew and Apollyon in Greek, and is portrayed as a being whose name means destroyer (Revelation 9:11).

introduce: Abner was the son of Ner, the uncle of King Saul, and served as commander of the house of Saul. Even after Saul's death he set up Ish-bosheth as king and was the man of real power in Israel, who tried to maintain the house of Saul.
lifetime: He is recorded as Saul's commander (1 Samuel 14:50), and after Saul died he took Saul's son Ish-bosheth, crossed over to Mahanaim, and made him king (2 Samuel 2:8-9). Afterward he met Joab, a servant of David, at the pool of Gibeon (2 Samuel 2:13), and after a quarrel with Ish-bosheth he sent messengers to David proposing a covenant (2 Samuel 3:7-12), but when he returned to Hebron he was stabbed by Joab at the gate of the city and died (2 Samuel 3:27).
event: He took Saul's son Ish-bosheth, crossed over to Mahanaim, and made him king over Gilead, the Asherites, Jezreel, Ephraim, Benjamin, and all Israel (2 Samuel 2:8-9). When Asahel pursued him in battle, he told him several times to turn aside, but since Asahel would not listen, he struck him in the belly with the butt end of his spear and killed him, and this affected his relationship with Asahel's brother Joab (2 Samuel 2:19-23). After his quarrel with Ish-bosheth he sent messengers to David to ask for a covenant, and spoke to the elders of Israel and to the Benjaminites to bring all Israel over to David (2 Samuel 3:12-21).
character: He is portrayed as a man of very strong loyalty to the house of Saul (2 Samuel 2:8). Excelling in military ability, he had the charisma to command the army of Israel (2 Samuel 3:6), and possessed a realistic judgment that made political decisions as circumstances changed (2 Samuel 3:17-18). At the same time, he also showed a restrained attitude in direct confrontation, as when he warned Asahel several times to turn away before killing him (2 Samuel 2:21-22).

meaning: Father of many nations, ancestor of many peoples
introduce: Abraham is the son of Terah and the father of Isaac, a figure recorded as the ancestor of the Hebrew people. In Genesis 17 and 18, he makes a covenant with God and has his name changed, practices circumcision, and receives a visit from God, encountering major turning points in history.
lifetime: God changed his name from Abram to Abraham, which means that he would be the father of many nations (Genesis 17:5). God commanded Abraham and his descendants to keep the covenant throughout their generations (Genesis 17:9). God also told him to change the name of his wife Sarai to Sarah, and said that He would give a son through Sarah (Genesis 17:15-16). When Abraham heard this word, he fell on his face and laughed, and said in his heart, "Shall a child be born to a man who is a hundred years old?" (Genesis 17:17). He told God that he wished Ishmael to live before Him (Genesis 17:18). After God finished speaking with him and went up from him (Genesis 17:22), Abraham took on that very day his son Ishmael and all who were born in his house or bought with his money, every male among the men of his house, and circumcised the flesh of their foreskins (Genesis 17:23). Abraham was ninety-nine years old when he was circumcised (Genesis 17:24). Abraham and Ishmael were circumcised on the same day (Genesis 17:26). Afterward the LORD appeared to Abraham by the oaks of Mamre (Genesis 18:1).
event: As God had commanded him, Abraham circumcised his son Ishmael and every male among the men of his house (Genesis 17:23). He was ninety-nine years old when he circumcised the flesh of his foreskin (Genesis 17:24). He also responded by falling on his face and laughing when he heard God's word that He would give a son through Sarah (Genesis 17:15-17). Afterward the LORD appeared to him by the oaks of Mamre (Genesis 18:1).
character: Abraham bowed down in reverence before the historic event of God's covenant and the accompanying change of his name (Genesis 17:17). He showed affection for his son Ishmael and pleaded that he might live before God (Genesis 17:18). He also showed an obedient side by promptly carrying out the circumcision God commanded (Genesis 17:23).

기타관계: Melchizedek#920(king of Salem, priest of God Most High)

call: Wise woman of Carmel (wife of David)
introduce: A woman from Carmel who was the wife of Nabal, a wealthy landowner of Maon, and who afterward became David's wife. She is recorded as one who recognized David's power and, by exercising diplomatic skill, saved her household from crisis.
lifetime: She was the wife of Nabal the Carmelite (1 Samuel 25:3). When Nabal insulted David's envoys and David resolved on revenge, she persuaded him and averted his wrath (1 Samuel 25:18-35). After Nabal died she became David's wife (1 Samuel 25:39-42), and when David came to Ziklag she was taken captive by the Amalekites, but David recovered and rescued her (1 Samuel 30:1-5, 18). Afterward, when David was at Hebron, she bore him his son Chileab (2 Samuel 3:2-3).
event: In the situation of conflict with David arising from Nabal's arrogant attitude, she quickly prepared provisions, went to David's camp, and wisely apologized, thereby causing David to withdraw his plan to kill Nabal and his household (1 Samuel 25:18-34). Also, after Nabal's death she became David's wife and joined David's household (1 Samuel 25:40-42).
character: The Bible describes her as an intelligent woman of beautiful appearance (1 Samuel 25:3). In calming David's anger, she used eloquence that acknowledged her own husband Nabal to be a fool and exalted David (1 Samuel 25:25-28), and showed a cool sense of reality that judged the situation accurately and responded to it (1 Samuel 25:24-31).

call: Man of Kiriath-jearim (keeper of the ark)
introduce: He lived on the hill at Kiriath-jearim; the men of Kiriath-jearim took the ark of the LORD that had returned from the Philistines and brought it into his house. The ark remained at Kiriath-jearim a long time, twenty years from the day it came there (1 Samuel 7:1-2).
lifetime: The men of Kiriath-jearim brought the ark of the LORD into his house, and his son Eleazar was consecrated to keep the ark (1 Samuel 7:1). When David moved the ark, his sons Uzzah and Ahio drove the new cart (2 Samuel 6:3).
event: The ark of the LORD, returned from the Philistines, was brought by the men of Kiriath-jearim into the house of Abinadab on the hill, and stayed there a long time (1 Samuel 7:1-2). Afterward, when the ark was placed on a new cart and brought out of his house, Uzzah, a son of Abinadab, drove the cart together with Ahio; when the oxen stumbled, Uzzah put out his hand and took hold of the ark of God, and the anger of the LORD was kindled against Uzzah, and He struck him down there, and he died beside the ark (2 Samuel 6:3-7).

introduce: Abinoam is a figure who appears in the Old Testament book of Judges, the father of Barak of Kedesh in the tribe of Naphtali.
lifetime: Abinoam is recorded as the father of Barak. In the text his name appears only in the expression "Barak son of Abinoam," and his son Barak is the one whom Deborah summoned from Kedesh in Naphtali to go to Mount Tabor (Judges 4:6). The Bible has no record of Abinoam's own residence, life, or death.
event: There is no historical achievement or event directly shown; in Judges his name is mentioned mainly in the expression "Barak son of Abinoam," a phrase that identifies Barak (Judges 4:6, 4:12, 5:1, 5:12).

introduce: Abida is a figure recorded as a son of Midian and one of the descendants born between Abraham and Keturah.
lifetime: He was born as one of the five sons of Midian, whom Keturah, Abraham's later wife, bore (Genesis 25:4).
event: In the biblical text no concrete record of independent achievements or particular events of Abida himself can be found (Genesis 25:4).

introduce: Abidan is a figure who appears in the Old Testament book of Numbers, the son of Gideoni of the tribe of Benjamin. He is recorded as a chief of the tribe of Benjamin in the census after the exodus, in the process of presenting the dedication offerings of the altar, and in the march in the wilderness.
lifetime: Abidan took part in the census as a commander of the descendants of Benjamin (Numbers 1:11), and after the tabernacle was set up he took part in the ceremony in which the commanders of each tribe presented offerings (Numbers 7:60). He also played the role of leading the army of the tribe of Benjamin in the march in the wilderness (Numbers 10:24).
event: On the day Moses set up the tabernacle and anointed the altar, when the chiefs presented the dedication offerings of the altar one man each day, Abidan, on the ninth day, as chief of the descendants of Benjamin, offered one silver platter, one silver bowl, one gold dish, and burnt offerings, sin offerings, and peace offerings (Numbers 7:10-11, 7:60-65). He also led the army of the tribe of the descendants of Benjamin during the journey in the wilderness (Numbers 10:24).

introduce: Abital is the woman who bore David's fifth son (2 Samuel 3:4).
lifetime: She became David's wife during the time when King David ruled the tribe of Judah at Hebron (2 Samuel 3:4).
event: During the seven years and six months of his reign at Hebron, she bore Shephatiah, the fifth of the sons whom David had at Hebron (2 Samuel 3:4-5, 1 Chronicles 3:3-4).

introduce: Abitub is a figure who appears in the genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin, a son of Shaharaim.
lifetime: He was born as a son whom Shaharaim of the tribe of Benjamin had by his wife Hushim (1 Chronicles 8:11).
event: No specific deeds of Abitub are recorded in the Bible; his name appears only as a son whom Shaharaim had by his wife Hushim, together with his brother Elpaal (1 Chronicles 8:11).

introduce: Abiram is a figure who appears in the Old Testament book of Numbers, a son of Eliab of the tribe of Reuben, and one of the key figures who, together with Dathan, rose up against the leadership of Moses.
lifetime: A descendant of the tribe of Reuben and a son of Eliab, he attempted a rebellion against Moses together with Dathan and On (Numbers 16:1). In the course of the march in the wilderness, he opposed the leadership and in the end received judgment and ended his life (Numbers 16:32).
event: In league with Korah, he rose up against Moses with two hundred fifty chiefs of the congregation of Israel, men of renown (Numbers 16:1-2). Moses sent to call Dathan and Abiram, but they said they would not come up, and accused Moses of bringing them up out of a land flowing with milk and honey to kill them in the wilderness, and of not bringing them into a land flowing with milk and honey or giving them an inheritance (Numbers 16:12-14). In this incident Abiram, together with Dathan, his wife and children and little ones, stood at the door of his tent, and the earth opened its mouth and swallowed them and all that belonged to them, and they went down alive into Sheol and perished from among the assembly (Numbers 16:27-33).
character: He showed a disobedient tendency, asserting his own vested rights and openly challenging the authority of the leader (Numbers 16:13). In the course of refusing Moses' summons he maintained a domineering and confrontational attitude, and displayed a hard-line stance of not yielding his position to the end (Numbers 16:12-14).

introduce: Abimael is a descendant of Shem, son of Noah, and is mentioned as one of the thirteen sons of Joktan. He is recorded as part of the ancient genealogy of humanity shown through the genealogy of Shem.
lifetime: Abimael was born as a son of Joktan, the son of Eber (Genesis 10:28). Other than his birth, no concrete dates or activities concerning his life appear in Scripture.

call: Abimelech I, king of Gerar (ally of Abraham)
introduce: Abimelech, king of Gerar, is a figure who appears in the book of Genesis; he is the king who, when Abraham was sojourning in Gerar, took Sarah, and after receiving a warning from God in a dream, made a covenant with Abraham.
lifetime: When Abraham moved to the Negev and was sojourning in Gerar, he took Sarah on the strength of Abraham's saying that she was his sister, but at night God appeared to him in a dream and warned him that he would die because the woman was another man's wife (Genesis 20:1-3). Afterward he gave sheep, oxen, and male and female servants to Abraham, and sent back his wife Sarah, and told him to dwell wherever he pleased in his land (Genesis 20:14-15). Later he came to Abraham with Phicol, the commander of his army, and made a covenant at Beersheba (Genesis 21:22-32).
event: Abimelech summoned Abraham and demanded of him why he had done this (Genesis 20:9-10). When Abraham reproved him about the servants of Abimelech having seized a well by force, he answered that he did not know who had done it, and that he had heard of it only that day (Genesis 21:25-26). When Abraham told him to take seven ewe lambs as a witness that he had dug the well, the two swore an oath to each other and called the place Beersheba, and after making the covenant at Beersheba, Abimelech and Phicol returned to the land of the Philistines (Genesis 21:27-32).
character: He showed a generous attitude toward foreigners living in his kingdom, and had a pragmatic side that gave priority to diplomatic agreement over military clash in conflict situations (Genesis 21:22-23). In his relationship with Abraham, he shows the disposition of a reasonable and moderate ruler, acknowledging the God (Elohim) of the other party and regarding the treaty with him as sacred (Genesis 21:22, 21:31).

introduce: Abishag was a young woman from Shunem who was brought in to attend King David in his old age.
lifetime: When David was old and could not keep warm even when covered with bedclothes, his servants looked for a young virgin to keep the king warm and wait on him (1 Kings 1:1-2). Abishag was chosen for this purpose and waited on David and served him, but the king did not lie with her (1 Kings 1:3-4). After David died, Adonijah asked, through Bathsheba the mother of Solomon, that Abishag be given him as a wife (1 Kings 2:17).
event: Abishag attended King David at his side when he was very old (1 Kings 1:15). Afterward, when Adonijah asked through Bathsheba that Abishag be given him as a wife, Solomon said that asking Abishag the Shunammite for Adonijah was the same as asking for the kingdom (1 Kings 2:22). Solomon swore by the LORD that Adonijah, having spoken thus, would be put to death that day, and sent Benaiah, who struck Adonijah down and killed him (1 Kings 2:23-25).
character: The Bible describes Abishag as a very beautiful young woman (1 Kings 1:4). While attending King David she served the king with great devotion, but it is stated explicitly that she had no physical relations with the king (1 Kings 1:4). Afterward nothing concrete is recorded about her personal character or deeds.

introduce: Abishalom is a figure mentioned in 1 Kings as the father of Maacah, who is recorded as the mother of Abijam and Asa, kings of Judah (1 Kings 15:2, 1 Kings 15:10).
lifetime: 1 Kings 15:2 and 15:10 record Maacah as the mother of Abijam and the mother of Asa, calling her "the daughter of Abishalom." The Bible has no record concerning the life of Abishalom himself.
event: The Bible has no record of Abishalom's own deeds. It does record that because his daughter Maacah had made a detestable image of Asherah, King Asa removed her from her position as queen mother, cut down the image, and burned it by the brook Kidron (1 Kings 15:13).
character: The Bible records that Abishalom was involved in the act of idol worship for Asherah, and as a result she was deprived of her political authority by King Asa (1 Kings 15:13).
