event: He is recorded as the officer over Zebulun in the list of those in charge of the tribes of Israel (1 Chronicles 27:16, 27:19). Apart from this verse, none of his deeds appears.

introduce: Ishmerai appears in the genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin, a member of the house of Benjamin recorded as a son of Elpaal (1 Chronicles 8:18).
lifetime: Ishmerai was born as a son of Elpaal, a descendant of Benjamin (1 Chronicles 8:18). Within the genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin he is stated to be one of the descendants whom Elpaal fathered (1 Chronicles 8:18).

introduce: Ishbah appears in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah; he is a son of Mered and is recorded as the ancestor of Eshtemoa (1 Chronicles 4:17).
lifetime: He was born as a son of Mered, a descendant of the tribe of Judah (1 Chronicles 4:17).
event: Mered fathered Miriam, Shammai, and Ishbah, the ancestor of Eshtemoa (1 Chronicles 4:17). The following verse records these as the sons of Bithiah, the daughter of Pharaoh, whom Mered had taken (1 Chronicles 4:18). There is no record of any personal event of Ishbah himself.

introduce: Ishbak is one of the six sons born to Abraham and his later wife Keturah, a person recorded in the genealogy as a descendant of Abraham.
lifetime: Ishbak is a son born to Keturah, whom Abraham took as a later wife (Genesis 25:1-2). He is listed among the sons born to Abraham's concubine Keturah (1 Chronicles 1:32). There is a record that Abraham gave possessions to the sons of his concubines and sent them away to the east, away from his son Isaac, during his lifetime (Genesis 25:6), but Ishbak's name is not mentioned directly.
event: There is no record in the Bible that Ishbak took the lead in any independent event or left any personal achievement. He merely served, as a person making up Abraham's family line, the role of being entered in the genealogy (Genesis 25:2, 1 Chronicles 1:32).

introduce: Ishpan is a person recorded in the genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin, a descendant of Benjamin who is mentioned as one of the sons of Shashak (1 Chronicles 8:22, 8:25).
lifetime: Ishpan, as a son of Shashak, is placed within the family line of the tribe of Benjamin, and these sons are all recorded as heads of families and chiefs throughout their generations who lived in Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 8:25, 8:28).

introduce: Ish-bosheth was a son of King Saul who, after Saul's death, was set up as king of Israel by Saul's commander Abner. He is understood to be the same person as Esh-baal, who is recorded as Saul's son in 1 Chronicles 8:33 and 9:39, and during the time when the house of Judah followed David, he was king of Israel in the midst of the war between the house of Saul and the house of David (2 Samuel 2:8-10, 3:1).
lifetime: Saul's commander Abner took Saul's son Ish-bosheth across to Mahanaim and made him king over Israel (2 Samuel 2:8-9). He was forty years old when he became king over Israel, and he reigned for two years (2 Samuel 2:10). When he rebuked Abner over the matter of Saul's concubine Rizpah, he was afraid of Abner's angry words and could not answer him a word (2 Samuel 3:7-11). In the end, his captains Baanah and Rechab came into his house and killed him (2 Samuel 4:2, 4:5-7).
event: While the war between the house of Saul and the house of David went on for a long time, the house of Saul grew weaker and weaker (2 Samuel 3:1). When Ish-bosheth rebuked Abner over the matter of Saul's concubine Rizpah, Abner became angry, and afterward Abner sent messengers to David to ask for a covenant (2 Samuel 3:7-12). When David demanded that Michal be given back, Ish-bosheth sent men and took Michal from her husband Paltiel son of Laish (2 Samuel 3:14-15). Afterward the captains Rechab and Baanah came into his house, struck him down as he lay on his bed in his bedchamber, cut off his head, and presented the head to David at Hebron (2 Samuel 4:5-8).
character: It can be seen that the base of his power depended heavily on the commander Abner (2 Samuel 3:11). When all Israel fell into confusion after Abner's death, he failed to show strong leadership capable of governing it, and he showed a weak side in that he could neither prevent nor control it when his subordinates plotted treason (2 Samuel 4:1).

introduce: Ishbi-benob is a Philistine recorded as one of the descendants of the giant. In the days of King David, when the Philistines attacked Israel, he carried a bronze spear weighing three hundred shekels and wore a new sword, and he tried to kill David (2 Samuel 21:15-16).
lifetime: When the Philistines attacked Israel again, Ishbi-benob tried to kill David in the battle in which David and his servants went down to fight, but Abishai son of Zeruiah came to David's aid and struck down that Philistine and killed him (2 Samuel 21:15-17).
event: Carrying a bronze spear weighing three hundred shekels and wearing a new sword, he tried to kill David (2 Samuel 21:16). This happened when David was weary (2 Samuel 21:15), and Abishai son of Zeruiah came to David's aid and struck down Ishbi-benob and killed him (2 Samuel 21:17). After this, David's men swore to David and asked that the king no longer go out with them to the battle (2 Samuel 21:17).
character: He was a descendant of the Rephaim and is described as a man of huge build (2 Samuel 21:16). He had the strength to use a bronze spear weighing three hundred shekels (2 Samuel 21:16), and he was a warrior who confronted David carrying a new weapon (2 Samuel 21:16).

introduce: Ishvah is recorded as one of the four sons of Asher, a son of Jacob (Genesis 46:17). He is mentioned as one of the principal members who make up the genealogy of the tribe of Asher (1 Chronicles 7:30).
lifetime: Ishvah was born as a son of Asher (Genesis 46:17), and his family has the hereditary background of having moved along with Jacob's family when it left Canaan and migrated to Egypt (Genesis 46:17). Afterward, through the record of 1 Chronicles 7:30, it is confirmed that, as a descendant of Asher, he occupies a place in that genealogy (1 Chronicles 7:30).

introduce: Ishvi is a person who appears in the Old Testament, a son of Asher recorded in the genealogy of the tribe of Asher, and he is listed third, after Imna and Ishvah (Genesis 46:17, 1 Chronicles 7:30).
lifetime: He was born as a son of Asher, and he was among those included when Jacob's family moved to Egypt (Genesis 46:17). He became the ancestor of the descendants of Ishvi (Numbers 26:44).
character: Nothing about his personal character or any unusual event is mentioned in the biblical record, and his name appears only in the genealogical lists (1 Chronicles 7:30).

introduce: Izhar is a son of Kohath of the tribe of Levi and a brother of Amram, Hebron, and Uzziel (Exodus 6:18). He was the father of Korah, Nepheg, and Zichri, and corresponds to the ancestor of the house of the descendants of Korah (Exodus 6:21).
lifetime: As a son of Kohath, he is recorded as Kohath's second son in the genealogy of the tribe of Levi (Exodus 6:18). He had three sons, Korah, Nepheg, and Zichri, and these formed the family line of the Levites (Exodus 6:21). The Bible contains no record of specific activities related to his life or of the time of his death.
character: No description of Izhar's personal character or specific traits is found in the biblical record (Exodus 6:18, 6:21).

introduce: Ishhod is a person mentioned in 1 Chronicles 7:18 of the Old Testament, a man who appears in the genealogy of the tribe of Manasseh. In the context of recording the descendants of Gilead, he is recorded as one of the sons born to "his sister" Hammoleketh (1 Chronicles 7:17-18).
lifetime: Ishhod is recorded as a son born to Hammoleketh (1 Chronicles 7:18). Hammoleketh is introduced as "his sister" in the context of recording the descendants of Gilead (the son of Machir and grandson of Manasseh) (1 Chronicles 7:17-18). Ishhod is recorded together with Hammoleketh's other sons Abiezer and Mahlah (1 Chronicles 7:18).

introduce: Izliah is a person who appears in the genealogy of the family of the tribe of Benjamin and is recorded as one of the sons of Elpaal (1 Chronicles 8:18).
lifetime: As a son of Elpaal, his name is entered in the genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin (1 Chronicles 8:18).

introduce: Ishi is a person mentioned in 1 Chronicles 2 and is recorded, in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah, as a descendant of Jerahmeel, the firstborn son of Hezron, and as a son of Appaim.
lifetime: Within the genealogy of the tribe of Judah he was born as a son of Appaim (1 Chronicles 2:31). He is a descendant of Onam, a son of Jerahmeel, Hezron's firstborn, and the line passes through Appaim, the son of Nadab, the son of Shammai (1 Chronicles 2:25, 2:28, 2:30-31).
event: In the biblical record, no specific achievement or historical event carried out by the person called Ishi appears, and he appears only as a name in the genealogy (1 Chronicles 2:31).

introduce: A person belonging to the tribe of Manasseh among the tribes of Israel, a descendant of Gilead who appears in the genealogy of the house of Abiezer.
lifetime: He was born as a descendant of Gilead, and from him came the family of Iezer (Numbers 26:30).
event: Apart from being mentioned in the census list of Numbers 26 as the ancestor of the family of Iezer among the descendants of Gilead, no special activity or event is recorded of him (Numbers 26:30).

introduce: Eve appears in the book of Genesis in the Old Testament; she is the first woman, whom God made from Adam's rib, and the wife of Adam (Genesis 2:22, 3:20). In the New Testament, in 2 Corinthians and 1 Timothy, her name is written in its Greek form, "Eua."
lifetime: She was made by God from Adam's rib and became Adam's helper (Genesis 2:18, 2:22-23). She was with Adam in the garden of Eden (Genesis 3:8), and listening to the serpent's words, she ate the fruit of the forbidden tree and also gave it to her husband Adam to eat with her (Genesis 3:1-6). After being driven out of the garden of Eden, she bore Cain and Abel (Genesis 3:23, 4:1-2), and after Cain killed Abel, she bore a son and named him Seth (Genesis 4:25).
event: Adam named her Eve because she was to become the mother of all the living (Genesis 3:20). The serpent's leading her astray by its craftiness is recorded (Genesis 3:1-6, 2 Corinthians 11:3), and the apostle Paul says that Adam was formed first, and Eua afterward (1 Timothy 2:13).

introduce: Ikkesh is recorded as the father of Ira among the 37 mighty men of David, the military organization of King David of ancient Israel. He is known by the name Ikkesh of Tekoa (2 Samuel 23:26).
lifetime: He was a man from Tekoa, a hill town of the tribe of Judah (2 Samuel 23:26).
event: His son Ira was chosen as one of David's Thirty mighty men, and he was also appointed commander of the sixth division, for the sixth month of the year, with 24,000 men (1 Chronicles 27:9).

기타관계: David#468(kinsman of the tribe of Judah)

introduce: Igdaliah is a person recorded in the book of Jeremiah as the father of Hanan, the man of God (Jeremiah 35:4).
lifetime: The Bible contains no record of Igdaliah's own life; it records only that his son Hanan is called "a man of God" and that the chamber of Hanan's sons was in the house of the LORD (Jeremiah 35:4).
event: The Bible contains no record of anything Igdaliah himself did. He is introduced merely as the father of Hanan, in the context where, when Jeremiah took the Rechabites to a chamber in the house of the LORD, he brought them into the chamber of the sons of Hanan, the man of God, son of Igdaliah (Jeremiah 35:2-4).

call: son of Helem (chief of the mighty men of Asher)
introduce: Imna is a descendant of the tribe of Asher and a son of Helem. He is a person who can be identified through the genealogy of 1 Chronicles 7:35.
lifetime: Imna is recorded as a son of Helem, the younger brother of Shomer (1 Chronicles 7:34-35). Together with his brothers Zophah, Shelesh, and Amal, he makes up the family line of the tribe of Asher (1 Chronicles 7:35).

call: Chief of the priestly family of the 16th division
introduce: Immer was the head of a priestly family recorded in 1 Chronicles, and the man in charge of the sixteenth of the twenty-four divisions of the priests established in the time of David.
lifetime: When David, together with Zadok of the descendants of Eleazar and Ahimelech of the descendants of Ithamar, divided the descendants of Aaron and assigned them their duties (1 Chronicles 24:3), Immer was recorded as the head of the sixteenth division (1 Chronicles 24:14). Maasai, who is introduced as a priest after the return from exile, is recorded as a fifth-generation descendant of Immer (1 Chronicles 9:10-12). Among the priests in the list of returnees, the descendants of Immer numbered one thousand and fifty-two (Ezra 2:36-37, Nehemiah 7:39-40).
event: In the time of Ezra, Hanani and Zebadiah, among the descendants of Immer, are recorded as being among the priests who had taken foreign women (Ezra 10:18, 10:20). The priests who had taken foreign women pledged, giving their hands, to send away their wives (Ezra 10:19).

introduce: Nimshi is a man recorded in 2 Chronicles 22:7 as the father of Jehu. His identity and genealogy are not stated beyond this verse.
lifetime: The Bible has no record of Nimshi's own life; he is mentioned only as the father of his son Jehu, whom the LORD anointed to destroy the house of Ahab (2 Chronicles 22:7).
event: The Bible has no record of anything Nimshi himself did. He is mentioned only as Jehu's father, in the context of Ahaziah going out with Joram to meet Jehu son of Nimshi (2 Chronicles 22:7).

introduce: Jephthah was a man of Gilead in the period of the judges, who was raised up as Israel's military leader in the war against the Ammonites and served as a judge. Although he was a son of Gilead, he was driven out of the family because he was the son of another woman, and then was called back, a distinctive history.
lifetime: Jephthah was a son of Gilead, born to a prostitute rather than to Gilead's wife (Judges 11:1). Driven out by his half-brothers, he lived in the land of Tob and gathered a band of worthless men around him (Judges 11:3). When the Ammonites attacked Israel, he was brought in as leader by the elders of Gilead and carried out the office of judge (Judges 11:6). After judging Israel for six years, he died and was buried in a city of Gilead (Judges 12:7).
event: Before the war with the Ammonites he attempted peaceful diplomatic negotiation and argued the legitimacy of the land Israel had taken (Judges 11:12-28). He won a great victory over the Ammonites; he struck twenty cities from Aroer to Minnith and as far as Abel-keramim with a great slaughter, and subdued the Ammonites (Judges 11:33). Before the battle he vowed to offer to the LORD as a burnt offering whoever came out of the doors of his house to meet him (Judges 11:30-31), and when he returned, the first to come out and meet him was his only child, his daughter (Judges 11:34); after two months she returned, and he did to her as he had vowed (Judges 11:35-39). When the men of Ephraim picked a quarrel with him because he had not called them when he fought the Ammonites, he gathered the men of Gilead and struck and defeated Ephraim, and at the fords of the Jordan he identified the men of Ephraim by their pronunciation of "Shibboleth" and killed them (Judges 12:1-6).
character: In negotiating with the elders who had driven him out, he showed a compromising attitude, seeking a clear guarantee of his position and authority (Judges 11:9-10). In diplomatic bargaining with the hostile power, he showed a logical and diplomatic side, accurately citing past history (Judges 11:12-28). He had a stubborn and tenacious side, being determined to fulfill his vow without retracting it (Judges 11:35). His conduct in the conflict with the tribe of Ephraim reveals an aspect of a resolute and exclusive temperament (Judges 12:4-6).

introduce: Ibzan was one of the judges of Israel recorded in the book of Judges, a man of Bethlehem. He became judge of Israel after Jephthah (Judges 12:7-8).
lifetime: Ibzan was a man of Bethlehem who became judge of Israel after Jephthah and served seven years (Judges 12:8-9). When he died, he was buried in Bethlehem (Judges 12:10).
event: He had thirty sons and thirty daughters; he gave his daughters in marriage outside his clan and brought in thirty women from outside for his sons (Judges 12:9). The Bible contains no record of any specific military activity or ruling he carried out as judge (Judges 12:8-10).
character: Ibzan had many children and followed the practice of forming alliances between families by marrying them to foreigners or to other tribes (Judges 12:9). The Bible gives no separate evaluation of his personal character (Judges 12:8-10).

introduce: Ibsam is a man found in the genealogy of the tribe of Issachar, recorded as a son of Tola and a descendant of Issachar (1 Chronicles 7:2).
lifetime: Ibsam was born as a son of Tola, the son of Issachar (1 Chronicles 7:1-2). Together with Tola's sons Uzzi, Rephaiah, Jeriel, Jahmai, Ibsam, and Shemuel, he was called head of his father Tola's house (1 Chronicles 7:2).
event: No event of Ibsam's own is recorded. All the sons of Tola were heads of their father Tola's house and mighty warriors in their generations, and in the days of David their number reached twenty-two thousand six hundred (1 Chronicles 7:2).

introduce: Ibhar was one of the sons David had in Jerusalem, a person included in the list of David's sons and one of the genealogical members of David's house (2 Samuel 5:14-15).
lifetime: Ibhar was a son born in Jerusalem after David moved his seat of rule from Hebron to Jerusalem (2 Samuel 5:15). In 1 Chronicles 3 and 14, his birth and name are confirmed once more within the genealogies listing David's sons (1 Chronicles 3:6, 1 Chronicles 14:5).

call: a man of Gath (David's loyal general)
introduce: Ittai was a Philistine from Gath, a foreign general who served as a close aide and military leader during the reign of King David.
lifetime: When David left Jerusalem to escape Absalom's rebellion, six hundred men from Gath followed the king (2 Samuel 15:18), and Ittai the Gittite also crossed over with all his men and the little ones who were with him (2 Samuel 15:22). David called him an exile and urged him to turn back, but he swore that he would follow David to the end (2 Samuel 15:19-21). Afterward David divided the people into three parts and put a third under the command of Ittai the Gittite (2 Samuel 18:2).
event: During Absalom's rebellion, as David fled, he urged Ittai to go back, but Ittai swore by the life of the LORD and the life of the king that wherever the king might be, whether for death or for life, his servant would be there too (2 Samuel 15:19-21). When David put a third of the army each under Joab, Abishai, and Ittai, Ittai took command of one of those divisions (2 Samuel 18:2).
character: He was a man of deep loyalty and faithfulness to King David, who had received him (2 Samuel 15:21). Beyond ties of blood or ethnic background, he showed devotion to the lord he had chosen, even at the risk of his life (2 Samuel 15:21). He is regarded as a man with the command of the ranks and the leadership ability that David trusted fully in military operations (2 Samuel 18:2).

call: father of Ahinadab (father of one of Solomon's officers)
introduce: Iddo is the father of Ahinadab, one of the twelve officers who administered the districts of Israel during the reign of King Solomon.
lifetime: Nothing specific is recorded about Iddo's life; his existence is mentioned only through the fact that his son Ahinadab, as an officer of Solomon, was responsible for the region of Mahanaim (1 Kings 4:14).
event: The Bible has no record of anything Iddo himself did. In the list of Solomon's twelve officers, he is mentioned only as the father of Ahinadab, in the words "Ahinadab the son of Iddo, in Mahanaim" (1 Kings 4:14).

introduce: Idbash is a man who appears in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah, recorded as one of the descendants of the father of Etam (1 Chronicles 4:3).
lifetime: He is recorded in the genealogy of Judah as a descendant of the father of Etam, and is mentioned together with Jezreel and Ishma. Hazzelelponi is recorded as their brother-in-law (1 Chronicles 4:3).
event: The biblical text records no specific deed or special event performed by Idbash (1 Chronicles 4:3).

기타관계: Hazzelelponi#2999(kinsman of the tribe of Judah)

introduce: Issachar was the fifth son born to Jacob and Leah and the ninth son of Jacob (Genesis 30:18). He became the ancestor of the tribe of Issachar, one of the twelve tribes of Israel (Genesis 46:13).
lifetime: Leah lay with Jacob in exchange for mandrakes and bore him, and she named him Issachar (Genesis 30:16-18). Afterward he left Canaan with the family of Jacob and migrated to Egypt (Genesis 46:13). When Jacob blessed his sons before he died, he compared him to a strong donkey and prophesied his destiny (Genesis 49:14-15).
event: His descendants, the tribe of the sons of Issachar, received as an inheritance, by their families, a territory that included Jezreel, Shunem, Tabor, and other places (Joshua 19:17-23). Later, when they were about to make David king, there were among the sons of Issachar two hundred chiefs who understood the times and knew what Israel ought to do (1 Chronicles 12:32).
character: Jacob described him as a strong donkey crouching between the sheepfolds (Genesis 49:14). He received the prophetic assessment that he would see that a resting place was good and the land pleasant, and would bend his shoulder to bear the burden and become a servant under forced labor (Genesis 49:15).

직업/직위: progenitor of the tribe of Issachar

introduce: A person who appears in the genealogy recorded in 1 Chronicles 7, a descendant of the tribe of Issachar and a son of Izrahiah.
lifetime: He was a son of Izrahiah, the son of Uzzi, and a descendant of Tola, the son of Issachar (1 Chronicles 7:1-3).
event: Together with his brothers Michael, Obadiah, and Joel, he was a chief (1 Chronicles 7:3), and the troops of the fighting army with them numbered thirty-six thousand (1 Chronicles 7:4).

introduce: Hacaliah is a person who appears in the book of Nehemiah in the Old Testament, recorded as the father of Nehemiah.
lifetime: Hacaliah's existence is confirmed through the record "Nehemiah son of Hacaliah," as Nehemiah's father (Nehemiah 1:1). Beyond that, the Bible gives no specific record of his birth, activities, or death.
event: The Bible contains no record of any independent achievement or particular event of Hacaliah himself. He is mentioned only as the father of his son Nehemiah, in the historical course of Nehemiah's rebuilding of the walls of Jerusalem as governor of Judah (Nehemiah 1:1, 10:1).

introduce: Hagabah is a person who appears in the books of Ezra and Nehemiah in the Bible, and refers to a family of the Nethinim, among the descendants who returned from the Babylonian exile to Jerusalem.
lifetime: He is mentioned as the ancestor of a family among the Nethinim who, having ended the Babylonian exile, returned to Jerusalem under the leadership of Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:45). Later, the descendants of this family were recorded in the list drawn up in the course of Nehemiah's rebuilding of the walls of Jerusalem and the census (Nehemiah 7:48).
event: The descendants of Hagabah are listed among the Nethinim in the list of the people of Israel who came out with Zerubbabel and others, recorded in Ezra 2 (Ezra 2:2, 2:43-45). They are also listed as Nethinim in the register that Nehemiah found of those who came up at the first (Nehemiah 7:5, 7:46-48).

introduce: Hagar was a maidservant of Sarai, Abram's wife, and was a person of Egyptian origin (Genesis 16:1). She appears in the biblical narrative as the surrogate who conceived Abram's offspring and as the mother of Ishmael (Genesis 16:3, Genesis 16:15).
lifetime: When Sarai could not bear children, she gave her maidservant, Hagar the Egyptian, to her husband Abram as a concubine (Genesis 16:1-3). Hagar realized that she had conceived and despised her mistress; when Sarai then mistreated her, she fled from her, but she met the angel of the LORD and was told to return to her mistress and submit to her (Genesis 16:4-9). She bore a son, and Abram named him Ishmael (Genesis 16:15). Later, when Sarah saw Ishmael mocking Isaac and told Abraham to cast out this maidservant and her son, Abraham gave Hagar bread and a skin of water and sent her away (Genesis 21:9-14). Hagar wandered in the wilderness of Beersheba, and when the water ran out she placed the child under a bush and wept aloud, but God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of water and gave the child a drink; Ishmael lived in the wilderness of Paran (Genesis 21:14-21).
event: Hagar bore Abram's son Ishmael (Genesis 16:15). Fleeing from Sarai's mistreatment, she met the angel of the LORD by a spring in the wilderness, the spring on the way to Shur (Genesis 16:6-7). When Sarah saw the son of Hagar, whom she had borne to Abraham, mocking Isaac, she had Hagar and her son cast out (Genesis 21:9-14); afterward, while Ishmael lived in the wilderness of Paran, his mother took a wife for him from the land of Egypt (Genesis 21:21). In the New Testament, Hagar is used as an allegory of the one who bears children into slavery from Mount Sinai (Galatians 4:24-25).
character: After conceiving, she showed an attitude of contempt toward her mistress, Sarai (Genesis 16:4). She could not endure her mistress's mistreatment and attempted to flee, and when she and her son were in danger of dying in the wilderness, she showed an emotional response, sitting down at a distance and weeping aloud because she could not bear to see her son die (Genesis 16:6, Genesis 21:16).

introduce: Hagab is one of the families of the Nethinim among the people of Israel who were released from the Babylonian exile and returned to Jerusalem and Judah with Zerubbabel and others (Ezra 2:1-2, 2:43-46).
lifetime: Among the descendants of those who had been carried captive to Babylon, who were released and returned to Jerusalem and Judah with Zerubbabel and others, he is recorded as one family of the Nethinim (the descendants of Hagab) (Ezra 2:1-2, 2:46).
event: The descendants of Hagab, who belonged to the Nethinim whom David and the officials had appointed to serve the Levites (Ezra 8:20), are listed in the list of returnees in Ezra 2 (Ezra 2:43-46).

introduce: Haggedolim is a man recorded in Nehemiah 11:14 as the father of Zabdiel.
lifetime: In the list of priests in Nehemiah 11:10-14, it is recorded that his son Zabdiel became the overseer of 128 of his brothers, mighty men of valor (Nehemiah 11:14). The Bible contains no other record concerning Haggedolim himself.
event: No deeds of Haggedolim himself are recorded in the Bible. His son Zabdiel became the overseer of 128 of his brothers, mighty men of valor (Nehemiah 11:14).

introduce: Hagri is a man recorded in the list of David's mighty men in 1 Chronicles 11:38 as the father of "Mibhar the son of Hagri."
lifetime: Hagri's son Mibhar is listed in the roll of David's mighty men together with Joel the brother of Nathan (1 Chronicles 11:26, 11:38). The Bible has no record of Hagri's own birth or activities.
event: Hagri's own deeds are not recorded in the Bible; it is confirmed only that his son Mibhar is on the list of mighty men in 1 Chronicles 11 (1 Chronicles 11:38).

introduce: Hakupha is a family of the Nethinim who returned from the Babylonian exile, a name recorded in the lists of Ezra 2 and Nehemiah 7 (Ezra 2:43, 2:51, Nehemiah 7:46, 7:53).
lifetime: The descendants of Hakupha are recorded in the list of the Nethinim who were released from the Babylonian exile and returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel and others (Ezra 2:2, 2:51). Nehemiah found the genealogical register of those who had come up at the first, and the descendants of Hakupha are also listed among the Nethinim recorded there (Nehemiah 7:5, 7:53).
event: The descendants of Hakupha are listed among the Nethinim, together with the descendants of Bakbuk and the descendants of Harhur, in the list of returnees in Ezra 2 (Ezra 2:51), and they are recorded in the same order in the genealogical register of Nehemiah 7 (Nehemiah 7:53).

introduce: A descendant of the tribe of Levi who was in charge of the ministry of praise in the temple in the time of David, recorded as one of the sons of Heman.
lifetime: When David, together with the commanders of the army, set apart for service some of the sons of Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun (1 Chronicles 25:1), he was recorded as one of Heman's fourteen sons (1 Chronicles 25:4-5). Under the direction of his father, he served by singing in the house of the LORD God with cymbals, harps, and lyres (1 Chronicles 25:6).
event: When duties were assigned by casting lots, small and great alike, teacher as well as pupil (1 Chronicles 25:8), Hananiah was chosen sixteenth, together with his sons and brothers, twelve in all (1 Chronicles 25:23). Together with the sons of Heman, he served by singing in the house of the LORD with cymbals, harps, and lyres (1 Chronicles 25:6).

introduce: Hanani was a Levite who was active in the time of David and served as a member of the temple choir. He is mentioned as one of the sons of Heman of the descendants of Korah, and Heman was one of the chief persons in charge of praise in the time of David and Solomon.
lifetime: Hanani is included in the list of the singers whom David appointed (1 Chronicles 25:4). Together with his brothers, he took part in the casting of lots to perform the duty of playing instruments and praising in the temple under David's direction (1 Chronicles 25:8).
event: As a son of Heman, he belonged to the temple choir together with his father and was assigned his duty as eighteenth in order (1 Chronicles 25:25). This means that he was a member of a systematic organization that carried out musical service in the temple in a fixed order.

introduce: Hanamel was a man who owned a field in Anathoth, a son of Shallum, the uncle of the prophet Jeremiah, and a cousin of Jeremiah. He is recorded as the one who sold his field in Anathoth to Jeremiah at the time when the army of Babylon was besieging Jerusalem (Jeremiah 32:2, 32:7-9).
lifetime: In the tenth year of Zedekiah king of Judah, which was the eighteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar, when the army of Babylon was besieging Jerusalem and Jeremiah was shut up in the court of the guard (Jeremiah 32:1-2), Hanamel came to Jeremiah in the court of the guard and told him to buy his field at Anathoth (Jeremiah 32:7-8). Jeremiah knew that this was the word of the LORD, and bought the field (Jeremiah 32:8-9).
event: Hanamel urged Jeremiah to buy his field at Anathoth in the land of Benjamin, and Jeremiah weighed out seventeen shekels of silver and bought the field (Jeremiah 32:8-9). It was Jeremiah who wrote the deed, sealed it, called witnesses, and weighed out the silver on the scales (Jeremiah 32:10), and Hanamel is recorded as one of those who were present when he handed the deed of purchase to Baruch (Jeremiah 32:12). In connection with this matter, the LORD said that houses, fields, and vineyards would again be bought in this land (Jeremiah 32:15).

introduce: Hanan is a man recorded as one of the sons of Shashak in the genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin in 1 Chronicles 8 (1 Chronicles 8:23-25).
lifetime: Hanan is listed together with Abdon and Zichri, and is recorded as one of the sons of Shashak, along with Ishpan, Eber, Eliel, Abdon, Zichri, Hanan, Hananiah, Elam, Anthothijah, Iphdeiah, and Penuel (1 Chronicles 8:22-25). The rest of his life is not recorded in the Bible.

introduce: Hanoch is one of the sons of Midian, who was born to Abraham and his later wife Keturah. As a descendant of Abraham, he is a person included in the genealogy of the Midianite clan (Genesis 25:1-4).
lifetime: He was born to Midian, the son of Abraham, and is recorded as the third of Midian's five sons (Ephah, Epher, Hanoch, Abida, and Eldaah) (Genesis 25:4, 1 Chronicles 1:33). The Bible does not describe in detail any specific place of residence or personal deeds in Hanoch's life.
character: As a son of Midian, he occupies a genealogical position in the formation of the origins of the Midianite clan (Genesis 25:4). The name Hanoch carries in Hebrew the meaning "dedicated" or "beginning," but no specific event of character that he personally carried out appears in the Bible (Genesis 25:4).

call: king of the Ammonites (son of Nahash)
introduce: He was a son of Nahash king of the Ammonites and succeeded Nahash to the throne. He is the one who, by insulting the delegation of condolence that David sent, set off a large-scale war between Israel and Ammon.
lifetime: When his father Nahash died, he succeeded him as king (2 Samuel 10:1). When David, remembering Nahash's kindness, sent a delegation of condolence, Hanun mistook them for spies, and an incident occurred in which he shaved off half of the delegation's beards and cut off their garments in the middle before sending them back (2 Samuel 10:2-4). As a result they went to war with Israel, and Ammon allied with the Aramean army, but they were finally defeated by the army of Israel led by Joab and Abishai (2 Samuel 10:6-14). Afterward, when Aram gathered its forces again and attacked, David himself led his army out and defeated them at Helam (2 Samuel 10:15-18).
event: Hanun listened to the words of the princes of the Ammonites, seized David's servants whom David had sent to show kindness, shaved off half of their beards, and cut off their garments in the middle as far as the buttocks before sending them back, and so became odious to David (2 Samuel 10:2-4). Hanun and the Ammonites sent a thousand talents of silver to Aram-naharaim, to Aram-maacah, and to Zobah to hire chariots and horsemen (1 Chronicles 19:6). In the battle, the Arameans fled before Joab, and the Ammonites fled before Abishai and went into the city (2 Samuel 10:13-14).
character: He tended to suspect the goodwill of others and interpret it from a hostile viewpoint (2 Samuel 10:3). He was easily swayed by the slanders of his officials, and by shaming David's delegation he showed himself impulsive and lacking in diplomatic wisdom (2 Samuel 10:3-4). After he recognized the seriousness of the situation, he showed a style of rule that was defensive and inclined to confrontation, such as hiring the armies of the foreign power Aram (2 Samuel 10:6).

introduce: Hathach was a eunuch who attended Queen Esther in the court of Ahasuerus king of Persia; at Esther's command he went to Mordecai to find out the circumstances and carried messages between Esther and Mordecai (Esther 4:5-12).
lifetime: Hathach was a eunuch whom Esther had appointed to attend her by the king's command (Esther 4:5). When Esther heard that Mordecai was wearing sackcloth, she was distressed and sent clothing, but when Mordecai would not accept it, she called Hathach and commanded him to go to Mordecai and learn what this was (Esther 4:4-5), and Hathach went out to Mordecai in the open square of the city in front of the king's gate (Esther 4:6).
event: Hathach heard Mordecai tell him all that had happened to him and the exact sum of silver that Haman had promised to pay into the king's treasuries for the destruction of the Jews; Mordecai gave him a copy of the written decree for their destruction and charged him to have Esther go in to the king and plead earnestly for her people (Esther 4:7-8). Hathach returned and told Mordecai's words to Esther (Esther 4:9), conveyed the message that Esther told him to give to Mordecai (Esther 4:10-12), and Mordecai had him carry back a reply to Esther (Esther 4:13).
character: He was a person who had gained Esther's trust, and he possessed the confidence needed to carry sensitive information secretly between the queen and Mordecai, an outsider (Esther 4:5-10). The prudence he showed in carrying out his duty reflects the orderly way of handling business of a court eunuch of that time (Esther 4:9).

introduce: Hadad was a king of Edom, the man who became king in place of Baal-hanan the son of Achbor after he died (Genesis 36:39). In 1 Chronicles 1:50 he is recorded under a variant spelling of the name.
lifetime: He became king of Edom after Baal-hanan the son of Achbor died (Genesis 36:39, 1 Chronicles 1:50).
event: The name of his city was Pau (Pai in 1 Chronicles 1:50), and his wife's name was Mehetabel, the daughter of Matred and granddaughter of Me-zahab (Genesis 36:39, 1 Chronicles 1:50).

introduce: Esther was a Jewish woman who became queen of King Ahasuerus, and she is recorded as Hadassah, that is, Esther (Esther 2:7). Her life is recorded centering on the event in which the Jews in all the provinces of the king were delivered from the crisis of annihilation through Haman's scheme.
lifetime: She was the daughter of Abihail of the tribe of Benjamin; she lost her parents early and grew up under the care of her cousin Mordecai (Esther 2:7, 2:15). In the selection of a queen for King Ahasuerus she entered the palace, won the king's favor, and became queen (Esther 2:17). When Haman, an intimate of the king, made a plan to annihilate the Jews, she resolved to go in to the king, fasting, in order to save her people (Esther 4:16). Afterward she accused Haman's plot to the king and played the role of saving the Jews (Esther 7:3-6).
event: When Haman plotted to kill Mordecai, Esther went in to the king, made known the plight of the Jews, and exposed Haman's treachery (Esther 7:4-6). Through this event Haman was executed, and the king had a new decree issued allowing the Jews to protect themselves (Esther 8:11). Also, at the instruction of Esther and Mordecai, the feast of Purim was established to commemorate the deliverance of the Jews (Esther 9:20-22).
character: She was obedient to the instructions of her cousin Mordecai and faithfully followed his guidance even after she became queen (Esther 2:20). In a time of crisis she showed bold decisiveness and courage, going in before the king with the attitude "if I perish, I perish" (Esther 4:16). She had a strategic side, using her position for the fate of her people (Esther 5:4, 7:3).

introduce: Hadadezer was king of Zobah, appearing in 2 Samuel and 1 Chronicles, a son of Rehob (2 Samuel 8:3). He was defeated by David while seeking to extend his power at the river Euphrates (2 Samuel 8:3, 1 Chronicles 18:3).
lifetime: As a son of Rehob and king of Zobah, he was struck by David as he went to the river Euphrates to restore his power (2 Samuel 8:3). The Arameans of Damascus came to help Hadadezer, but David struck down twenty-two thousand of the Arameans, and when David put garrisons in Aram of Damascus, the Arameans became servants to David and brought tribute (2 Samuel 8:5-6). Later, in the war with Ammon, Hadadezer sent and brought out the Arameans who were beyond the River, and they came to Helam but were defeated before Israel (2 Samuel 10:16-19).
event: David captured from him seventeen hundred horsemen and twenty thousand foot soldiers, and hamstrung all the chariot horses except enough for a hundred chariots (2 Samuel 8:4). David also took the gold shields that were carried by the servants of Hadadezer and brought them to Jerusalem, and from Betah and Berothai, cities of Hadadezer, took a very large amount of bronze (2 Samuel 8:7-8). The kings who were subject to Hadadezer, when they saw that they had been defeated before Israel, made peace with Israel and served them (2 Samuel 10:19).
character: He was a conquering monarch with an active will for territorial expansion, to the point of trying to extend his power as far as the Euphrates (2 Samuel 8:3). When David's power grew, he allied with the surrounding small states and even mobilized the Aramean forces of Damascus, showing a strategic side in responding in an organized way (2 Samuel 10:16). Even after defeat he did not submit but formed a coalition army again to attempt a comeback, and he appears to have had a stubborn and resistant temperament (2 Samuel 10:17).

introduce: Hadoram is a descendant of Shem the son of Noah, recorded as one of the thirteen sons born to Joktan. He is mentioned in the same way in the genealogy of Genesis 10 and the genealogy of 1 Chronicles 1, and is a member of the family line that continues in the genealogy of Shem through Arphaxad, Shelah, and Eber to Joktan (Genesis 10:24-27).
lifetime: As a son of Joktan, Hadoram is among the descendants of Shem, and his name is entered in the genealogy of the descendants of Noah in Genesis (Genesis 10:27). In the genealogy of 1 Chronicles 1 he is likewise mentioned again as one of the sons of Joktan (1 Chronicles 1:21).

introduce: Hadlai is a man recorded in 2 Chronicles 28:12 as the father of Amasa, one of the chiefs of the sons of Ephraim.
lifetime: When northern Israel struck Judah in the time of King Ahaz and came back with captives, Hadlai's son Amasa rose up together with several chiefs of the sons of Ephraim and stood against those coming from the battle (2 Chronicles 28:5-12). The Bible contains no other record concerning Hadlai himself.
event: Hadlai's son Amasa rose up together with Azariah the son of Johanan, Berechiah the son of Meshillemoth, and Jehizkiah the son of Shallum, and said that they must not bring the captives of Judah in here (2 Chronicles 28:12-13). These chiefs took the captives, clothed them, fed them, gave them drink, and anointed them, set the feeble ones on donkeys, brought them to Jericho, the city of palm trees, to their brothers, and then returned to Samaria (2 Chronicles 28:15).
character: His personal character is not recorded in the Bible. The ones who stood against those returning from the war and demanded that the captives not be brought in were Amasa son of Hadlai and the other chiefs of Ephraim (2 Chronicles 28:12-13).

introduce: Hatita is the name of a family belonging to the descendants of the gatekeepers among the people of Israel who returned from the Babylonian exile, and it appears in the lists of returnees in Ezra and Nehemiah (Ezra 2:42, Nehemiah 7:45).
lifetime: As one family of the descendants of the gatekeepers who returned from Babylon to Jerusalem and Judah (the descendants of Hatita), it is recorded in the list of returnees together with the descendants of Shallum, Ater, Talmon, Akkub, and Shobai (Ezra 2:42, Nehemiah 7:45).
event: The descendants of the gatekeepers (the descendants of Shallum, Ater, Talmon, Akkub, Hatita, and Shobai) are recorded in all as one hundred thirty-nine in Ezra 2:42 and one hundred thirty-eight in Nehemiah 7:45. The number of the descendants of Hatita alone is not recorded separately.

introduce: The descendants of Hatipha are recorded as one family among the Nethinim who returned to Jerusalem from the Babylonian exile (Ezra 2:43, 2:54, Nehemiah 7:56).
lifetime: They are included in the list of the Nethinim who returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel and others after the Babylonian exile (Ezra 2:2, 2:54, Nehemiah 7:56).
event: The descendants of Hatipha, together with the descendants of Neziah among the Nethinim, are recorded in the lists of returnees in Ezra 2 and Nehemiah 7 (Ezra 2:54, Nehemiah 7:56).

introduce: Hattil is a name recorded in the list of the people of Israel who returned from the Babylonian exile, belonging to the group of the descendants of Solomon's servants (Ezra 2:55-57).
lifetime: The descendants of Hattil are included in the list of those who returned to Jerusalem and Judah with Zerubbabel and others after the Babylonian exile (Ezra 2:2, 2:57).
event: The descendants of Hattil are mentioned as one of the descendants of Solomon's servants who returned from Babylon to Jerusalem (Ezra 2:57).

introduce: Hareph is a man recorded as "the father of Beth-gader" in the list of the sons of Hur, the firstborn of Ephrathah, among the descendants of Caleb in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah (1 Chronicles 2:50-51).
lifetime: Hareph is one of the sons of Hur, the firstborn of Ephrathah, among the descendants of Caleb, and is listed together with Shobal and Salma (1 Chronicles 2:50-51).
event: Hareph is recorded as "the father of Beth-gader" (1 Chronicles 2:51). Beyond that, no specific deeds are recorded in the Bible.

introduce: Haroeh is a man recorded in the genealogy as a descendant of Shobal, the father of Kiriath-jearim, among the descendants of Caleb of the tribe of Judah (1 Chronicles 2:50, 2:52). This entry is regarded as the same person as "Reaiah the son of Shobal" in 1 Chronicles 4:2.
lifetime: Haroeh is recorded as a descendant of Shobal, the son of Hur, the firstborn of Ephrathah (1 Chronicles 2:50, 2:52). 1 Chronicles 4:2 records that Reaiah the son of Shobal fathered Jahath, and Jahath fathered Ahumai and Lahad, and that these were the clans of the Zorathites (1 Chronicles 4:2).
event: Haroeh is listed, together with half of the Manahathites, among the descendants of Shobal, the father of Kiriath-jearim (1 Chronicles 2:52). The Bible does not record his specific deeds.

introduce: Harumaph is a man mentioned in Nehemiah 3:10 only as "Jedaiah the son of Harumaph," the father of Jedaiah who repaired the wall of Jerusalem (Nehemiah 3:10).
lifetime: There is no record of Harumaph himself; he is mentioned only as the father in the verse where his son Jedaiah appears as a repairer of the wall (Nehemiah 3:10).
event: Nothing Harumaph himself did is recorded. His son Jedaiah repaired the part opposite his own house (Nehemiah 3:10).

introduce: Haruz was a man of Jotbah, recorded as the father of Meshullemeth, the mother of Amon king of Judah (2 Kings 21:19).
lifetime: He was from Jotbah, and his daughter Meshullemeth was the mother of Amon king of Judah (2 Kings 21:19).

introduce: Harnepher is a man who appears in the genealogy of the tribe of Asher, a son of Zophah and a descendant of the tribe of Asher (1 Chronicles 7:36).
lifetime: Harnepher was born as a son of Zophah and has his name entered in the genealogy of a family of the tribe of Asher (1 Chronicles 7:36).

introduce: Harbona was one of the seven eunuchs who served King Ahasuerus of the Persian Empire, an official who attended in the king's palace.
lifetime: He is recorded as one of the seven eunuchs of the royal presence whom King Ahasuerus commanded, when his heart was merry with wine, to bring Queen Vashti (Esther 1:10). Later, as one of the eunuchs who attended the king, he told the king that Haman had prepared a gallows fifty cubits high for hanging Mordecai and had set it up at his house (Esther 7:9).
event: King Ahasuerus commanded the seven eunuchs of the royal presence to bring Queen Vashti before the king, but Vashti refused to come at the king's command conveyed by the eunuchs (Esther 1:10-12). Harbona was one of those seven. Later he told the king that the gallows fifty cubits high, which Haman had prepared for hanging Mordecai, stood at Haman's house, and the king said to hang Haman on it (Esther 7:9). When Haman was hanged on it, the king's wrath subsided (Esther 7:10).
character: As an official well informed about the affairs of the court, he played the role of quickly conveying Haman's plot to the king and turning the course of events (Esther 7:9). He is regarded as a man faithful to his duty as a eunuch trusted by the king (Esther 1:10).

introduce: Harim is one of the priestly families recorded in 1 Chronicles, and the man in charge of the third division when the priestly organization was divided into twenty-four divisions in the time of King David.
lifetime: When David organized the priests for the service of the temple, he was appointed by lot as the priest of the third division (1 Chronicles 24:8).
event: His is the family recorded as the third division in the order determined by lot among the divisions of the priests (1 Chronicles 24:5, 24:7-8).

call: ancestor of a family that returned with Zerubbabel
introduce: Hariph is the name of a family recorded as "the descendants of Hariph" in the list of those who returned from Babylon, and the same list in Ezra 2:18 reads "the descendants of Jorah" (Nehemiah 7:24, Ezra 2:18).
lifetime: The descendants of Hariph are recorded in the list of the returnees from the Babylonian exile as one hundred twelve (Nehemiah 7:24, Ezra 2:18).
event: Apart from the record of one hundred twelve descendants of Hariph in the list of returnees, no specific deeds under this name are recorded in the Bible (Nehemiah 7:24).

introduce: A high official who enjoyed the king's favor in the time of King Ahasuerus of the Persian Empire, and a main figure in the book of Esther. He is known as a descendant of Agag the Amalekite; he planned to massacre the Jews but failed and was executed.
lifetime: King Ahasuerus appointed him to a position higher than all the officials, and arranged that all the king's servants at the king's gate should bow down to him (Esther 3:1-2). When Mordecai would not bow down to him, he became furious, made a plan to annihilate all the Jews, and obtained the king's permission (Esther 3:5-6, 11). Invited to the banquet that Queen Esther gave, he nevertheless, out of hatred for Mordecai, had a high gallows set up on which to hang him (Esther 5:9-14). Afterward he lost the king's favor and, exposed by Esther, was hanged and executed on the gallows he had set up himself (Esther 7:9-10).
event: Through the king's decree he issued an order to kill all the Jews in the empire and plunder their property on the thirteenth day of the month of Adar (Esther 3:13). In accordance with the king's command to honor Mordecai, he suffered the humiliation of having to clothe him in the king's robe and lead him through the city on horseback (Esther 6:10-11). When his wickedness was exposed by Queen Esther's accusation, he was reduced to begging Esther for his life in the presence of the king (Esther 7:7-8). After his death, all ten of Haman's sons were executed (Esther 9:7-10).
character: He was so vengeful and willful that, because of the attitude of one man, Mordecai, who would not bow down to him, he tried to destroy a whole people (Esther 3:5-6). Relying on the king's power, he showed an arrogant tendency to flaunt his position (Esther 5:11-12). When he realized that his plan would not be carried out, he showed extreme mental agitation and terror (Esther 7:6).

introduce: A Hivite of the area of Shechem in the land of Canaan, the father of Shechem, the chief of the land, and the one who led the negotiation with the household of Jacob. His name derives from the Hebrew word meaning donkey.
lifetime: When Jacob came from Paddan-aram and pitched his tent before the city of Shechem, he bought that parcel of ground from the sons of Hamor for a hundred pieces of silver (Genesis 33:18-19). Hamor was the father of Shechem, the chief of the land, and after his son Shechem violated Jacob's daughter Dinah, he proposed intermarriage with Jacob's household and living together (Genesis 34:2-8). He accepted the condition of circumcision that Jacob's sons set, and spoke together with his son Shechem to the men of their city at the city gate, and every male of the city was circumcised, but on the third day, in the surprise attack of Simeon and Levi, he was killed by the sword together with his son Shechem (Genesis 34:18-26).
event: As the father of Shechem he came to speak with Jacob, and proposed that the two families intermarry, live together, and trade (Genesis 34:6-10). He and his son Shechem thought well of the conditions Jacob's sons stated, and at the city gate he told the men of the town to be circumcised and to live with them (Genesis 34:18-24).
character: In resolving the wrong his son had committed, he took a practical approach and led the diplomatic negotiation (Genesis 34:8-12). To his own tribesmen he stressed the economic benefit of being able to share the property and livestock of Jacob's household in exchange for accepting circumcision, and so persuaded them (Genesis 34:21-23). From this he appears to have been a ruler who put the interests and political stability of his tribe first, but he is characterized as having entered the negotiation without fully grasping the other side's intentions (Genesis 34:20-24).

introduce: Hamutal is a woman recorded as the wife of Josiah and the mother of the kings of Judah Jehoahaz and Zedekiah (2 Kings 23:31, 24:18).
lifetime: Hamutal was the daughter of Jeremiah of Libnah (2 Kings 23:31). She is the mother of Josiah's sons Jehoahaz (Shallum) and Zedekiah (Mattaniah) (2 Kings 23:30-31, 24:17-18, Jeremiah 22:11).
event: Her son Jehoahaz was twenty-three years old when he began to reign and reigned three months in Jerusalem (2 Kings 23:31), and her other son Zedekiah was twenty-one years old when he began to reign and reigned eleven years in Jerusalem (2 Kings 24:18).

introduce: Hamul was a son born to Perez the son of Judah, and became the ancestor of the Hamulite clan. He is mentioned in the course of the succession of the family line of the tribe of Judah in the genealogical records of the Bible.
lifetime: Hamul was a grandson of Judah and a son of Perez (Genesis 46:12, 1 Chronicles 2:5). Genesis 46:8, 12 records Perez's son Hamul in the list of the family of Israel who went down to Egypt.
event: Hamul became the founder of the Hamulite clan, which was recorded as one of the main families within the tribe of Judah when the census of the tribes of Israel was taken in later times (Numbers 26:21). His name is entered in the same way in the genealogy of Chronicles, showing the continuity of the family (1 Chronicles 2:5).

introduce: Hemdan is a man who appears in the genealogy of the descendants of Edom, a son of Dishon, a descendant of Seir (1 Chronicles 1:41).
lifetime: Hemdan is recorded as a son of Dishon and a grandson of Anah, of the Horite clan who lived in the land of Edom (1 Chronicles 1:41).

introduce: Habazziniah is a man mentioned as the grandfather when Jeremiah 35:3 introduces Jaazaniah as "the son of Jeremiah, the son of Habazziniah" (Jeremiah 35:3).
lifetime: Habazziniah is recorded only as the grandfather of Jaazaniah (Jeremiah 35:3). The Bible has no record of what activities he engaged in during his lifetime.
event: Habazziniah's own deeds are not recorded. In the scene where Jeremiah brings the Rechabites into a chamber of the house of the LORD and urges them to drink wine, Jaazaniah, who was brought along, is introduced only as the "grandson of Habazziniah" (Jeremiah 35:2-5).

introduce: One of the people of Israel who returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel after the Babylonian exile, a person classified as belonging to one of the priestly families.
lifetime: He is included, as "the descendants of Hobaiah," in the list of returnees who ended the Babylonian exile and returned to Jerusalem under Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:61; recorded as the descendants of Hobaiah in Nehemiah 7:63). This family searched for their registration among those enrolled by genealogy but did not find it, and so were regarded as unclean and could not carry out the priestly office (Ezra 2:62, Nehemiah 7:64).
event: The descendants of Hobaiah were recorded among the priests together with the descendants of Hakkoz and the descendants of Barzillai (Ezra 2:61). They searched for their registration among those enrolled by genealogy but did not find it, and were regarded as unclean, and the governor ordered that they should not eat of the most holy things until a priest arose with Urim and Thummim (Ezra 2:62-63).

meaning: one who embraces; one who wrestles
introduce: Habakkuk was a prophet who was active in the last period of the kingdom of Judah and the author of one of the minor prophetic books. His name carries the meaning of one who embraces or one who wrestles, and the Bible gives no specific information about his family or place of origin.
lifetime: At a time when the corruption and violence of Judah had reached their height, Habakkuk carried out his prophetic activity by putting questions to God (Habakkuk 1:2). He heard God's plan to raise up the Chaldeans of Babylon to discipline Judah, and argued and conversed with God about it (Habakkuk 1:6, 1:13). Afterward he stood on the watchtower, waiting for God's answer, and left a record (Habakkuk 2:1).
event: Through his dialogue with God, he asked about the tyranny of the Chaldeans and the wickedness of Judah, and recorded God's righteous judgment concerning them (Habakkuk 1:12-17). He also left the key phrase "the righteous shall live by his faith" (Habakkuk 2:4). Proclaiming that God's rule would come upon all the earth, he wrote at the end a song of prayer to God (Habakkuk 3:1-19).
character: Rather than blindly accepting the will of God, Habakkuk showed an analytical attitude of actively raising questions and seeking answers (Habakkuk 1:3). Even in desperate circumstances where the situation did not change, rather than clinging to his own logic, he showed a posture of acknowledging and accepting the sovereignty of God (Habakkuk 3:17-19).

introduce: Hasadiah is one of the persons listed as sons of Zerubbabel in the genealogy of the house of David, recorded as five persons together with Hashubah, Ohel, Berechiah, and Jushab-hesed (1 Chronicles 3:19-20).
lifetime: Hasadiah is recorded as one of the five persons listed after Zerubbabel's sons Meshullam and Hananiah and their brother-in-law Shelomith (1 Chronicles 3:19-20). His other deeds are not recorded in the Bible.
event: Hasadiah is mentioned as one of the five persons together with Hashubah, Ohel, Berechiah, and Jushab-hesed (1 Chronicles 3:20). His specific deeds are not recorded in the Bible.

introduce: Hashabiah was a descendant of the tribe of Levi, a descendant of Merari the son of Levi. Among those whom David appointed to sing, he is recorded in the ancestral line of Ethan, who served at the left hand of the descendants of Merari, as the son of Amaziah and the father of Malluch (1 Chronicles 6:44-47).
lifetime: He was the son of Amaziah and the father of Malluch (1 Chronicles 6:45). His ancestry runs through Amaziah, Hilkiah, Amzi, Bani, Shemer, Mahli, Mushi, Merari, and Levi (1 Chronicles 6:45-47).
event: Hashabiah's own deeds are not recorded. His descendant Ethan is recorded as one who served at the left hand of the descendants of Merari among the singers whom David appointed (1 Chronicles 6:31, 6:44-45).

introduce: Hazaiah is a man recorded in Nehemiah 11:5 as the great-grandfather of Maaseiah, who lived in Jerusalem (Nehemiah 11:5).
lifetime: Hazaiah is recorded as the great-grandfather of Maaseiah, the son of Baruch and grandson of Col-hozeh (Nehemiah 11:5). The Bible has no record of Hazaiah's own activity or residence.
event: Nothing Hazaiah himself did is recorded. Nehemiah 11:4-5, enumerating those who lived in Jerusalem, mentions Hazaiah as his great-grandfather when introducing Maaseiah's lineage (Nehemiah 11:4-5).

introduce: Hazael was king of Aram of Damascus around the ninth century BC, a man who pressed the kingdoms of northern Israel and southern Judah and had a great influence on the affairs of the surrounding nations. According to the biblical record, the LORD commanded Elijah to anoint Hazael as king over Aram (1 Kings 19:15), Elisha said that the LORD had shown him that he would be king over Aram (2 Kings 8:13), and afterward he became king in place of Ben-hadad king of Aram (2 Kings 8:15).
lifetime: When the prophet Elisha visited Damascus, Hazael met Elisha as the messenger of the sick Ben-hadad king of Aram (2 Kings 8:7-9). Elisha wept, knowing the evil that Hazael would do to the people of Israel (2 Kings 8:11-12). The next day Hazael dipped a cloth in water and spread it over the king's face, and when the king died he became king in his place (2 Kings 8:15). Afterward he struck Israel in the days of Jehu and Jehoahaz, and Judah in the days of Joash (2 Kings 10:32, 2 Kings 12:17-18, 2 Kings 13:3).
event: During the reign of Jehu king of Israel, Hazael struck Israel on every side, reaching all the land of Gilead east of the Jordan, as far as Bashan (2 Kings 10:32-33). In the days of Joash king of Judah, he fought against Gath and took it, and set his face to go up against Jerusalem; Joash sent the sacred things and the gold found in the temple and the king's house to Hazael, and Hazael went away from Jerusalem (2 Kings 12:17-18). After Hazael died, his son Ben-hadad became king in his place (2 Kings 13:24).
character: To achieve his own ambition, he had the cold and opportunistic side to murder his lord Ben-hadad (2 Kings 8:15). When he heard Elisha's prophecy, he reacted negatively, comparing himself to a dog, but after actually becoming king he showed himself a military leader who cruelly oppressed Israel, as prophesied (2 Kings 8:13).

introduce: Hashabnah was one of the group of leaders of Israel who pledged to keep the law of God after the rebuilding of the wall of Jerusalem in the time of Nehemiah (Nehemiah 10:25).
lifetime: Hashabnah appears as one of the names who took part in the sealed covenant that the people of Judah made in order to keep the law of God after completing the wall of Jerusalem (Nehemiah 10:1). He is recorded in the list of the chiefs of the people (Nehemiah 10:14, 10:25).
event: On behalf of the leaders of Israel, he took part in the sealing by which they swore to follow the law given through Moses the servant of God and to keep his commandments and ordinances (Nehemiah 10:28-29). His participation in the covenant was part of the process of announcing the religious reform of the community of Israel and its observance of the law after the historic event of rebuilding the wall (Nehemiah 10:25).

call: father of Hattush (father of a wall repairer)
introduce: Hashabneiah is a man who appears in the book of Nehemiah, recorded as the father of Hattush, who took part in the repair work at the time of the rebuilding of the wall of Jerusalem.
lifetime: Hashabneiah's son Hattush, in the repair of the wall of Jerusalem led by Nehemiah, repaired the section next to the part repaired by Jedaiah the son of Harumaph (Nehemiah 3:10). Apart from the family information about his son Hattush, there is no record of Hashabneiah's own life in the Bible.
event: There is no record that Hashabneiah himself took part in the rebuilding of the wall; it is mentioned that his son Hattush, as part of the work of repairing the wall, repaired the section next to the part repaired by Jedaiah the son of Harumaph (Nehemiah 3:10).

introduce: Hashem is a man recorded in the list of David's mighty men (1 Chronicles 11:34) in the expression "the sons of Hashem the Gizonite"; he was from Gizon and is mentioned as the father of those mighty men. The parallel passage in 2 Samuel 23:32 reads "Jonathan the son of Jashen."
lifetime: He was a Gizonite, and his sons are recorded in the list of David's mighty men in 1 Chronicles 11:34. Hashem's own deeds are not recorded in the Bible.
event: Jashen's own events are not recorded in the Bible. His son Jonathan is on the list of David's mighty men (2 Samuel 23:32), and in 1 Chronicles 11:34 also "Jonathan the son of Shagee the Hararite" appears in the list of mighty men.

introduce: Hazo is recorded as the fifth of the eight sons born to Nahor, Abraham's brother, and his wife Milcah (Genesis 22:20-23). He is recorded as a member of the house of Nahor.
lifetime: Hazo was born as one of the children that Abraham's brother Nahor had through Milcah (Genesis 22:22). In the biblical record no further information appears about his deeds or residence after his birth.

introduce: Sophereth is a person recorded as "the descendants of Sophereth" in the list of those who returned from the Babylonian exile, and belongs to the descendants of Solomon's servants (Ezra 2:55).
lifetime: He is recorded as one of the descendants of Solomon's servants in the list of returnees who came back to Jerusalem and Judah from the Babylonian captivity (Ezra 2:55). In the parallel list of Nehemiah 7:57 the same entry appears as "the descendants of Sophereth" (Nehemiah 7:57).
event: No historical event that Sophereth himself performed is recorded in the Bible; his descendants are recorded in the list of returnees as members of the descendants of Solomon's servants (Ezra 2:55). When Nehemiah found the genealogical register of those who had come back at the first, the same entry was recorded as "the descendants of Sophereth" (Nehemiah 7:5, 7:57).

introduce: Hashubah is a man of the tribe of Judah recorded in 1 Chronicles 3, a descendant of the house of David mentioned as one of the sons of Zerubbabel, the leader of Judah who returned from Babylon.
lifetime: In 1 Chronicles 3:19, after Zerubbabel's sons Meshullam and Hananiah and their brother-in-law Shelomith are listed, in 3:20 Hashubah is recorded first among those listed as "five persons" together with Ohel, Berechiah, Hasadiah, and Jushab-hesed (1 Chronicles 3:19, 3:20). His name is entered in the genealogy of the house of David in the period of the return from the Babylonian exile (1 Chronicles 3:20).
character: Five of Zerubbabel's sons, Hashubah, Ohel, Berechiah, Hasadiah, and Jushab-hesed, are listed together (1 Chronicles 3:20). The order of listing alone cannot establish the order of birth, and his personal character is not recorded.

introduce: Hazzelelponi is a person who appears in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah, recorded as the "brother-in-law" of Jezreel, Ishma, and Idbash, descendants of the father of Etam (1 Chronicles 4:3).
lifetime: Hazzelelponi appears in the genealogy of the sons of Judah (1 Chronicles 4:1) together with Jezreel, Ishma, and Idbash, "the descendants of the father of Etam," and is recorded as their brother-in-law (1 Chronicles 4:3). The rest of his life is not recorded in the Bible.

call: ancestor of a family that returned with Zerubbabel
introduce: Hashum is a person mentioned in Ezra 2 and Nehemiah 7, recorded as one of the ancestors of the families of Israel who ended the Babylonian exile and returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel.
lifetime: The family of Hashum is included in the list of those who returned from the Babylonian exile, and they were among the first returnees who came back to Jerusalem and Judah (Ezra 2:19). His descendants are likewise mentioned in the list of returnees compiled by Nehemiah (Nehemiah 7:22).
event: Two hundred twenty-three descendants of Hashum returned to Jerusalem under the leadership of Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:19). Later, when Ezra investigated those who had taken foreign women as wives, it was found that there were also among the descendants of Hashum those who had made foreign women their wives, and this was dealt with (Ezra 10:33).

introduce: Hassenaah is a man whose name appears in the passage of Nehemiah 3, in the record of the rebuilding of the wall of Jerusalem, saying that "the sons of Hassenaah" built the Fish Gate, and he is mentioned as the ancestor of that family (Nehemiah 3:3).
lifetime: The descendants of Hassenaah built the Fish Gate of the wall of Jerusalem (Nehemiah 3:3).
event: The descendants of Hassenaah, when the wall of Jerusalem was being built, built the Fish Gate, laid its beams, set up its doors, and fitted its locks and bars (Nehemiah 3:3).

introduce: Hasrah is a man whose name appears in 2 Chronicles 34:22 when the lineage of Shallum, husband of the prophetess Huldah, is introduced, recorded as the grandfather of Tokhath. In the parallel passage of 2 Kings 22:14 it reads "Shallum the son of Tikvah, the son of Harhas" (2 Chronicles 34:22, 2 Kings 22:14).
lifetime: Hasrah's name appears only within the lineage introduced in 2 Chronicles 34:22 as "Shallum the son of Tokhath, the son of Hasrah," and there is no other record of his life in the Bible (2 Chronicles 34:22).
event: Nothing Hasrah himself did is recorded in the Bible. When Hilkiah and the men sent by King Josiah went to the prophetess Huldah, Huldah was introduced as "the wife of Shallum the son of Tokhath, the son of Hasrah, the keeper of the wardrobe," and so Hasrah's name appears only there (2 Chronicles 34:22).

introduce: Hash-baddanah is a person recorded in the Old Testament, in the time of Nehemiah, as one of those who stood beside Ezra at the reading and interpretation of the law that took place after the rebuilding of the wall of Jerusalem.
lifetime: Hash-baddanah is mentioned as one of those who stood at Ezra's left when Ezra read the law to the people in the square before the Water Gate (Nehemiah 8:4). Beyond that, no record of his birth, death, or other life events appears in the Bible.
event: When Ezra the scribe stood on the wooden platform specially built and opened the book of the law to read to the people, Hash-baddanah was one of those who stood at Ezra's left (Nehemiah 8:3-5). His specific deeds or contributions after that are not described in the Bible.

introduce: Haziel is a Levite mentioned in 1 Chronicles 23, one of the sons of Shimei, a descendant of Gershon (1 Chronicles 23:7, 23:9).
lifetime: Haziel is recorded as a son of Shimei, a descendant of Gershon, together with Shelomoth and Haran, and these are called "the heads of the families of Ladan" (1 Chronicles 23:9).
event: When David divided the Levites into divisions (1 Chronicles 23:6), he was recorded as a son of Shimei, together with Shelomoth and Haran, as "the heads of the families of Ladan"; beyond that, no record exists of any particular historical event or personal deed (1 Chronicles 23:9).

introduce: Haahashtari is a person who appears in Chronicles in the Old Testament, a son of Ashhur mentioned in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah.
lifetime: He was a son born to Naarah, wife of Ashhur, the father of Tekoa of the tribe of Judah, by Ashhur (1 Chronicles 4:5-6).
event: Haahashtari's personal deeds are not recorded in the Bible; he is recorded only as one of the children of Naarah, together with Ahuzzam, Hepher, and Temeni (1 Chronicles 4:6).

call: son of Cush (ancestor of a tribe of the line of Ham)
introduce: Havilah is a person recorded as a son of Cush, the son of Ham, the son of Noah.
lifetime: Havilah is recorded as one of the sons of Cush: Seba, Havilah, Sabtah, Raamah, and Sabteca (Genesis 10:6-7, 1 Chronicles 1:9). The Bible has no further record of his later life or personal deeds.

introduce: Hakkatan is a man recorded as the father of Johanan of the descendants of Azgad, among the heads of families who came up from Babylon to Jerusalem with Ezra (Ezra 8:12).
lifetime: The Bible has no record of Hakkatan's own life. Ezra 8:12 records that "of the sons of Azgad, Johanan the son of Hakkatan" was there with one hundred ten males, and this list is the genealogical register of the heads of families who came up from Babylon with Ezra in the time of King Artaxerxes (Ezra 8:1, 8:12).
event: Nothing Hakkatan himself did is recorded. His son Johanan, as head of the descendants of Azgad, was entered with one hundred ten males in the list of the heads of families who came up with Ezra (Ezra 8:12).

call: founder/representative of the priestly family of Hakkoz
introduce: The head of the seventh of the twenty-four divisions into which the priestly office was divided in the time of David (1 Chronicles 24:10). In Nehemiah 3:4 and 3:21 he is mentioned as the grandfather of Uriah (given there under a variant spelling of the name), and Uriah's son Meremoth took part in the rebuilding of the wall of Jerusalem in the time of Nehemiah and repaired one section (Nehemiah 3:4, 21). The line of Hakkoz is understood to be connected with the family of Hakkoz that appears as the seventh priestly division in the time of David (1 Chronicles 24:10; Ezra 2:61; Nehemiah 7:63).
event: As a priest of the line of Aaron, he became the head of the seventh priestly division. These twenty-four divisions were appointed to enter the house of the LORD in turn and carry out the priestly duties. Therefore the name of Hakkoz remained not as a mere entry in a list but as a name representing one of the priestly divisions responsible for the service of the temple.

introduce: Haggi was a son of Gad, the son of Jacob, one of the descendants of Gad who went with Jacob's family when it migrated to Egypt (Genesis 46:16). Afterward he is recorded as the ancestor of the Haggite clan, a family of the tribe of Gad mentioned at the census in Numbers (Numbers 26:15).
lifetime: When Jacob migrated to Egypt with his sons, he first appeared in the list as a son of Gad (Genesis 46:16). When Moses and Eleazar took a census of the people of Israel on the plains of Moab after the wilderness of Sinai, Haggi is mentioned again as the ancestor who formed the Haggite clan of the tribe of Gad (Numbers 26:15).
event: In the census taken in the wilderness after the exodus of Israel, his name was left in the record as the ancestor of the Haggite clan, one of the several clans that arose from the descendants of the tribe of Gad (Numbers 26:15). As a son of Gad, he was one of the early family members who migrated to Egypt with his father (Genesis 46:16).

introduce: Haggiah is a man who appears in the genealogy of the descendants of Levi in 1 Chronicles 6, belonging to the family line of the descendants of Merari (1 Chronicles 6:30).
lifetime: Haggiah was the son of Shimea and a descendant of Mahli, who was born to Merari (1 Chronicles 6:29-30). No specific time or deeds are recorded in the Bible in connection with his life (1 Chronicles 6:30).

introduce: Haggith was one of David's wives, who bore her son Adonijah in Hebron.
lifetime: Haggith bore Adonijah, David's fourth son, while David was in Hebron (2 Samuel 3:2, 3:4). Afterward she is mentioned again in David's old age, in the course of her son Adonijah's attempt to make himself king (1 Kings 1:5).
event: Her name appears as his mother in the incident in which, when David was old and advanced in years, Haggith's son Adonijah exalted himself, saying "I will be king," and prepared for himself chariots, horsemen, and fifty men to run before him (1 Kings 1:1, 1:5). Also, 1 Chronicles 3:1-2 records "Adonijah the son of Haggith" as the fourth among the sons whom David had in Hebron.

introduce: Hachmoni is a man recorded as the father of Jehiel in the record concerning David's royal household in 1 Chronicles 27 (1 Chronicles 27:32).
lifetime: Hachmoni's own life is not recorded in the Bible. 1 Chronicles 27:32 records that "Jehiel the son of Hachmoni" attended to the king's sons (1 Chronicles 27:32).
event: Nothing Hachmoni himself did is recorded in the Bible. His son Jehiel attended to the king's sons (1 Chronicles 27:32).
character: He is described as a wise and learned man, and in the royal household of David he held a role requiring specialized insight, such as that of a scribe or teacher (1 Chronicles 27:32). He was also a kinsman of David, a person who assisted with the affairs of the royal household from a position of trust (1 Chronicles 27:32).

introduce: The wife of Elkanah, a man of the tribe of Ephraim, and the mother of Samuel; she is recorded as an important figure in the history of Israel at the time of transition from the period of the judges to the period of the monarchy.
lifetime: She lived in Ramathaim-zophim in the hill country of Ephraim and was a wife of Elkanah together with Peninnah (1 Samuel 1:1-2). Being childless, she prayed at Shiloh, then conceived and gave birth to Samuel (1 Samuel 1:20). After raising the child until he was weaned, she brought him to the sanctuary at Shiloh and entrusted him to Eli the priest (1 Samuel 1:24-28). Afterward, going up to Shiloh every year with her husband, she made a little robe and brought it to Samuel (1 Samuel 2:19). After Samuel she bore three more sons and two daughters (1 Samuel 2:21).
event: Suffering from having no child, she made a vow in prayer to God at the sanctuary at Shiloh (1 Samuel 1:10-11). Though she was misunderstood by Eli the priest, she explained her innocence and received his blessing (1 Samuel 1:14-17). After giving birth to Samuel, in order to fulfill her vow to dedicate him to God, she left the young Samuel at the house of the LORD at Shiloh (1 Samuel 1:28). Hannah also left a song containing her feelings and prayer, which is recorded in 1 Samuel 2:1-10.
character: She showed such earnestness that, in anguish of heart, she prayed weeping bitterly (1 Samuel 1:10). Even when misunderstood by Eli the priest, she did not become angry but explained her situation calmly and politely (1 Samuel 1:15-16). She had the practical resolve to keep faithfully what she had vowed, and she had a devoted attitude, not forgetting her child but caring for him every year (1 Samuel 1:28, 2:19).
