introduce: Obadiah was a high official who, in the time of Ahab of the kingdom of Northern Israel, served as palace administrator and was responsible for the household of the royal court. He is recorded as one who kept his faith, fearing the LORD even in the time when Baal worship was at its height.
lifetime: Obadiah was appointed palace administrator of King Ahab and held the position of overseeing the affairs of the royal court (1 Kings 18:3). When Ahab's wife Jezebel was persecuting the prophets of the LORD, he hid a hundred of them, fifty to a cave, and supplied them with food and water so that they survived (1 Kings 18:4). Afterward, when the famine became severe, as Ahab said he divided the land with Ahab to search for sources of water and went along a different road, and on the road Elijah met him (1 Kings 18:5-7).
event: While keeping the high position of palace administrator under Ahab's rule, he took the risk of sheltering and protecting a hundred prophets of the LORD, carrying out a weighty role (1 Kings 18:4). During the famine, on the road as he was going to look for water as Ahab had said, he met Elijah; and when Elijah told him to tell Ahab, "Elijah is here," he declined for fear that Ahab would kill him (1 Kings 18:8-14), but when Elijah swore that he would show himself to Ahab that day, he went and told Ahab (1 Kings 18:15-16).
character: Obadiah was a man who feared the LORD greatly from his youth (1 Kings 18:12). He held such strong moral conviction that he protected the prophets of the LORD at the risk of his own life, and although he was a high official of the royal court, he maintained an attitude of acknowledging religious authority, to the point of showing extreme respect and fear before the prophet Elijah (1 Kings 18:7). Also, he had an obedient disposition that accepted without doubt the will of God that Elijah spoke (1 Kings 18:15-16).

call: son of Gershom (priest of the tribe of Dan)
introduce: Jonathan was a Levite who lived in the hill country of Ephraim and became a priest of the tribe of Dan. He is recorded as a grandson of Moses and a son of Gershom (Judges 18:30).
lifetime: Having lived as a sojourner in Bethlehem of Judah, he stayed in the house of a man named Micah in the hill country of Ephraim and became his priest (Judges 17:7-13). Afterward he met the spies of the tribe of Dan and blessed their way ahead (Judges 18:5-6). When the tribe of Dan went to conquer Laish, he took Micah's ephod, teraphim, and graven image and went with them (Judges 18:18-20), and afterward he became priest to the descendants of Dan and carried on that office with his descendants (Judges 18:30).
event: When the five men of the tribe of Dan went into Micah's house and took out the graven image, the ephod, the teraphim, and the molten image, the priest was glad in his heart and took the ephod, the teraphim, and the graven image and went in among the people (Judges 18:18-20). After the tribe of Dan conquered Laish and called the city Dan, they set up the image there and made Jonathan and his descendants priests (Judges 18:29-31).
character: He showed an attitude of putting his own economic interest and the security of his position first, and an opportunistic tendency of readily changing patrons appears (Judges 18:20). Despite being of the lineage of Moses, he played a central role in idolatry (Judges 18:30-31).

call: nephew of David (a very shrewd man)
introduce: Jonadab, the son of David's brother Shimeah and thus the nephew of King David, is known as a friend of Amnon, David's eldest son. He was deeply involved in the political dynamics within the royal house, and in particular played a decisive role in planning Amnon's crime.
lifetime: Jonadab was born the son of Shimeah, David's brother (2 Samuel 13:3). He was a friend of David's son Amnon and is recorded as a very shrewd man (2 Samuel 13:3). When Amnon grew haggard from being in love with Tamar, he advised him of a scheme to lie down on his bed and pretend to be ill (2 Samuel 13:4-5), and afterward, at the time when Absalom killed Amnon, he told David, "Let not my lord suppose that all the young men the king's sons are dead; only Amnon is dead" (2 Samuel 13:32-33).
event: To Amnon, who was in love with Tamar, he gave the concrete method of pretending to be ill and having Tamar summoned to prepare food for him, thereby creating the occasion for the crime (2 Samuel 13:4-5). At the time when Absalom killed Amnon, who had dishonored Tamar, he told the king that not all the king's sons had been killed but only Amnon was dead (2 Samuel 13:32-33).
character: The Bible describes him directly as a very shrewd man (2 Samuel 13:3). He had the resourcefulness to grasp the surrounding situation objectively, but he was a man who used it not for a moral purpose but to instigate events within the royal house and to control information.

introduce: Jezreel is a person who appears in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah recorded in 1 Chronicles 4 of the Old Testament, classified as one of the descendants of Etam.
lifetime: In the line of descendants of Hur, the son of Judah, he is recorded together with Ishma and Idbash as "the sons of the father of Etam" (1 Chronicles 4:3).
event: No special achievement performed by Jezreel himself, or specific event recorded about him, appears in the biblical record. (-)
character: The biblical text contains no description of Jezreel's character, physical features, or personality. (-)

기타관계: Hazzelelponi#2999(kinsman of the tribe of Judah)

introduce: Eshtaol is recorded as a person belonging to the genealogy of the descendants of Kiriath-jearim, one of the families of the tribe of Judah (1 Chronicles 2:53).
lifetime: From these clans of Kiriath-jearim, namely the Ithrites, the Puthites, the Shumathites, and the Mishraites, came the Eshtaolite clan and the Zorathite clan (1 Chronicles 2:53).

call: prophet of Tekoa (author of the book of Amos)
introduce: Amos was a prophet from Tekoa in the land of Judah, a man who was active during the reign of Jeroboam II of Northern Israel. By original occupation he was neither a prophet nor a son of a prophet, but a shepherd and a farmer who tended sycamore-fig trees (Amos 7:14).
lifetime: In the days of Uzziah king of Judah and of Jeroboam the son of Jehoash king of Israel, he lived as one of the shepherds of Tekoa (Amos 1:1). He received from God the call to go to Northern Israel and prophesy (Amos 7:15). While serving at Bethel he was accused by the priest Amaziah and faced the danger of being expelled from there (Amos 7:10-13).
event: He proclaimed judgment on the nations around Israel, such as Damascus, Gaza, Tyre, Edom, Ammon, and Moab (Amos 1:3-2:3). He strongly criticized the social injustice and the formal religious practices within Northern Israel and prophesied the judgment of God (Amos 5:21-24). Through the vision of the plumb line and the vision of a basket of summer fruit, he conveyed visually the inevitability of the destruction that would come upon Israel (Amos 7:7-9, 8:1-2). He confronted the priest Amaziah of Bethel head-on and made clear that his calling came from the command of God and not from human authority (Amos 7:16-17).
character: He had an honest and unpretentious attitude, to the point of declaring openly that he had no professional background as a prophet (Amos 7:14). He showed uncompromising resolve and a blunt manner of speech toward the unjust accumulation of wealth by the powerful and the oppression of the poor (Amos 4:1, 8:4-6). Coming from a rural background, he often used metaphors drawn from nature and agricultural life as instruments of his prophecy (Amos 3:4-5, 9:13).

call: the prophet Zephaniah (author of the book of Zephaniah)
introduce: Zephaniah was a prophet who was active in the time of King Josiah of the kingdom of Judah, recorded as a great-great-grandson of Hezekiah. His name carries the meaning "the LORD has hidden" or "protects," and at the opening he states the information about his name and his lineage.
lifetime: Zephaniah received the word of the LORD during the reign of King Josiah (Zephaniah 1:1). He records a specific genealogy: a great-great-grandson of Hezekiah, a great-grandson of Amariah, a grandson of Gedaliah, and a son of Cushi (Zephaniah 1:1).
event: He criticized the idolatry of Judah and Jerusalem and warned that the day of the LORD was near (Zephaniah 1:4). He proclaimed messages of judgment not only against Judah but against surrounding nations such as the Philistines, Moab, Ammon, Cush, and Assyria (Zephaniah 2:4-15). He also carried out the activity of pointing out the sins of the corrupt officials, prophets, and priests of Jerusalem (Zephaniah 3:1-4).
character: As one of the lineage of the royal house of Judah, he maintained a critical view of the social and religious corruption of the time (Zephaniah 1:1). While stressing the day of judgment, he also showed a resolute yet restoration-oriented attitude, delivering the promise of salvation to the remnant who rely on the LORD (Zephaniah 3:12-13).

introduce: The priest Zephaniah is a priest recorded as the son of Maaseiah, a man sent to Jeremiah in the time of Zedekiah king of Judah (Jeremiah 21:1, 37:3). In the letter from Babylon it is recorded that the LORD appointed him in place of the priest Jehoiada as chief officer in the house of the LORD (Jeremiah 29:25-26). The second priest Zephaniah was taken captive at the fall of Jerusalem (Jeremiah 52:24).
lifetime: When Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon was attacking, King Zedekiah sent Pashhur the son of Malchijah and the priest Zephaniah the son of Maaseiah to Jeremiah and asked him to inquire of the LORD (Jeremiah 21:1-2). He also sent Jehucal the son of Shelemiah and the priest Zephaniah the son of Maaseiah to Jeremiah and asked him to pray (Jeremiah 37:3). Shemaiah, who was in Babylon, sent a letter to Zephaniah saying that the LORD had made him priest in place of the priest Jehoiada and appointed him chief officer in the house of the LORD (Jeremiah 29:25-26), and Zephaniah read Shemaiah's letter in the hearing of the prophet Jeremiah (Jeremiah 29:29). At the fall of Jerusalem the second priest Zephaniah was seized by the captain of the guard, was brought to the king of Babylon at Riblah, and was struck down there (2 Kings 25:18-21).
event: Sent by King Zedekiah, he went to Jeremiah and asked him to inquire of the LORD and pray in the face of the attack of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon (Jeremiah 21:1-2, 37:3). He read Shemaiah's letter in the hearing of the prophet Jeremiah (Jeremiah 29:29). As second priest, at the fall of Jerusalem he was seized by the captain of the guard, was brought to the king of Babylon at Riblah, and was struck down (2 Kings 25:18-21, Jeremiah 52:24-27).
character: In a national crisis he showed the disposition of an official who faithfully carried out the royal commands as a confidant of the king (Jeremiah 21:1). He served as a bridge between the royal house and the forces opposed to the prophet Jeremiah, but he took a prudent and procedural stance, as when he did not immediately put Jeremiah to death but informed him of the contents of the letter (Jeremiah 29:29). As a leading priest of the temple, he held such high standing that the Babylonian army singled him out as a person of note (2 Kings 25:18).

introduce: Nehemiah is a figure of the age of the return from the Babylonian exile, a son of Hacaliah (Nehemiah 1:1). In the time of King Artaxerxes he was in the citadel of Susa and became the king's cupbearer (Nehemiah 1:1, 1:11).
lifetime: While serving as the king's cupbearer in the citadel of Susa, Nehemiah heard of the condition of Jerusalem, grieved, and fasted (Nehemiah 1:4). He asked King Artaxerxes to send him to the city of the tombs of his fathers in the land of Judah that he might rebuild it, and he received permission (Nehemiah 2:5-7), and was appointed governor of the land of Judah (Nehemiah 5:14). When Ezra the scribe read the book of the law and all the people wept, Governor Nehemiah, together with Ezra and the Levites, told the people not to mourn or weep (Nehemiah 8:9). Afterward, in the thirty-second year of Artaxerxes king of Babylon, he went to the king, then asked for leave and returned to Jerusalem, where he learned of the evil that Eliashib had done in preparing a chamber for Tobiah (Nehemiah 13:6-7).
event: He directed the work that completed the wall of Jerusalem in fifty-two days (Nehemiah 6:15). In the course of rebuilding the wall, in response to the threats of the opposing forces, he stationed armed men and strengthened the guard (Nehemiah 4:16-18). He also resolved the problem of the people of Judah suffering under unjust usury and ordered the nobles to return the land (Nehemiah 5:10-12). When the population of Jerusalem was short, he selected residents by casting lots and had them dwell there (Nehemiah 11:1); when the people heard the law, they separated the mixed multitude from Israel (Nehemiah 13:3); and he rebuked the men of Judah for taking foreign women as wives and made them swear by God that they would not give or take their daughters and sons in marriage with them (Nehemiah 13:23-25).
character: As a close associate of the king, upon hearing the news of Jerusalem, Nehemiah showed the prudence of responding immediately with fasting and prayer (Nehemiah 1:4). During the twelve years he served as governor he did not take his own allowance, showing the integrity of lightening the economic burden of the people (Nehemiah 5:14-15). He is portrayed as a man with the resolution and drive to press ahead with the work on the wall, unshaken by outside slander and threats (Nehemiah 6:3).

introduce: Daniel was a man of the noble lineage of the kingdom of Judah who, after being taken captive to Babylon, was educated in the Babylonian royal palace and appointed to office. He was taken to Babylon in the time of Jehoiakim king of Judah and served in the court of King Nebuchadnezzar (Daniel 1:1, 1:6).
lifetime: Born a descendant of the nobility of Judah, he was taken captive to Babylon (Daniel 1:3-6). In the Babylonian royal palace he learned the literature and language of the Chaldeans (Daniel 1:4). After he interpreted the dream of King Nebuchadnezzar, the king exalted him and made him chief over all the wise men of Babylon (Daniel 2:48). Afterward, in the time of King Belshazzar, he became the third ruler in the kingdom (Daniel 5:29), and in the time of Darius the Mede he also kept office as one of the three presidents (Daniel 6:1-2).
event: He interpreted the dream that King Nebuchadnezzar dreamed and resolved the king's distress (Daniel 2:24-45). At the feast of King Belshazzar he interpreted the meaning of the writing that appeared on the wall (Daniel 5:17-28). During the reign of Darius the Mede he was appointed one of the presidents and ran the affairs of state, but because he violated the decree forbidding prayer to any god other than the king, he was thrown into the lions' den and survived (Daniel 6:1-23). He saw visions concerning the future on several occasions and left them in writing (Daniel 7:1, 8:1).
character: He resolved not to defile himself with the king's food and wine and volunteered to eat vegetables and drink water (Daniel 1:8, 1:12). Despite the king's decree, he kept the habit of opening his window toward Jerusalem and kneeling in prayer three times a day (Daniel 6:10). It is recorded that the kings and officials could find in him no fault or corruption (Daniel 6:4).

introduce: Isaiah was a prophet of the kingdom of Southern Judah, recorded as the son of Amoz (Isaiah 1:1). Active in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, he spoke the word of God concerning Judah and Jerusalem (Isaiah 1:1).
lifetime: In the year that King Uzziah died, Isaiah saw a vision of God in the temple and was called as a prophet (Isaiah 6:1). In the time of King Ahaz, Rezin king of Aram and Pekah king of Israel went up against Jerusalem but could not overcome it (Isaiah 7:1), and the LORD told Isaiah to go out with his son Shear-jashub to meet Ahaz and say to him, "Take heed, be quiet, and do not fear" (Isaiah 7:3-4). In the time of King Hezekiah, in the matter of Rabshakeh sent by the king of Assyria, when the king sent Eliakim the palace administrator and others to Isaiah, Isaiah delivered the word of the LORD (Isaiah 37:2-7). No record of his death can be confirmed in the biblical text.
event: Isaiah presented the sign of Immanuel to King Ahaz (Isaiah 7:14), and when King Hezekiah was threatened by Sennacherib king of Assyria, through prayer he delivered God's answer of saving Jerusalem (Isaiah 37:21). He also delivered the word of God concerning healing when King Hezekiah was sick (Isaiah 38:5), and afterward, when men came from Babylon, he delivered to Hezekiah the word of the LORD that everything in the royal palace would be carried to Babylon and that some of the king's descendants would become eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon (Isaiah 39:6-7).

introduce: Joab was the son of Zeruiah, David's sister, and a man who served as commander of King David's army. He was a brother of Abishai and Asahel, and a key commander who laid the military foundation of the Davidic dynasty (2 Samuel 2:18, 1 Chronicles 2:16).
lifetime: When David became king in Hebron, Joab the son of Zeruiah went out with the servants of David and met the party of Ish-bosheth by the pool of Gibeon (2 Samuel 2:13). At the time of Absalom's rebellion he commanded David's army and led it to victory, but he killed Absalom in disobedience to David's command (2 Samuel 18:14). In David's last years he supported Adonijah's attempt to succeed to the throne (1 Kings 1:7), and afterward, by the command of King Solomon, while holding the horns of the altar at the tabernacle, he was put to death by Benaiah (1 Kings 2:34).
event: When David said that whoever struck the Jebusites first would be made chief and commander, Joab the son of Zeruiah went up first and became chief (1 Chronicles 11:6), and he repaired the rest of the city (1 Chronicles 11:8). In the battle against the coalition of Aram and Ammon he employed strategy and won (2 Samuel 10:11). When Abner returned to Hebron, Joab took him aside into the gateway as if to speak with him quietly and stabbed him in the stomach and killed him, on account of the blood of his brother Asahel (2 Samuel 3:27). After David commanded by letter that Uriah be put at the front of the fiercest fighting (2 Samuel 11:14-15), Joab placed Uriah at a place where he knew there were valiant men, so that he died (2 Samuel 11:16-17). He also stabbed Amasa in the stomach with a sword and killed him (2 Samuel 20:10).
character: He tended to interpret the king's commands arbitrarily, or to refuse them, in order to maintain his own power (2 Samuel 18:14). He did not hesitate to assassinate those in a hostile relationship with him, and he made ruthless decisions to achieve his aims (2 Samuel 3:27, 2 Samuel 20:10). While enjoying the trust of King David, he at the same time habitually took political actions that conflicted with the king's will (1 Kings 2:5).

introduce: Baruch was a man who, at the end of the kingdom of Judah, served as scribe to the prophet Jeremiah. He was the son of Neriah and the grandson of Mahseiah (Jeremiah 32:12), and his brother Seraiah was the man who went to Babylon with Zedekiah king of Judah (Jeremiah 51:59).
lifetime: Baruch took on the role of writing in a scroll the words of the LORD dictated by Jeremiah (Jeremiah 36:4). As Jeremiah commanded, in the house of the LORD he read the words of the LORD from the book to all the people (Jeremiah 36:8-10), and afterward he read the same to the high officials (Jeremiah 36:15). Afterward Johanan and all the commanders of the forces took the prophet Jeremiah and Baruch and entered the land of Egypt (Jeremiah 43:5-7).
event: In the fourth year of King Jehoiakim, when Jeremiah called him, he wrote on a scroll, from the mouth of Jeremiah, all the words that the LORD had spoken to him (Jeremiah 36:1, 36:4). When King Jehoiakim burned the scroll, Jeremiah took another scroll and gave it to Baruch, who wrote on it, from the mouth of Jeremiah, all the words of the book that had been burned, and many similar words were added besides (Jeremiah 36:32). Also Jeremiah gave to Baruch, in the presence of the witnesses and of all the men of Judah, the deed of purchase of the field at Anathoth, and was commanded to put the sealed deed and the open deed in an earthenware vessel to be preserved for many days (Jeremiah 32:12-14).
character: He showed himself lamenting over the suffering he received, but he received from the LORD the promise that his life would be saved (Jeremiah 45:3-5). As a scribe who faithfully carried out Jeremiah's instructions, he completed the concrete task of recording and reading the prophecies (Jeremiah 36:4-10).

introduce: Hadad was of the royal family of Edom, a man whom the LORD raised up in the time of Solomon to be an adversary to Solomon (1 Kings 11:14). When Joab, commander of David's army, struck down and killed every male in Edom, he, as a little child, fled to Egypt with some Edomites of his father's servants and survived (1 Kings 11:15-17).
lifetime: Hadad, as a descendant of the king of Edom, fled to Egypt when Joab killed every male in Edom (1 Kings 11:14-17). In Egypt he found great favor in the sight of Pharaoh, who gave him in marriage the sister of his wife, and by her he fathered a son, Genubath (1 Kings 11:19-20). After he heard that David and Joab were dead, Hadad asked Pharaoh to send him to his own country, and though Pharaoh tried to dissuade him, he said, "Only let me depart" (1 Kings 11:21-22).
event: Because Solomon turned his heart away from the LORD, the God of Israel, the LORD raised up Hadad the Edomite as an adversary to Solomon (1 Kings 11:9, 11:14). The Bible records that the trouble that Hadad caused lasted throughout Solomon's lifetime (1 Kings 11:25).

introduce: Pekah was a king of the kingdom of Northern Israel, the son of Remaliah, who killed the king (Pekahiah), Argob, and Arieh and came to the throne (2 Kings 15:25). He ruled Israel in Samaria for twenty years (2 Kings 15:27).
lifetime: Pekah was originally an officer of the king, the son of Remaliah, but with fifty men of Gilead he killed the king in the citadel of the king's palace in Samaria and became king in his place (2 Kings 15:25). He ruled Israel for twenty years but did evil in the sight of the LORD and did not depart from the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, who caused Israel to sin (2 Kings 15:27-28). In the last years of his reign Hoshea the son of Elah conspired against him, struck him down and killed him, and reigned in his place (2 Kings 15:30).
event: In the time of Pekah, Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria invaded and captured Ijon, Abel-beth-maacah, Janoah, Kedesh, Hazor, Gilead, Galilee, and all the land of Naphtali, and took the people captive and carried them to Assyria (2 Kings 15:29). Also, in the time of Ahaz the son of Jotham king of Judah, he made an alliance with Rezin king of Aram and came up to attack Jerusalem, but could not capture it (2 Kings 16:5).

introduce: In the Bible, Pharaoh is used as the official royal title referring to the ruler of Egypt. This title, derived from the Hebrew Par'oh, is not the name of a particular individual but a common noun for the Egyptian monarch, and from Genesis to Kings and the book of Jeremiah it was used in common when referring to several kings of Egypt.
lifetime: There was a king who took Sarai into his palace when Abram went down to Egypt to escape the famine (Genesis 12:15); the king who made Joseph ruler over all the land of Egypt (Genesis 41:41) and the king who let Joseph's father and brothers dwell in the land of Goshen are recorded (Genesis 47:5-6). Afterward, in the time of Moses, there was the Pharaoh who refused Israel's demand to leave Egypt and said, "Who is the LORD?" (Exodus 5:2), and that Pharaoh made ready his chariot and took his people with him and pursued Israel (Exodus 14:6). In later times there are mentioned Pharaoh king of Egypt, with whom Solomon made an alliance and whose daughter he took (1 Kings 3:1), Pharaoh Neco king of Egypt, who killed Josiah at Megiddo (2 Kings 23:29), and Pharaoh Hophra, whom Jeremiah prophesied he would give into the hand of his enemies (Jeremiah 44:30).
event: Pharaoh made Joseph, who interpreted his dream, ruler over all the land of Egypt (Genesis 41:15-16, 41:41). In Exodus, Pharaoh refused Moses' demand and increased the brick labor of the sons of Israel (Exodus 5:6-9), and afterward Pharaoh's army, pursuing Israel, entered the sea and was covered by the waters, so that not one of them remained (Exodus 14:23-28). In the time of Solomon, Pharaoh king of Egypt came up and captured Gezer, burned it with fire, and gave that city as a present to his daughter, Solomon's wife (1 Kings 9:16).
character: He showed despotic authority, as when he was angry with the magicians who could not interpret his dream (Genesis 41:8), and when oppressing the people of Israel he held consistently to a hardened heart and refused their demand (Exodus 8:15). As a ruler with divine authority, he also revealed the political traits of deifying himself or employing diplomatic strategy for the interests of the state (2 Kings 23:29).

meaning: one who gathers and heaps up
introduce: Asaph was a descendant of Gershon of the tribe of Levi, and one of the chief musicians who were in charge of praise in the temple in the time of David and Solomon. He formed the family known as the sons of Asaph and became the founder who passed on the duty of praise in the worship of the temple until after the return from the Babylonian exile.
lifetime: King David appointed singers from among the Levites, and at that time Asaph, together with Heman and Ethan, was appointed to sound the cymbals (1 Chronicles 15:17). When the ark of God was set inside the tent that David had pitched for it, and David appointed Levites to minister before the ark of the LORD, Asaph was the chief of them and sounded the cymbals loudly (1 Chronicles 16:1, 16:4-5). After Solomon finished building the temple, the sons of Asaph led the praise (2 Chronicles 5:12), and afterward, in the time of King Hezekiah as well, they praised the LORD with the words of Asaph (2 Chronicles 29:30). Even after returning from the Babylonian exile, the sons of Asaph continued to carry out the duty of praise in the temple (Ezra 2:41).
event: Asaph was the man whom David appointed, together with his brothers, at the time he placed the ark in the tent, to give thanks to the LORD first, and he became its chief (1 Chronicles 16:5, 16:7). King Hezekiah, together with the officials, had the Levites praise the LORD with the words of David and of Asaph the seer (2 Chronicles 29:30), and the descendants of Asaph were called the sons of Asaph and carried on the duty of praise (1 Chronicles 25:1). In the time of Nehemiah as well, the sons of Asaph are recorded as the singers of the temple, confirming the continuity of that duty (Nehemiah 11:22).

introduce: Pontius Pilate was a historical person, the governor of the Roman Empire in the region of Judea, who presided over the trial and execution of Jesus. He is recorded as governor of Judea in the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar (Luke 3:1).
lifetime: While serving as governor of Judea, Pilate received Jesus handed over for trial and sentenced him to death (Matthew 27:2). He insisted on Jesus' innocence and tried to release him, but yielded to the strong pressure of the Jews and approved the crucifixion (John 19:12-16). No detailed record of his life or death afterward appears in the Bible.
event: He asked whether Jesus was a Galilean, and when he learned that he belonged to Herod's jurisdiction, he sent Jesus to Herod (Luke 23:6-7). Also, in the process of releasing one prisoner according to the Passover custom, he asked whether they wanted him to release the King of the Jews (Mark 15:6-9), but he released Barabbas and, after scourging Jesus, handed him over to be crucified (Mark 15:15). He also wrote a notice reading "Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews" and had it attached to Jesus' cross (John 19:19).
character: In the course of questioning Jesus he found in him no crime worthy of death (Luke 23:22), and he was also warned by his wife, who called Jesus a righteous man on account of what she had suffered in a dream because of him, not to have anything to do with him (Matthew 27:19). Although he strove to release Jesus, he felt the political burden of the opinion of the Jews, which appealed to loyalty to the Roman emperor, and showed the weak side of reversing his own decision (John 19:12). In the middle of the trial he washed his hands and publicly claimed innocence in this matter, trying to evade responsibility (Matthew 27:24).

introduce: Benjamin was the youngest of the twelve sons whom Jacob had, and he was a full brother of Joseph, by Rachel (Genesis 35:18). Born last of Jacob's twelve sons, he became the ancestor of the tribe of Benjamin among the twelve tribes of Israel (Genesis 46:21).
lifetime: Benjamin was born in the land of Canaan near Ephrath, and his mother Rachel died of a difficult labor as she gave birth to Benjamin (Genesis 35:16-18). Afterward Jacob cherished Benjamin greatly, and because of the famine Benjamin went down with his brothers to Egypt, where Joseph was, to buy grain (Genesis 42:4, 43:15). Benjamin, on reaching adulthood, had ten sons (Genesis 46:21), and afterward he lived in Egypt with Jacob's family and made his descendants multiply (Genesis 46:21-27).
event: There occurred the incident in which Joseph, in order to test his brothers, hid a silver cup in Benjamin's sack (Genesis 44:2). When because of this Benjamin was in danger of being seized as Joseph's slave, Judah pleaded to become a slave in his place (Genesis 44:33). Also, when Jacob blessed his children just before his death, he compared Benjamin to a ravenous wolf and left a prophecy foretelling the strength of his tribe (Genesis 49:27).

introduce: Gedaliah was a man appointed by Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, after the Babylonian invasion of Judah, as governor over those left in the land of Judah. He was the grandson of Shaphan and the son of Ahikam, and immediately after the fall of Jerusalem he governed the remnant of Judah with Mizpah as his center.
lifetime: Gedaliah was born the grandson of Shaphan and the son of Ahikam (2 Kings 25:22). After the Babylonian army conquered Judah, the king of Babylon appointed Gedaliah governor over the cities of Judah and entrusted to him the men, women, children, and the poor who had not been carried off to Babylon (Jeremiah 40:5, 40:7). Living at Mizpah, he swore to the commanders of the forces and their men and urged them not to fear serving the Chaldeans but to dwell in the land and serve the king of Babylon (Jeremiah 40:7-10). Afterward Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, the grandson of Elishama, of the royal family, came with ten men and struck Gedaliah down and killed him (2 Kings 25:25).
event: At Mizpah, Gedaliah sought stability by urging the remnant of the people of Judah to serve the Chaldeans, to gather wine, summer fruit, and oil and store them, and each to dwell in the cities he had taken (Jeremiah 40:9-10). Johanan the son of Kareah and the commanders of the forces informed him that Baalis king of the sons of Ammon had sent Ishmael the son of Nethaniah to take his life, but Gedaliah did not believe it, and when Johanan asked permission to kill Ishmael, he did not allow it (Jeremiah 40:13-16). In the end Ishmael and the ten men with him struck Gedaliah down with the sword and killed him, and they also killed all the Jews who were with Gedaliah at Mizpah and the Chaldean soldiers who were there (Jeremiah 41:2-3).

introduce: Boaz was a man of standing in the region of Bethlehem, the son of Salmon and of Rahab (Ruth 2:1, Matthew 1:5). He is mentioned as the great-grandfather of King David and an ancestor of Jesus Christ (Ruth 4:21-22, Matthew 1:5).
lifetime: Boaz was one who owned a field in Bethlehem and oversaw the harvest (Ruth 2:3). He discovered Ruth the Moabite gleaning in his field and learned of her circumstances (Ruth 2:5-11). Afterward, in order to exercise the right of the kinsman-redeemer, he carried out the proceedings before the elders at the gate, and he bought Naomi's land connected with the house of Elimelech and took Ruth as his wife (Ruth 4:1-10). A son named Obed was born to him and Ruth (Ruth 4:13, 17).
event: Boaz provided for Ruth to glean safely in his field and gave her food (Ruth 2:8-16). To fulfill his legal duty as kinsman-redeemer, he consulted with the other kinsman-redeemer, and at the gate, with the elders and the people as witnesses, he formalized the buying from the hand of Naomi of all that had belonged to Elimelech, Chilion, and Mahlon, and the taking of Ruth as his wife (Ruth 4:1-10). In this process the other kinsman-redeemer said to Boaz, "Buy it for yourself," and took off his sandal and handed over his right (Ruth 4:7-8).
character: Boaz maintained a good relationship with his servants, as when he greeted his workers with "The LORD be with you" (Ruth 2:4). He knew of Ruth's diligence and devotion to her mother-in-law, and he praised her for it and encouraged her (Ruth 2:11-12). Also, while fulfilling the responsibility of a kinsman-redeemer, he showed an attitude of observing proper legal procedure and custom in the process (Ruth 4:1-10).

introduce: Korah was a great-grandson of Levi, a grandson of Kohath, and the son of Izhar, a man who appears in the period of Israel's wilderness journey (Numbers 16:1). As a descendant of Kohath, he was a member of the family that held the duty of caring for the furnishings of the tabernacle (Numbers 4:15).
lifetime: Korah rose up against Moses together with two hundred fifty well-known chiefs among the congregation, chosen from the assembly of the sons of Israel (Numbers 16:2). He gathered renowned leaders from among the congregation and opposed Moses and Aaron (Numbers 16:2). Afterward, according to Moses' word, he took a censer and stood at the door of the tent of meeting with Moses and Aaron, and he gathered the whole congregation at the door of the tent of meeting and intended to oppose the two men, but the earth split open and swallowed him with all who belonged to Korah (Numbers 16:16-19, 16:31-32).
event: Korah conspired with Dathan and Abiram, the sons of Eliab, of the descendants of Reuben, and On the son of Peleth, and questioned the leadership of Moses and Aaron (Numbers 16:1). He protested that all the congregation was holy and that the LORD was among them, so why did Moses exalt himself above the assembly of the LORD (Numbers 16:3). Because of this incident Korah and those who belonged to him, with their houses and possessions, were all buried underground as the earth split open (Numbers 16:32). Also fire came out from the LORD and consumed the 250 men who were offering incense (Numbers 16:35).

introduce: Felix is a figure who appears in the book of Acts as the governor of the Roman Empire over Judea (Acts 23:24).
lifetime: When Paul was escorted to Caesarea, Felix, as governor, read the letter and asked Paul what province he was from, and learned that he was from Cilicia (Acts 23:33-34). He had Paul kept in Herod's Praetorium (Acts 23:35), and postponed the case, saying he would decide it when Lysias the commander came down (Acts 24:22). After two years had passed, Porcius Festus succeeded Felix, and Felix, wishing to win the favor of the Jews, left Paul in custody (Acts 24:27).
event: Having received the letter of the commander Claudius Lysias, he had Paul stand before him, said he would hear him when his accusers came, and had him kept in Herod's Praetorium (Acts 23:33-35). When the high priest Ananias came down with some elders and an orator named Tertullus and accused Paul before the governor, he heard it (Acts 24:1). When Paul discoursed on righteousness, self-control, and the coming judgment, Felix was afraid and said, "Go away for now; when I have an opportunity I will send for you" (Acts 24:25). Hoping that money would be given to him by Paul, he sent for him more often and talked with him, but in the end he did not release him (Acts 24:26).
character: He showed an attitude of putting his own political interest first in order to win the favor of the Jews (Acts 24:27). He showed material greed, to the point of sending for Paul frequently and conversing with him in the hope of obtaining a bribe from him (Acts 24:26). Although he reacted with fear on hearing Paul's discourse, he showed a double-sided character in continuing Paul's unjust detention in order to strengthen his own political standing (Acts 24:25).

introduce: Leah was the elder daughter of Laban of Paddan-aram, the daughter of Laban, who was Jacob's mother's brother and became his father-in-law (Genesis 29:16). She was Jacob's first wife and the woman who bore the ancestors of six of the twelve tribes of Israel (Genesis 29:23, 29:32-35, 30:17-20).
lifetime: Laban gave Leah in marriage to Jacob before her younger sister Rachel (Genesis 29:23). By Jacob, Leah bore Reuben, Simeon, Levi, and Judah in succession (Genesis 29:32-35), and afterward she bore Issachar, Zebulun, and a daughter, Dinah (Genesis 30:18-21). Leah accompanied Jacob when he returned to Canaan (Genesis 31:17), and later she was buried in the cave of Machpelah, where Jacob was also buried (Genesis 49:31).
event: She bore Jacob's firstborn son Reuben, and also Simeon, Levi, and Judah (Genesis 29:32-35). When the LORD saw that Leah was unloved, he opened her womb (Genesis 29:31). When she stopped bearing, Leah gave her maid Zilpah to Jacob to be a concubine (Genesis 30:9), and over the mandrakes that her son Reuben found in the field, she made a bargain with Rachel and lay with Jacob that night (Genesis 30:14-16).
character: The Bible describes Leah as a person with weak eyes (Genesis 29:17). From the biblical text one can confirm that she longed for the love of her husband Jacob but was in a position of relative neglect compared with Rachel (Genesis 29:30-31). Also, each time she bore children she named each son while mentioning that God had seen her affliction and given her a son (Genesis 29:32-35).

introduce: Silas was a man called a leading man among the brothers of the church in Jerusalem in the early church, and he is also recorded under the name Silvanus (Acts 15:22, 1 Peter 5:12). Paul chose him and set out together with him, traveling through Syria and Cilicia and strengthening the churches (Acts 15:40-41).
lifetime: He was called a leading man among the brothers in the church in Jerusalem and was chosen, together with Paul and Barnabas, as a man to be sent to Antioch (Acts 15:22). After Paul and Barnabas parted, Paul chose Silas and set out for Syria and Cilicia (Acts 15:39-41). At Philippi he was dragged with Paul before the magistrates, beaten, and thrown into prison (Acts 16:19-24), and at midnight a great earthquake came, the prison doors were opened, and everyone's bonds were unfastened (Acts 16:25-26). Afterward Paul and Silas were sent away by the brothers by night to Berea (Acts 17:10), and even after Paul left, Silas stayed in Berea with Timothy (Acts 17:14). He came down from Macedonia with Timothy and joined Paul (Acts 18:5). In 1 Peter 5:12 Peter says he writes his letter of exhortation through Silvanus, whom he regards as a faithful brother.
event: He was sent together with Judas to tell the church in Antioch by word of mouth the decision of the apostolic council in Jerusalem (Acts 15:27). At Philippi, though he was beaten and thrown into prison with Paul, at midnight he prayed and sang praises to God with Paul (Acts 16:23-25), and the word of the Lord was spoken to the jailer and all his household (Acts 16:31-32). He came down from Macedonia with Timothy and joined Paul (Acts 18:5). In 1 Peter 5:12 it is said that Peter wrote his letter through Silvanus, whom he regards as a faithful brother.
character: He was a man recognized by the apostles and elders at the time of the Jerusalem council as a leader among the brothers (Acts 15:22). He was called a prophet, and he had the ability to exhort and strengthen believers by preaching the gospel (Acts 15:32). Even in the suffering of being thrown into prison he did not despair but kept his integrity of faith, to the point of singing praises (Acts 16:25). Peter judged him a faithful brother and placed his trust in him (1 Peter 5:12).

introduce: Haggai was a prophet who was active in the land of Judah in the time of King Darius after the return from the Babylonian exile (Haggai 1:1). He is recorded as a prophet who, together with Zechariah, prophesied to the Jews who were in Judah and Jerusalem (Ezra 5:1).
lifetime: Haggai began to deliver the word of God on the first day of the sixth month of the second year of King Darius (Haggai 1:1). He delivered a message urging Zerubbabel, governor of Judah, and Joshua the high priest to resume the work of rebuilding the temple (Haggai 1:1). Also, on the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month of the same year, he put a question about the law to the priests and stressed the importance of building the temple (Haggai 2:10-11).
event: By getting the interrupted building of the temple started again, he contributed to the completion of the temple work on the third day of the month Adar in the sixth year of King Darius (Haggai 1:14, Ezra 6:15). To Zerubbabel, governor of Judah, Haggai delivered the word of the LORD: "On that day I will take you and make you like a signet ring, for I have chosen you" (Haggai 2:23).

introduce: Achan is a man recorded as a great-grandson of Zerah of the tribe of Judah, a grandson of Zabdi, and a son of Carmi (Joshua 7:1). He is known as one who, in the period when Israel was carrying out the war of conquest of Canaan, took spoil in the city of Jericho and violated the discipline of the community.
lifetime: As a member of the tribe of Judah he took part in Israel's entry into Canaan (Joshua 7:1). At the capture of Jericho he took what was devoted to the LORD (Joshua 7:1, 21). Afterward, when Joshua had Israel come near by tribe, clan, family, and each man, Achan was taken (Joshua 7:16-18), and in the Valley of Achor all Israel stoned him (Joshua 7:24-25).
event: In the battle of the city of Jericho he took the forbidden spoil — a beautiful robe from Mount Shinar, two hundred shekels of silver, and a bar of gold weighing fifty shekels — and hid them in the ground inside his tent (Joshua 7:21). Because of this the sons of Israel could not stand against their enemies and were defeated before the men of Ai (Joshua 7:5, 11-12). When Joshua had Israel come near by tribe, Achan was taken, and he confessed that he had sinned against the LORD, the God of Israel (Joshua 7:18, 20). As a result Achan, with his silver, the robe, the bar of gold, his sons and daughters, his oxen, donkeys, and sheep, his tent, and all that belonged to him, was brought up to the Valley of Achor, stoned, and burned (Joshua 7:24-25).

introduce: The Philistines were a people who lived on the coastal plain of the Mediterranean in the ancient Near East, and in the Bible they are portrayed as a power in continual conflict with Israel from the time of the conquest of Canaan. They formed a confederation centered on five major cities — Gaza, Ashdod, Ashkelon, Gath, and Ekron — and the rulers of each city were called lords.
lifetime: The Philistines came from the Casluhites, who were descendants of Ham (Genesis 10:14), and are recorded as a people who came up from Caphtor (Amos 9:7). After settling in the land of Canaan, from the period of the judges of Israel until the reign of David, they bordered the territory of Israel and kept up military hostility with it (Judges 3:3).
event: The Philistines, fearing that the Hebrews would make swords or spears, saw to it that there was no smith in all the land of Israel (1 Samuel 13:19-20), and when, in the dispute connected with Samson's wife, they burned that woman and her father (Judges 15:6), they were greatly slaughtered by Samson (Judges 15:7-8). Also, in the battle of Ebenezer they captured the ark of God, but when the ark had been in the country of the Philistines for seven months, they sent it back (1 Samuel 4:11, 1 Samuel 6:1). Goliath of Gath appears as the champion who challenged to battle from the Philistine camp (1 Samuel 17:4). David struck the Philistines and subdued them, and took Gath and its towns out of the hand of the Philistines (1 Chronicles 18:1).
character: The Bible describes the Philistines as a people in a hostile relationship with Israel, and, religiously, they are characterized by worshiping the god Dagon (1 Samuel 5:2). They are portrayed as a warlike group with their own military organization and system of government, and they played the role of oppressing Israel and of exerting continual military pressure during Israel's process of establishing the monarchy (1 Samuel 13:19).

introduce: Naphtali was a son born to Jacob and Rachel's maidservant Bilhah, the sixth son of Jacob and the ancestor of the tribe of Naphtali, one of the twelve tribes of Israel (Genesis 30:8).
lifetime: As the second son born to Jacob and Rachel's maid Bilhah (Genesis 30:7-8), he is recorded among the sons of Jacob together with Gad and Asher, the sons of Leah's maid Zilpah, and Dan, the son of Rachel's maid Bilhah (Genesis 35:25-26). The sons of Naphtali, namely Jahzeel, Guni, Jezer, and Shillem, are recorded among the descendants who went down to Egypt with Jacob (Genesis 46:8, 24-26), and later became the clans of the descendants of Naphtali (Numbers 26:48-49).
event: He was the second son whom Rachel obtained through her maidservant Bilhah, and when he was born Rachel named him Naphtali, in the sense that she had prevailed in the contest (Genesis 30:8). When Jacob blessed his sons before his death, he compared him to a doe and described him as one who gives beautiful words (Genesis 49:21).

introduce: Shelah is a man recorded as the son of Arphaxad and the father of Eber (Genesis 10:24). A descendant of Shem and a great-grandson of Noah, he was one of the patriarchs who carried on the line of humanity after the flood (1 Chronicles 1:18).
lifetime: Arphaxad fathered Shelah at the age of thirty-five, and after fathering Shelah he lived 403 years and fathered sons and daughters (Genesis 11:12-13). Shelah fathered Eber at the age of thirty, and after fathering Eber he lived 403 years and fathered sons and daughters, and he enjoyed a total of 433 years (Genesis 11:14-15).
event: As a descendant of Shem, he played the role of a middle link in the central genealogy by which the line of humanity after the flood runs from Arphaxad through Shelah and Eber (1 Chronicles 1:24).

introduce: Judah was the fourth son born to Jacob and Leah, the ancestor of the tribe of Judah, one of the twelve tribes of Israel (Genesis 29:35). He is recorded as one who played a leading role among his brothers (Genesis 43:8).
lifetime: Judah married the daughter of Shua the Canaanite and had three sons: Er, Onan, and Shelah (Genesis 38:2-5). Afterward, through his daughter-in-law Tamar, he fathered Perez and Zerah (Genesis 38:29-30). He proposed that instead of killing Joseph they sell him to the Ishmaelites (Genesis 37:26-27), and later, when Jacob's family moved to Egypt, Jacob sent Judah ahead to Joseph to guide them to Goshen (Genesis 46:28).
event: At the time Joseph was sold into Egypt, Judah proposed that instead of killing him they sell him to the Ishmaelites (Genesis 37:26-27). In connection with his daughter-in-law Tamar, after his sons died he tried not to give her his son Shelah, but when Tamar produced the pledge he acknowledged his own wrong, saying, "She is more righteous than I" (Genesis 38:11, 38:26). When going to Egypt during the famine to seek food, he pledged to his father that he would be surety for Benjamin (Genesis 43:8-9), and before Joseph he pleaded to remain as a slave in place of Benjamin (Genesis 44:18, 33).
character: Within the family he played the role of spokesman for his brothers (Genesis 43:8), and when his wrong was exposed he showed himself acknowledging it (Genesis 38:26). Also, giving deep consideration to the grief of his father Jacob, he showed a responsible attitude of protecting Benjamin to the end (Genesis 44:33).

introduce: Kohath was a son of Levi and a grandson of Jacob (Genesis 46:11). Within the tribe of Levi he was the ancestor of the family of the sons of Kohath, whose descendants, the Kohathites, were given the work concerning the most holy things in the tent of meeting and the carrying of the furnishings of the sanctuary (Numbers 4:4, 15).
lifetime: Kohath was born a son of Levi, one of the descendants of Jacob who went down to Egypt (Genesis 46:11). The years of his life were one hundred thirty-three, and he had four sons: Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel (Exodus 6:18). His son Amram fathered Aaron and Moses (Exodus 6:20), and to Amram were born Aaron, Moses, and their sister Miriam (Numbers 26:59). Therefore Kohath was the grandfather of Aaron, Moses, and Miriam.
event: Kohath, rather than through direct activity, formed through his descendants the central family of the duties connected with the carrying of the tabernacle. As a son of Levi, Kohath's descendants were later given the task of carrying the furnishings of the tabernacle during the wilderness journey (Numbers 4:15).

introduce: Asa was the third king of the kingdom of Judah, the son of Abijam, the grandson of Rehoboam, and a descendant of David (1 Kings 15:8, 14:31). He reigned in Jerusalem forty-one years (1 Kings 15:10).
lifetime: Asa succeeded to the throne after his father Abijam died (1 Kings 15:8). During his reign he was at war with Baasha king of Northern Israel all his days (1 Kings 15:16). In the thirty-sixth year of his reign, when Baasha king of Israel built Ramah to keep the people of Judah from coming and going, Asa sent the silver and gold from the treasuries of the house of the LORD and of the royal palace to Ben-hadad king of Aram and asked for a treaty, and Ben-hadad attacked the cities of Israel (2 Chronicles 16:1-4). In the thirty-ninth year since Asa became king, his feet became diseased, and his disease was severe, yet he did not seek the LORD but the physicians (2 Chronicles 16:12), and in the forty-first year of his reign he died and was buried in the city of David (2 Chronicles 16:13-14).
event: Asa drove out the male cult prostitutes from Judah and removed all the idols that his fathers had made (1 Kings 15:12), and because his mother Maacah had made an Asherah pole, he removed her from the position of queen mother, cut down her idol, and burned it by the brook Kidron (1 Kings 15:13). Militarily, there was the incident in which he repulsed Zerah the Cushite when he came with an army of a million men (2 Chronicles 14:9-13). Also, in the fifteenth year of King Asa, he led a ceremony in which they gathered at Jerusalem, offered sacrifices to the LORD, and renewed the covenant (2 Chronicles 15:10-12). He took the building materials of Ramah that Baasha had been building and used them to build Geba and Mizpah (1 Kings 15:22).
character: Asa did what was right in the eyes of the LORD from the beginning of his reign (1 Kings 15:11), and his heart is judged to have been wholly devoted to the LORD all his days (1 Kings 15:14). However, near the end of his reign, when the seer Hanani rebuked him for relying on the king of Aram, he was angry with him, put him in prison, and oppressed some of the people (2 Chronicles 16:10).

introduce: Balak was the king of Moab, the son of Zippor, and a ruler of a neighboring people whom the people of Israel encountered on their way to the land of Canaan (Numbers 22:2).
lifetime: When the sons of Israel camped on the plains of Moab, Moab was greatly afraid because of the multitude of the people of Israel, and at that time Balak the son of Zippor was king of Moab (Numbers 22:1, 3-4). He sent messengers to Pethor, the home of Balaam the son of Beor, to summon Balaam and have him curse this people (Numbers 22:5-6). Balak again sent more and higher-ranking nobles, saying that he would exalt Balaam and honor him greatly, and asked him to come and curse this people (Numbers 22:15-17); and when he heard that Balaam was coming, he went out as far as the city on the Arnon at the border of Moab to meet him (Numbers 22:36). Afterward Balak led Balaam in turn to the high places of Baal, the top of Pisgah, and the top of Peor (Numbers 22:41, 23:13-14, 23:28), but Balaam blessed three times (Numbers 24:10). Revelation 2:14 says that Balaam taught Balak to put a stumbling block before Israel, to eat food sacrificed to idols and to commit sexual immorality.
event: In order to curse Israel, he sent messengers to Balaam and asked him to come and curse this people (Numbers 22:5-7). As Balaam said, he built seven altars, prepared seven bulls and seven rams, and offered a bull and a ram on each altar with Balaam (Numbers 23:1-2), and at the top of Pisgah in the field of Zophim (Numbers 23:14) and at the top of Peor (Numbers 23:28-30) he likewise built altars and offered sacrifices in the same way. When Balaam blessed three times, Balak was angry and struck his hands together and said, "Flee to your place now," and that he had intended to honor him greatly, but that the LORD had kept him back from honor (Numbers 24:10-11).
character: He showed himself greatly afraid on seeing that the people of Israel were numerous and mighty (Numbers 22:3). He relied on Balaam, a diviner of another nation, in an attempt to restrain Israel, and used reward and payment as means to attain his purpose (Numbers 22:16-17). A hot-tempered side is evident in the way he reproached Balaam for failing to receive wealth and honor as the price of prophecy and openly expressed his own feelings (Numbers 24:10-11).

introduce: Cyrus was the king of Persia who, in the first year of his reign, issued a decree that the people of Judah might go up to Jerusalem and build the house of the LORD (Ezra 1:1-3). In the Bible he appears as a foreign king whom the LORD called "my anointed, Cyrus" (Isaiah 45:1).
lifetime: In the first year of Cyrus king of Persia, in order to fulfill the word of the LORD spoken by the mouth of Jeremiah, the LORD stirred up his spirit, and he made a proclamation throughout all his kingdom and issued a decree (2 Chronicles 36:22, Ezra 1:1). In that decree he said that the LORD, the God of heaven, had given him all the kingdoms of the earth and had charged him to build a house at Jerusalem in Judah (Ezra 1:2).
event: In the decree Cyrus said that all of his people should go up to Jerusalem in Judah and build the house of the LORD (2 Chronicles 36:23, Ezra 1:3), and that the men of the places where the remaining people sojourned should help them with silver and gold, with goods, and with beasts, besides freewill offerings (Ezra 1:4). King Cyrus brought out the vessels of the house of the LORD that Nebuchadnezzar had carried away from Jerusalem and put in the house of his gods (Ezra 1:7), and commanded Mithredath the treasurer to count them out and number them to Sheshbazzar the prince of Judah (Ezra 1:8).
character: The Bible calls Cyrus the one anointed by the LORD, and stresses that God called him by name even though he did not know God (Isaiah 45:4). He pursued a lenient policy toward the conquered peoples in his realm, and in particular showed a manner of rule that allowed the peoples brought captive to return to their homeland and to have religious freedom (Ezra 1:3).

introduce: The son of Jehoiada the priest, who was active in the time of Joash king of Judah, and who was put to death by stoning in the court of the temple in Jerusalem.
lifetime: In the time of King Joash, after Jehoiada died, the princes of Judah came and bowed down to the king, and the king listened to them and abandoned the house of the LORD and served the Asherah poles and idols (2 Chronicles 24:17-18). Then Zechariah the son of Jehoiada the priest stood before the people and warned them, and the crowd conspired together and, at the command of the king, stoned him in the court of the house of the LORD (2 Chronicles 24:20-21). King Joash did not remember the kindness that Zechariah's father Jehoiada had shown him, and killed his son (2 Chronicles 24:22). Matthew 23:35 mentions Zechariah the son of Berechiah, who was killed between the temple and the altar, but from the text alone it cannot be determined whether this person is the same as Zechariah the son of Jehoiada.
event: Zechariah the son of Jehoiada the priest, moved by the Spirit of God, warned the people about their abandonment of the commandments of the LORD (2 Chronicles 24:20).
character: Moved by the Spirit of God, he showed the boldness to speak the right word even in a hostile situation (2 Chronicles 24:20). He had the firm attitude of delivering the will of God face to face to the king who had forgotten the kindness shown by his father Jehoiada and had betrayed it (2 Chronicles 24:22).

introduce: Puah is a man recorded as a son of Issachar. In 1 Chronicles 7:1 he appears together with Tola, Jashub, and Shimron as one of the four sons of Issachar (1 Chronicles 7:1).
lifetime: Puah is recorded as one of the four sons of Issachar: Tola, Puah, Jashub, and Shimron (1 Chronicles 7:1).

introduce: Jonah was a prophet, the son of Amittai, from Gath-hepher (2 Kings 14:25). He was active in the time of Jeroboam II of Israel and carried out the task of speaking the word of God (2 Kings 14:25).
lifetime: Jonah received the command to go to Nineveh and cry out against it according to the word of the LORD, but he refused and tried to flee to Tarshish (Jonah 1:3). While sailing from Joppa he met a great storm and was thrown into the sea, and he remained three days and three nights in the belly of a great fish (Jonah 1:4, 1:15, 1:17). Afterward, after being vomited out by the fish, he went again to Nineveh and delivered the word of God (Jonah 2:10, 3:3).
event: In the time of Jeroboam II he prophesied that the territory of Israel would be restored from the entrance of Hamath to the Sea of the Arabah (2 Kings 14:25). He entered the city of Nineveh and proclaimed that after forty days Nineveh would be overthrown, and as a result the king and people of Nineveh fasted and repented (Jonah 3:4, 3:5). Afterward, when the destruction of Nineveh was withheld, he was displeased, built a booth east of the city, and sat watching what would become of the city (Jonah 4:5).
character: He showed an attitude of evading the command of God and trying to go to another region (Jonah 1:3). When he learned of God's merciful disposition toward Nineveh, he was greatly angry and distressed (Jonah 4:1). When the vine grew up over the city and then withered, his emotions changed so greatly that he wished that his life be taken (Jonah 4:6, 4:8).

introduce: He was the son of Buzi, a man of a priestly family who was active in the time of the Babylonian exile (Ezekiel 1:3). He began to receive the word of God in the fifth year after King Jehoiachin of Judah was taken captive (Ezekiel 1:2).
lifetime: While among the captives by the River Kebar in the land of the Chaldeans, he saw visions of God (Ezekiel 1:1, 1:3). He continued his prophetic activity concerning the destruction of Jerusalem and the restoration of Israel, and when his wife died in the evening, he did as he had been commanded in the morning and did not mourn (Ezekiel 24:16-18). In the twenty-fifth year of the captivity, the fourteenth year after the city was struck down, on the tenth day of the first month, the hand of the LORD was upon him, and in visions he was brought to the land of Israel and set down on a very high mountain (Ezekiel 40:1-2).
event: He performed several symbolic acts of prophecy signifying the imminent destruction of Jerusalem (Ezekiel 4:1-3, 5:1-4). He proclaimed the iniquity of Judah and the judgment of God that followed, and afterward recorded visions of Israel's being restored again (Ezekiel 37:1-10, 47:1-12). In the visions he saw on a high mountain in the land of Israel a man whose appearance was like bronze, standing with a line of flax and a measuring reed, and he was commanded to look with his eyes, hear with his ears, and declare to the house of Israel all that he saw (Ezekiel 40:2-4).

introduce: Hezron was the son of Perez and the grandson of Judah, a man who carried on the family line of the tribe of Judah (Genesis 46:12; 1 Chronicles 2:5). He is recorded as a great-grandson of Jacob and an ancestor of King David (Ruth 4:18-22).
lifetime: Hezron is recorded as a son of Perez in the list of the family of Israel when Jacob and his sons went down to Egypt (Genesis 46:8, 46:12). Later, in the census of the sons of Israel, the Hezronite family, descended from Hezron, is recorded among the descendants of Perez (Numbers 26:21).
event: The sons whom Hezron fathered were Jerahmeel, Ram, and Caleb (1 Chronicles 2:9). Also, at the age of sixty he went in to the daughter of Machir the father of Gilead and she bore him Segub, and Segub fathered Jair (1 Chronicles 2:21-22). In the genealogy of the book of Ruth, Perez fathered Hezron and Hezron fathered Ram, and this line reaches David (Ruth 4:18-22).

기타관계: Oren#2656(kinsman of the tribe of Judah)

introduce: Cushan-rishathaim is a man recorded as the king of Mesopotamia, a king whom the sons of Israel served for eight years (Judges 3:8).
lifetime: The LORD was angry with Israel and sold them into the hand of Cushan-rishathaim king of Mesopotamia, and the sons of Israel served him eight years (Judges 3:8).
event: When the sons of Israel cried out to the LORD, the LORD raised up as a deliverer Othniel the son of Kenaz, Caleb's younger brother, and the LORD gave Cushan-rishathaim into the hand of Othniel, and Othniel prevailed over him (Judges 3:9-10).

introduce: Peleg was a descendant of Shem and a son of Eber, one of the patriarchs who carried on the line of humanity after Noah's flood (Genesis 11:10-16). It is recorded that to Eber were born two sons, and the name of the one was Peleg, for in his days the earth was divided (Genesis 10:25).
lifetime: Peleg was born a son of Eber (Genesis 11:16) and fathered Reu at the age of thirty (Genesis 11:18). After fathering Reu he lived two hundred nine years and fathered sons and daughters, so that he lived 239 years in all (Genesis 11:18-19). He belongs to the line that runs from Shem through Arphaxad, Shelah, and Eber (Genesis 11:10-16), and in the genealogy of Luke he is also recorded as an ancestor of Abraham (Luke 3:34-35).
event: It is recorded that to Eber were born two sons, and the name of the one was Peleg, for in his days the earth was divided (Genesis 10:25). This verse itself does not record the specific content of the dividing of the earth.

introduce: Phygelus is a person who appears in 2 Timothy in the New Testament, whose name is mentioned in connection with the matter of those in Asia forsaking Paul (2 Timothy 1:15).
lifetime: In his letter to Timothy, Paul, speaking of the matter that all who are in Asia had turned away from him, said that among them were Phygelus and Hermogenes (2 Timothy 1:15). No other record of his birth or life is found in the Bible.
event: It is recorded that among all those in Asia who forsook Paul, Phygelus was one of them, together with Hermogenes (2 Timothy 1:15).

introduce: Barzillai the Gileadite was a wealthy man from Rogelim who supplied provisions and food to King David and the army that followed him when David fled to the east side of the Jordan to escape Absalom's rebellion (2 Samuel 17:27).
lifetime: While David stayed at Mahanaim fleeing from Absalom, Barzillai welcomed David's company together with Shobi and Machir (2 Samuel 17:27). After David had put down Absalom's revolt, Barzillai came out to escort him as he crossed the Jordan (2 Samuel 19:31). Remembering Barzillai's kindness, David offered to have him stay with him in Jerusalem, but Barzillai declined on account of his great age and wished to return to his hometown of Rogelim (2 Samuel 19:32-37). Before his death David charged Solomon to show kindness to the sons of Barzillai and to let them be among those who ate at the king's table (1 Kings 2:7).
event: Together with Shobi and Machir, he helped David in his flight, saying that David and the people with him must be hungry, weary, and thirsty in the wilderness, and bringing bedding, basins, earthen vessels, wheat, barley, flour, roasted grain, beans, lentils, roasted seeds, honey, curds, sheep, and cheese for them to eat (2 Samuel 17:27-29).
character: He stated that he was eighty years old and called himself an old man, and he showed an attitude of not wishing to burden the king (2 Samuel 19:32-35). He was a man of material abundance, a wealthy man (2 Samuel 19:32), and he had the discernment to decline the king's favor courteously and a regard for his hometown and the grave of his father and mother (2 Samuel 19:36-37).

call: Sanhedrin teacher of the law (Paul's teacher)
introduce: Gamaliel was a Pharisee and a teacher of the law who was honored by all the people in the Sanhedrin (Acts 5:34). He is the man at whose feet the apostle Paul said he had been trained (Acts 22:3).
lifetime: Gamaliel was a teacher of the law, honored by all the people (Acts 5:34). He is the one whom the apostle Paul mentioned directly as his teacher, and Paul testified that at his feet he had been strictly trained in the law of the fathers (Acts 22:3). There is no further detailed biblical record concerning his personal birth or the end of his life.
event: When Peter and the apostles were being examined before the Sanhedrin council, Gamaliel had the apostles put outside for a little while and then counseled the council members to act with caution. Citing the cases of Theudas and Judas, he argued that if the apostles' undertaking was of human origin it would fall by itself, but if it was from God it could not be stopped, and he proposed that the apostles be released (Acts 5:35-39).
character: Gamaliel was a prudent and moderate man who, rather than resorting to immediate physical suppression, chose to wait and see how matters would turn out (Acts 5:38-39). He was regarded as a man who combined scholarly authority and social influence within the Judaism of his day (Acts 5:34).

introduce: A figure who appears in the genealogy of Jesus Christ in the Gospel of Luke, where he is recorded as the son of Arphaxad and the father of Shelah (Luke 3:35-36). He does not appear in the genealogies of Genesis and 1 Chronicles, but is a person attested in the record of Luke.
lifetime: According to the genealogy in Luke, he appears as the son of Arphaxad and the father of Shelah (Luke 3:35-36).

introduce: Gaius was a Christian known to be from Derbe, who accompanied the apostle Paul on his third missionary journey.
lifetime: After Paul had spent three months in Greece and then resolved to return through Macedonia, Gaius is recorded as one of those who went with him as far as Asia (Acts 20:3-4).
event: Among those who accompanied Paul as far as Asia was Gaius of Derbe; they went on ahead and waited for Paul and his party at Troas (Acts 20:4-5).

introduce: A believer of the early church living in Corinth, who was baptized at the time when the apostle Paul was carrying out his evangelistic work in Corinth. He is recorded as having helped Paul's ministry and played a hospitable role in the church community. The Third Epistle of John records a letter sent by the elder to Gaius (3 John 1:1), but the text does not make clear whether this Gaius is the same person as the Gaius of Corinth.
lifetime: When Paul preached the gospel in Corinth, Gaius was baptized by Paul himself (1 Corinthians 1:14). Afterward, while Paul stayed in Corinth and wrote the Epistle to the Romans, Gaius actively supported Paul's missionary work and provided him with lodging (Romans 16:23). Meanwhile, in the Third Epistle of John, the elder rejoiced when he heard the brothers' testimony that Gaius walks in the truth (3 John 1:3).
event: During the time Paul stayed in Corinth, he served as host, providing lodging and support to Paul and to the whole church (Romans 16:23). When mentioning the divisions within the church at Corinth, the apostle Paul named Gaius among the few people whom he had baptized himself, making his existence clear (1 Corinthians 1:14). In the Third Epistle of John, the elder said that what Gaius did for the brothers, strangers though they were, was a faithful work, and that they had testified to his love before the church (3 John 1:5-6).
character: He was devoted to the apostle and the community to the point of being described by Paul as host to the whole church, that is, one who served the entire church (Romans 16:23). He maintained a close relationship with Paul, so close that Paul baptized him personally, and he firmly supported Paul's ministry (1 Corinthians 1:14). Gaius is portrayed as one who walks in the truth and has genuine faith (3 John 1:3). He showed a character marked by generosity and charity toward others and faithful adherence to the apostle's teaching (3 John 1:5-6).

introduce: Kain, which appears in Numbers 24:21 and Judges 4:11, is understood to be a name designating the Kenite clan, or the ancestor of that clan. It refers to a group of people distinct from Cain, the son of Adam recorded in Genesis.
lifetime: The name Kain appears in Balaam's prophecy, in the course of mentioning the secure dwelling place of the Kenites (Numbers 24:21). Later, Judges tells us that Heber the Kenite, one of the descendants of Hobab, the father-in-law of Moses, left his clan and pitched his tent by the great tree of Zaanannim near Kedesh (Judges 4:11).
event: It is mentioned when Balaam, looking at the Kenites, sang that their dwelling place was secure and their nest was set in a cliff (Numbers 24:21). There is also the record that Heber the Kenite left his clan and pitched his tent by the great tree of Zaanannim near Kedesh (Judges 4:11).

introduce: Galal is a Levite recorded in 1 Chronicles, the father of Shemaiah and a descendant of Jeduthun. He is recorded as the grandfather of the Levite Obadiah (1 Chronicles 9:16).
lifetime: Galal was the father of Shemaiah, and his grandson Obadiah is recorded as a great-grandson of Jeduthun (1 Chronicles 9:16). The Bible has no record of Galal's own birth or life.
event: The Bible has no record of any event or achievement of Galal himself (1 Chronicles 9:16).

call: Fourth son of Reuben (ancestor of the Carmite clan)
introduce: Carmi is recorded as the fourth of the four sons of Reuben, the firstborn of Jacob, and in the genealogy of the tribes of Israel he is the ancestor of the Carmite clan within the tribe of Reuben.
lifetime: Carmi, as a son of Reuben, is recorded in the list of the family of Israel when Jacob and his sons went down to Egypt (Genesis 46:8-9). Later, in the census of Israel on the plains of Moab, the Carmite clan descended from Carmi, among the descendants of Reuben, was recorded as one family unit (Numbers 26:3-6).
event: Carmi's existence is confirmed through the genealogical records of the tribe of Reuben rather than through any individual activity of his own. When Moses and Eleazar the priest counted the Israelites on the plains of Moab, the Carmite clan descended from Carmi was recorded among the descendants of Reuben (Numbers 26:3-6).

introduce: Gad was a seer and prophet who was active in the time of King David, and during David's reign he carried out the ministry of delivering to the king the messages he had received from God.
lifetime: When David was in the stronghold fleeing from Saul, he told David not to stay there but to go into the land of Judah (1 Samuel 22:5). When David sinned by taking a census, he set before David three options of punishment (2 Samuel 24:11-13). He left a written record of the acts related to David's reign (1 Chronicles 29:29).
event: When David was conscience-stricken after he had taken the census, Gad came to David with the word of the LORD and demanded that he choose one of seven years of famine, three months of being pursued by his enemies, or three days of plague (2 Samuel 24:10-13). Afterward Gad told David to build an altar to the LORD on the threshing floor of Araunah (2 Samuel 24:18). It is also recorded that in the time of Hezekiah, the stationing of the Levites with cymbals, harps, and lyres was according to the command of David, of Gad the king's seer, and of Nathan the prophet (2 Chronicles 29:25).
character: Even in the presence of the king, he showed the strictness of his office by conveying God's judgment and commands directly and without hesitation (2 Samuel 24:11-13). He is regarded as the seer who recorded the history of David's reign (1 Chronicles 29:29).

call: Gershom, son of Moses (father of Jonathan)
introduce: Gershom was the firstborn son of Moses and Zipporah, born in the land of Midian (Exodus 2:22). He is a different person from the Gershonites of the tribe of Levi, and is mentioned as the father of Jonathan, who became a priest of the tribe of Dan in the book of Judges (Judges 18:30).
lifetime: He was the first son born to Moses when Moses left Egypt and stayed in the house of Jethro, the priest of Midian, and took Zipporah as his wife (Exodus 2:21-22). He went along when Moses was about to return to Egypt (Exodus 4:20), and later was reunited with him when Moses' father-in-law Jethro brought Zipporah and her two sons to Moses (Exodus 18:3-4). It is recorded that his descendant Jonathan later became a priest of the tribe of Dan (Judges 18:30).
event: Moses named his son Gershom in the sense that he had become a foreigner (Exodus 2:22). According to the record in Judges, his son Jonathan stayed in the house of Micah in the hill country of Ephraim and served as a priest for the idol, and afterward the tribe of Dan took him and made him priest to the descendants of Dan (Judges 18:18-30).

introduce: A descendant of Phinehas and a man of the tribe of Levi, a descendant of a priestly family who returned to Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile.
lifetime: A man of a priestly family who returned from Babylon to Jerusalem with Ezra, he is a descendant of Phinehas (Ezra 8:2).
event: He is recorded as one of the priests who accompanied Ezra when he returned from Babylon to Jerusalem (Ezra 8:2).

call: Chief officer over the contributions in Hezekiah's time
introduce: Conaniah was a Levite who, in the time of Hezekiah king of Judah, carried out the duty of managing the temple's contributions, tithes, and dedicated gifts. Following his Levitical descent, he held an important role within the administrative system that oversaw the altar and the affairs of the temple.
lifetime: Conaniah was a Levite who, in the time of King Hezekiah, was in charge of the contributions, tithes, and dedicated things that had been faithfully brought into the house of the LORD (2 Chronicles 31:12). His brother Shimei was second (2 Chronicles 31:12).
event: Conaniah, together with his brother Shimei, took charge of and managed the contributions, tithes, and dedicated things brought into the temple, and Jehiel, Azaziah, Nahath, Asahel, Jerimoth, Jozabad, Eliel, Ismachiah, Mahath, and Benaiah became overseers under Conaniah and Shimei. This was by the appointment of King Hezekiah and of Azariah, who managed the house of God (2 Chronicles 31:12-13).
character: The Bible suggests that Conaniah was a man of diligence and honesty in carrying out his duties. Carrying out the post to which he was appointed within the hierarchy of the tribe of Levi, he showed practical ability in managing the goods under the direction of the king and the overseer of the temple (2 Chronicles 31:12-13).
