introduce: Meshullam is a figure who inherited the bloodline of the royal house of David, recorded in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah, after the return from the Babylonian exile, as a son of Zerubbabel.
lifetime: A descendant of Zerubbabel in the generation after the Babylonian exile, he is included in the lineage of the royal house of David through the genealogy of 1 Chronicles (1 Chronicles 3:19).
event: The Bible records no specific achievement or individual event carried out by this figure (1 Chronicles 3:19).

call: Head of the tribe of Gad
introduce: Meshullam is a figure who appears in 1 Chronicles; he is one of the ancestors recorded in the genealogy of the tribe of Gad.
lifetime: He is recorded as one of the seven sons of Abihail among the Gadites who lived in the land of Bashan (1 Chronicles 5:11, 13-14).
event: His name is included in the list of the Gadites recorded in the genealogy in the days when Jotham was king of Judah and Jeroboam was king of Israel (1 Chronicles 5:13, 5:17).

introduce: A figure recorded in the genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin, one of the sons of Elpaal (1 Chronicles 8:17-18).
lifetime: He is recorded as a son of Elpaal and a member of a family belonging to the tribe of Benjamin; Zebadiah, Hizki, Heber, Ishmerai, Izliah, and Jobab are his brothers (1 Chronicles 8:17-18).

introduce: Meshullam is a figure who appears in 1 Chronicles; he is recorded as a descendant of the tribe of Benjamin, the son of Hodaviah and the grandson of Hassenuah.
lifetime: Coming from a family of the descendants of Benjamin, he is recorded as the son of Hodaviah and the father of Sallu (1 Chronicles 9:7). His son Sallu is recorded as one of the descendants of Benjamin who lived in Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 9:3, 7).
event: The Bible has no record of Meshullam's own deeds (1 Chronicles 9:7).

call: Priest of the house of Zadok
introduce: Meshullam is a figure who appears in 1 Chronicles 9; he is a member of the priestly genealogy belonging to the house of Zadok. He is recorded as having the family background connected with the temple service in the Jewish community that returned to Jerusalem.
lifetime: He is the son of Zadok and the father of Hilkiah, the grandson of Meraioth and the great-grandson of Ahitub (1 Chronicles 9:11). His grandson Azariah is recorded as the one in charge of the house of God (1 Chronicles 9:11).
event: The Bible has no record of Meshullam's own deeds, and Nehemiah 11:11 records, in the same genealogy, that his grandson Seraiah was the one in charge of the house of God (Nehemiah 11:11).

call: Priest of the house of Immer
introduce: Meshullam is a man of the house of Immer recorded in the priestly genealogy of 1 Chronicles 9; he is the son of Meshillemith and the father of Jahzerah.
lifetime: He is recorded as the grandson of Immer, the son of Meshillemith, and the father of Jahzerah. His great-grandson Maasai is recorded as a priest who lived in Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 9:12).
event: The Bible has no record of this figure's own deeds (1 Chronicles 9:12).
character: He is recorded as a priest who faithfully carried out his duties within the genealogy of the house of Immer (1 Chronicles 9:12). There is no biblical record of specific personal character or distinctive features.

call: Leader in the time of Ezra
introduce: Meshullam is one of the heads whom Ezra summoned at the canal that flows to Ahava at the time of the return from the Babylonian exile (Ezra 8:15-16).
lifetime: He was summoned as one of the heads on the journey in which Ezra returned to Judah after the Babylonian exile (Ezra 8:16). He is one of those whom Ezra summoned when the company assembled at the canal that flows to Ahava (Ezra 8:15-16).
event: Ezra summoned the heads, Eliezer, Ariel, Shemaiah, Elnathan, Jarib, Elnathan, Nathan, Zechariah, and Meshullam, and sent them to Iddo, the head of the place Casiphia, to bring those who would minister for the house of God (Ezra 8:16-17).

call: Opponent of the investigation of foreign marriages
introduce: Meshullam is recorded as a figure who, in the time of Ezra, helped Jonathan son of Asahel and Jahzeiah son of Tikvah when they opposed the handling of the matter of marriages with foreign women.
lifetime: After the return from the Babylonian exile, in the time of Ezra, when Jonathan and Jahzeiah rose up against the handling of the matter of marriages with foreign women, he helped them together with Shabbethai the Levite (Ezra 10:15).
event: In Ezra 10, when Jonathan and Jahzeiah opposed the handling of the matter of marriages with foreign women, Meshullam helped them together with Shabbethai the Levite (Ezra 10:15).
character: Meshullam showed a cooperative attitude, actively taking part in communal undertakings such as the rebuilding of the wall, but at the same time he was a man of independent judgment who voiced dissent against Ezra's policy of expelling the foreign women (Ezra 10:15). It is mentioned that Jehohanan son of Tobiah took the daughter of Meshullam as his wife, which shows that he was closely connected with persons who built up influence through marriage relations within the noble society of that time (Nehemiah 6:18).

introduce: Meshullam is one of the descendants of Bani who took foreign women as wives in the time of Ezra, after the return from the Babylonian exile (Ezra 10:29).
lifetime:
He was born as a descendant of Bani (Ezra 10:29).
Living as part of the community that had returned to Judah, he took a foreign woman as wife (Ezra 10:29).
No record of his specific birth or death appears in the Bible (Ezra 10:29).
event: When Ezra investigated the people of Israel who had intermarried with foreign women, he was recorded in that list (Ezra 10:29, 10:44).

introduce: Meshullam is a figure who appears in the Bible, the son of Berechiah, who took part in the rebuilding of the wall of Jerusalem. He is recorded as a man who was active in the time of Nehemiah.
lifetime: He was born as the son of Berechiah (Nehemiah 3:4). In the work of rebuilding the wall of Jerusalem led by Nehemiah, he took part in repairing the section opposite his own bedchamber (Nehemiah 3:30).
event: He repaired a section of the wall of Jerusalem (Nehemiah 3:4). He also took part in the work of repairing the section opposite his own room, and as the son of Berechiah he took charge of the labor of building the wall (Nehemiah 3:30).

introduce: Meshullam was a Jew living under the rule of the Persian Empire, who repaired a section of the wall of Jerusalem when Nehemiah rebuilt it. He is recorded as the son of Besodeiah (Nehemiah 3:6).
lifetime: He was active as a member of the Jewish community that returned to Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile. He is recorded as the son of Besodeiah (Nehemiah 3:6). Afterward he took part in the rebuilding of the wall of Jerusalem carried out under the leadership of Nehemiah, and together with Joiada son of Paseah he repaired the Jeshanah Gate (Nehemiah 3:6).
event: Meshullam took the role of repairing the Jeshanah Gate of the wall of Jerusalem (Nehemiah 3:6). He took part directly at the site of the work of repairing a section of the wall and contributed to the building of the wall (Nehemiah 3:6).

call: Fellow minister at the reading of the law
introduce: A figure of the time of Nehemiah, one of those who stood at the left of the wooden platform on which Ezra stood when the scribe Ezra read the book of the law (Nehemiah 8:3-4).
lifetime: The Bible mentions his name only as one who stood beside Ezra in Nehemiah 8:4; the rest of his life is not recorded (Nehemiah 8:4).
event: In the seventh month, when Ezra read the book of the law in the square in front of the Water Gate (Nehemiah 8:1-3), he stood at the left of the wooden platform on which Ezra stood, together with Pedaiah, Mishael, Malchijah, Hashum, Hash-baddanah, and Zechariah (Nehemiah 8:4).

introduce: One of the priests who sealed the covenant document after the rebuilding of the wall of Jerusalem in the time of Nehemiah.
lifetime: His name is recorded as one of the priests who sealed the covenant in the time of Nehemiah (Nehemiah 10:7-8). This covenant was an oath with a curse to keep the law given through Moses the servant of God (Nehemiah 10:29).
event: He put his name on the list of priests who sealed the covenant, swearing to separate from the foreign peoples and to keep the law of God (Nehemiah 10:1, 10:7-8, 10:28-29).

call: Leader in the time of Nehemiah
introduce: A figure whose name is recorded among the heads of the people who sealed the covenant in the time of Nehemiah (Nehemiah 10:14, 10:20).
lifetime:
No record of his specific birth, family, or death appears in the Bible (Nehemiah 10:20).
After the return from the exile, he was active in Jerusalem as one of the leaders of the people (Nehemiah 10:14, 10:20).
The name Meshullam appears among those who followed in the procession at the dedication of the wall (Nehemiah 12:32-33), but the text does not make clear whether he is the same person as the one in 10:20.
event:
When the people of Israel put their seal to the covenant made with God, swearing to keep the law, he put his name among the heads of the people (Nehemiah 10:14, 10:20).
At the dedication of the wall, when the great company giving thanks and praise divided into two groups and marched on top of the wall, the name of Meshullam appears together with Hoshaiah and half of the princes of Judah, Azariah, and Ezra among those who followed one of the groups (Nehemiah 12:31-33).

introduce: Meshullam is a man of the tribe of Benjamin, recorded as the son of Joed and the father of Sallu (Nehemiah 11:7).
lifetime: In the genealogy of Nehemiah 11:7 he is recorded as the son of Joed and the father of Sallu. In the generations above him, Joed was the son of Pedaiah, Pedaiah the son of Kolaiah, Kolaiah the son of Maaseiah, Maaseiah the son of Ithiel, and Ithiel the son of Jeshaiah (Nehemiah 11:7).
event: The one recorded as a descendant of Benjamin who lived in Jerusalem is his son Sallu (Nehemiah 11:4, 11:7). The Bible does not record Meshullam's own deeds.

call: Priest of the family of Ezra
introduce: He is recorded as the head of the family of Ezra in the list of the heads of the priests in the days of Joiakim in Nehemiah 12 (Nehemiah 12:12-13).
lifetime: Among the heads of the priestly families in the days of Joiakim, his name is recorded as the one representing the family of Ezra (Nehemiah 12:12-13). The rest of his life is not recorded in the Bible.
event: As a head of the priests in the days of Joiakim, he remained on record as representing the family of Ezra (Nehemiah 12:12-13).

call: Priest of the family of Ginnethon
introduce: Meshullam is recorded as the head of the family of Ginnethon in the list of the heads of the priests in the days of Joiakim in Nehemiah 12 (Nehemiah 12:12, 12:16).
lifetime: Among the heads of the priestly families in the days of Joiakim, his name is recorded as the one representing the family of Ginnethon (Nehemiah 12:16). The rest of his life is not recorded in the Bible.
event: As a head of the priests in the days of Joiakim, he remained on record as representing the family of Ginnethon (Nehemiah 12:12, 12:16).

introduce: Meshullam is a figure recorded as a gatekeeper in Nehemiah 12 (Nehemiah 12:25).
lifetime: He is recorded as one of the gatekeepers who lived in the days of Joiakim, the governor Nehemiah, and Ezra the priest and scribe (Nehemiah 12:25-26).
event: Together with Mattaniah, Bakbukiah, Obadiah, Talmon, and Akkub, he served as a gatekeeper, guarding the storerooms at the gates by turns, according to the division (Nehemiah 12:25).
character: He showed a disposition of faithfully fulfilling his duty, handing down the office of temple gatekeeper through the generations of his family (1 Chronicles 9:19). As a gatekeeper responsible for the security of Jerusalem, he also worked together within the administrative organization and contributed to the rebuilding of the community (Nehemiah 11:19).

call: Father of Delaiah (grandfather of the false prophet)
introduce: Mehetabel is introduced in Nehemiah 6 as the father of Delaiah, and is the grandfather of Shemaiah the son of Delaiah (Nehemiah 6:10). Shemaiah is the man who took a bribe from Tobiah and Sanballat and prophesied falsely to Nehemiah (Nehemiah 6:10-13).
lifetime: The Bible does not record Mehetabel's own deeds; his name appears in the introduction "Shemaiah the son of Delaiah, the son of Mehetabel" (Nehemiah 6:10).
event: He is mentioned as a member of the family line in connection with the incident in which his grandson Shemaiah, having been bribed by Tobiah and Sanballat, prophesied falsely in order to frighten Nehemiah into sinning (Nehemiah 6:10-13).

call: Son of Shimei (a descendant of Reuben)
introduce: A figure who appears in the genealogy of the tribe of Reuben recorded in 1 Chronicles 5; he is the son of Shimei and the father of Reaiah (1 Chronicles 5:4-5).
lifetime: In the genealogy of Joel he is recorded as the son of Shimei, following Shemaiah, Gog, and Shimei, and his son is Reaiah (1 Chronicles 5:4-5). His great-grandson Beerah, a head of the Reubenites, is the one who was carried into exile by Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria (1 Chronicles 5:5-6).

introduce: Mica was a Levite, belonging to the genealogy of the descendants of Asaph, and is recorded as the father of Mattaniah (1 Chronicles 9:15, Nehemiah 11:17).
lifetime: In the genealogy of the Levites who lived in Jerusalem after the return from exile he is recorded as the son of Zichri, and his sons are Bakbakkar, Heresh, Galal, and Mattaniah (1 Chronicles 9:15).
event: His son Mattaniah became the chief who led the thanksgiving in prayer in Jerusalem (Nehemiah 11:17). Mica's own deeds are not recorded in the Bible.

introduce: A Levite, the son of Uzziel, a figure mentioned in the process of the division of the duties of the Levites in the time of David.
lifetime: As a son of Uzziel he is recorded as a head among the Levites in the time of David (1 Chronicles 23:20). His younger brother is Isshiah, and among his sons is Shamir (1 Chronicles 24:24-25).
event: King David surveyed the genealogies of the Levites and assigned their duties, and at that time Micah put his name on the list as a descendant of Uzziel (1 Chronicles 23:20). Also, when David set the order of the duties of the priests and Levites by casting lots, Micah is identified as one of the representative names of the descendants of Uzziel (1 Chronicles 24:24).

call: The Moreshite (author of the book of Micah)
introduce: Micah the Moreshite is a prophet who was active in the days of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah (Micah 1:1). He came from the southern kingdom of Judah and foretold the destruction of Samaria and Jerusalem.
lifetime: Micah is known to have come from Moresheth in Judah (Micah 1:1). He was active through the days of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah, and received a vision concerning Samaria and Jerusalem (Micah 1:1). The book of Jeremiah also mentions that Micah prophesied in the time of King Hezekiah (Jeremiah 26:18).
event: Micah prophesied that Samaria would become a heap in the field and that its foundations would be laid bare (Micah 1:6). He also warned that Jerusalem would become a heap of rubble and that the mountain of the temple would become like the high places of a forest (Micah 3:12). In the time of King Hezekiah, Micah's prophecy became the occasion for changing the king's attitude, with the result that the intention of judgment against Jerusalem was turned back (Jeremiah 26:18-19).

introduce: Mica is the son of Mephibosheth, who was the grandson of Saul, the first king of Israel, and the son of Jonathan. He is recorded as one of the persons who continued the genealogy of the house of Saul.
lifetime: Mica is recorded as the son of Mephibosheth (2 Samuel 9:12), and Chronicles says that Merib-baal, the son of Jonathan, fathered Mica (1 Chronicles 8:34, 9:40). His sons are Pithon, Melech, Tarea, and Ahaz (1 Chronicles 8:35, 9:41).
event: When King David showed favor to the one remaining of the house of Saul, restoring the fields of Saul to Mephibosheth and having him eat at the king's table, Mica was mentioned as the young son of Mephibosheth (2 Samuel 9:1-12).

introduce: The Mica who appears in Nehemiah 10 was one of the Levites who, after the return from the Babylonian exile, signed the covenant sealed in Jerusalem under the leadership of Nehemiah.
lifetime: His name is recorded as one of the Levites who sealed the covenant in which they swore to keep the law of God in the time of Nehemiah (Nehemiah 10:9-11).
event: He put his name on the list of the Levites who sealed the covenant to keep the law given through Moses the servant of God, and so took part in that oath (Nehemiah 10:9-11, 10:28-29).

introduce: Micaiah is recorded as the father of Achbor, an envoy in the time of Josiah king of Judah (2 Kings 22:12). In 2 Chronicles 34:20 the name of the same person appears as Micah.
lifetime: The Bible does not record Micaiah's own deeds; his name appears in the introduction "Achbor the son of Micaiah" (2 Kings 22:12).
event: His son Achbor, at the command of King Josiah, went with the priest Hilkiah, Ahikam, the scribe Shaphan, and Asaiah to the prophetess Huldah and inquired of the LORD concerning the words of the book that had been found (2 Kings 22:12-14).

introduce: Maacah was the wife of Rehoboam king of Judah and the mother of Abijah; 1 Kings 15:10 and 2 Chronicles 15:16 also record her as the mother of King Asa. 2 Chronicles 13:2 records her under the name Micaiah and introduces her as the daughter of Uriel of Gibeah, while 1 Kings 15:2 records her as the daughter of Abishalom.
lifetime: Rehoboam married Maacah the daughter of Absalom, and she bore Abijah, Attai, Ziza, and Shelomith (2 Chronicles 11:20). She is recorded as the mother of Abijah (1 Kings 15:2) and also as the mother of King Asa (1 Kings 15:10). After Asa came to the throne, she was removed from her position as queen mother because she had made a detestable image of Asherah (1 Kings 15:13).
event: She made a detestable image of Asherah (1 Kings 15:13). King Asa chopped down and crushed the Asherah pole that Maacah had made and burned it in the Kidron Valley (2 Chronicles 15:16). Because of this incident Maacah was removed from the position of queen mother (1 Kings 15:13).
character: She took her own religious course, to the point of personally making a detestable object that promoted idol worship by using her power (1 Kings 15:13). Since she remained in the palace as queen mother for a considerable time even after Asa became king and exercised influence, her political standing was strong (1 Kings 15:10). In some records she is also called Micaiah, and the genealogical information that she was the daughter of Uriel of Gibeah is stated explicitly (2 Chronicles 13:2).

introduce: One of the officials who, in the days of Jehoshaphat king of Judah, were summoned by the king and carried out the task of teaching the people (2 Chronicles 17:7).
lifetime: In the third year of the reign of King Jehoshaphat, the king sent his servants Ben-hail, Obadiah, Zechariah, Nethanel, and Micaiah to teach in the cities of Judah (2 Chronicles 17:7).
event: At the command of King Jehoshaphat, he went around the cities of Judah with the book of the law and carried out the ministry of teaching the people (2 Chronicles 17:7, 2 Chronicles 17:9).

introduce: Micaiah, the son of Gemariah and grandson of Shaphan, was active in the time of Jehoiakim son of Josiah king of Judah; he is the man who heard the words of Jeremiah read by Baruch and reported them to the officials (Jeremiah 36:1, 36:11-13).
lifetime: Micaiah is the grandson of the scribe Shaphan and the son of Gemariah (Jeremiah 36:11). He heard Baruch reading the words of Jeremiah in the house of the LORD, and went to the chamber of the scribe in the king's palace and reported it to the officials (Jeremiah 36:11-12).
event: Micaiah heard the sound of Baruch reading the prophecy of Jeremiah to the people in the upper court of the house of the LORD (Jeremiah 36:10). Afterward he told all the words that Baruch had read to all the officials gathered in the chamber of Elishama, the king's scribe (Jeremiah 36:13). This became the occasion for the officials to summon Baruch and have him read the scroll again (Jeremiah 36:14-15).

meaning: who is a man like God
introduce: A figure recorded in 1 Chronicles 5; he is one of the seven kinsmen of the clan of the tribe of Gad and is a son of Abihail (1 Chronicles 5:13-14).
lifetime: As a son of Abihail he is recorded as one of the seven kinsmen of the clan: Michael, Meshullam, Sheba, Jorai, Jacan, Zia, and Eber (1 Chronicles 5:13-14).
event: The Gadites lived in Bashan and Gilead, its towns, and all the pasturelands of Sharon (1 Chronicles 5:16), and this genealogy was recorded in the days of Jotham king of Judah and Jeroboam king of Israel (1 Chronicles 5:17).

call: Son of Jeshishai (head of the tribe of Gad)
meaning: who is a man like God
introduce: A figure who appears in the genealogy of the tribe of Gad in 1 Chronicles 5; he is the son of Jeshishai and the father of Gilead, and Abihail is his great-great-grandson (1 Chronicles 5:14).
lifetime: In the genealogy of the tribe of Gad he is recorded as the son of Jeshishai, and Abihail is introduced as the great-grandson of Gilead and the great-great-grandson of Michael (1 Chronicles 5:14).
event: The genealogy of the Gadites in which he is included was recorded in the days of Jotham king of Judah and Jeroboam king of Israel (1 Chronicles 5:17). The Bible does not record his own deeds.

meaning: who is a man like God
introduce: A figure of the family of Gershom among the descendants of Levi, one person in the genealogy who is an ancestor of Asaph.
lifetime: He belongs to the genealogy of Gershom the son of Levi (1 Chronicles 6:43), and is recorded as the son of Baaseiah and the father of Shimea (1 Chronicles 6:40). Asaph is the descendant of his son Shimea, in the generation of a grandson (1 Chronicles 6:39).

meaning: who is a man like God
introduce: The son of Izrahiah, a figure who appears in the genealogy of the tribe of Issachar recorded in 1 Chronicles 7.
lifetime: As the grandson of Uzzi of the tribe of Issachar and the son of Izrahiah, he was a chief together with Obadiah, Joel, and Isshiah (1 Chronicles 7:3).
event: He became a chief together with Obadiah, Joel, and Isshiah, and the troops fit for war that were with them numbered thirty-six thousand men (1 Chronicles 7:3-4).

meaning: who is a man like God
introduce: One of the chiefs of the tribe of Benjamin, the son of Beriah and a leader of a family that lived in Jerusalem.
lifetime: He is recorded as a son of Beriah of the tribe of Benjamin, and is a brother of Ishpah and Joha (1 Chronicles 8:16).
event: He is included in the list of the chiefs who lived in Jerusalem, and is mentioned as one of the principal figures of the tribe of Benjamin who were active centered on Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 8:28).

call: Commander of a thousand of Manasseh (warrior at Ziklag)
meaning: who is a man like God
introduce: A commander of a thousand from the tribe of Manasseh who joined David's army when David stayed at Ziklag in the land of the Philistines, fleeing from King Saul.
lifetime: He is one of the chiefs of the tribe of Manasseh who joined David to help him when David lived at Ziklag to escape the pursuit of Saul (1 Chronicles 12:20). He held the office of commander of a thousand, leading a thousand men in the tribe of Manasseh (1 Chronicles 12:20).
event: He is recorded as one of the commanders of a thousand who came over to David from Manasseh when David went to Ziklag (1 Chronicles 12:20); this company helped David against the band of raiders, and all of them were mighty men of valor and commanders in the army (1 Chronicles 12:21).
character: According to the biblical record he is described as a mighty man of valor, and he is regarded as a person who had the military ability and leadership to serve as a commander in David's army (1 Chronicles 12:21).

call: Father of Omri (father of the chief of Issachar)
meaning: who is a man like God
introduce: A figure recorded in 1 Chronicles as the father of Omri, the chief officer of Issachar.
lifetime: 1 Chronicles 27:18 records the chief officer of Issachar as "Omri the son of Michael"; Michael appears only as the father (1 Chronicles 27:18). There is no record in the Bible about Michael's own life.
event: When the officers in charge of the tribes of Israel in the time of David are listed, the one recorded as the chief officer of Issachar is Omri the son of Michael (1 Chronicles 27:16, 18). There is no record of any specific political event or achievement of Michael himself.

meaning: who is a man like God
introduce: A figure recorded as one of the sons of Jehoshaphat king of Judah. According to the record of Chronicles, King Jehoshaphat had many sons, and their father gave them generous gifts, but the kingdom passed to the firstborn Jehoram, and Jehoram killed all his brothers.
lifetime: He is recorded as a son of Jehoshaphat king of Judah (2 Chronicles 21:2). His father Jehoshaphat gave his sons great gifts of silver, gold, and valuables, along with fortified cities in Judah, but gave the kingdom to Jehoram, the firstborn (2 Chronicles 21:3). After Jehoshaphat died and Jehoram took the throne, Jehoram, when he had gained power, killed all his brothers with the sword (2 Chronicles 21:1, 4).
event: After Jehoram gained power he killed all his brothers with the sword, and since Michael is recorded as a brother of Jehoram, he was among the objects of that slaughter (2 Chronicles 21:2, 4). There is no record that he left any particular political achievement during his lifetime.

call: Father of Zebadiah (one who returned with Ezra)
meaning: who is a man like God
introduce: A figure recorded as the father of Zebadiah, head of the descendants of Shephatiah, in the list of the heads who returned, in Ezra 8 (Ezra 8:8).
lifetime: Ezra 8:8 says "from the descendants of Shephatiah, Zebadiah the son of Michael" and records Michael only as the father of Zebadiah (Ezra 8:8). There is no record in the Bible about Michael's own life.
event: In the genealogical register of the heads who came up from Babylon with Ezra in the time of King Artaxerxes, his son Zebadiah is recorded as a head, with eighty men (Ezra 8:1, 8).

meaning: who is a man like God
introduce: In the Bible, Michael is mentioned as one of the angels of God, and is described mainly as a commander of the heavenly host or the chief of angels who possess mighty power. The Hebrew etymology carries the meaning of the question, "Who is like God?"
lifetime: When the one who was speaking to Daniel was held up for twenty-one days by the prince of the kingdom of Persia, Michael, one of the chief princes, came and helped him (Daniel 10:13). He is prophesied as one who will rise up at the time of the end to stand guard over the people of Israel (Daniel 12:1). In the war that broke out in heaven he appears as one who fights against the dragon and his angels (Revelation 12:7). There is a record that he disputed with the devil and contended over the body of Moses (Jude 1:9).
event: When the one who was speaking to Daniel was held up by the prince of the kingdom of Persia, Michael came and helped him (Daniel 10:13). When there was war in heaven, Michael and his angels fought against the dragon, and the dragon and his angels did not prevail, and no place was found for them in heaven any longer (Revelation 12:7-8). When he opposed the devil over the body of Moses, he did not presume to pronounce a slanderous judgment but said, "The Lord rebuke you," and withdrew (Jude 1:9).
character: He is called by the title of archangel and is described as one with higher authority than other angels (Jude 1:9). As an agent of God, he has the strength to engage directly with hostile spiritual forces (Daniel 10:13). Even in confrontation with the devil, he does not respond emotionally but shows a restrained attitude, relying on the authority of the Lord (Jude 1:9).

call: Officer of David's division of the second month
introduce: A figure recorded as the head of the division of the second month in the structure of the army of Israel organized in the time of King David. The leader of the same division is recorded as Dodai the Ahohite (1 Chronicles 27:4).
lifetime: 1 Chronicles 27 records that the divisions of the people of Israel were arranged to come in and go out by turns month by month throughout the year (1 Chronicles 27:1), and Mikloth became the head of the division of the second month among them (1 Chronicles 27:4). That division numbered twenty-four thousand (1 Chronicles 27:4).
event: Within the system of divisions that came in and went out by turns each month, Mikloth became the head of the division of the second month, and that division numbered twenty-four thousand (1 Chronicles 27:1, 4). The leader of the same division was Dodai the Ahohite (1 Chronicles 27:4). His other specific deeds are not recorded in the Bible.

call: Head of a priestly family that returned with Zerubbabel
introduce: Miniamin is the name of a priest in Nehemiah 12; in the list of the priestly clans in the time of Joiakim he appears as "Miniamin, of Moadiah" (Nehemiah 12:17), and he is also recorded as one of the priests who held trumpets at the dedication of the wall of Jerusalem (Nehemiah 12:41).
lifetime: In the list of the heads of the priests in the time of Joiakim in Nehemiah 12, he appears as "of Miniamin, of Moadiah, Piltai," and the head of this clan is recorded as Piltai (Nehemiah 12:12, 17). At the dedication after the wall of Jerusalem was completed, the priests Eliakim, Maaseiah, Miniamin, and others held trumpets (Nehemiah 12:27, 41).
event: At the dedication of the wall of Jerusalem he was one of the priests who held trumpets, together with the priests Eliakim, Maaseiah, Micaiah, Elioenai, Zechariah, and Hananiah (Nehemiah 12:41).

call: Persian official who accused to King Artaxerxes
introduce: Mithredath is a figure recorded in Ezra 4, one of those who wrote a letter to the king, together with Bishlam, Tabeel, and their associates, in the time of Artaxerxes king of Persia (Ezra 4:7).
lifetime: He is recorded as one who wrote a letter to the king, together with Bishlam, Tabeel, and their associates, in the time of Artaxerxes king of Persia (Ezra 4:7). That letter was written in Aramaic script and in the Aramaic language (Ezra 4:7).
event: Together with Bishlam, Tabeel, and their associates, he sent a letter to Artaxerxes king of Persia (Ezra 4:7). The specific content of this letter is not recorded in 4:7. In 4:8 and following there is recorded a letter that the commander Rehum and the scribe Shimshai sent to King Artaxerxes accusing the people of Jerusalem, but the name of Mithredath does not appear in that letter.

call: Descendant of Ezra of the tribe of Judah
introduce: A figure who appears in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah, recorded as one of the children born to Mered, a son of Ezra (1 Chronicles 4:17).
lifetime: In the genealogy of Judah she is recorded as one of those whom Mered fathered: Miriam, Shammai, and Ishbah the father of Eshtemoa (1 Chronicles 4:17). These are recorded as the sons of Bithiah the daughter of Pharaoh, whom Mered took (1 Chronicles 4:18).
event: She is mentioned only as the name of a child born to Mered in the genealogy, and no specific deeds of Miriam as an individual are recorded in the Bible (1 Chronicles 4:17).

call: Fellow minister at Ezra's reading of the law
introduce: Mishael is a figure active in the time of Ezra and Nehemiah in the Old Testament, one of those who stood beside Ezra when Ezra read the book of the law before the people of Israel.
lifetime: After the return from the Babylonian exile, he is recorded as one who stood at the left of the platform when Ezra read the book of the law in Jerusalem (Nehemiah 8:4).
event: When Ezra stood on the wooden platform in the square in front of the Water Gate and opened the book of the law, he was one of those who stood at its left, and was present at the public occasion of the reading of the law (Nehemiah 8:4).

introduce: Mishma is a descendant of Simeon the son of Jacob, a figure who appears in the genealogy of the tribe of Simeon. He is the son of Mibsam, and Hammuel is recorded as the son of Mishma (1 Chronicles 4:25-26).
lifetime: A descendant of Shaul the son of Simeon, he is recorded as the son of Mibsam the son of Shallum (1 Chronicles 4:24-25). His son Hammuel, and his son Zaccur, and his son Shimei form the line of the genealogy that continues from him (1 Chronicles 4:26).
event: According to the biblical record there is no record of any independent deeds or specific events of Mishma as an individual; he is mentioned only as one of the persons who make up the family tree of the tribe of Simeon (1 Chronicles 4:26).

meaning: one born of the right hand, blessed
introduce: Mijamin was a member of the community of Israel in the time of Ezra, a figure recorded among the descendants of Parosh in the list of those who had taken foreign women as wives (Ezra 10:25).
lifetime: He was a member of the community of Israel in the time of Ezra, and when Ezra commanded them to sever ties with foreign women and investigated the matter, he was included in the list of the men who had taken foreign women as wives (Ezra 10:10-11, 16-17, 25).
event: When Ezra commanded that the foreign women be put away (Ezra 10:11), his name was entered in the list of those who had taken foreign women as one of the descendants of Parosh (Ezra 10:25).

meaning: one born of the right hand, blessed
introduce: Mijamin is a figure recorded as one of the priests who sealed the covenant in the time of Nehemiah (Nehemiah 10:7-8).
lifetime: At the renewal of the covenant led by Nehemiah, he took part in the sealing as one of the priests (Nehemiah 10:7-8).
event: At the ceremony of the oath of the covenant renewal recorded in Nehemiah 10, he sealed the covenant document together with Nehemiah as one of the priests (Nehemiah 10:1, 7-8), and this signifies the formal pledge of the community of Israel to keep the law of God.

call: Daughter of Zelophehad (heir of an inheritance)
introduce: Milcah is a figure who appears in the book of Numbers in the Old Testament, one of the five daughters of Zelophehad the son of Hepher of the tribe of Manasseh. She is a woman who took part in establishing a legal precedent concerning the right of inheritance within the family, in a situation where her father had no sons.
lifetime: Milcah was born as a daughter of Zelophehad of the tribe of Manasseh (Numbers 26:33). After her father died in the wilderness, she stood with her sisters Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, and Tirzah at the entrance of the tent of meeting before Moses, Eleazar the priest, the leaders, and the whole congregation (Numbers 27:1-2). Afterward she asked that an inheritance be given so that her father's name would not be removed from among his family, and in this process she obtained the ruling in which the LORD said that the daughters of Zelophehad were right in what they said and that their father's inheritance should be given to them (Numbers 27:4, 6-7). Later, as the LORD had commanded Moses, she was married to the sons of her father's brothers and so preserved the inheritance within the tribe of Manasseh (Numbers 36:10-12).
event: The daughters of Zelophehad, on the ground that their father had died in the wilderness but had not joined the company of Korah, raised the claim that when there is no son the daughter should inherit the father's inheritance (Numbers 27:3-4). When Moses brought their case before the LORD (Numbers 27:5), the LORD commanded the people of Israel a statute of judgment that if a man dies and has no son, his inheritance shall be given to his daughter (Numbers 27:6-11). Milcah was one of the parties to this case, and by the daughters of Zelophehad marrying the sons of their father's brothers, the inheritance remained in the tribe of their father's family (Numbers 36:11-12).
character: Milcah did not stay silent about her rights but showed an independent attitude, expressing her intention boldly before Moses, the highest leader, and the congregation (Numbers 27:2). She is also described as a person of prudence and realistic judgment, who respected the legal norms and traditions of the tribe and obeyed the command to marry the sons of her uncles so that the inheritance she received would not pass to another tribe (Numbers 36:10-11).

introduce: Mibsam is a figure recorded in the genealogy of the tribe of Simeon in 1 Chronicles 4; he is the son of Shallum the son of Shaul, and the father of Mishma (1 Chronicles 4:25).
lifetime: A descendant of Shaul the son of Simeon, he is recorded as the son of Shallum the son of Shaul (1 Chronicles 4:24-25). His son is Mishma (1 Chronicles 4:25).

introduce: Bani is a figure who appears in 1 Chronicles 6 of the Old Testament, belonging to the descendants of Merari of the tribe of Levi. As an ancestor of Ethan, he is recorded as one of the persons who continue the line of Merari in the genealogy.
lifetime: Bani is the son of Shemer and the father of Amzi, a descendant of Mushi the son of Merari (1 Chronicles 6:46-47). No specific record of his birth or death appears in the Bible; he is mentioned only as a member of the line that makes up the genealogy of the Levites (1 Chronicles 6:46).
event: His name is entered as an ancestor who continues the line of the descendants of Merari in the process of organizing the choir of the tabernacle and the temple (1 Chronicles 6:44-47). Ethan is recorded as his descendant, and Bani occupies one part of the genealogy that confirms the lineal legitimacy of the Levites (1 Chronicles 6:46).

introduce: Bani is a figure recorded in 1 Chronicles 9 of the Old Testament, belonging to the descendants of Perez the son of Judah, and the father of Imri. He is mentioned in the genealogy as the great-great-grandfather of Uthai, who lived in Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 9:3-4).
lifetime: 1 Chronicles 9:4 records Uthai as "the son of Ammihud, the grandson of Omri, the great-grandson of Imri, and the great-great-grandson of Bani," which shows that Bani was the father of Imri and an ancestor of Uthai (1 Chronicles 9:4). There is no specific record about his life in the Bible.
event: His name is entered in the genealogy only as an ancestor of Uthai, a descendant of Perez who lived in Jerusalem, and Bani's own deeds are not recorded in the Bible (1 Chronicles 9:4).

call: Ancestor of a family that returned with Zerubbabel
introduce: Bani is a name that appears in the book of Ezra in the Old Testament as the founder of the descendants of Bani, and refers to the ancestor of the family of the descendants who returned with Zerubbabel after the Babylonian exile (Ezra 2:1-2, 10).
lifetime: The descendants of Bani are included in the list of those who returned with Zerubbabel and others at the return from the Babylonian exile, and the descendants of Bani numbered 642 (Ezra 2:1-2, 10).
event: The Bible does not record any deeds of Bani himself, and the number of his descendants is recorded in the list of those who returned (Ezra 2:10). In the time of Ezra, some of the descendants of Bani were entered in the list of those who had taken foreign women as wives (Ezra 10:34).

call: Founder of the family of the descendants of Bani
introduce: Bani is the name that appears in Ezra 10 as "descendants of Bani" in the list of those who had taken foreign women as wives. It was not Bani himself who was entered in this list, but several of his descendants.
lifetime: Ezra 10:29 records Meshullam, Malluch, Adaiah, Jashub, Sheal, and Jeremoth among the descendants of Bani, and Ezra 10:34 records Maadai, Amram, Uel, and others among the descendants of Bani as those who had taken foreign women (Ezra 10:29, 34). There is no record about Bani himself.
event: When those who had taken foreign women were investigated and the list was drawn up in the time of Ezra (Ezra 10:16-17), the persons above among the descendants of Bani were entered in that list (Ezra 10:29, 34, 44).

call: Descendant of Bani who married foreign women
introduce: Bani is a figure whose name is recorded in the list of those who had taken foreign women as wives in the time of Ezra (Ezra 10:38, 44).
lifetime: When Ezra appointed the heads to investigate those who had taken foreign women, his name was entered in the list drawn up then, and in the list of the descendants of Bani that continues from Ezra 10:34 it is recorded as "Bani, and Binnui, and Shimei" (Ezra 10:16-17, 34, 38).
event: When Ezra commanded that the foreign women be put away (Ezra 10:11), his name was entered in the list of those who had taken foreign women (Ezra 10:38, 44).

call: Father of Rehum (father of a wall repairer)
introduce: Bani is a figure recorded as the father of Rehum, who was in charge of the practical work in the historic process of rebuilding the wall of Jerusalem in the time of Nehemiah.
lifetime: Bani appears as the father of Rehum, one of those who divided the sections and carried out the repair work when Nehemiah rebuilt the wall of Jerusalem (Nehemiah 3:17).
event: His son Rehum, as the son of Bani, took part directly in the work of repairing one section of the wall of Jerusalem (Nehemiah 3:17).

introduce: Bani is a Levite who appears in the books of Ezra and Nehemiah in the Old Testament, a figure who, after the return from exile, read the law in Jerusalem and carried out the role of interpreting its meaning to the people.
lifetime: Bani is recorded as a Levite who was active in Jerusalem in the time of Ezra and Nehemiah (Nehemiah 9:4). In the time of Ezra, as a Levite, he held the duty of teaching the law before the people (Nehemiah 8:7). Also, Bani's name is recorded in the list of the Levites who sealed the covenant led by Nehemiah (Nehemiah 10:13).
event: When Ezra read the book of the law in the square in front of the Water Gate, Bani, together with his fellow Levites, carried out the role of making the people understand the law and interpreting its meaning (Nehemiah 8:7). Afterward, when the people of Israel gathered fasting, wearing sackcloth, and with dust on their heads, Bani went up on the platform of the Levites, praised God in a loud voice, and joined in the prayer that confessed the past history on behalf of the people (Nehemiah 9:4). Also his name is recorded in the sealing of the covenant led by Nehemiah (Nehemiah 10:13).
character: Bani went beyond merely reading the law aloud and performed an instructional function that helped the people understand its meaning (Nehemiah 8:7). As a Levite he was skilled in religious ceremonies and administrative procedures, and he was seen cooperating with his fellows in the process of strengthening the faith-bond of the community (Nehemiah 9:4).

introduce: Bani was a member of the community of Israel after the exile, and is a figure recorded as one of the heads of the people who sealed the covenant in the time of Nehemiah (Nehemiah 10:14).
lifetime: When Nehemiah, together with the people, made a firm covenant before God, wrote it down, and put the seal to it (Nehemiah 9:38), his name is recorded among the heads of the people who sealed, following Parosh, Pahath-moab, Elam, and Zattu (Nehemiah 10:14).
event: He put his name as one of the heads of the people among those who sealed the covenant document together with Nehemiah (Nehemiah 10:1, 14).

call: Father of Uzzi (father of the overseer of the Levites)
introduce: A figure recorded as the father of Uzzi, the overseer of the Levites who lived in Jerusalem in the time of Nehemiah (Nehemiah 11:22).
lifetime: He is recorded as the father of Uzzi in the genealogy of the descendants of Asaph the singer, and Uzzi is introduced as the great-great-grandson of Mica, the great-grandson of Mattaniah, and the grandson of Hashabiah (Nehemiah 11:22). There is no record in the Bible about Bani's own life.
event: His son Uzzi became the overseer of the Levites who lived in Jerusalem and took charge of the work of the house of God (Nehemiah 11:22). No specific deeds of Bani himself are recorded.

call: Judas Barsabbas (envoy of the Jerusalem Council)
introduce: Judas, who was called Barsabbas, was a figure active in the early Christian community, one of the leaders whom the apostles and elders sent to convey the decision of the Jerusalem Council to the Gentile churches.
lifetime: Judas Barsabbas appears in the book of Acts as a leading figure of the church in Jerusalem, and is mentioned as a representative sent to Antioch after the Jerusalem Council (Acts 15:22). Afterward, in Antioch, he carried out the ministry of exhorting and comforting the brothers (Acts 15:32). After finishing his ministry he returned to Jerusalem (Acts 15:33).
event: He was a member of the delegation that officially conveyed to the church in Antioch the regulations concerning the Gentile believers decided at the Jerusalem Council (Acts 15:22). Sent to Antioch together with Barnabas and Paul, he read out the letter of the Council, and in that course exhorted and strengthened the brothers with many words (Acts 15:27, 15:32).
character: He was a man esteemed as a leader among the brothers within the early church in Jerusalem (Acts 15:22), and according to the biblical record he had the qualities of a prophet (Acts 15:32).

introduce: Pashhur is one of the priests who sealed the covenant that the people of Israel renewed with God in the time of Nehemiah the governor, after the return from the Babylonian exile (Nehemiah 10:3).
lifetime:
No record of his specific birth or death appears in the Bible.
After the return from the Babylonian exile, when the rebuilding of the wall of Jerusalem was completed and the people understood the law and sealed the covenant made with God, he took part in the capacity of a priest (Nehemiah 10:3).
event: Together with Nehemiah the governor of Judah and the other priests such as Seraiah and Azariah, he put his seal on the document of the firm covenant swearing to walk in the law of God (Nehemiah 10:1-3).

call: Son of Immer (chief overseer of the temple)
introduce: Pashhur is the son of Immer and a priest who served as chief overseer of the temple of Jerusalem. He is recorded as a figure who opposed and persecuted the prophet Jeremiah at the end of the kingdom of Judah.
lifetime: Pashhur came from the house of Immer and carried out the office of priest (Jeremiah 20:1). He held the authoritative position of chief overseer of the temple (Jeremiah 20:1); having heard Jeremiah prophesying in the temple court, he had him beaten and then imprisoned him by putting him in the stocks at the Gate of Benjamin of the temple (Jeremiah 20:2). Afterward he released Jeremiah, but through Jeremiah he received the message of judgment that his name would be changed to Magor-missabib (Jeremiah 20:3-6).
event: Taking issue with what Jeremiah prophesied in the temple, he inflicted the physical punishment of beating him and putting him in the stocks (Jeremiah 20:2). After this incident Jeremiah proclaimed to him the prophecy that he would be taken captive to Babylon and die there (Jeremiah 20:6). It is also recorded together that all the wealth, the produce, and the precious things of this city, and the treasures of the kings of Judah, would be given into the hand of the enemy and carried off to Babylon (Jeremiah 20:5).
character: Using his authority as chief overseer of the temple, he showed a coercive attitude, directly punishing a prophet who held an opposing opinion (Jeremiah 20:2). By ignoring the prophet's warning and persecuting him, he is portrayed as a figure who starkly reveals the conflict between the established priestly order and the company of the prophets (Jeremiah 20:3).

introduce: Pashhur the son of Malchijah, a high official of Jerusalem at the end of the kingdom of Judah, was one of the officials in the time of King Zedekiah. He is recorded together with the officials who, having heard what Jeremiah said to the people, asked the king to put Jeremiah to death (Jeremiah 38:1, 38:4).
lifetime: King Zedekiah sent Pashhur the son of Malchijah and the priest Zephaniah to Jeremiah to inquire of the word of the LORD (Jeremiah 21:1). At that time Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon was attacking Judah (Jeremiah 21:1). Afterward, together with Shephatiah, Gedaliah, and Jucal, he heard what Jeremiah was saying to all the people (Jeremiah 38:1), and the officials asked the king to put Jeremiah to death (Jeremiah 38:4).
event: When Jeremiah delivered the word of the LORD that those who remain in this city will die but those who surrender to the Chaldeans will live (Jeremiah 38:2), the officials asked the king to put him to death, saying that Jeremiah was not seeking the welfare of the people but their harm, and was weakening the hands of the soldiers and of all the people who were left in this city (Jeremiah 38:4). Pashhur is recorded as one who heard these words together with Shephatiah, Gedaliah, and Jucal (Jeremiah 38:1). Then Jeremiah was cast into the cistern of Malchijah, the king's son, which was in the court of the guard (Jeremiah 38:6).
character: He shows the features of a typical hard-line official who puts his own political convictions and the survival of the state first (Jeremiah 38:4). He took a realist attitude of trusting the king's power and military defense rather than the supernatural authority of the prophet, and had a resolute and hostile disposition that sought to eliminate prophecy that conflicted with his own thinking (Jeremiah 38:1-4).

introduce: Baal-hanan was an overseer who managed the olive trees and sycamore trees of the plain, which were royal property, in the reign of King David of ancient Israel. He was a Gederite, and one of those placed over the property of King David (1 Chronicles 27:28, 27:31).
lifetime: Among those placed over the property of King David were men over the king's storehouses, over the storehouses in the fields, cities, villages, and fortresses, over the farmers who tilled the soil, and over the vineyards and the wine cellars (1 Chronicles 27:25-27), and Baal-hanan the Gederite was over the olive trees and sycamore trees of the plain (1 Chronicles 27:28, 27:31).
event: Among those placed over the property of King David, he was over the olive trees and sycamore trees of the plain (1 Chronicles 27:28, 27:31). His other specific deeds are not recorded in the Bible.

call: Son of Laish (Palti, husband of Michal)
introduce: Paltiel is the second husband of Michal, daughter of King Saul, a figure also called Palti in the Bible. He is the son of Laish, from Gallim.
lifetime: King Saul took his daughter Michal away from David and gave her to Palti, the son of Laish, who was from Gallim (1 Samuel 25:44). Afterward, when David sent messengers to Ish-bosheth and demanded that his wife Michal be returned, Ish-bosheth took Michal from Paltiel the son of Laish (2 Samuel 3:14-15), and Paltiel followed Michal weeping as far as Bahurim (2 Samuel 3:16). There, when Abner told him to go back, he went back (2 Samuel 3:16).
event: When David sought to bring Michal back again, Ish-bosheth took her from her husband Paltiel, and so Paltiel was parted from Michal (2 Samuel 3:13-15). He followed weeping as far as Bahurim when Michal left, but when Abner told him to go back, he went back from there (2 Samuel 3:16).
character: Since he followed weeping as far as Bahurim when his wife Michal was being forcibly sent back to David, he appears to have been a man with considerable attachment to Michal (2 Samuel 3:16).

call: Son of Ephraim (founder of the Becher clan)
introduce: Becher is a figure mentioned as a son of Ephraim in the genealogy of the tribe of Ephraim, and he became the origin of the Becherite clan, having him as its founder. The marginal note of Numbers 26:35 writes "Bered," and there is a view that he is the same person as Bered the son of Shuthelah in 1 Chronicles 7:20 (Bered #4795), but since this is not settled by the text, he is kept as a separate entry.
lifetime: As a son of Ephraim he formed the Becherite clan, and he is recorded as one of the principal families of the tribe of Ephraim (Numbers 26:35).

call: Son of Judah and Tamar (direct ancestor of David and Jesus)
introduce: Perez is the firstborn of the twins born between Judah the son of Jacob and his daughter-in-law Tamar. He is a key figure continuing the family line of the tribe of Judah, and is recorded as an ancestor in the genealogies of King David and of Jesus.
lifetime: Tamar conceived twins by Judah, and at the birth one put out a hand first but it drew back, and Perez was born first (Genesis 38:27-29). Afterward Perez fathered Hezron and Hamul and became the founder of the family of the tribe of Judah (Genesis 46:12, Numbers 26:20-21). Through the generations after that he became an ancestor of David, and he appears repeatedly in the genealogical records of the Bible (Ruth 4:18-22, Matthew 1:3).
event: In the process of the birth he broke through the opening of the womb and came out first, and so was called Perez, which means "one who has broken through" (Genesis 38:29). In Ruth 4:12 his name is mentioned in the blessing that the house of Boaz might be like "the house of Perez, whom Tamar bore to Judah" (Ruth 4:12), and his sons Hezron and Hamul are recorded (1 Chronicles 2:5).

call: Ben-hadad II, king of Aram (adversary of Ahab)
introduce: The ruler of Damascus in the ancient kingdom of Aram, who continually pressed on Israel during the reign of Ahab king of northern Israel. He gathered all his army and, with thirty-two kings who were with him, besieged Samaria (1 Kings 20:1).
lifetime: As king of Aram he assembled his army, besieged Samaria, and threatened Israel by demanding of Ahab silver and gold and the fairest of his wives and children (1 Kings 20:1-6). After being defeated in the first battle with Ahab, the next year he mustered the Arameans again and went up to Aphek and clashed with Israel once more (1 Kings 20:26). Defeated in the battle of Aphek, he fled and entered an inner chamber in the city, but as his servants advised he went to Ahab and sought his life; he was released on the agreement that he would return the cities and let Ahab make streets for himself in Damascus (1 Kings 20:30-34). Later, in the course of opposing the king of Israel and Jehoshaphat king of Judah, who went up to Ramoth-gilead, the king of Aram commanded the thirty-two commanders of his chariots to fight only with the king of Israel (1 Kings 22:29-31).
event: With thirty-two kings he besieged Samaria and demanded of Ahab king of Israel silver and gold and the fairest of his wives and children (1 Kings 20:1-3). Defeated at Aphek, he hid in an inner chamber and sought his life from Ahab, and was released on the agreement that he would return the cities and let Ahab make streets for himself in Damascus (1 Kings 20:30-34). Afterward, when the king of Aram was fighting against Israel and consulting about where to encamp, Elisha made known the plan to the king of Israel, and so Israel was on guard not once or twice (2 Kings 6:8-12). When Ben-hadad was sick, he sent Hazael to Elisha to ask the LORD whether he would recover from his illness (2 Kings 8:7-9), and the next day Hazael took a cloth, dipped it in water, and spread it over the king's face, so that the king died and Hazael became king in his place (2 Kings 8:15).
character: Over-trusting his military superiority, he showed an arrogant attitude, not hesitating to make excessive demands of an enemy country (1 Kings 20:5-6). When the tide of the war turned against him, he showed the flexibility to accept the proposal of his servants and to plead for his life with a humility that was almost servile (1 Kings 20:31-32). In the course of spying on the forces of Israel and gathering information, he was so sensitive in judging the strategic situation that he perceived the presence of the prophet as a threat (2 Kings 6:11-12). When his illness worsened, he had a strong attachment to survival, to the point of sending an envoy even to the prophet of an enemy country to seek an answer (2 Kings 8:8).

call: Ben-hadad III, king of Aram (son of Hazael)
introduce: Ben-hadad III was king of Damascus in Aram and succeeded to the throne after his father Hazael. He was in military opposition to northern Israel, and it is recorded that the LORD gave Israel into the hand of Hazael and the hand of his son Ben-hadad (2 Kings 13:3).
lifetime: He succeeded to the throne after his father Hazael died (2 Kings 13:24). He fought with northern Israel, then ruled by Joash the son of Jehoahaz, was defeated three times, and lost a couple of cities to Israel (2 Kings 13:25).
event: Joash the son of Jehoahaz struck down Ben-hadad the son of Hazael three times and recovered from his hand a couple of cities. These cities were the ones that Joash's father Jehoahaz had lost in the war (2 Kings 13:25). Through this event a part of the territory of Israel that Aram had held came again under the control of Israel.
character: The biblical record gives no specific description of his personality, but he appears as a ruler who inherited the military strength of Aram that his father Hazael had built up and kept up a continual conflict with Israel (2 Kings 13:24).

introduce: A son of Ham and one of the descendants of Noah; in the Bible it is a people, or a member of it, used mainly as the name of a place or of a particular nation.
lifetime: He is mentioned in the genealogy as a son of Ham and a brother of Cush (Genesis 10:6). Afterward his name is mentioned, together with Cush, Lud, and others, as a people of the land allied with Egypt (Ezekiel 30:5).
event: In the Bible Put appears as a military ally or as soldiers. In Ezekiel 27:10, together with Persia and Lud, they were warriors in the army of Tyre and hung up shields and helmets; in Jeremiah 46:9, together with the Cushites, they are mentioned as shield-bearers who will come out in the army of Egypt. Again, in Ezekiel 38:5 they are listed, together with Persia and Cush, equipped with shields and helmets, with the army of Gog.
character: The Bible emphasizes, as an outward characteristic of the Put people, the skilled military ability of holding the shield and drawing the bow (Jeremiah 46:9). They are sometimes identified with the region of Libya in northern Africa, and are described as a group that formed a formidable infantry force amid the struggles for supremacy in the ancient Near East (Nahum 3:9).

introduce: Put, mentioned as one of the clans of Kiriath-jearim, is a name that designates a person or a family who appears in 1 Chronicles 2:53. It is recorded as one of the four clans that make up the inhabitants of Kiriath-jearim.
lifetime: He is mentioned as a member of a clan that formed among the descendants of the tribe of Judah who lived in Kiriath-jearim (1 Chronicles 2:53). No information about the life, birth, or death of any particular individual is recorded.
event: It is stated explicitly that the Puthites were a clan that came from the people of Kiriath-jearim (1 Chronicles 2:53). Apart from this, no specific deeds of taking part in historical events or records are found.

introduce: Penuel is a figure recorded in 1 Chronicles of the Old Testament, mentioned in the genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin as a son of Shashak.
lifetime: Penuel is a son of Shashak and is recorded as one of the chiefs of the tribe of Benjamin who lived in Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 8:25, 8:28).

call: Father of Zerubbabel (descendant of King David)
introduce: Pedaiah is a figure recorded in the genealogy of Chronicles, classified as the father of Zerubbabel and one who continues the bloodline of the royal house of David. Pedaiah, a son of King Jeconiah of the tribe of Judah, is recorded in the genealogy of the royal house of David in 1 Chronicles 3.
lifetime: Pedaiah is recorded as the son of Jeconiah and the father of Zerubbabel (1 Chronicles 3:17-19). There is no record of the rest of his life in the Bible.
event: In the biblical record there is no separate account of any historical event or specific achievement that Pedaiah led himself. He is recorded only in the genealogy of the royal house of David as the son of Jeconiah and the father of Zerubbabel (1 Chronicles 3:17-19).

call: Father of Joel (father of the chief officer of Manasseh)
introduce: Pedaiah is a figure recorded as the father of Joel. In the time of King David, the chief officer of the half-tribe of Manasseh was his son Joel (1 Chronicles 27:20).
lifetime: In the Bible Pedaiah appears only as the father of Joel, in the expression "Joel the son of Pedaiah" (1 Chronicles 27:20). Among the chief officers of the tribes organized by David, the chief officer of the half-tribe of Manasseh was not Pedaiah himself but his son Joel (1 Chronicles 27:20).
event: Pedaiah's own deeds or office are not recorded in the Bible. The one who served as chief officer of the half-tribe of Manasseh in the time of David was his son Joel (1 Chronicles 27:20).

introduce: Pedaiah is a figure who appears in the book of Nehemiah in the Old Testament, one of the descendants of Parosh, who took part in Nehemiah's work of rebuilding the wall of Jerusalem.
lifetime: He is recorded in Nehemiah 3:25 as the son of Parosh. In the work of repairing the wall of Jerusalem, he repaired the section next to the part repaired by Palal the son of Uzai (Nehemiah 3:25).
event: When repairing the wall of Jerusalem, he repaired the section next to the part repaired by Palal the son of Uzai (Nehemiah 3:25). The boundaries of the section he was in charge of are not recorded separately in the text.

call: Leader who stood at Ezra's left
introduce: Pedaiah is a figure who appears in Nehemiah 8 in the Old Testament, one of those who stood at Ezra's left when Ezra read the law in Jerusalem after the return from the Babylonian exile.
lifetime: As a member of the community of Israel that had returned from the Babylonian exile, he is recorded as one of those who stood at the left of Ezra, who stood on the wooden platform, when Ezra read the book of the law in the square in front of the Water Gate (Nehemiah 8:1-3) (Nehemiah 8:4).
event: When Ezra stood on the wooden platform to read the book of the law, he was one of those who stood at its left (Nehemiah 8:4).

introduce: Pedaiah is a descendant of Benjamin who appears as the great-grandfather of Sallu in the genealogy of Nehemiah 11:7. Sallu, a descendant of Benjamin who lived in Jerusalem, is recorded as the son of Meshullam, the grandson of Joed, and the great-grandson of Pedaiah (Nehemiah 11:7).
lifetime: Pedaiah's name appears only in the genealogy of Sallu in Nehemiah 11:7, and there is no record in the Bible about his own life. The one recorded as a descendant of Benjamin who lived in Jerusalem after the return from the exile is his great-grandson Sallu (Nehemiah 11:4, 11:7).
event: Pedaiah's own events or deeds are not recorded in the Bible. His great-grandson Sallu was recorded as a descendant of Benjamin who lived in Jerusalem (Nehemiah 11:7).

introduce: Pethahiah is one of the Levites who returned from the Babylonian exile in the time of Ezra, and a figure recorded as having married a foreign woman.
lifetime: He is recorded as a Levite who returned after the Babylonian exile in the time of Ezra, and the rest of his life is not recorded in the Bible (Ezra 10:23). He is one of those mentioned in the list in the course of Ezra's measures prohibiting and severing marriage with foreign women (Ezra 10:23).
event: At the time of the reform movement led by Ezra, he was included in the list of those who had married foreign women, and entered his name (Ezra 10:23). This incident appears as a case of the application of strict rules for the sake of religious purity and the preservation of the lineage that arose in the returned community at the time (Ezra 10:18-23).

introduce: Pethahiah is one of the Levites who took part in the ceremony in which, after the rebuilding of the wall of Jerusalem, the people of Israel repented and renewed the covenant (Nehemiah 9:5).
lifetime: In Nehemiah 9, when the people of Israel were fasting, wearing sackcloth, and with dust on their heads (Nehemiah 9:1), his name is recorded as one of the Levites (Nehemiah 9:5). The rest of his life is not recorded in the Bible.
event: Together with the Levites Jeshua, Kadmiel, Bani, Hashabneiah, Sherebiah, Hodiah, and Shebaniah, he told the people to bless the LORD their God, who is from everlasting to everlasting (Nehemiah 9:5). Nehemiah 9:4 separately records that the Levites stood on the platform and cried out in a loud voice, but Pethahiah's name is not in that list.

call: Attendant of the king of Persia (descendant of Judah)
introduce: Pethahiah is a descendant of Zerah the son of Judah and the son of Meshezabel, recorded in Nehemiah 11 as one who was at the king's hand in all matters concerning the people (Nehemiah 11:24).
lifetime: Pethahiah is recorded as a descendant of Zerah the son of Judah and the son of Meshezabel (Nehemiah 11:24). He was at the king's hand in all matters concerning the people (Nehemiah 11:24). The rest of his life is not recorded in the Bible.
event: He held the duty of being at the king's hand in all matters concerning the people (Nehemiah 11:24).

introduce: Pethuel is a figure mentioned as the father of the prophet Joel, who is known as the author of the book of Joel in the Old Testament.
lifetime: In the biblical record there is no information about his life other than the fact that he is the father of the prophet Joel (Joel 1:1).

introduce: Beriah is a figure of the tribe of Ephraim, a son whom Ephraim obtained after he went through the calamity of his sons being killed by the men of Gath. His name carries the meaning that there was evil in the house at the time he was born.
lifetime: After the sons of Ephraim were killed by the men of Gath, Ephraim lay with his wife, and she bore a son, and he named him Beriah (1 Chronicles 7:23). Rephah and Resheph are recorded as the sons of Beriah, and the son of Resheph is Telah, and his son is Tahan (1 Chronicles 7:25).
event: Beriah is recorded as one born when calamity came upon his house (1 Chronicles 7:23). He appears as the one who carries on the line of the family after the incident in which the sons of Ephraim, who had tried to plunder the livestock in the region of Gath, were killed (1 Chronicles 7:21-23). The Bible states that he named him Beriah because evil had come upon his house (1 Chronicles 7:23).

introduce: Beriah is a figure who appears in the genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin, recorded as a son of Elpaal and as one of the heads of the inhabitants of Aijalon.
lifetime: Beriah, as a son of Elpaal, is a figure who makes up the family line of the tribe of Benjamin, and together with Shema he became a head of the inhabitants of Aijalon and drove out the inhabitants of Gath (1 Chronicles 8:13).
event: Together with Shema he became a head of the inhabitants of Aijalon and drove out the inhabitants of Gath (1 Chronicles 8:13).

call: Fourth son of Shimei (Levite of Gershon)
introduce: Beriah is a figure belonging to the family line of the descendants of Gershon of the tribe of Levi, one of the four sons of Shimei. His name is recorded within the system of the duties of the Levites organized in the time of King David.
lifetime: Beriah is a descendant of Gershon the son of Levi, and is recorded as the fourth of the four sons of Shimei (1 Chronicles 23:7, 23:10). Among the sons of Shimei, Jeush and Beriah did not have many sons, so they were counted as one clan (1 Chronicles 23:11).
event: When King David, in his old age, divided the Levites into divisions according to the clans of Gershon, Kohath, and Merari (1 Chronicles 23:1, 23:6), Beriah was included in that list, together with Jahath, Zina, and Jeush, as one of the persons who make up the family line of the descendants of Shimei (1 Chronicles 23:10).

introduce: Beeri is a figure mentioned in recording the family information of Hosea, as the father of the prophet Hosea in the Old Testament.
lifetime: There is no specific information recorded about Beeri's life; his name is mentioned only as the father of the prophet Hosea (Hosea 1:1).
event: In the biblical record there is no special achievement or event performed by Beeri as an individual; he is presented only as the lineal basis of the prophet Hosea (Hosea 1:1).

call: Son of Ishi (chief of the tribe of Simeon)
introduce: Pelatiah is a figure who appears in 1 Chronicles in the Old Testament, the son of Ishi and one of the chiefs of the tribe of Simeon.
lifetime: He is recorded as a man of the tribe of Simeon and a son of Ishi. Five hundred of the descendants of Simeon went to Mount Seir with Pelatiah, Neariah, Rephaiah, and Uzziel, the sons of Ishi, as their leaders (1 Chronicles 4:42).
event: Five hundred of the descendants of Simeon, with Pelatiah, Neariah, Rephaiah, and Uzziel, the sons of Ishi, as their leaders, went to Mount Seir, struck down the remnant of the Amalekites who had escaped, and have lived there to this day (1 Chronicles 4:42-43).

introduce: Pelatiah is one of the leaders of the people of Israel who returned to Jerusalem in the time of Nehemiah and put their seal to the covenant made with God (Nehemiah 10:22).
lifetime: As a member of the community that returned after the Babylonian exile, he took part in the covenant renewal movement led by Nehemiah and put his seal to it (Nehemiah 10:1). He appears as one of the leaders recorded in that list, and his name was listed in the course of the sealing by the priests, the Levites, and the heads of the people (Nehemiah 10:22).
event: He joined in the event of signing the document in which the people of Israel pledged to keep the law of God and maintain a holy community (Nehemiah 10:22). This covenant included the pledges not to intermarry with the peoples of the land, not to buy goods on the Sabbath and holy days, and to give a third of a shekel yearly for the house of God (Nehemiah 10:30-32).

introduce: Pelatiah is a figure who appears in the book of Ezekiel, the son of Benaiah and one of the officials of the people. He is one of the twenty-five men whom Ezekiel saw in a vision at the east gate of the house of the LORD, and is recorded as belonging to those who devise iniquity and give wicked counsel in this city.
lifetime: Pelatiah is the son of Benaiah, and is recorded as an official of the people among the twenty-five men whom Ezekiel, brought by the Spirit, saw at the east gate of the house of the LORD (Ezekiel 11:1).
event: As one of the twenty-five men, he belonged to those whom God called "the men who plot evil and give wicked counsel in this city" (Ezekiel 11:2). Their saying was: "Is not the time near to build houses? The city is the cooking pot, and we are the meat" (Ezekiel 11:3). While Ezekiel was prophesying against them, Pelatiah the son of Benaiah died, and Ezekiel fell on his face and cried out whether the LORD was going to make a complete end of the remnant of Israel (Ezekiel 11:4, 11:13).
character: The Bible assesses Pelatiah as a leader who proposed unjust schemes to the people and devised wicked counsel (Ezekiel 11:2). Even in the situation before God's judgment, he showed a political bent of misjudging reality and deceiving the people so as to lead them on a wrong path (Ezekiel 11:3). That he suddenly met his death in the midst of Ezekiel's prophecy represents his evil influence and his corruption as a leader (Ezekiel 11:13).

introduce: Pelaiah is one of the Levites included in the list of those who made a covenant with God after the rebuilding of the wall of Jerusalem in the time of Nehemiah (Nehemiah 10:9).
lifetime: In the time of Nehemiah his name is recorded in the list of the Levites who sealed the covenant, among "their kinsmen Shebaniah, Hodiah, Kelita, Pelaiah, Hanan" (Nehemiah 10:9-10). The rest of his life is not recorded in the Bible.
event: When the people of Israel swore to keep the law and put their seal to it, his name was recorded as one of the Levites who sealed (Nehemiah 10:9-10).

call: Levite leader who returned from exile
introduce: Pelaiah is a Levite active in the time of Ezra and Nehemiah in the Old Testament, who appears as one who stood by in the work of making the people understand the law when Ezra read the book of the law after the return from the Babylonian exile.
lifetime: When Ezra read the book of the law to the people gathered in the square in front of the Water Gate, Pelaiah, together with Jeshua, Bani, Sherebiah, and others, made the people who stood in their places understand the law (Nehemiah 8:1, 8:7).
event: When Ezra read the book of the law and interpreted its meaning so that all the people understood (Nehemiah 8:8), Pelaiah, together with the other Levites, took part in the work of making the people understand the law (Nehemiah 8:7).

call: Ancestor of a family that returned with Zerubbabel
introduce: Bigvai is a figure who represents one of the families of the people of Israel who returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel, in accordance with the decree of Cyrus king of Persia, after the Babylonian exile. His name is recorded in the list of those who returned from exile and appears as a member of the community.
lifetime: He is one of those who, while living in exile in Babylon, returned to Jerusalem and Judah in accordance with King Cyrus's decree of return (Ezra 2:2). In the list of those who returned, the descendants of Bigvai are recorded as 2,056 (Ezra 2:14) and 2,067 (Nehemiah 7:19).
event: His name was entered in the list recording the number of the people of Israel who came out with Zerubbabel, Jeshua, and others (Ezra 2:2). The name Bigvai also appears in the list of those who sealed the covenant in Nehemiah 10:16 (whether it is the same person is not made clear in the text).

call: Ancestor of a family that returned with Ezra
introduce: Bigvai is a figure who appears in the books of Ezra and Nehemiah in the Old Testament, an ancestor of a particular family among the people of Israel who returned from the Babylonian exile, and one who stands for the name of the family.
lifetime: In the list of the heads who came up from Babylon with Ezra in the time of King Artaxerxes, it is recorded: "from the descendants of Bigvai, Uthai and Zabbud, and with them seventy men" (Ezra 8:1, 8:14). In the list of those who returned with Zerubbabel, the number of the descendants of Bigvai is recorded separately, as 2,056 in Ezra 2:14 and 2,067 in Nehemiah 7:19.
event: Of the descendants of Bigvai, Uthai and Zabbud, together with seventy men who were with them, were entered in the list of the heads who came up from Babylon with Ezra (Ezra 8:1, 8:14). The name Bigvai also appears in the list of those who sealed the covenant in Nehemiah 10:16.

introduce: Bigvai was a member of the Judean community that returned to Jerusalem in the era under Persian rule after the Babylonian exile, and is one of the leader-level figures who sealed the covenant together with Nehemiah.
lifetime: In the covenant pledge led by Nehemiah, when the people swore to keep the law of God, his name is recorded in the list of "the heads of the people" among those who sealed, as "Adonijah, Bigvai, Adin" (Nehemiah 10:1, 10:14, 10:16).
event: Apart from taking part in the covenant signing ceremony led by Nehemiah and officially putting his seal on behalf of the people, there is no recorded achievement (Nehemiah 10:16).

introduce: One of the two sons of Eli, the priest of Israel, who carried out the duties of priest at the tabernacle at Shiloh. Together with his brother Hophni he showed improper conduct as a priest, and for this reason he is one of the figures who receive a negative evaluation in the history of Israel.
lifetime: Born as a son of Eli the priest, he inherited the office of priest according to the tradition of the family (1 Samuel 1:3). Active at Shiloh, he persisted in moral corruption, such as lying with the women who served at the entrance of the tent of meeting (1 Samuel 2:22). He did not listen even to the rebuke of his father Eli (1 Samuel 2:25), and in the end he went out to the battlefield with the ark of the covenant of God carried before him in the battle of Aphek against the Philistines, and was killed (1 Samuel 4:11).
event: The sons of Eli despised the sacrifice of the LORD, as when the priest's servant forcibly took meat from the one who was offering the sacrifice, and their sin was very great before the LORD (1 Samuel 2:13-17). When Israel was defeated before the Philistines, the people brought the ark of the covenant from Shiloh, and the two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, were there with the ark of the covenant of God (1 Samuel 4:3-4). The ark of God was captured, and the two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, were put to death (1 Samuel 4:11). When the messenger spoke of the ark of God, their father Eli fell backward from his seat, broke his neck, and died (1 Samuel 4:17-18), and the wife of Phinehas, hearing the news that the ark of God had been captured and that her father-in-law and her husband were dead, gave birth and then died (1 Samuel 4:19-21).
character: He had a greedy and unnatural disposition, to the point of despising the sacrifice of the LORD (1 Samuel 2:12). He was so stubborn that he rejected the admonition of his father, Eli the priest, and showed an irresponsible attitude of putting his own selfish desires before the authority of God (1 Samuel 2:25).

call: Father of Eleazar (father of one who returned with Ezra)
introduce: Phinehas is a figure mentioned only in the expression "Eleazar the son of Phinehas" in Ezra 8:33, the father of Eleazar. The Bible does not record Phinehas's own deeds.
lifetime: The Bible has no record of Phinehas's life. His name appears only as an introduction of "Eleazar the son of Phinehas," who was present when the silver, gold, and vessels were weighed out in the house of God on the fourth day (Ezra 8:33).
event: Phinehas's own actions are not recorded. When his son Eleazar weighed out the silver, gold, and vessels and put them into the hand of Meremoth the son of Uriah the priest, he was there together with Jozabad the son of Jeshua the Levite and Noadiah the son of Binnui (Ezra 8:33).

introduce: A figure who appears in the time of Ezra and Nehemiah, one of the descendants of Pahath-moab, who took a foreign woman as wife and then repented of it.
lifetime: He was a member of the community of Israel that returned to Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile (Ezra 10:30). In the course of resolving the matter of marriages with foreign women led by Ezra, he is included in the list of those who pledged to send away their wives (Ezra 10:30).
event: In Ezra's religious reform he was singled out as one of those who had married foreign women, and joined in the pledge to send away the foreign wives and children for the purity of the community (Ezra 10:30).

introduce: A figure who existed in the community of Israel after the return from the Babylonian exile, recorded as one of those who took foreign women as wives in the course of Ezra's reform.
lifetime: As one of the people of Israel who returned from the Babylonian exile, his name was entered in the list in the course of the severing of ties with foreign women and the purification of the community led by Ezra (Ezra 10:38).
event: When Ezra, repenting of the sin of Israel, resolved before the temple of Jerusalem to send away the foreign women, he was included in the list of those singled out as subjects of it (Ezra 10:38).
